[p. 80]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsir** (exegesis) of Surat al-Ma'ida

This surah is Madani (revealed after the Hijra to Madina) by **ijma'** (scholarly consensus). It is narrated that it was revealed as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was returning from al-Hudaybiya. al-Naqqash mentioned, on the authority of Abu Salama, that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiya, he said: 'O 'Ali, were you aware that the Surah al-Ma'ida has been revealed to me? And what a benefit it is.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In my view, this does not resemble the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Some of this surah was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and some was revealed in the year of the Conquest (of Makka). The latter is His saying, ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾, and the verse continues. Every part of the Qur'an revealed after the Prophet's (ﷺ) Hijra is Madani, whether it was revealed in Madina, during a journey, or in Makka. What is designated as Makki is only that which was revealed before the Hijra. It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Surah al-Ma'ida is called in the Kingdom of Allah 'the Deliverer'; it delivers its companion from the hands of the angels of punishment."

[p. 81]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿O you who have believed, fulfil (your) contracts. Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you, but not hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval.﴾

'Alqama said: Everything in the Qur'an that begins with "O you who have believed" is Madani. The discussion of this has already preceded. It is said that "wafa" and "awfa" have one meaning (to fulfil). Allah, exalted is He, commanded the believers in general to fulfil contracts, and these are the binding of the speech. This may be in a pledge of righteousness, or in a marriage contract, or a sale, or otherwise. The word "the believers" encompasses the believers among the People of the Book, since between them and Allah there is a covenant regarding the discharge of the trust concerning what is in their Book about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). The word "contracts" encompasses the contracts of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) that were founded on righteousness, such as repelling injustice and the like. As for all their pacts founded on injustice and raids, Islam has demolished them. So the meaning of the verse is the command to all believers to fulfil a contract that proceeds according to the pattern of the Shari'a.

Some people explained the word "contracts" as "covenants" (ʿuhud), and some of them mentioned certain contracts by way of example. Among that is the saying of Qatada, ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾, its meaning: with the covenant of the Jahiliyya. It was transmitted to us from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Fulfil the contract of the Jahiliyya, but do not introduce a contract in Islam."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The understanding (fiqh) of this hadith is that the contract of the Jahiliyya was restricted to the two contracting parties, since the majority were upon injustice and misguidance. Islam has bound everyone together and made the believers brothers. So whoever wishes that the two contracting parties alone be bound by it, the Shari'a has bound them with other Muslims. Except that if the pact is to repel one of the calamities of injustices, then in Islam it is obligatory to pledge to repel that and to fulfil that covenant. Or it may be a specific covenant for something that might occur, restricted to those who pledge to look after it and benefit from it, as was the case in the Jahiliyya; this does not exist in Islam.

[p. 82]

al-Tabari said: It is mentioned that "Furat ibn Hayyan al-'Ijli asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the alliance of the Jahiliyya, and he said: 'Perhaps you are asking about the alliance of Lakhm and Taym Allah.' He said: 'Yes, O Prophet of Allah.' He said: 'Islam only increases it in strength.'"

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾, its meaning is: "by what Allah has made lawful, by what He has made unlawful, by what He has obligated, and by what He has set as limits in all matters." This was said by Mujahid and others.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Ibn Zayd, and others said: The "contracts" in the verse are everything that a person binds upon himself, whether a sale, a marriage, or otherwise.

Ibn Zayd and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayda said: The contracts are five: the contract of faith, the contract of marriage, the contract of covenant, the contract of sale, and the contract of alliance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: They may be reduced to fewer than five. Ibn Juraij said: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿"Fulfil the contracts"﴾ — he said: These are the contracts which Allah took from the People of the Book, that they would act upon what came to them. Ibn Shihab said: "I read the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) which he wrote to 'Amr ibn Hazm when he sent him to Najran, and at its beginning was: 'This is a declaration from Allah and His Messenger: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾,' and he wrote the verses from it until His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 4]."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The most correct thing said in the explanation of this verse is that its wording be generalised to the full extent of what it encompasses. So the word "the believers" is generalised as a whole to those manifesting faith, even if they do not conceal it, and to the believers in truth. And the word "contracts" is generalised to every binding by a statement that agrees with the truth and the Shari'a.

From the word "'aqd" (contract) is the saying of al-Hutay'a:

*A people who, when they make a pact for their neighbour,*
*They tighten the 'inaj and tighten the karaba over it.*

[p. 83]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾ is addressed to everyone who has adopted faith in its proper form and completeness. The Arabs had customs regarding livestock, such as the sa'iba, the bahira, the ham, and other things, so this verse was revealed abrogating (**naskh**, i.e. lifting the ruling of) all of that.

There is a difference of opinion regarding the meaning of "bahimat al-an'am" (grazing livestock). al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Qatada, and al-Dahhak said: It is all of the cattle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is as if He said: "The cattle are lawful for you," so He attributed the genus to something more specific than it. al-Hasan said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means camels, cows, and sheep. It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means the foetuses that come out at the slaughter of the mothers, so they are eaten without slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: These foetuses are of the grazing livestock. al-Tabari said: Some people said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means their wild animals, such as gazelles, wild cattle, wild asses, and other things. Someone other than al-Tabari mentioned this from al-Dahhak.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a good view, because al-an'am are the eight pairs, and whatever is added to them of the rest of the animals is also called "an'am" together with them. The predatory animals, such as the lion and every animal with fangs, have left the category of an'am, so they have a different status. Thus "bahimat al-an'am" is the grazing one of the four-footed creatures. This, as it has been said, is an attribution of a thing to itself, like "the abode of the Hereafter" and "the mosque of the congregation," but to me it is only the attribution of a thing to its genus. The Qur'an has explicitly made them lawful, and the verse agrees with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be blessings and peace: "Every animal with fangs of the predators is unlawful." This view is supported by the two exceptions that follow, since in the first, specific individuals are excepted that have received certain attributes, and those attributes commonly occur in grazing animals; and in the second, a state of the addressees is excepted, which is the state of ihram (pilgrim consecration), and hunting is only of animals other than the eight pairs. So the two exceptions are arranged within the grazing four-footed animals.

"Al-Bahima" in the speech of the Arabs is that which is ambiguous (mubham) in terms of lacking speech and understanding. From it comes: "a closed door" (bab mubham), "a closed wall" (ha'it mubham), "a dark night" (layl bahim), and "buhma," used for a brave man whose attack cannot be anticipated.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from what was recited in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], and the verse continues. The word "ma" is in the accusative position according to the basic principle of exception. Some of the Kufans permitted that it be in the nominative position, as an apposition (badal), and that "illa" be a conjunction (ʿatifa); but according to the Basrans this is not permitted except after an indefinite noun or what is close to it among the generic nouns, such as your saying: "The men came, except Zayd," as if you said: "other than Zayd" (ghayr Zayd), in the nominative.

﴿"Not hunting"﴾: "ghayr" is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the kaf and mim in His saying: "Lawful for you" (uhillat lakum). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ghayru" in the nominative, and its grammatical analysis (**i'rab**) is that it is an adjective (sifa) of the pronoun in "yutla" (is recited), because "ghayr muhilli al-sayd" has the meaning of "one who does not make lawful [hunting] when it is game." Or it may be explained as an adjective of "bahima," considering the meaning of the speech, as I have mentioned.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: People have confused themselves at this point regarding the accusative of "ghayr," and they supposed in it advancements and postponements, and all of that is unsatisfactory, because the speech is well-formed in its consistency as a sequence of exceptions after exceptions.

"Hurum" is the plural of "haram," meaning one in the state of ihram. From it is the saying of the poet:

*I said to her, "Turn back to me, for I am*
*in ihram, and yet after that I am wise,"*

meaning: one who recites the talbiya (the pilgrim's call). al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and Yahya ibn Wathab read "hurm" with the ra' sukun (quiescent). Abu al-Hasan said: This is a Tamimi dialect, where they say "rusl" for "rusul" and "kutb" for "kutub," and similar.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾ is a reinforcement of these legal rulings that oppose the familiar rulings of the Arabs; that is, "you, O listener, be alert to the abrogation of those covenants which were familiar, for indeed Allah, who is the owner of everything, ordains what He wills; none can repel His judgment."

This verse is among those whose eloquence and abundance of meanings become apparent, despite the fewness of its words, to everyone with insight into speech and to whoever has even a little perception. For it contains five rulings: the command to fulfil contracts; the making lawful of the grazing livestock; the exception of what is recited afterwards; the exception of the state of ihram regarding what is hunted; and what the meaning of the verse requires, namely the permissibility of hunting for one who is not in ihram.

al-Naqqash related that the companions of al-Kindi said to al-Kindi: "O wise one, produce for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes... I will produce something like a part of it." So he secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, I am not able to do it, and no one can bear this. I opened the codex (mushaf), and the Surah al-Ma'ida came out; I looked, and behold, it commands fulfilment, forbids breaking covenants, makes lawful in a general way, then makes exceptions after exceptions, then informs about His power and wisdom, in two lines; and no one can produce this except in large volumes."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ is an address to the believers in truth, that they should not transgress the limits of Allah in any matter.

"Al-sha'a'ir" is the plural of "sha'ira": that is, "Allah has made known that it is His limit and His obedience." So it has the meaning of "the markers of Allah." The expressions of the exegetes differed regarding what is meant by the sha'a'ir, by which this general ruling concerning the sha'a'ir was revealed. al-Suddi said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "the sanctities (hurum) of Allah." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "the rites of the Hajj." The polytheists used to perform the Hajj, make 'Umra, bring offerings, slaughter, and glorify the places of the Hajj; so the Muslims wanted to raid them, and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are what He has set as a limit of prohibition in the state of ihram. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: [p. 86] "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "all that He has commanded or forbidden." This is the preferred view that has preceded. Ibn al-Kalbi said: Most of the Arabs did not count al-Safa and al-Marwa among the sha'a'ir, and the Quraysh did not stand at 'Arafat, so they were forbidden by this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, is a singular noun that denotes the category of all the sacred months. They are, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban." It was attributed to Mudar because they were the ones who specifically declared it sacred and would remove weapons during it and take the heads off their spears. They called it "Munsil al-Asinna" (the one that unsheathes spear-points) and called it "al-Asamm" (the deaf), because no sound of weapons could be heard during it. The Arabs were in agreement regarding "Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram," and its sanctity would extend over them, and they would refrain from raids for three months. Therefore they adopted the nasi' (intercalation, i.e. the manipulation of the calendar), which is that the speaker, Nu'aym ibn Tha'laba and others, would make al-Muharram lawful for them and declare Safar sacred in its place. Allah forbade that by this verse and by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. Al-Muharram was made the first month of the year because the Hajj and the season were the culmination and fruit of the year; by it the year is completed, and then another year begins. For this reason, and Allah knows best, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab recorded the registers (al-dawawin) beginning with it. So the meaning of His saying, ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, is: do not make it lawful through fighting, nor raiding, nor alteration, for altering it is making its sanctity lawful.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What is more apparent to me is that by "the sacred month" is meant Rajab, so that its matter would be strengthened, because it was specific to Quraysh, then it spread among Mudar. Evidence for this is the saying of 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas:

"And the month of the sons of Umayyah, and the offerings, when the blood has stained their necks [red]."

Abu 'Ubayda said: He meant Rajab, because it is a month that the elders of Quraysh used to venerate, so he attributed it to the sons of Umayyah. al-Akhfash mentioned this in al-Mufaddaliyyat. Al-Tabari said: The intended meaning in this verse is Rajab of Mudar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The reason for this specification is, as I have mentioned, that Allah, may He be exalted, strengthened the matter of this month, since the Arabs did not agree upon it.

'Ikrimah said: The intended meaning in this verse is Dhu al-Qa'dah, since it is the first of them. Our saying "first" here is an approximation and a figurative usage, since the months are cyclical; the "first" is only ordered according to a particular event or some indication specific to a people.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor the offering, nor the garlands﴾: As for the offering (al-hadyu), there is no disagreement that it refers to what is offered of livestock to the House of Allah with the intention of drawing near to Him. So Allah commanded that it not be made lawful and that raids not be launched against it.

People differed regarding the garlands (al-qala'id). Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the garlands are the garlanded offering, and that the offering is only called "hadyu" when it has not been garlanded. So it is as if he said: "Nor the offering that has not been garlanded, nor that which is garlanded."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What al-Tabari said is an imposition upon the wording of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It does not follow from Ibn 'Abbas's statement that "hadyu" is only applied to what has not been garlanded. Rather, it only implies that Allah forbade making the offering lawful in general, then mentioned the garlanded one specifically for emphasis and to heighten the warning about the sanctity of the garlanding.

The majority of scholars said: "Hadyu" is general to all types of what is offered as an act of drawing near to Allah, and "qala'id" are what people used to hang around themselves for security. Qatadah said: In the Jahiliyyah, when a man set out intending Hajj, he would hang around himself a garland of acacia (al-samur), and no one would harm him, since that was the sign of his ihram and his pilgrimage. 'Ata' and others said: Rather, when people left the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) for their needs, they would hang around themselves [something] from the trees of the Haram and its bark, and this indicates that they were from its people or from its pilgrims, so they would be secure thereby. So Allah, may He be exalted, forbade making lawful [harm to] anyone who was made sacred by any of these meanings. Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Rather, the verse is a prohibition to the believers against making lawful the taking of garlands from the trees of the Haram, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do. This was also said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir and others.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾: its meaning is: "Do not make them lawful, so that you raid them." Allah, may He be exalted, through this verse forbade the believers from deliberately targeting the disbelievers who were heading to the Sacred House for the purpose of worship and drawing near [to Allah].

Everything in this verse that is a prohibition concerning a polytheist, or the observance of the sanctity of such a person through a garland, or those who make for the House, and similar things, all of it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword, in His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

It has been related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam ibn Hind al-Bakri, brother of the Banu Dubay'a ibn Tha'laba. The reason was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day to his companions: "A man from Rabi'a will enter upon you today, speaking with the tongue of a devil." Al-Hutam came and left his horses outside Madinah, and entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented Islam to him and invited him to Allah, he said: "Let me think, perhaps I will embrace Islam; I see harshness in your matter, and I have someone I consult." So he went out, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He entered with the face of a disbeliever, and departed with the heel of a treacherous one." Then he passed by a herd of livestock belonging to Madinah, drove them off, and departed with them, saying:

"The night has wrapped them with a driver, al-Hutam,
Not a shepherd of camels nor of sheep,
Nor a butcher upon the back of a stout beast;
They spent the night asleep, while the son of Hind did not sleep.
He spent the night tormenting them, a youth like an arrow-shaft,
Thick-calved, with light-stepping feet."

Then al-Hutam came back the following year, performing Hajj and driving an offering. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to send [someone] to him, and some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) hastened toward him, and this verse was revealed.

Ibn Jurayj said: This verse is a prohibition against the pilgrims having their roads cut off, and the verse was revealed because of al-Hutam, and he mentioned something similar. Ibn Zayd said: The verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Makkah: "Some people from the polytheists came, performing Hajj and 'Umrah, and the Muslims said: O Messenger of Allah, these are only polytheists, so we will not leave them except by raiding them. Then the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Everything in this verse that can be conceived of regarding a Muslim pilgrim is muhkam (definitive), and whatever in it concerns the disbelievers is mansukh. Ibn Mas'ud and his companions read: "Nor those who make for the House," with the genitive construction to "the House."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾: The majority of exegetes said regarding it: its meaning is "they seek bounty in profits through trade, and they seek with that also His good pleasure, in their assumption and hope." Others said: "Bounty" and "good pleasure" in the verse have one meaning, namely the pleasure of Allah and His bounty, through mercy and reward. Among the Arabs there were those who believed in a reward after death, but most of them only hoped for reward and good pleasure in this world: gain, abundance of children, and they drew near (through sacrifices) hoping for an increase in these meanings. al-A'mash read: "wa-ruḍwānan" with a dammah on the ra'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This verse is an act of winning hearts (istil'af) from Allah, may He be exalted, toward the Arabs, and a kindness to them, so that souls would be at ease, people would mix together, they would attend the season, hear the Qur'an, faith would enter their hearts, and the proof would be established for them, as had happened. This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, and Allah, may He be exalted, abrogated all of that after a year, in the year nine, when Abu Bakr performed Hajj and the people were proclaimed to with the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah).

[p. 80]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*They tighten the 'inaj and tighten the karaba over it.*

[p. 83]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾ is addressed to everyone who has adopted faith in its proper form and completeness. The Arabs had customs regarding livestock, such as the sa'iba, the bahira, the ham, and other things, so this verse was revealed abrogating (**naskh**, i.e. lifting the ruling of) all of that.

There is a difference of opinion regarding the meaning of "bahimat al-an'am" (grazing livestock). al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Qatada, and al-Dahhak said: It is all of the cattle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is as if He said: "The cattle are lawful for you," so He attributed the genus to something more specific than it. al-Hasan said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means camels, cows, and sheep. It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means the foetuses that come out at the slaughter of the mothers, so they are eaten without slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: These foetuses are of the grazing livestock. al-Tabari said: Some people said: "Bahimat al-an'am" means their wild animals, such as gazelles, wild cattle, wild asses, and other things. Someone other than al-Tabari mentioned this from al-Dahhak.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a good view, because al-an'am are the eight pairs, and whatever is added to them of the rest of the animals is also called "an'am" together with them. The predatory animals, such as the lion and every animal with fangs, have left the category of an'am, so they have a different status. Thus "bahimat al-an'am" is the grazing one of the four-footed creatures. This, as it has been said, is an attribution of a thing to itself, like "the abode of the Hereafter" and "the mosque of the congregation," but to me it is only the attribution of a thing to its genus. The Qur'an has explicitly made them lawful, and the verse agrees with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be blessings and peace: "Every animal with fangs of the predators is unlawful." This view is supported by the two exceptions that follow, since in the first, specific individuals are excepted that have received certain attributes, and those attributes commonly occur in grazing animals; and in the second, a state of the addressees is excepted, which is the state of ihram (pilgrim consecration), and hunting is only of animals other than the eight pairs. So the two exceptions are arranged within the grazing four-footed animals.

"Al-Bahima" in the speech of the Arabs is that which is ambiguous (mubham) in terms of lacking speech and understanding. From it comes: "a closed door" (bab mubham), "a closed wall" (ha'it mubham), "a dark night" (layl bahim), and "buhma," used for a brave man whose attack cannot be anticipated.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from what was recited in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], and the verse continues. The word "ma" is in the accusative position according to the basic principle of exception. Some of the Kufans permitted that it be in the nominative position, as an apposition (badal), and that "illa" be a conjunction (ʿatifa); but according to the Basrans this is not permitted except after an indefinite noun or what is close to it among the generic nouns, such as your saying: "The men came, except Zayd," as if you said: "other than Zayd" (ghayr Zayd), in the nominative.

﴿"Not hunting"﴾: "ghayr" is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the kaf and mim in His saying: "Lawful for you" (uhillat lakum). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ghayru" in the nominative, and its grammatical analysis (**i'rab**) is that it is an adjective (sifa) of the pronoun in "yutla" (is recited), because "ghayr muhilli al-sayd" has the meaning of "one who does not make lawful [hunting] when it is game." Or it may be explained as an adjective of "bahima," considering the meaning of the speech, as I have mentioned.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: People have confused themselves at this point regarding the accusative of "ghayr," and they supposed in it advancements and postponements, and all of that is unsatisfactory, because the speech is well-formed in its consistency as a sequence of exceptions after exceptions.

"Hurum" is the plural of "haram," meaning one in the state of ihram. From it is the saying of the poet:

*I said to her, "Turn back to me, for I am*
*in ihram, and yet after that I am wise,"*

meaning: one who recites the talbiya (the pilgrim's call). al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and Yahya ibn Wathab read "hurm" with the ra' sukun (quiescent). Abu al-Hasan said: This is a Tamimi dialect, where they say "rusl" for "rusul" and "kutb" for "kutub," and similar.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾ is a reinforcement of these legal rulings that oppose the familiar rulings of the Arabs; that is, "you, O listener, be alert to the abrogation of those covenants which were familiar, for indeed Allah, who is the owner of everything, ordains what He wills; none can repel His judgment."

This verse is among those whose eloquence and abundance of meanings become apparent, despite the fewness of its words, to everyone with insight into speech and to whoever has even a little perception. For it contains five rulings: the command to fulfil contracts; the making lawful of the grazing livestock; the exception of what is recited afterwards; the exception of the state of ihram regarding what is hunted; and what the meaning of the verse requires, namely the permissibility of hunting for one who is not in ihram.

al-Naqqash related that the companions of al-Kindi said to al-Kindi: "O wise one, produce for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes... I will produce something like a part of it." So he secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, I am not able to do it, and no one can bear this. I opened the codex (mushaf), and the Surah al-Ma'ida came out; I looked, and behold, it commands fulfilment, forbids breaking covenants, makes lawful in a general way, then makes exceptions after exceptions, then informs about His power and wisdom, in two lines; and no one can produce this except in large volumes."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ is an address to the believers in truth, that they should not transgress the limits of Allah in any matter.

"Al-sha'a'ir" is the plural of "sha'ira": that is, "Allah has made known that it is His limit and His obedience." So it has the meaning of "the markers of Allah." The expressions of the exegetes differed regarding what is meant by the sha'a'ir, by which this general ruling concerning the sha'a'ir was revealed. al-Suddi said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "the sanctities (hurum) of Allah." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "the rites of the Hajj." The polytheists used to perform the Hajj, make 'Umra, bring offerings, slaughter, and glorify the places of the Hajj; so the Muslims wanted to raid them, and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "Sha'a'ir Allah" are what He has set as a limit of prohibition in the state of ihram. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: [p. 86] "Sha'a'ir Allah" are "all that He has commanded or forbidden." This is the preferred view that has preceded. Ibn al-Kalbi said: Most of the Arabs did not count al-Safa and al-Marwa among the sha'a'ir, and the Quraysh did not stand at 'Arafat, so they were forbidden by this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, is a singular noun that denotes the category of all the sacred months. They are, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban." It was attributed to Mudar because they were the ones who specifically declared it sacred and would remove weapons during it and take the heads off their spears. They called it "Munsil al-Asinna" (the one that unsheathes spear-points) and called it "al-Asamm" (the deaf), because no sound of weapons could be heard during it. The Arabs were in agreement regarding "Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram," and its sanctity would extend over them, and they would refrain from raids for three months. Therefore they adopted the nasi' (intercalation, i.e. the manipulation of the calendar), which is that the speaker, Nu'aym ibn Tha'laba and others, would make al-Muharram lawful for them and declare Safar sacred in its place. Allah forbade that by this verse and by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. Al-Muharram was made the first month of the year because the Hajj and the season were the culmination and fruit of the year; by it the year is completed, and then another year begins. For this reason, and Allah knows best, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab recorded the registers (al-dawawin) beginning with it. So the meaning of His saying, ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, is: do not make it lawful through fighting, nor raiding, nor alteration, for altering it is making its sanctity lawful.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What is more apparent to me is that by "the sacred month" is meant Rajab, so that its matter would be strengthened, because it was specific to Quraysh, then it spread among Mudar. Evidence for this is the saying of 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas:

"And the month of the sons of Umayyah, and the offerings, when the blood has stained their necks [red]."

Abu 'Ubayda said: He meant Rajab, because it is a month that the elders of Quraysh used to venerate, so he attributed it to the sons of Umayyah. al-Akhfash mentioned this in al-Mufaddaliyyat. Al-Tabari said: The intended meaning in this verse is Rajab of Mudar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The reason for this specification is, as I have mentioned, that Allah, may He be exalted, strengthened the matter of this month, since the Arabs did not agree upon it.

'Ikrimah said: The intended meaning in this verse is Dhu al-Qa'dah, since it is the first of them. Our saying "first" here is an approximation and a figurative usage, since the months are cyclical; the "first" is only ordered according to a particular event or some indication specific to a people.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor the offering, nor the garlands﴾: As for the offering (al-hadyu), there is no disagreement that it refers to what is offered of livestock to the House of Allah with the intention of drawing near to Him. So Allah commanded that it not be made lawful and that raids not be launched against it.

People differed regarding the garlands (al-qala'id). Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the garlands are the garlanded offering, and that the offering is only called "hadyu" when it has not been garlanded. So it is as if he said: "Nor the offering that has not been garlanded, nor that which is garlanded."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What al-Tabari said is an imposition upon the wording of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It does not follow from Ibn 'Abbas's statement that "hadyu" is only applied to what has not been garlanded. Rather, it only implies that Allah forbade making the offering lawful in general, then mentioned the garlanded one specifically for emphasis and to heighten the warning about the sanctity of the garlanding.

The majority of scholars said: "Hadyu" is general to all types of what is offered as an act of drawing near to Allah, and "qala'id" are what people used to hang around themselves for security. Qatadah said: In the Jahiliyyah, when a man set out intending Hajj, he would hang around himself a garland of acacia (al-samur), and no one would harm him, since that was the sign of his ihram and his pilgrimage. 'Ata' and others said: Rather, when people left the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) for their needs, they would hang around themselves [something] from the trees of the Haram and its bark, and this indicates that they were from its people or from its pilgrims, so they would be secure thereby. So Allah, may He be exalted, forbade making lawful [harm to] anyone who was made sacred by any of these meanings. Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Rather, the verse is a prohibition to the believers against making lawful the taking of garlands from the trees of the Haram, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do. This was also said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir and others.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾: its meaning is: "Do not make them lawful, so that you raid them." Allah, may He be exalted, through this verse forbade the believers from deliberately targeting the disbelievers who were heading to the Sacred House for the purpose of worship and drawing near [to Allah].

Everything in this verse that is a prohibition concerning a polytheist, or the observance of the sanctity of such a person through a garland, or those who make for the House, and similar things, all of it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword, in His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

It has been related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam ibn Hind al-Bakri, brother of the Banu Dubay'a ibn Tha'laba. The reason was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day to his companions: "A man from Rabi'a will enter upon you today, speaking with the tongue of a devil." Al-Hutam came and left his horses outside Madinah, and entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented Islam to him and invited him to Allah, he said: "Let me think, perhaps I will embrace Islam; I see harshness in your matter, and I have someone I consult." So he went out, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He entered with the face of a disbeliever, and departed with the heel of a treacherous one." Then he passed by a herd of livestock belonging to Madinah, drove them off, and departed with them, saying:

"The night has wrapped them with a driver, al-Hutam,
Not a shepherd of camels nor of sheep,
Nor a butcher upon the back of a stout beast;
They spent the night asleep, while the son of Hind did not sleep.
He spent the night tormenting them, a youth like an arrow-shaft,
Thick-calved, with light-stepping feet."

Then al-Hutam came back the following year, performing Hajj and driving an offering. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to send [someone] to him, and some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) hastened toward him, and this verse was revealed.

Ibn Jurayj said: This verse is a prohibition against the pilgrims having their roads cut off, and the verse was revealed because of al-Hutam, and he mentioned something similar. Ibn Zayd said: The verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Makkah: "Some people from the polytheists came, performing Hajj and 'Umrah, and the Muslims said: O Messenger of Allah, these are only polytheists, so we will not leave them except by raiding them. Then the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Everything in this verse that can be conceived of regarding a Muslim pilgrim is muhkam (definitive), and whatever in it concerns the disbelievers is mansukh. Ibn Mas'ud and his companions read: "Nor those who make for the House," with the genitive construction to "the House."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾: The majority of exegetes said regarding it: its meaning is "they seek bounty in profits through trade, and they seek with that also His good pleasure, in their assumption and hope." Others said: "Bounty" and "good pleasure" in the verse have one meaning, namely the pleasure of Allah and His bounty, through mercy and reward. Among the Arabs there were those who believed in a reward after death, but most of them only hoped for reward and good pleasure in this world: gain, abundance of children, and they drew near (through sacrifices) hoping for an increase in these meanings. al-A'mash read: "wa-ruḍwānan" with a dammah on the ra'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This verse is an act of winning hearts (istil'af) from Allah, may He be exalted, toward the Arabs, and a kindness to them, so that souls would be at ease, people would mix together, they would attend the season, hear the Qur'an, faith would enter their hearts, and the proof would be established for them, as had happened. This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, and Allah, may He be exalted, abrogated all of that after a year, in the year nine, when Abu Bakr performed Hajj and the people were proclaimed to with the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

(p. 90) His saying, exalted is He:
﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And let not the hatred of a people, because they blocked you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2] ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored by another, and that which a beast of prey has eaten, except what you slaughter.﴾

The permission to hunt came directly after the strictness regarding the sanctuary of humans, which is an excellent eloquence of speech. His saying, exalted is He, "then hunt" (fa-istadu), is an imperative form, and its meaning is permission, by the consensus of the people.

The scholars differed regarding the imperative form "if"al" (if'al, "do"), when it occurs without any clear indication of one of its possible meanings. The jurists (fuqaha') said: it indicates obligation (wujub) until a proof indicates otherwise. The theologians (mutakallimun) said: it is suspended (waqf) until an indicator (qarinah) is established, and no command is free of an indicator. A group said: it indicates permission (ibahah) until a proof indicates otherwise. Another group said: it indicates recommendation (nadb) until a proof indicates otherwise. The view of the jurists is the most cautious, the view of the theologians is the most analogically sound, and anything else is weak.

The form "if'al" may come for obligation, as in His saying: ﴿Establish prayer﴾ [al-An'am: 72]; it may come for recommendation, as in His saying: ﴿And do good﴾ [al-Hajj: 77]; it may come for permission, as in His saying: ﴿then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], and ﴿And seek of the bounty of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10] and ﴿then disperse in the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. The seeking of Allah's bounty may be a recommendation. It may come for a threat, as in His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]; and it may come for challenge (ta'jiz), as in His saying: ﴿Be stones﴾ [al-Isra': 50].

(p. 91) Abu Waqid, al-Jarrah, Nubayh and al-Hasan ibn 'Imran recited "fi-istadu" with a kasrah on the fa'. This is a problematic reading. One way to explain it is that the reader observed the kasrah of the hamzat al-wasl when you begin, so you say "istadu" and he gave the fa' a kasrah out of consideration and as a reminder of the kasrah of the hamzat al-wasl.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And let not ... lead you"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2] means: "and let not ... earn for you." "Jarama al-rajul" means "kasaba" (he earned), and it is transitive to two objects, as "kasaba" is transitive. In a hadith: "and you earn what is nonexistent." Abu 'Ali said: "ajrama," with the alif, has the same meaning: earning, in sins and wrongdoings. Al-Kisa'i said: "jarama" and "ajrama" are two dialects with one meaning, namely "kasaba." A group said: "yajrimannakum" means "it is due to you (yahiqqu lakum)," just as ﴿la jarama anna lahumu al-nar﴾ [al-Nahl: 62] means "it is due to them that the Fire is theirs." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "yajrimannakum" means "yahmilannakum" (lead you / bear you to).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All these sayings are close in meaning. The interpretation that is specific to the word is the meaning of earning (kasb), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"A predator of a nesting bird on the top of a cliff, you see the bones it has gathered as a cross."

Its meaning: "a strong earner of food." It is said: "So-and-so is the earner (jarimat) of his people," if he is the one who earns for them. Ibn Mas'ud and others recited "yujrimannakum" with a dammah on the ya'; the meaning is also "lā yukṣibannakum" (let not earn for you). As for the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyaynah a blow, and Fazarah earned after it that they become angry."

(p. 92) Its meaning: "Fazarah earned anger after it." It has been explained otherwise, with things close to this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"the hatred of a people"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "shana'anu" with a vowelled nun; Ibn 'Amir recited "shan'anu" with a sukun on the nun; and there is a difference of report from 'Asim and Nafi'. It is said: "shana'tu al-rajul shan'an" with a fatha on the shin, "shana'anan" with a fatha on the nun, and "shan'anan" with a sukun on the nun. The fatha is more common. All of this is used when you hate him. Sibawayh said: every masdar on the pattern "fa'alan" with a fatha on the 'ayn does not have a transitive verb, unless something anomalous occurs, like "shana'an." "Shana'tu" became transitive because it has the meaning of "abghadtu" (I hated), just as "al-rafath" became transitive with "ila" because it has the meaning of "al-ifda'" (going unto).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: As for the one who recites "shana'anu" with a fatha on the nun, the most evident reading is that it is a masdar, as if He said: "let not the hatred of a people, because they blocked you, earn for you aggression against them and injustice toward them." Masadir on this pattern are numerous, like "al-nazawan," "al-ghalayan," "al-tawafan," "al-jaraayan," and others. "Al-shana'an," with a fatha on the nun, may also be an adjective, so the meaning becomes: "let not the hatred of a people, or the enmity of a people, earn for you aggression."

Among what came on this pattern as an adjective is their saying: "a donkey qatawan," when it is not easy in its walk; and their saying: "a run wa-saman," meaning heavy, like the run of an old man, and similar to that, besides other things that are not as numerous as masadir. Among it is what Abu Zayd recited:

"And before you, men did not fear my wrongful claim, and I put out the eye of the arrogant, ... (al-Ashwas al-Abayan)."

With a fatha on the ba'. As for the one who recites "shan'anu" with a sukun on the nun, it may be a masdar, and the masdar has come on this pattern in their saying: "lawaytuhu dayanahu lawyanan" (I twisted his debt for him, a twisting), and in the saying of al-Ahwas:

(p. 93) "... and if the one with the shanan blamed him and rejected him."

It is only a lightening of "shan'an," which is a masdar with a sukun on the nun, because he deleted the hamzah and placed its vowel on the sakin. This is the analogical lightening. Abu 'Ali said: whoever claims that "fa'alan," when its 'ayn is made sakin, is not a masdar, has erred. The reading with a sukun on the nun may also be an adjective, since it has been reported: "a man shan'an, and a woman shan'anah." The analogy of this is that it derives from an intransitive verb, though one word may derive both a transitive verb and an intransitive verb. So the meaning would be: "let not the hateful (baghid) of a people, or the enmity (baghda') of a people, earn for you aggression." If the word is taken as a masdar, then it is a masdar with the object (al-maf'ul) as its genitive. Among what came as an adjective on the pattern "fa'lan" is what Sibawayh related from their saying: "khamsan" (lean); and from this their saying: "nadman" (regretful). The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: From this is "rahman" (the Merciful).

This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest (fath), when the believers wanted to overpower Quraysh and their confederates among the tribes, those who had backed each other in blocking the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, and his companions, in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. That was in the sixth year after the Hijrah. Thereby hatred entered the hearts of the believers and rancor (hasikah) among the disbelievers. So it was said to the believers, in the year of the Conquest, which is the eighth year: "Let not that hatred, or those enemies, lead you, because they blocked you, to transgress against them, since Allah has in them an intention of good, and in His knowledge that among them are those who will believe," just as happened.

Al-Mahdawi related from a group that it was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, because when the Muslims were blocked from the House, a group from the people of Najd passed by them wanting the House. They said: "We will block these as we were blocked." So the verse was revealed.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited "in sadduku-m" with a kasrah on the hamzah; the rest recited "an sadduku-m" with a fatha on the hamzah, referring to the blocking that occurred. This is the reading of the majority and is more fitting in meaning. The kasrah of the hamzah means: "if such a thing occurs in the future."

Ibn Mas'ud recited "in yasuddukum," and this supports the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded everyone to cooperate in righteousness (al-birr) and piety (al-taqwa). Some said: these are two words with one meaning, and He repeated them with different wording for emphasis and exaggeration, since every righteousness is piety and every piety is righteousness.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this there is some looseness. The custom in the meaning of these two words is that righteousness covers the obligatory and the recommended, while piety is the observance of the obligatory. If one of them is made to replace the other, that is by metaphorical usage. Then He, exalted is He, forbade cooperation in sin (ithm), which is the ruling that applies to crimes, and in aggression ('udwan), which is wronging people. Then He commanded piety and threatened, in general terms, with severity of punishment. It has been related that this verse was revealed forbidding the pursuit of pre-Islamic blood feuds (dhuhul al-jahiliyyah), when a group of believers wanted that. Mujahid said so, and a confederate of Abu Sufyan from Hudhayl had been killed in that way.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ ... the verse. It is an enumeration of what is recited to the community of what is excepted from the livestock (bahimat al-an'am). Carrion (al-maytah) is every animal that has a flowing soul, whose soul has left its body by other than the prescribed method of slaughter (dhakah), except fish and locusts. Regarding locusts, many scholars held that an action must be performed on them that functions like slaughter.

Most people recited "al-maytah" with a sukun on the ya'. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "al-mayyitah" with a shaddah on the ya'. Al-Zajjaj said: they have the same meaning. Some people of the language said: "al-mayt" with a sukun on the ya' is what has died, and "al-mayyit" is said of what has died and of what has not died yet but is still alive, and it is not said of it "mayt" without the shaddah. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and cited as evidence for his rejection the saying of the poet:

"He who has died and found rest is not a mayt; rather the mayt is the mayyit of the living."

(p. 95) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The verse may be interpreted as evidence against it, not for it. Some have interpreted "istarah" (found rest) in this verse as "iktasaba raihah" (acquired a smell), since its speaker was a pre-Islamic man who did not see rest in death.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"and blood"﴾ means "al-masfuh" (poured out, flowing), because blood is restricted to this in other verses, so the absolute is referred back to the restricted. The community has agreed on the permissibility of blood mixed with meat, and of the spleen and the like. The pre-Islamic Arabs used to consider blood lawful, and from this is their saying: "whoever is bled for is not forbidden." "Al-'ilhiz" is blood and wool, which they used to eat in times of distress.

﴿"And the flesh of swine"﴾ implies its fat by consensus. There was disagreement about using its hair and its skin after tanning: some permitted it and some forbade it. Every part of the swine is forbidden by consensus, whether skin or bone.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ means what is slaughtered for other than Allah, exalted is He, and intended for an idol or a human being, as the Arabs used to do; and so did the Christians. The custom of the slaughterer is to name the one he intends and to call out to him; that is his "ihlal" (dedication). From it comes "istihlal" of a newborn, when it cries out at birth; and from it "ihlal al-hilal" (the proclamation of the crescent), that is, calling out its matter upon seeing it. From "ihlal" is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

(p. 96) "They proclaim at al-Farqad their riders, as the pilgrim in ihram proclaims."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And the strangled"﴾ means that which dies by strangling (khanq), which is the restriction of breath, whether a human did that to it, or it happened to it on a rock, a tree, a rope, or the like. This is by consensus. Qatadah mentioned that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to strangle sheep and other animals; when they died they ate them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned something similar.

﴿"And the beaten to death"﴾ is that which is struck or beaten with a stick, a stone, or the like, and it seems to be that which is pelted (tuhdhaf) with it. Al-Farazdaq said:

"A stumbling-woman who kicks the young camel with her leg, a flyer over the forefeet of the virgin she-camels."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-mawqudhah" is that which is beaten with wood until it is stunned and dies. Qatadah said: the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do that and eat it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: From this word is the saying of Mu'awiyah: "As for Ibn 'Umar, he is a man whom scrupulousness (al-wara') has stunned, and it has sufficed for his matter and his impetuousness." Al-Dahhak said: "They used to strike the livestock with wood for their gods until they killed them, and then they would eat them." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi said: "There is no mawqudhah except in your property (malik); and there is no waqidh in hunting."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to Malik and other jurists, regarding game (al-sayd), its ruling is the ruling of the one struck to death (al-waqidh). This is explicit in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the mi'rad (a blunt, heavy-headed hunting stick): "If it strikes with its width, do not eat it, for it is waqidh."

﴿And the one that falls to death (al-mutaraddiyah)﴾: this is the one that falls from a height to a lower place and dies, whether that is from a mountain, or into a well, or the like. It is of the form mutafa''ilah, from al-radaa (ruin/destruction), which is perishing. The Jahiliyyah used to eat the one that fell to death, and the Arabs did not consider as carrion (maytah) anything except what died of illness and the like, without any known cause. As for these causes, they regarded them as equivalent to slaughter (dhakah). So the Law restricted slaughter to a specific manner, and all of these remained carrion.

And ﴿the one gored to death (al-nativah)﴾: it is fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, and it is the sheep that another butts, or other than that, so that it dies. Some scholars interpreted al-nativah in the sense of al-natihah (the one that butts), because two sheep may butt each other and both die. Others said: if it meant the sheep, it would have been said "wa al-shatu al-natih," as one says "kaffun khadib" (a dyed hand) and "lihyatun dahin" (an oiled beard). Since the noun was not mentioned, the feminine ending was added so that the matter would not be ambiguous: is it masculine or feminine in intent? Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: al-nativah is the sheep that is butted by another sheep so that both die, or the sheep that is gored by a cow or sheep.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Everything that dies from being pressed (dagh't) is nativ. Abu Maysarah recited: "wa al-mantuhah."

As for His words ﴿and what the beast of prey has eaten﴾: he means every animal that is preyed upon by one having fangs and claws, such as the lion, the panther, the fox, the wolf, the hyena and the like. All of these are sibā' (beasts of prey). Some Arabs restrict the term sabu' to the lion. The Arabs, when a beast of prey seized a sheep and killed it, and then it escaped from it, would eat it; and likewise if it ate part of it. This is said by Qatadah and others. Al-Hasan, al-Fayyad, Talhah ibn Sulayman and Abu Haywah recited: "wa ma akala al-sab'" with a sukun on the ba', and this is the dialect of the people of Najd. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him, also recited thus. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa akilatu al-sabu'," and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas recited: "wa akilu al-sabu'."

The scholars differed concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿except what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Qatadah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Tawus, (p-98) 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and the majority of scholars said: the exception applies to these enumerated categories. Thus whatever of them is reached while it still blinks with an eye, or moves a leg, or moves a tail, and in general whatever is certain not to have had its soul depart but still has life, it is slaughtered according to the sunnah of slaughter and may be eaten. Whatever its soul has departed from is in the ruling of carrion through illness and the like, according to what the Jahiliyyah believed. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, once held this view. He also said, and this is the well-known position from him and from his companions from the people of Madinah: the words of Exalted Allah ﴿"except what you have slaughtered"﴾ mean: from these enumerated categories, at a time when their slaughter is valid, which is when their vital organs have not been destroyed and it is certain that they will not live. Once they reach this limit, they are in the ruling of carrion.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Some exegetes said: the exception is connected (muttasil) according to the majority's view, and disconnected (munqati') according to Malik's view, because its meaning for him is: "but what you have slaughtered of those that may validly be slaughtered, then eat it." Some of them even said the meaning is: "except what you have slaughtered of other than these, then eat it." In my view there is a problem with this. Rather, the exception according to Malik is connected, but he differs regarding the state in which the slaughter of these enumerated categories is valid. Al-Tabari said: the exception according to Malik is from the prohibition, not from the prohibited things.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this expression there is considerable figurative usage, and with it the meaning becomes coherent.

Dhakah in the speech of the Arabs means slaughter. Tha'lab said this. Ibn Sidah said: the Arabs say: "The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is only a hadith (a saying transmitted in such form).

"Dhakkā al-hayawān" means he slaughtered the animal, and from it is the poet's saying:
﻿"It is slaughtered by the spear-shaft"

(p-99) Among the arguments the Malikis used for Malik's view that "whatever is certainly known to die from these accidents is in the ruling of carrion" is this: if these whose death is certain were not prohibited except by dying, then mentioning carrion first would have sufficed for them. The opponent's argument is that they were mentioned because the Arabs believed these accidents to be like slaughter; so if nothing had been mentioned for them except carrion, they would have thought they were carrion through illness, as they were accustomed to.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 5, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted:
﴿Also forbidden to you is that which is sacrificed on the stone altars (nuṣub), and that you seek decisions by divining arrows (azlām). That is defiance (fisq). Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, without inclining toward sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: Lawful for you are the good things, and what the trained hunting animals have caught for you, which you train, teaching them from what Allah has taught you.﴾

His saying: ﴿"And that which is sacrificed"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] is conjoined to the prohibited things mentioned. "Al-nuṣub" is a plural whose singular is "niṣāb." It is said to be a singular noun, with the plural "anṣāb." They are stones that are set up. Around the Kaʿbah there were three hundred and sixty of them. The people of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance) would venerate them, slaughter upon them for their gods, and also smear them with blood, placing the flesh upon them in pieces so that people might eat. Mujāhid, Qatādah and others said: "al-nuṣub" are stones upon which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to slaughter. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "and they would invoke (the name of others) over them." Ibn Juraij said: "al-nuṣub are not idols; the idol is shaped and carved, whereas these are stones that are set up."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Arabs had in their lands stone altars which they worshipped, and they related about them the altars of Makkah. Among them is the stone called "Saʿd" and others. Ibn Juraij said: The Arabs used to slaughter in Makkah, sprinkle the blood on whatever part of the House faced them, and cut the meat and place it upon the stones. When Islam came, the Muslims said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We have more right to honour this House with these acts," and it seemed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not dislike that. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Its flesh does not reach Allah, nor its blood, but what reaches Him is your piety﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 37]; and this verse was revealed: ﴿And that which is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning and intention in it is the veneration of the altars. Mujāhid said: The people of Makkah would exchange those stones for whatever they liked, when they found something more pleasing to them than them. Ibn Zayd said: "That which is sacrificed on the altars" and "that over which other than Allah has been invoked" are one and the same thing.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "That which is sacrificed on the altars" is a part of "that over which other than Allah has been invoked," but it was singled out for mention after its genus because of the fame of the matter, the nobility of the place, and the veneration that souls had for it. The idol may also be called "nuṣub," because it is set up. It has been related that al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan recited: "wa mā dhubiḥa ʿalā al-naṣb" with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād, and said: "upon the idol." Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif recited: "ʿalā al-nuṣb" with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited: "ʿalā al-naṣab" with a fatḥah on the nūn and the ṣād. It was related from him that he also recited with a ḍammah on the nūn and the ṣād, like the recitation of the majority.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you seek decisions by the azlām﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. By this, He, may He be exalted, forbade the seeking of a share or allotment (qism, with a fatḥah on the qāf, which is the verbal noun) by means of the azlām, which are arrows. Its singular is "zalam," with a ḍammah or fatḥah on the zāy. The azlām of the Arabs are of three kinds. Among them are the three that every person would keep for himself: on one of them is written "Do," on another "Do not," and the third is blank with nothing on it. He would place them in a bag with him, and when he wanted to do something, he would put his hand in, while they were alike, and take out one of them, and would act or refrain according to what came out for him. If the arrow with nothing on it came out, he would repeat the drawing. This is the type with which Suraqah ibn Mālik ibn Juʿshum drew lots when he pursued the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abū Bakr at the time of the Hijrah.

The second type was seven arrows which were with Hubal inside the Kaʿbah, in which were the rulings of the Arabs and what occurred among the people of new events. On one of them was written "the blood-money (ʿaql) in matters of compensation"; on another "from among you"; on another "from other than you"; on another "attached"; and on the rest were rulings about water and other matters. These were the ones with which lots were drawn over the sons of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, when he had vowed to sacrifice one of them if they completed ten. This is the lengthy narrative found in the biography of Ibn Isḥāq. These seven are also kept with every soothsayer (kāhin) of the Arabs and their judges, in the same manner as they were in the Kaʿbah with Hubal.

The third type is the arrows of the maysir (the game of chance), which are ten: seven of them have markings, each with a share according to its number, and three are blank. They would cast them for gambling, so there is in them amusement for those who seek it, and play. Their intelligent men would intend by them to feed the poor and the destitute in the time of winter, when the cold was severe and earning was difficult. Among the Arabs there were some who sought by them a share of gain and of risk for himself. I have explained their matter more fully than this in Surah al-Baqarah, in the commentary on the maysir. So seeking by all of this is seeking an allotment and a share, and it is from consuming wealth falsely, and it is forbidden. Every gambling with pigeons, or with backgammon, or with chess, or with other such games, is seeking by means of that which has the meaning of the azlām, and all of it is forbidden.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"That is defiance (fisq)"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] is a reference to seeking by the azlām. Fisq (defiance) is going out from a contained, gathered place. It is said: "the date (ruṭabah) went out (fasaqat) from its skin," and "the mouse from its hole." The term has been used in the Sharīʿah for one who goes out from the encompassing and enclosure of the legal matter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. Its meaning according to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, is: that you would return to their religion. This was said also by al-Suddī and ʿAṭāʾ. The apparent state of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, and the manifestation of his religion, indicates that the despair of the disbelievers regarding a return to their religion had occurred long before. Rather, in my view this despair is from the collapse of the affair of Islam and the corruption of its community, because this was a matter that those among the disbelievers who remained hoped for. Do you not see the saying of the brother of Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah on the day of Hawāzin, when the Muslims were routed and he thought it a defeat: "Has not magic been nullified today?" And other examples besides this. This verse was revealed in the wake of the Farewell Pilgrimage (Ḥajjat al-Wadāʿ). It was said: on the day of ʿArafah. The polytheists at that time were only in a state of scarcity, and none of them attended the season. On that day the matter of polytheism was erased from the sacred places (mashāʿir) of the Hajj. The saying of Allah, "today," may also refer to that very day, especially in the view of the majority, such as ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and others, who said that it was revealed on the evening of ʿArafah, on the day of Friday, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the standing-place on his camel, and there was no polytheist in the season. It may also be that "today" refers to the time and period, meaning: at this time the disbelievers have despaired of your religion.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] encompasses the polytheists of the Arabs and others, such as the Romans, the Persians, and other than them. This strengthens that the despair concerns the dissolution of the affair of Islam and the loss of its power, and it strengthens that the reference by "today" is to the time whose beginning is the day of ʿArafah, when there was no polytheist at the season. This is supported by the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. He forbade the believers from fearing all kinds of disbelievers, and commanded them to fear Him, may He be exalted, which is the head of every act of worship, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, and the key to all good. It was related from Abū ʿAmr that he recited "yayisa" without a hamzah, and this is the recitation of Abū Jaʿfar.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. "Today" may refer to what we have mentioned. This perfection, according to the majority, is the manifestation (of the religion) and the comprehensiveness of the greatest of the obligations, and of what is permitted and forbidden. They said: after that much Qur'an was revealed, the verse on usury was revealed, the verse on kalālah was revealed, and so on. Rather, the greatest part of the religion was perfected, and the matter of the Hajj was that they performed it while there was no polytheist with them. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī said: it is a complete perfection, and after that day no permission or prohibition or obligation was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarī related from some of those who held this view that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not live after the revelation of this verse except eighty-one nights.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent view is that he (peace be upon him) lived a few more days than that. It has been related that when this verse was revealed on the Day of the Greatest Pilgrimage (yawm al-ḥajj al-akbar), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, wept. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "It made me weep that we were in an increase of our religion, but now that it has been completed, nothing is completed except that it decreases." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have spoken the truth."

It was related that a Jew said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him: "There is a verse in your book that you recite; if it had been revealed to us, the Jews, we would have taken that day as a festival." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Which verse is it?" He said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We know that day and the place. It was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was standing at ʿArafah on the day of Friday."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: So on that day there are two festivals for the people of Islam until the Day of Resurrection.

Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind said to al-Shaʿbī: "The Jews say: how did the Arabs not preserve this day on which Allah perfected their religion?" Al-Shaʿbī said: "Did you not preserve it?" Dāwūd said: "I said: which day is it?" He said: "The day of ʿArafah."

ʿĪsā ibn Jāriyah al-Anṣārī said: "We were sitting in the diwān (register office), and a Christian said to us what the Jew had said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and none of us answered him. So I met Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī and informed him. He said: 'Why did you not answer him?'" ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "It was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was standing on the mountain on the day of ʿArafah."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Ikrimah related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Surah al-Mā'idah was revealed in Madinah on Monday." Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: Surah al-Mā'idah was revealed during the journey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the Farewell Pilgrimage. All of this indicates that the surah is Madinan, after the Hijrah. The completion of the favour lies in the manifestation of Islam, the light of the beliefs, the perfection of the religion, the expansion of conditions, and other things that this upright monotheistic creed (milla ḥanīfiyyah) encompasses, up to entering Paradise and abiding in the mercy of Allah. All of these are the favours of Allah, completed for us.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I have approved Islam as your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The word "riḍā" (approval) in this place may mean "will" (irādah). It may also be an attribute of action, an expression for Allah's manifestation of it, because riḍā is among the attributes that lie between the attributes of the Essence (ṣifāt al-dhāt) and the attributes of action (ṣifāt al-afʿāl). Allah, may He be exalted, willed Islam for us and approved it for us, and there are things that Allah, may He be exalted, wills to occur but does not approve. Islam in this verse is the same as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19]. It is the same as was explained in Jibrīl's question to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is faith (īmān), deeds, and branches (shuʿab).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] means: whoever is driven by necessity to eat carrion and the rest of those prohibited things. It was asked of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When does carrion become lawful?" He said: "When you do not have a morning drink, nor an evening drink, and do not gather for it any herbs (baql)."

"Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: 'This is an example of the case where there is no food, to the point that it leads to the loss of strength and of life.'"

Ibn Muhayṣin recited: "fa-manit-ṭurra" (فَمَنِ اطُّرَّ), with the ḍād assimilated into the ṭā'. This is not in accordance with the regular analogy (qiyās), but the Arabs used it frequently in a few words. The discussion of the rulings on necessity (idṭirār) in the parallel verse in Surat al-Baqarah has already been presented.

Al-makhmaṣah (المَخْمَصَة) is hunger, by which the stomachs become empty, i.e., shrunken. Al-khamṣ (الخَمْص) is the shrinking of the belly. Thus, a slim build is considered beautiful in women, and from it is said khumṣāna (خُمْصانَة, a slender woman) and baṭnun khamīṣ (بَطْنٌ خَمِيصٌ, a flat belly). From it also comes akhmaṣ al-qadam (أَخْمَصُ القَدَمِ, the arch of the foot). This is used frequently for hunger and emptiness. From it is the saying of al-A'shā:

"You sleep in winter with your bellies full,
while your neighbours' women, hungry, sleep as slender ones."

That is, they are folded over hunger, their bellies made lean.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿غَيْرَ مُتَجانِفٍ لإثْمٍ﴾ (ghayra mutajānifin li-ithm, "not inclining toward sin"), it has the meaning of ﴿غَيْرَ باغٍ ولا عادٍ﴾ (ghayra bāghin wa-lā ʿādin, "neither rebellious nor transgressing"). Its explanation and jurisprudence have already been given in Surat al-Baqarah. Al-janaf (الجَنَف) is inclination. Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī recited: "ghayra mutajannifin" (غَيْرَ مُتَجَنِّفٍ), without the alif. This is more emphatic in meaning than mutajānif, because doubling the ʿayn (shadd) implies intensification, deep penetration into the meaning, and the firm establishment of its ruling. The form tafāʿala (تَفاعَلَ) only signifies imitating a thing and approaching it. Do you not see that when you say "tamāyala al-ghuṣnu" (the branch swayed), it implies swaying and approaching an inclination? But when you say "tamayyala," you have firmly established the ruling of inclination. Likewise: taṣāwana and taṣawwana, taghāfala and taghaffala.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿فَإنَّ اللهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ (fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm, "indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"), it stands in place of "then there is no sin upon him," with the addition of what it contains of increased promise and comfort for souls. In the speech there is an elided element indicated by what is mentioned; its estimated sense is: "so he ate from those forbidden things that were mentioned."

The occasion of revelation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ ماذا أُحِلَّ لَهُمْ﴾ (They ask you what has been made lawful for them): "Jibrīl, peace be upon him, came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and found a dog in the house, so he did not enter. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him: 'Enter.' He said: 'I do not enter a house in which there is a dog.' So the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the killing of dogs, and they were killed until they reached al-ʿAwālī. Then ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, Saʿd ibn Khaythama and ʿUwaymir ibn Sāʿida came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us of these dogs?'"

Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: This occasion was also related by Abu Rāfiʿ, the freed slave of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he was the one in charge of killing the dogs. ʿIkrima and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī also related it, as a statement traced back to them both (mawqūfan). The apparent meaning of the verse is that a questioner asked about what was made lawful to people of food, because the words of the Exalted: ﴿قُلْ أُحِلَّ لَكُمُ الطَيِّباتُ﴾ (Say: "Lawful for you are the good things") are not an answer to "What is lawful for us from keeping dogs?" unless this is answering the questioner with more than what he asked about. This is found frequently from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as his answer concerning the clothing of the one in ihram and other matters. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the explainer of the Sharia, so he answers by extending the instruction for his community.

Al-ṭayyibāt (الطَّيِّباتُ) means the lawful. This is the meaning according to Mālik and others, and it is not restricted to what is pleasant or not. Al-Shāfiʿī said: al-ṭayyibāt is the lawful that is pleasant, and everything disgusting, such as the gecko, beetles and others, is among the khabāʾith (the foul things), and forbidden.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَما عَلَّمْتُمْ مِنَ الجَوارِحِ﴾ (and what you have trained of the hunting animals), its estimated sense is: "and the hunting of what you have trained," or "the keeping of what you have trained." The highest degrees of training are that the animal is sent and it goes, is called and it responds, and is restrained after it has caught the prey so that it stops, and that it does not eat from its catch.
