If a dog has these qualities, and is not an entirely black dog, then the community agrees on the permissibility of hunting with it, on condition that it was trained by a Muslim and hunts for a Muslim. Here consensus is established. If any of what we have mentioned is missing, disagreement enters.

If what is used for hunting is other than a dog, such as the leopard and what is similar to it, and the falcon, the hawk and similar birds, then the majority of the community holds that whatever hunts after training is a jāriḥ, that is, a earner (kāsib). It is said "jaraḥa fulān" and "ijtaraḥa" when he earned. From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَيَعْلَمُ ما جَرَحْتُمْ بِالنَهارِ﴾ (And He knows what you have earned by day) [al-Anʿām: 60], that is, "what you have earned of good and evil."

Ibn ʿUmar used to say: it is only hunting by dogs. As for what is hunted by hawks and other birds, whatever you reach its slaughter, slaughter it, and it is lawful for you; otherwise do not eat it. Ibn al-Mundhir related this thus. He said: Abu Jaʿfar was asked about the hawk and the falcon: is their game lawful? He said: "No, unless you reach its slaughter." He said: "A group made an exception for the hawks and permitted their hunting, on account of the ḥadīth of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: 'I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the game of the hawk, and he said: "If it holds for you, then eat."'"

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī said: ﴿وَما عَلَّمْتُمْ مِنَ الجَوارِحِ مُكَلِّبِينَ﴾ refers to dogs only. If the dog is entirely black, al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī disliked its game. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: "I know of no one who grants leniency in it if it is entirely black," and Ibn Rāhawayh said likewise. As for the common scholars of Medina and Kufa, they hold the permissibility of the game of every trained dog.

As for eating from the game by the dog: Ibn ʿAbbās, Abu Hurayra, al-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abu Thawr, al-Nuʿmān and his companions said: "What remains is not eaten, because it only held for itself, and did not hold for its master." This view is strengthened by the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim concerning the trained dog: "And if it has eaten, do not eat, for it has held only for itself." These scholars interpreted the words of the Exalted: ﴿فَكُلُوا مِمّا أمْسَكْنَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (Eat of what they hold for you) as complete holding; whenever it eats, it has not held for the hunter. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, Abu Hurayra also, and Salmān al-Fārisī, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "When the hunting animal eats, what remains is eaten, even if only a small piece is left." This is the view of Mālik and all his companions, as far as I know. They interpreted the words of the Exalted: ﴿مِمّا أمْسَكْنَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ on the generality of holding; so whenever holding occurs, even in a small part, its eating is lawful. It is related from al-Nakhaʿī, the people of opinion (Aṣḥāb al-Ra'y), al-Thawrī and Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān that they granted leniency in what the hawk eats of, specifically regarding the hawk.

Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: It seems that more than this is not possible in its case, because the limit of its training is that it is called and responds, and that it is sent and goes. If the hunting animal drinks from the blood of the game, the majority of people hold that this game is eaten. ʿAṭāʾ said: drinking blood is not eating. Al-Shaʿbī and Sufyān al-Thawrī disliked eating that game.

Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: "There is no animal that accepts complete training except the dog, in rare cases," and most of them eat from the game. For this reason Mālik did not consider that among the conditions of training. As for birds, Rabīʿa said: whatever of them answers when called is the trained, hunting one.

Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: because most animals by nature are sent. The companions of Abu Ḥanīfa said: if the dog hunts and holds three times consecutively, then training has been achieved in it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: al-Nuʿmān did not set a number in this. Others said: if it does this once, it has become trained. If the dog is trained by a Jew or a Christian, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī disliked hunting with it. As for the dog, falcon and hawk of a Magian, Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Thawrī, Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abu Ḥanīfa and their companions disliked hunting with them. They agree on the permissibility of hunting with their dogs when the hunter is a Muslim; they said: this is like his knife. As for when the hunter is one of the People of the Book, the majority of the community holds the permissibility of his hunting, except Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, who did not permit the hunting of a Jew or Christian, and distinguished between that and their slaughter. He recited the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿تَنالُهُ أيْدِيكم ورِماحُكُمْ﴾ (Your hands and your spears can reach it) [al-Mā'ida: 94], and said: Allah did not mention Jews or Christians with this. Ibn Wahb and Ashhab said: the game of a Jew or Christian is lawful, like their slaughter. In the Kitāb of Muḥammad: the game of the Ṣābi'a is not permitted, nor their slaughter, and they are a people between Jews and Christians with no religion of their own. As for when the hunter is a Magian, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abu Ḥanīfa and their companions, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd and the majority of people forbade eating his game. Abu Thawr had two opinions on it: one like the view of these, and the other that the Magians are People of a Book and their game is permissible.

The majority of people recited: "wa-mā ʿallamtum" (وَما عَلَّمْتُمْ) with a fatḥa on the ʿayn and the lām. Ibn ʿAbbās and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya recited: "ʿullimtum" (عُلِّمْتُمْ) with a ḍamma on the ʿayn and a kasra on the lām, meaning: the command of the hunting animals and hunting with them.

Al-jawāriḥ (الجَوارِحُ) are the earners (al-kawāsib), as previously stated. Ibn al-Mundhir related from a group that they said: "al-jawāriḥ" is derived from "al-jarrāḥ," that is, the animal that has a fang, a claw or a talon with which it wounds its prey.

Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: This is a weak view; the people of language are against it. The majority of people recited: "mukallibīn" (مُكَلِّبِينَ) with a fatḥa on the kāf and a shadda on the lām. Al-mukallib is the trainer of dogs and the one who sets them on prey. It is said of one who trains other than a dog: "mukallib," because he sends that animal like the dog. Al-Ḥasan and Abu Zayd recited: "mukliblīn" (مُكْلِبِينَ), with a sukūn on the kāf and a lightened lām, and its meaning is: owners of dogs. It is said: "amshā al-rajul" (he had many cattle walking), meaning his livestock increased; and "akhlaba" meant his dogs increased. Some exegetes said: al-mukallib, with a fatḥa on the kāf and a shadda on the lām, is the owner of dogs. Said the judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him: this is not a precise explanation.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿تُعَلِّمُونَهُنَّ مِمّا عَلَّمَكُمُ اللهُ﴾ (You train them with what Allah has taught you) mean: "You train them in the cunning of hunting and the patience for catching the animal." This is part of what Allah has taught mankind, so "min" is partitive; it may also be for the beginning of the end point. The pronoun in "tuʿallimūnahunna" (تُعَلِّمُونَهُنَّ) is feminine in consideration of the word al-jawāriḥ, since it is the plural of jāriḥa.

﴿So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of God over it, and fear God. Indeed, God is swift in reckoning.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]

﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. And [lawful are] the chaste women from among the believing women, and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you give them their due compensation, desiring chastity, not committing unlawful intercourse or taking secret lovers. And whoever rejects faith, his work has become worthless, and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]

God's statement: ﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]. It is possible that it means: "of what they catch and do not eat any of it." It is also possible that it means: "of what they catch, even if they eat some of the game." Scholars differed on the permissibility of eating game when the trained hunting animal has eaten from it, according to which of these two meanings is intended. This has already been discussed.

God's statement: ﴿and mention the name of God over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4] is a command to pronounce the basmalah (saying "In the name of God") when releasing the hunting animal at the game. The jurisprudence of hunting and slaughter, regarding the meaning of pronouncing the name, is one. Some scholars said: this command is obligatory. If the one who releases the animal or the slaughterer deliberately or forgetfully omits the pronouncement, the meat is not to be eaten. Among those reported to have disliked what was not slaughtered with God's name pronounced over it when forgotten were ash-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, Nafi', and Abu Thawr. Some scholars regarded this command as recommended (mandub). Ashhab inclined to this in his statement: "If one omits the pronouncement out of levity, the meat is not to be eaten; but if he omits it deliberately without knowing its exact status, yet is not dismissive of the sacred law, it is to be eaten." The position of Malik and the majority of scholars is that the pronouncement is obligatory when remembered and dropped when forgotten. Whoever omits it deliberately has invalidated the slaughtered animal and the game; whoever omits it forgetfully should pronounce it when eating, and the slaughtered animal is permissible. Most scholars recommended that no name other than God's be mentioned in the pronouncement, and that its wording be: "In the name of God; God is greatest." Some people said: if one adds to that a blessing upon the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) (ﷺ), it is permissible.

Then God commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) in general. The nearest reference is to what these verses contain of commands. The swiftness of reckoning is due to the fact that He, blessed and exalted, has encompassed everything in knowledge, so He has no need to attempt counting, and He calls all creatures to account at once. The verse may be a warning of the Day of Resurrection, as if He said: "The reckoning of God for you comes swiftly, since the Day of Resurrection is near." It is also possible that by "reckoning" (al-hisab) He means requital, so that He threatened in this world a swift and near requital if they do not fear God.

God's statement: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful﴾ indicates the time and the present moment. The address is to the believers. The discussion of "the good things" (al-tayyibat) has already preceded.

God's statement: ﴿and the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar), and "lawful" (hill) means permissible (halal). "Food" in this verse means slaughtered animals. This is what the people of tafsir said, because food that involves no processing, such as wheat and fruit and the like, is not harmed by the possession of anyone, and its very nature is not made unlawful by someone's ownership.

Food that involves processing falls into two kinds. One kind is that whose processing is a craft unconnected to religion, such as baking flour, pressing oil, and the like. If a dhimmi (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection) is avoided in this, it is out of distaste. The second kind is that which requires religion and intention. If the analogy were that their slaughtered animals should not be permissible, since you say they have no valid prayer, no valid fasting, and no accepted worship, God, blessed and exalted, granted a concession for their slaughtered animals to this community and removed them from analogy by textual evidence.

Then the scholars differed over the word "food" (ta'am). The majority said it refers to the entire slaughtered animal, and the ritual slaughter (tadhkiyah) of the dhimmi makes lawful for us all of the animal, including what is lawful for him and what is forbidden to him, because he has performed the ritual slaughter.

A group of scholars said: what is lawful for us of their food is only the slaughtered animal that is lawful for them (i.e., their lawful food). Their ritual slaughter does not make lawful what is not lawful to them. This group therefore prohibited the tarif (a particular part of the animal) and pure fats from the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book. This disagreement exists within the school of Malik, may God have mercy on him.

The scholars differed over the word "those who were given" (utu). One group said: only the slaughtered animals of the Children of Israel and the pure Christians, those to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, were made lawful for us. This group therefore prohibited the slaughtered animals of the Christians of the Banu Taghlib among the Arabs and of every newcomer to these two religions. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, used to forbid the slaughtered animals of the Christians of the Banu Taghlib, saying: "They did not hold to anything of Christianity except drinking wine."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: "This is not a prohibition of the slaughtered animals of the Christians who are genuine among them." The majority of the community, namely Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn al-Musayyib, ash-Sha'bi, 'Ata', Ibn Shihab, al-Hakam, Hammad, Qatada, Malik, may God have mercy on him, and others, said: "The slaughtered animal of every Christian is lawful, whether he is from the Banu Taghlib or from others, and likewise the Jews." They interpreted God's statement: ﴿whoever among you allies with them, then he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51] accordingly.

God's statement: ﴿and your food is lawful for them﴾ means your slaughtered animals. This is a concession for the Muslims, not for the People of the Book. Since the matter requires that something over which we have legislated ritual slaughter should be protected by us from them, God granted this concession in it, lifting hardship according to what is permitted.

God's statement: ﴿"and the chaste women" [al-Muhsanat]﴾ is conjoined to the lawful food. In the speech of the Arabs and in the usage of the sacred law, ihsan (chastity, or being protected) is derived from protection (al-man'ah), and from it comes "fortress" (al-hisn). It is conditioned by four things: Islam, chastity (iffah), marriage (nikah), and freedom (hurriyyah). In this context it cannot mean Islam, because the verse has explicitly stated that they are from the People of the Book. It cannot mean marriage, because a woman who is already married is not lawful. Only freedom and chastity remain, so the word bears both meanings. The scholars differed according to this possibility. Malik, may God have mercy on him, Mujahid, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and a group of scholars said: "The chaste women (al-muhsanat) in this verse are the free women." They therefore prohibited marriage to a Scripturary slave woman. A group of scholars said: "The chaste women in this verse are the chaste/virtuous women" (al-'afa'if). Among them is also Mujahid, along with ash-Sha'bi and others. They therefore permitted marriage to a Scripturary slave woman. Sufyan and as-Suddi also said this. Ash-Sha'bi said: "The ihsan of a dhimmiyyah is that she does not commit adultery and that she performs the ghusl (ritual bath) from major impurity." Abu Maysarah said: "The slave women of the People of the Book are in the position of their free women who are chaste; their marriage is lawful."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Some scholars prohibited marriage to a woman who is not chaste, on the basis of this verse. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "If a man discovers a grave indecency from his wife, he should separate from her." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, distinguished between the women of the people of war (ahl al-harb) and the women of the people of protection (ahl al-dhimmah). He said: "Among the People of the Book are those whose women are lawful to us, and they are all who pay the jizyah (poll tax); and among them are those whose women are not lawful to us, and they are the people of war." Malik, may God have mercy on him, disliked marrying the women of the people of war, out of fear of the loss of the child or the change of his religion.

The "due compensation" (ujur) in this verse means the bridal gifts (mahr). Scholars derived from the phrase ﴿"when you give them"﴾ that a husband should not consummate the marriage with his wife except after he has offered from the bridal gift that with which he makes her lawful to himself. Whoever permitted consummation without offering this, held that by the rule of the contract and the commitment, she is in the position of one who has been given (i.e., she is already his).

"Muhsinin" (desiring chastity) means: married according to the sunnah. Ihsan in this context is by marriage. "Musafih" means the adulterer, and sifah means adultery. A "musafihah" is the woman who does not turn away the hand of a toucher and commits adultery with everyone; they were the "owners of banners" in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period). "Mukhadanah" means that each of the two adulterers has devoted himself to the other. The parallel of this verse has already preceded and has been explained more fully than this.

God's statement: ﴿and whoever rejects faith﴾ may mean that disbelief is in the very faith itself. In this there is metaphor and figurative language, because faith cannot be conceived as being rejected; rather, disbelief is in the matters in which faith ought to be placed. The remainder of the verse is clear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He:
﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major impurity (janabah), purify yourselves. If you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself (al-ghaʾit), or you have touched women and find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. God does not desire to place upon you any hardship, but He desires to purify you and to complete His favour upon you, so that you may be grateful.﴾

There is no disagreement that this verse is the one in which, as 'Aisha (may God be pleased with her) said, the verse of tayammum (dry ablution) was revealed. It is the verse of wudu' (ablution). However, since wudu' was already established and in use among them, it is as if the verse added nothing to them regarding it except its recitation. It only gave them the benefit and the concession concerning tayammum. The existence of wudu' was inferred from the saying of 'Aisha (may God be pleased with her): "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led the people in prayer, and they were not near water, and there was no water with them." The verse of women was either revealed together with it or shortly after it. The story of tayammum took place during the journey of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the expedition of al-Muraysi', which is the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. In it, according to what has been related, there was the blowing of a wind, and in it was the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "If we return to Medina..." The story is long, and in it occurred the incident of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk).

Since attempting prayer is for the most part done standing, the expression "when you rise" came.

People differed concerning the indicator (qarīnah) that was intended along with the phrase "when you rise." One group said: "This is a general expression for every rising, whether the person is in a state of purity or is in a state of minor impurity (muḥdith). It is recommended for him, when he rises to prayer, that he perform wudu'." It is related that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) used to do this and would recite the verse. A similar report is transmitted from 'Ikrimah. Ibn Sirin said: "The caliphs used to perform wudu' for every prayer." It is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) performed a wudu' in which there was leniency, then said: "This is the wudu' of one who has not become impure." 'Abdullah ibn Hanzalah ibn Abi 'Amir al-Ghasil said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to perform wudu' for every prayer, and that was difficult for him, so he was commanded to use the siwak (toothstick), and the obligation of wudu' was lifted from him, except in cases of minor impurity."

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Many of the Companions, among them Ibn 'Umar and others, used to perform wudu' for every prayer, seeking to attain a virtue. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) also used to do so. Then he combined two prayers with one wudu' in the hadith of Suwayd ibn al-Nu'man, and on other occasions, until "on the day of the conquest (of Mecca), he (ﷺ) combined the five prayers with one wudu'," intending to clarify (the ruling) for his community. Ibn 'Umar related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever performs wudu' while already in a state of purity, ten good deeds are written for him," and he said: "I have only desired this."

Another group said: This verse was revealed as a concession specifically for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because he did not perform any action except while in a state of wudu', nor did he speak to anyone, nor return a greeting, and so on. So God informed him through this verse that wudu' is required only at the time of rising to prayer, and not for the rest of actions. This was said by 'Alqamah ibn al-Faghwa', who was among the Companions and was the guide of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to Tabuk. Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Suddi said: The meaning of the verse is: "When you rise to prayer from your beds," meaning from sleep.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The purpose of this interpretation is to include the causes of impurity (aḥdāth) in the mention, especially sleep, which is a matter of disagreement: is it in itself a cause of impurity? According to this interpretation, there is an inversion of order in the verse. Its implied meaning is: "O you who believe, when you rise to prayer from sleep, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women (meaning the minor touching), then wash..." Thus the rulings for one who is in a state of minor impurity are complete. Then He said: ﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾; this is the ruling of another category. Then He said to both categories together: ﴿And if you are sick or on a journey and you find no water, then seek clean earth﴾. Muḥammad ibn Maslamah, from the companions of Malik, may God have mercy on him, and others, held this interpretation.

The majority of scholars said: The meaning of the verse is: "When you rise to prayer while in a state of impurity (muḥdithīn)." According to this, there is no inversion or reordering in the verse. Rather, the ruling for one who finds water is set out in the verse up to His saying "then purify yourselves." The minor touching (mulāmasah al-ṣughrā) is included in His saying "muḥdithīn." Then, after that, He mentioned, with His saying ﴿And if you are sick﴾ to the end of the verse, the ruling for one who lacks water, from both categories together. The touching would have to be sexual intercourse (al-jimā') for the verse to mention the junub who lacks water as it mentioned the one who finds water. This is the interpretation of al-Shafi'i and others, and the statements of the Companions conform to it, such as those of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa, and others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wash your faces﴾. Ghasl (washing) linguistically means causing water to reach the thing washed, together with passing something over it, such as the hand or what takes its place. It varies according to the extent of immersion in water or the reduction of it. Washing the face in wudu' is by transferring water to it and passing the hand over it. The face (wajh) is that which faces and confronts the one who looks. Its limit in length is the place where hair grows above the forehead down to the bottom of the chin. Some people expressed it as "to what is before the chin." It was also said: its limit in length is the end of the hair.

The scholars differed concerning the passing of water through the beard (takhlīl al-liḥyah), in two opinions. Its passing through is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) through a hadith of Anas, which al-Tabari mentioned. They differed concerning its width: for a woman and a beardless youth, it is from the ear to the ear. For one who has a beard, there are three opinions. It was said: "from the hair to the hair," meaning the hair of the sideburns (al-ʿāriḍayn). It was said: "from the ear to the ear," and the whiteness that lies between the sideburn and the ear enters into the face. It was said: "that whiteness is washed as a recommended act (istiḥbāb)."

There was disagreement concerning the two ears. It was said: "They are part of the head." al-Zuhri said: "They are part of the face." It was said: "They are a limb standing on its own, neither part of the face nor part of the head." It was said: "What faces forward of them is part of the face, and what turns backward is part of the head."

There was disagreement concerning rinsing the mouth (al-madmaḍah) and sniffing water into the nose (al-istinshaq). The majority of the community consider them a sunnah, and these two inner parts are not, in their view, included in the face. Mujahid said: "Sniffing water into the nose is half of wudu'." Ḥammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Qatadah, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibn Rahawayh said: "Whoever leaves out rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose in wudu' must repeat the prayer." Ahmad said: "Whoever leaves out sniffing water into the nose must repeat, but whoever leaves out rinsing the mouth does not repeat." All people agree that the inside of the eyes does not require washing, except what is related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, that he used to splash water into his eyes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾. Linguistically, al-yad (the hand) applies to the limb that extends from the shoulder to the tips of the fingers. For this reason Abu Hurayrah used to wash all of it in wudu' at times, in order to lengthen the radiance (al-ghurrah). God specified the place of washing from it with His saying: ﴿"up to the elbows"﴾. Its singular is said to be "mirfaq" and "mirfiq," and the form with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa' is more well-known. The scholars differed: do the elbows enter into the washing or not? One group said: "They do not enter, because 'ila' (up to) is a limit that separates what comes before it from what comes after it." Another group said: "The elbows enter into the washing, because what comes after 'ila', if it is of the same kind as what precedes it, is included." Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad gave as an example of this that you say: "I bought the whole farm up to its border," or that you say: "I bought the farm up to the house," and His saying: ﴿Complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The precise formulation of this meaning is to say: "If what comes after 'ila' is not of the same kind as what precedes it, then the limit is the first of what is mentioned after it. If what comes after it is part of what precedes it, then caution requires that the limit be the last of what is mentioned after it." For this reason, the entry of both elbows into the washing is the preferred view. Both reports are preserved from Malik ibn Anas (may God be pleased with him): Ashhab related from him that the two elbows are not included in the limit, and it is also related from him that they are included.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and wipe your heads﴾. Al-masḥ (wiping) is to pass over a thing with something moistened with water. The sunnah of wiping the head is that water is taken with both hands, then they are sent forward, then the head is wiped with what has adhered to the two hands.

There is disagreement about wiping the head in several respects. Among them is the manner of wiping. One group, among them Malik, al-Shafi'i, and a number of the Companions and the Successors, said: "He begins with the front of his head, then takes his two hands to the back of his head, then returns them to the front." Another group said: "He begins from the back of the head until he comes to the front, then returns to the back." Another group said: "He begins from the middle of the head, bringing his two hands toward the face, then returns, so that they touch the inner hair. When he reaches the middle of the head, he passes his hands in the same way over the outer hair of the back of the head, then returns, touching its inner part, and stops at the middle of the head." Another group said: "He wipes his head from here and from there, without any order and without a defined starting point, until it is covered."

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: "All of this is a statement of generality (qawl bil-'umum)." There was disagreement about returning the two hands to the hair of the head: is it an obligation (farḍ) or a sunnah, given the consensus that the first wiping is obligatory by the Qur'an? The majority hold that it is a sunnah, and it was said: "It is an obligation."

Among the points of disagreement concerning wiping the head is the amount that must be wiped. A group said: "What is obligatory in wiping the head is its entirety." Then they differed about the manners mentioned above. Muhammad ibn Maslamah said: "If he wipes two-thirds of the head and leaves out a third, it suffices, because it is considered most of the head in several matters of the Shari'ah." Ashhab said: "If he wipes the forelock (al-nāṣiyah), it suffices."

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Everyone from whom I know the sufficiency of part of the head holds that this part is from the front of the head. This is because reports have been transmitted on this matter: in some of them the forelock is mentioned, and in some the front of the head is mentioned. Except what is related from Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi, who both said: "Whichever part of your head you wipe suffices for you." Salamah ibn al-Akwa' used to wipe the front of his head. It is related from Ibn 'Umar that he wiped only the crown of the head (al-yāfūkh). Ashab al-Ra'y (the jurists of opinion) said: "If he wipes with three fingers it suffices him; if the part wiped is less than what three fingers pass over, it does not suffice." Some people said: "It suffices the one who wipes the head to wipe once with one finger." al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "If the woman touches only one hair, it suffices her." al-Tabari and others reported from Sufyan al-Thawri that if a man wipes a single hair, it suffices him.

Among the points of disagreement concerning wiping the head is: with what limb is it wiped? There is consensus on the preference for wiping with both hands together, and on sufficiency if one wipes with one hand. There was disagreement about one who wipes with a single finger until he covers what he considers sufficient of the head. The well-known view is that this suffices. It was also said that it does not suffice.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is the more preferred view that it does not suffice, because it is a departure from the sunnah of wiping, and it seems like play. Unless it is due to the necessity of illness, in which case there should be no disagreement about its sufficiency.

Among the points of disagreement is the number of wipings. The majority hold that it is once. This suffices according to al-Shafi'i, though three is more beloved to him. It is related from Ibn Sirin that he wiped his head twice. It is related from Anas that he said: "The head is wiped three times." Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', and Maysarah also said this.

The bā' in His saying ﴿"with your heads"﴾ is emphatic and superfluous according to the one who holds that the whole head must be wiped. For him the meaning is: "and wipe your heads." According to the one who holds that part of the head suffices, it is for pure adherence (*ilṣāq al-maḥḍ*, meaning that the wiping is attached to the head without implying totality). As if the meaning is: "bring about a wiping with your heads." Whoever wipes a single hair has done that. Then they followed, in the measures they set for this, traditions and analogies, according to the *ijtihad* (independent scholarly effort) of the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿"wa-arjulikum"﴾ with a kasra (*khafḍ*, the genitive reading). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿"wa-arjulakum"﴾ with a fatha (*naṣb*, the accusative reading). Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim the khafḍ reading, and Hafs narrated from him the naṣb reading. al-Hasan and al-A'mash read ﴿"wa-arjulukum"﴾ with a ḍamma (*raf'*, the nominative reading), meaning: "then wash them." This reading is also narrated from Nafi'. Accordingly, the differences among the Companions and the Successors arise from these readings. Whoever reads with the naṣb makes the governing verb "wash" (*ighsilū*), and holds that the obligation for the feet is washing with water, not wiping. This is the position of the majority, and it is the practice of the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is what necessarily follows from his saying (ﷺ), when he saw people performing ablution while their heels were shining, and he called out in a loud voice: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."

Whoever reads with the khafḍ makes the governing verb the nearer of the two verbs. They differed. A group among them said: the obligation for the feet is wiping, not washing. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Wudu' (ablution) is two washings and two wipings." It is also narrated that al-Hajjaj delivered a sermon at al-Ahwaz, and he mentioned wudu' and said: "Wash your faces and your hands, and wipe your heads and your feet, for there is nothing of the son of Adam closer to his filth than his two feet, so wash their undersides, their upper surfaces, and their heels." Anas ibn Malik heard this and said: "Allah spoke the truth and al-Hajjaj lied." Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And wipe your heads and your feet﴾. The narrator said: Anas, whenever he wiped his feet, would moisten them. It is also narrated from Anas, who said: "The Qur'an was revealed with wiping, and the Sunnah with washing." Ikrima used to wipe over his feet, and there is no washing in the two feet; rather, wiping was revealed concerning them. al-Sha'bi said: "Jibril descended with wiping." Then he said: "Do you not see that tayammum (dry ablution) involves wiping what is normally washed, and cancels what is normally wiped?" It is narrated from Abu Ja'far that he said: "Wipe over your head and your two feet." Qatada said: "Allah obligated two washings and two wipings."

All those we have mentioned whose reading is ﴿"wa-arjulikum"﴾ with a kasra on the lam, and in this manner read 'Alqama, al-A'mash, al-Dahhak, and others. al-Tabari mentioned them under the heading of the position that holds wiping. Some people who acknowledge the kasra on the lam held that wiping of the two feet is in fact washing. It is narrated from Abu Zayd that the Arabs call a light washing "wiping," and they say: "I wiped myself for prayer," meaning: "I washed my limbs." Abu 'Ubayda and others, in explaining His saying ﴿so he began to strike﴾ [Sad: 33], said it means striking, and it is said: "He wiped his neck," when he struck it. Abu 'Ali said: "This strengthens that the intended meaning of wiping the two feet is washing. And among the evidence that wiping of the two feet is intended as washing is that the limit has been placed on them with ﴿ilā﴾ (up to), as it has been placed on the hands, which are washed, whereas no limit is placed on what is wiped."

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This interpretation is objected to by the absence of a limit on the face; so the ablution would have two washed members, one with a limit and one without, and two wiped members, one with a limit and one without. al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The wiping of the two feet is by making water reach them; then he wipes with his hands after that, so the person is both washing and wiping." He said: "For this reason most scholars disliked that the one performing wudu' put his feet in the water without passing his hands over them."

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This was permitted by a group, among them al-Hasan al-Basri and some jurists of the cities. The majority of the Ummah, from the Companions and the Successors, hold that the obligation for the two feet is washing, and that wiping does not suffice. This is narrated from al-Dahhak, and he used to read with the kasra on the lam.

The discussion of His saying ﴿"ilā al-ka'bayn"﴾ (up to the two ankles) is as previously mentioned in His saying ﴿"ilā al-marāfiq"﴾ (up to the elbows). The linguists differed about the *ka'bayn*. The majority hold that they are the two protruding bones on the two sides of the foot, and these are the limit of wudu', by consensus as far as I know. It was disputed whether they enter into the washing or not, as was mentioned regarding the elbow. Some people said: the *ka'b* is the protruding bone on the front of the foot, where the strap of the sandal meets.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: I know of no one who made the limit of wudu' reach this. But 'Abd al-Wahhab, in *al-Talqin*, came with a wording in this matter that contains confusion and ambiguity. al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: I know of no dissenter that the two ankles are the two bones at the junction of the shin joint. al-Tabari narrated from Yunus, from Ashhab, from Malik, who said: The two ankles to which washing is obligatory are the two bones attached to the shin, adjacent to the heel, and the ankle is not the protrusion on the front of the foot.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This becomes evident from the verse, from His saying concerning the hands: ﴿"ilā al-marāfiq"﴾; that is, each hand has an elbow. If it were the same for the feet, it would have said: "up to the *ku'ub*" (ankles). But since each foot has two ankles, they were singled out for mention.

The wording of the verse requires continuity (*muwālāt*) between the limbs. The scholars differed about this. Ibn Abi Salama and Ibn Wahb said: it is one of the obligations of wudu', whether one remembers or forgets. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: it is not an obligation while one remembers. Malik said: it is an obligation while one remembers, and it falls away in the case of forgetfulness.

Likewise the wording of the verse includes the sequence (*tartīb*). This too was disputed. al-Abhari said: the sequence is a Sunnah. The apparent position of the school is that for one who forgets, reversing the order suffices. It was disputed concerning one who does so deliberately. It is said: it suffices, and he should observe the sequence in the future. Abu Bakr al-Qadi and others said: it does not suffice, because he is playing.

As for His saying Exalted is He: ﴿"and if you are junub"﴾ (in a state of major impurity), the word *junub* is derived from *janb* (side), because a person's side usually touches the side of a woman. It is also derived from proximity and nearness; it is said: ﴿"and the neighbor who is junub"﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. The word *junub* may also come from distance, since distance is *janāba*, and from it "I *tajannabtu* the thing" means I kept far from it. As if he has avoided purity. On this basis it is possible that the *jār junub* means the neighbor who is distant, and that it stands in contrast to the companion by the side.

﴿"fa-ṭṭahharū"﴾ (then purify yourselves) is a command to wash with water. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Mas'ud and others held that the junub does not perform tayammum at all, but leaves prayer until he finds water. The majority of people said: rather, this expression is for one who finds water. The junub has also been mentioned afterward in the rulings for one who lacks water, with His saying ﴿"or you have touched women"﴾, since *mulāmasa* (touching) here means intercourse. The purification with water is characterized by the whole body being covered with water, and the hand being passed over it along with that. This is the well-known position of the school. Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Zahiri and others narrated from Malik that it suffices in the ghusl of janāba that a man immerse himself in water without rubbing. The explanation of His saying ﴿"and if you are sick"﴾ up to His saying ﴿"then wipe your faces and your hands with it"﴾, and the reading of the one who reads "min al-ghayṭ" (from the ground), has already been mentioned in Surat al-Nisa'.

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿"Allah does not desire to place upon you any hardship"﴾: *al-irāda* (will/desire) is an attribute of His essence. The verb came in the future tense, in consideration of the events that arise from the will, for they come newly, from the purification of the believers and the completion of blessings upon them.

The construction of *arāda* and what is derived from it with this *lām* is known in the speech of the Arabs. Among it is the saying of the poet:

*I wish to forget her remembrance, yet it is as if*
*Layla presents herself to me on every path.*

Sibawayh said: I asked him, may Allah have mercy on him, about this, and he said: The meaning is: my wish is to forget. Among it is also the saying of Qays ibn Sa'd:

*I intended that people would know that it is*
*the trousers of Qays, and the delegations are witnesses.*

It is possible that there is an omitted object in the speech to which the *lām* attaches. What al-Khalil said to Sibawayh is shorter and better. This possibility of an omitted object is objected to on the ground that *min* would become superfluous in an affirmative context. It is resolved by saying that the force of the negation at the beginning of the speech justifies the superfluity of *min*, even if the negation does not fall directly on the verb that governs the *ḥaraj*. There are parallels to this.

*Al-ḥaraj* (hardship) means narrowness. A *ḥarja* is a tree that is intertwined and constricted. From this it was said on the day of Badr about Abu Jahl: "He was in the midst of a *ḥaraj* of spears." In line with the meaning of this verse is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The religion of Allah is ease," and his saying (ﷺ): "I was sent with the tolerant, easy monotheism." The wording of the verse is general. The thing mentioned nearby is the matter of tayammum and the concession in it, and the removal of hardship in bearing the burden of water at all times. For this reason Usayd said: "This is not the first of your blessings, O family of Abu Bakr."

As for His saying Exalted is He: ﴿"But He desires to purify you"﴾ up to the end of the verse: it is an announcement of what cannot be matched by gratitude, of the magnitude of His bounty, blessed and exalted is He.

﴿"That perhaps you may be grateful"﴾: *la'alla* (perhaps) expresses hope regarding the human being. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read ﴿"yuṭhirakum"﴾ with the ṭā' sukūn and the hā' lightened.

(p-123)

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be steadfast in [standing firm for] Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

The address in His words "And remember" through to the end of the verse is to the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). "The favour of Allah" is a generic noun (ism jins) that encompasses Islam, the unity of the word, the honour of life, the wealth of property, and a good final outcome. All of these are favours of this religious community (millah).

The covenant mentioned is what took place with the Prophet (ﷺ) at the Pledge of 'Aqabah, the Pledge of al-Ridwan, and every occasion in which the people said, "We hear and we obey." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and a group of the exegetes (mufassirun). Mujahid said: the covenant mentioned is the one taken from the souls (nasam) when they were brought forth from the back of Adam. The first view is more preponderant (arjah) and more fitting to the style of the discourse.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, commanded the believers to continually stand firm (qiyam) in justice (qist), which is equity (al-'adl). A similar matter has already been mentioned in Surat an-Nisa'. And a counterpart of His words "and do not let the hatred of a people" was mentioned earlier at the beginning of this surah. The rest of the verse is clear and repeated; and Allah is the Helper.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 9–11:

His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – those are the companions of Hellfire.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah; and upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

This is a verse of promise to the believers of the concealing of their sins upon them and of Paradise; so it is the great reward. "Wa'ada" (promised) is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible to limit it to one of them; and so it is in this verse. The second object is implied; it is explained by and indicated by His statement: "for them is forgiveness." Then, may He be exalted, followed it with mention of the state of the disbelievers, to make the distinction clear.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8] is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. "Ni'ma" (favor) is the governing element of "idh" (when); and it is a specific favor. "Hamma al-rajul bi'l-shay'" (a man intended a thing) means that he wished to do it; and from it is the statement of the poet:

"Will the abundance of what you bequeath and the bundle of the sick-camel's ... benefit you today, if (a man) intends harm?"

And from it is the statement of another:

"I intended and did not do it, and I nearly... and I wish you had left the wives of Uthman weeping over him."

People differed concerning the occasion of this verse, and the incident in which the intent to extend the hand occurred, and the restraining of hands by God, may He be exalted. The majority said: the occasion of this verse is that "when the people of Bi'r Ma'una were killed, 'Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri escaped from the people, and a man with him; they met near Medina two men from Sulaym, who had taken a covenant from the Prophet (ﷺ) and had departed; 'Amr asked them: 'From whom are you?' They claimed kinship with the Banu 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who was the aggressor against the Muslims at Bi'r Ma'una; so 'Amr and his companion killed them, and brought their spoils to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'You have killed two persons; I will certainly pay their blood-money.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set about gathering the blood-money; and one day he went to the Banu al-Nadir seeking their help regarding the blood-money, and with him were Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them); so he spoke with them. They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim; alight until we prepare food for you and consider your assistance.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted in the shade of a wall, and they conspired among themselves to kill him, saying: 'You have never had a better chance against Muhammad than today.' Some of them said to others: 'Who will climb onto the wall and cast a stone upon him to crush him?' So 'Amr ibn Jahhash, as it is narrated, volunteered for that; and Jibril came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose from that place and headed to Medina; and the verse was revealed concerning that.» There are additions in the report that do not pertain to the verse; it was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq and others; and this view is preferred by what follows of the verses describing the treachery of the Children of Israel and their breaking of covenants.

A group of scholars said: the occasion of the verse was the act of a Bedouin in the expedition of "Dhat al-Riqa'"; and it was "the expedition of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the Banu Muharib ibn Khasafa ibn Qays ibn Aylan"; and that was because he alighted in a valley abundant with thorn trees, so the people dispersed into the shade, and a shady tree was left for the Prophet (ﷺ); he hung his sword upon it and slept. A man from Muharib came, drew the sword, and the Prophet (ﷺ) awoke with the sword drawn in his hand. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do you fear me?" He said: "No." He said: "Who will prevent me from you?" He said: "Allah." So he sheathed the sword and sat down. » In al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) called the people, and they gathered while he was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not punish him. Al-Waqidi and Ibn Abi Hatim, on the authority of his father, mentioned that he embraced Islam. Some people mentioned that he struck his head against the trunk of the tree until he died; and the verse was revealed because of that. In al-Bukhari, in the expedition of "Dhat al-Riqa'", the name of the man is given as Ghawrath ibn al-Harith – with a dotted ghayn; and some people related that his name was Da'thur ibn al-Harith.

Al-Tabari related that the verse was revealed because of a group of Jews who intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) with food; but Allah informed him of that. Then al-Tabari included under this heading, from Ibn 'Abbas, a report different from what it was headed with, namely that a group of Jews prepared food for the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions in order to kill him when he came to the food.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that Ibn 'Abbas was only describing the story of the Banu al-Nadir mentioned earlier.

(p-126) Qatada said: the occasion of the verse was what Muharib and Banu Tha'laba intended on the day of Dhat al-Riqa' regarding attacking the Muslims during the 'Asr prayer; so Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, informed him of that; and the prayer of fear was revealed; so that is the restraining of their hands from the Muslims.

Ibn Fawrak related from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that the verse was revealed because Quraysh sent a man to the Prophet (ﷺ) to assassinate him and kill him; so Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, made him aware of that and sufficed him against his evil.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What is preserved in this matter is the setting out of 'Umayr ibn Wahb for this purpose, after his agreement on that with Safwan ibn Umayya; and the full narration is in the Sira of Ibn Hisham.

Some exegetes – and al-Zajjaj alluded to it – mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]; so it is as if He, may He be blessed and exalted, enumerated for the believers His favors in that He made them victorious; and by that He restrained the hands of the disbelievers from them, which they had intended to extend against the believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is fitting – according to this view – that the verse was revealed following the Battle of the Trench, when Allah routed the confederates and sufficed the believers in fighting; and the remainder of the verse is a command to piety and reliance upon Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 9–11:

His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – those are the companions of Hellfire.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah; and upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

This is a verse of promise to the believers of the concealing of their sins upon them and of Paradise; so it is the great reward. "Wa'ada" (promised) is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible to limit it to one of them; and so it is in this verse. The second object is implied; it is explained by and indicated by His statement: "for them is forgiveness." Then, may He be exalted, followed it with mention of the state of the disbelievers, to make the distinction clear.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8] is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. "Ni'ma" (favor) is the governing element of "idh" (when); and it is a specific favor. "Hamma al-rajul bi'l-shay'" (a man intended a thing) means that he wished to do it; and from it is the statement of the poet:

"Will the abundance of what you bequeath and the bundle of the sick-camel's ... benefit you today, if (a man) intends harm?"

And from it is the statement of another:

"I intended and did not do it, and I nearly... and I wish you had left the wives of Uthman weeping over him."

People differed concerning the occasion of this verse, and the incident in which the intent to extend the hand occurred, and the restraining of hands by God, may He be exalted. The majority said: the occasion of this verse is that "when the people of Bi'r Ma'una were killed, 'Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri escaped from the people, and a man with him; they met near Medina two men from Sulaym, who had taken a covenant from the Prophet (ﷺ) and had departed; 'Amr asked them: 'From whom are you?' They claimed kinship with the Banu 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who was the aggressor against the Muslims at Bi'r Ma'una; so 'Amr and his companion killed them, and brought their spoils to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'You have killed two persons; I will certainly pay their blood-money.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set about gathering the blood-money; and one day he went to the Banu al-Nadir seeking their help regarding the blood-money, and with him were Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them); so he spoke with them. They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim; alight until we prepare food for you and consider your assistance.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alighted in the shade of a wall, and they conspired among themselves to kill him, saying: 'You have never had a better chance against Muhammad than today.' Some of them said to others: 'Who will climb onto the wall and cast a stone upon him to crush him?' So 'Amr ibn Jahhash, as it is narrated, volunteered for that; and Jibril came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose from that place and headed to Medina; and the verse was revealed concerning that.» There are additions in the report that do not pertain to the verse; it was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq and others; and this view is preferred by what follows of the verses describing the treachery of the Children of Israel and their breaking of covenants.

A group of scholars said: the occasion of the verse was the act of a Bedouin in the expedition of "Dhat al-Riqa'"; and it was "the expedition of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the Banu Muharib ibn Khasafa ibn Qays ibn Aylan"; and that was because he alighted in a valley abundant with thorn trees, so the people dispersed into the shade, and a shady tree was left for the Prophet (ﷺ); he hung his sword upon it and slept. A man from Muharib came, drew the sword, and the Prophet (ﷺ) awoke with the sword drawn in his hand. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do you fear me?" He said: "No." He said: "Who will prevent me from you?" He said: "Allah." So he sheathed the sword and sat down. » In al-Bukhari, the Prophet (ﷺ) called the people, and they gathered while he was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not punish him. Al-Waqidi and Ibn Abi Hatim, on the authority of his father, mentioned that he embraced Islam. Some people mentioned that he struck his head against the trunk of the tree until he died; and the verse was revealed because of that. In al-Bukhari, in the expedition of "Dhat al-Riqa'", the name of the man is given as Ghawrath ibn al-Harith – with a dotted ghayn; and some people related that his name was Da'thur ibn al-Harith.

Al-Tabari related that the verse was revealed because of a group of Jews who intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) with food; but Allah informed him of that. Then al-Tabari included under this heading, from Ibn 'Abbas, a report different from what it was headed with, namely that a group of Jews prepared food for the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions in order to kill him when he came to the food.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that Ibn 'Abbas was only describing the story of the Banu al-Nadir mentioned earlier.

(p-126) Qatada said: the occasion of the verse was what Muharib and Banu Tha'laba intended on the day of Dhat al-Riqa' regarding attacking the Muslims during the 'Asr prayer; so Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, informed him of that; and the prayer of fear was revealed; so that is the restraining of their hands from the Muslims.

Ibn Fawrak related from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that the verse was revealed because Quraysh sent a man to the Prophet (ﷺ) to assassinate him and kill him; so Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, made him aware of that and sufficed him against his evil.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What is preserved in this matter is the setting out of 'Umayr ibn Wahb for this purpose, after his agreement on that with Safwan ibn Umayya; and the full narration is in the Sira of Ibn Hisham.

Some exegetes – and al-Zajjaj alluded to it – mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]; so it is as if He, may He be blessed and exalted, enumerated for the believers His favors in that He made them victorious; and by that He restrained the hands of the disbelievers from them, which they had intended to extend against the believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is fitting – according to this view – that the verse was revealed following the Battle of the Trench, when Allah routed the confederates and sufficed the believers in fighting; and the remainder of the verse is a command to piety and reliance upon Allah.
