Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 12:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders. And Allah said, "Indeed, I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever of you disbelieves after that has certainly strayed from the sound way."﴾

These verses, which contain the report of their breaking the covenants of Allah, the Exalted, strengthen the view that the preceding verse about restraining hands was concerned with the affair of the Banu al-Nadir. The exegetes differed concerning the manner in which these nuqaba' (leaders) were sent, although there is consensus that the naqib (leader) is the chief of a people, the one who takes charge of their affairs and who inquires about them (yunaqqibu 'anha) and about their interests therein. The word "al-naqqab" refers to the great man who is, among all people, of this disposition. (p-127) From this it is said of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was indeed a naqqab. The nuqaba' are the guarantors; their singular is naqib, and he is the witness and surety of the people. Others said: the nuqaba' are the trustees over their people. All of this is close to one another. The naqib is higher in rank than the 'arif. Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: these nuqaba' were great men from each tribe, each of whom took responsibility for his tribe that they would believe and fear Allah, the Exalted.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Something similar were the nuqaba' on the night of the Pledge of al-'Aqabah with Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; it was the third 'Aqabah, in which seventy men and two women pledged allegiance. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, chose from the seventy twelve men and named them the nuqaba'. Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi and others said: the nuqaba' were sent from the Children of Israel only as trustees to spy upon the tyrants and test their strength and power. So they set out until a man of the tyrants met them, seized them all, and placed them in his waistband.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is in a long, weak narrative, whose implication is that they observed from the tyrants a great power and thought they had no means against them; so they agreed among themselves to conceal that from the Children of Israel and to inform Musa, peace be upon him, so that he might see in it the command of his Lord. When they returned to the Children of Israel, ten of them betrayed; they informed their relatives and those they trusted of their secret, so the news spread until the affair of the Children of Israel was distorted, and they said: "Go you and your Lord and fight; indeed, we are sitting here."

Al-Tabari related with a chain from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: The nuqaba' from the Children of Israel were sent by Musa, peace be upon him, to look at the city of the tyrants. They went and looked, and they brought back a grape from their fruit, the load of a man. They said: "Estimate the measure of the strength of a people whose fruit is this." That was the cause of the trial of the Children of Israel and their refusal.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ is: kings. He said that the verse is an enumeration of Allah's favor upon them in that He raised, for their reform, this number of kings. He said: (p-128) None of them fulfilled it except five: Dawud, peace be upon him, and his son Sulayman, peace be upon him; Talut; Hizqiyya; and his son. Seven disbelieved, altered, and killed the prophets. Between the twelve there emerged thirty-two tyrants, all of whom seized the kingship by the sword and spread corruption among them. The pronoun in "ma'akum" (with you) refers to the Children of Israel collectively, and this statement was addressed to them. Al-Rabi' said: rather, the pronoun refers to the twelve, and this statement was addressed to them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first view is more preferable. "Ma'akum" means: by My help, My protection, and My support. The lam in His saying "la-in" (if indeed) is the one that announces the coming of the lam of oath; and the lam of oath is His saying "la-ukaffiranna" (I will surely remove). The evidence that this lam is merely an announcing lam is that it may sometimes be dispensed with, and the speech is complete without it; had it been the lam of oath, that would not have been the case.

The establishment of prayer means fulfilling its conditions. Zakah here is, as some exegetes said, a portion of wealth that was obligatory; it may also be that the meaning is: "and you gave from yourselves everything in which there is zakah for you, as you were urged to do." He placed these before faith to honour prayer and zakah, since it is known and established that no deed benefits without faith. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "bi-rusli" with the sin unvowelled (sakinat al-sin) throughout the Qur'an.

"Wa 'azzartumuhum": its meaning is: you revered them, glorified them, and supported them. From it is the poet's saying:

"And how many a noble man for them is generous, and how many a lion is honoured in the assembly."

'Asim al-Jahdari read "wa 'azartumuhum" with a light zay wherever it occurs; and in Surah al-Fath he read "wa ta'uzzuruhu" with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the 'ayn, and a damma on the zay. The explanation of "iqrad" (lending) has already been given in Surah al-Baqarah.

The expiation of misdeeds is covering them by erasure and removal; so it is a metaphor. "Sawa' al-sabil" means its middle; from it comes "sawa' al-jahim" (the middle of the Hellfire); and from it is the Bedouin's saying: "my middle has been cut off" (qad inqata'a siwa'i). The middles of roads are their broad, well-trodden parts. The rest of what is in the verse is clear, and Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿So for their breaking their covenant We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

It is possible that "mā" (what) is extra (zā'idah), and the sense is: "fa-bi-naqdihim" (because of their breaking). It is also possible that it is an indefinite noun, and "al-naqḍ" (the breaking) is substituted for it as a substitution of a definite noun for an indefinite one. The sense then is: "because of an act which is their breaking of the covenant." This is the meaning under this interpretation, and something similar has already been mentioned in "al-Nisa'" (Surah 4).

As for "la'annāhum" (We cursed them), its meaning is: We removed them from all good.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "qāsiyatan" (hard) with an alif. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "qasiyyatan" without an alif, its pattern being "fa'iyalah." The evidence for the first reading is His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened (qāsiyah)﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], and His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened (qasat) after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. Qaswah (hardness) is the hardness of the heart, its remoteness from tenderness and admonition, and its firmness, such that it is not affected by good.

As for whoever reads "qasiyyatan," it is from this same meaning, "fa'iyalah" in the sense of "fā'ilah," like "shāhid" and "shahīd," and other such patterns. Al-Tabari related from some people that they said: "qasiyyatan" is not from the meaning of qaswah; rather, it is like the "qasiyy" of dirhams, which is that which has been mixed with adulteration and deception. Thus the hearts did not become pure for faith; rather, disbelief and corruption mixed into them. Among the evidence for this is the saying of Abu Zubayd:

"Its neighings in the deaf stillness, as when the qasiyyat cry out in the hands of the money-changers."

And among the same usage is the saying of another:

"They provided me with nothing but the rubbing off of a turban, and five hundred of them being qasiyy and counterfeit."

Abu 'Ali said: this word is arabicised (mu'arrabah) and is not an original part of the speech of the Arabs.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿They distort words﴾. A group, among them Ibn 'Abbas, said: their distortion is by interpretation (ta'wil), and they have no ability to change the wording in the Torah, nor is that possible for them. What indicates this is the survival of the verse of stoning, and their need for the reader to place his hand upon it. Another group said: rather, they distorted the speech and also changed it, and they did both as far as they were able.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The words of the Qur'an admit of both meanings. His saying, ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], implies alteration, and there is no doubt that they did both.

The majority of people read "al-kalim" with a fatha on the kaf and a kasra on the lam. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "al-kalam" with an alif. Abu Raja' read "al-kilm" with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ is a text on the evil of their own actions: that is, there was for them a great portion in what they were reminded of, but they forgot it and abandoned it. Then He, blessed and exalted, informed His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, that he would not cease, throughout the continuing course of time, to discover from them treachery, deceit, and corrupt matters. People differed concerning the meaning of "khā'inah" (treachery) in this place. A group said: "khā'inah" is a verbal noun, like "al-'āqibah," and like His saying: ﴿So they were destroyed by the overwhelming (al-ṭāghiyah)﴾ [al-Haqqah: 5]; so the meaning is: "upon treachery." Others said: the meaning is "upon a treacherous group," so it is an active participle describing a feminine noun. Others said: the meaning is "upon a treacherous man," and the "ha'" was added for emphasis, like "'allāmah" and "nassābah." Among the same usage is the saying of the poet:

"You told yourself of fidelity, yet you were not one who is treacherous to betrayal, with a crooked finger."

Al-A'mash read: "'alā khiyānatin minhum" (upon a betrayal from them). Then He, blessed and exalted, made an exception of the few from them. The exception may be in regard to persons, and it may be in regard to actions.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ is abrogated by what is in "Bara'ah" (Surah 9) of the command to fight them until they pay the jizyah. The remainder of the verse is a promise of reward for good conduct.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (*al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*) on Surah 5, verses 14–15:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of. So We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much.﴾

"Wa min" (وَمِن): it is attached to "akhadhna" (أخَذْنا, "We took"). The sense is: "And We took from those who say, 'We are Christians,' their covenant." It is possible that his saying "wa min" (وَمِنَ) is coordinated with His saying ﴿"a treacherous act from them"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and that His saying "akhadhna mithaqahum" ("We took their covenant") begins a new statement about them. The first reading is more likely. Their being Christians is attached to their own claim and assertion, in that "Christian" is a legal designation that implies supporting the religion of Allah. They applied this name to themselves without deserving it, and there was no resemblance between their deeds and their words. So this expression comes as a rebuke to them, pushing them away from the path of supporting the religion of Allah and His prophets.

As for His saying, ﴿"So We cast among them"﴾, its meaning is: We fixed it among them and affixed it. The word "al-ighra'" (الإغْراء, "incitement" or "fastening") is derived from "al-ghira'" (الغِراء, "glue"), with which something is stuck. The pronoun in "baynahum" (بَيْنَهُمُ, "among them") may refer to the Jews and the Christians, since enmity between them is present and continuous. It may also refer to the Christians alone, since they are a people who fight one another, with strife among them until the Day of Resurrection. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, threatened them with the punishment of the Hereafter, because informing them of their deeds is in fact an affirmation and a rebuke for the punishment, since their deeds are disbelief which necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"O People of the Scripture"﴾: this is a term that encompasses both the Jews and the Christians. However, the incidents of concealment, such as the stoning (al-rajm), and others, were preserved specifically for the Jews, because they were neighbours of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his place of migration. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "The first of this surah to be revealed were these two verses concerning the Jews and the Christians; then the rest of the surah was revealed at 'Arafah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage."

As for His saying "Our Messenger" (رَسُولُنا), it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). The verse contains evidence for the truthfulness of his prophethood, because his informing them of the hidden contents of their books, while he was unlettered (ummi), could not read and did not associate with the readers of scripture, is proof that this knowledge came to him from Allah, blessed and exalted.

The most famous of the incidents they concealed, which Allah revealed through the tongue of His Prophet, is the matter of stoning, and its account is well known. Among them are also the attributes of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things. "Min al-Kitab" (مِنَ الكِتابِ, "of the Scripture") means: of the Torah.

As for His saying, ﴿"and pardoning much"﴾: its meaning is that He leaves aside much that He does not expose them for, out of consideration for you. What is left aside is in the sense of their boasting, their describing the Days of Allah concerning themselves, and similar matters, which in the religion of Islam do not necessitate exposing them or denouncing them. The subject of "wa ya'fu" (وَيَعْفُو, "and pardons") is Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also possible that the verb is ascribed to Allah, blessed and exalted. If the pardon is from the Prophet (peace be upon him), then it is by the command of his Lord; and if it is from Allah, blessed and exalted, then it is through the tongue of His Prophet (peace be upon him). The two possibilities are close to one another.

(p-132)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (*al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*) on Surah 5, verses 14–15:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of. So We cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much.﴾

"Wa min" (وَمِن): it is attached to "akhadhna" (أخَذْنا, "We took"). The sense is: "And We took from those who say, 'We are Christians,' their covenant." It is possible that his saying "wa min" (وَمِنَ) is coordinated with His saying ﴿"a treacherous act from them"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and that His saying "akhadhna mithaqahum" ("We took their covenant") begins a new statement about them. The first reading is more likely. Their being Christians is attached to their own claim and assertion, in that "Christian" is a legal designation that implies supporting the religion of Allah. They applied this name to themselves without deserving it, and there was no resemblance between their deeds and their words. So this expression comes as a rebuke to them, pushing them away from the path of supporting the religion of Allah and His prophets.

As for His saying, ﴿"So We cast among them"﴾, its meaning is: We fixed it among them and affixed it. The word "al-ighra'" (الإغْراء, "incitement" or "fastening") is derived from "al-ghira'" (الغِراء, "glue"), with which something is stuck. The pronoun in "baynahum" (بَيْنَهُمُ, "among them") may refer to the Jews and the Christians, since enmity between them is present and continuous. It may also refer to the Christians alone, since they are a people who fight one another, with strife among them until the Day of Resurrection. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, threatened them with the punishment of the Hereafter, because informing them of their deeds is in fact an affirmation and a rebuke for the punishment, since their deeds are disbelief which necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"O People of the Scripture"﴾: this is a term that encompasses both the Jews and the Christians. However, the incidents of concealment, such as the stoning (al-rajm), and others, were preserved specifically for the Jews, because they were neighbours of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his place of migration. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "The first of this surah to be revealed were these two verses concerning the Jews and the Christians; then the rest of the surah was revealed at 'Arafah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage."

As for His saying "Our Messenger" (رَسُولُنا), it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). The verse contains evidence for the truthfulness of his prophethood, because his informing them of the hidden contents of their books, while he was unlettered (ummi), could not read and did not associate with the readers of scripture, is proof that this knowledge came to him from Allah, blessed and exalted.

The most famous of the incidents they concealed, which Allah revealed through the tongue of His Prophet, is the matter of stoning, and its account is well known. Among them are also the attributes of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things. "Min al-Kitab" (مِنَ الكِتابِ, "of the Scripture") means: of the Torah.

As for His saying, ﴿"and pardoning much"﴾: its meaning is that He leaves aside much that He does not expose them for, out of consideration for you. What is left aside is in the sense of their boasting, their describing the Days of Allah concerning themselves, and similar matters, which in the religion of Islam do not necessitate exposing them or denouncing them. The subject of "wa ya'fu" (وَيَعْفُو, "and pardons") is Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also possible that the verb is ascribed to Allah, blessed and exalted. If the pardon is from the Prophet (peace be upon him), then it is by the command of his Lord; and if it is from Allah, blessed and exalted, then it is through the tongue of His Prophet (peace be upon him). The two possibilities are close to one another.

(p-132)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 16–17:

(p-133) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15]. ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path﴾. ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary." Say, "Who then could prevent Allah at all if He intended to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?" And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent﴾.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15]. It is possible that it means Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, and this is the apparent meaning of the words. It is also possible that it means Musa (peace be upon him) and the Torah, meaning: "If you had followed it with the truest following, you would have believed in Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), since it commands that and gives good news of him." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Zuhri, Salam, Humayd and Muslim ibn Jundub recited "bihi Allahu" with a dammah on the ha' wherever it occurs similarly.

"Followed His pleasure" means: by earning, by intention, and by turning towards it. "Al-subul" means the paths. The recitation of "ridwanahu" with a dammah on the ra' and with a kasrah are two dialects, and this has been mentioned previously. Ibn Shihab and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "subula" with a sukun on the ba'. "Al-salam" in this verse may be one of the names of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, so the meaning is: "the paths of Allah Most High which He commanded His servants and prescribed for them." It may also be a verbal noun like "al-salamah," so the meaning is: "the paths of salvation and safety from the Fire."

His saying, "and brings them out": it means those who follow the pleasure, so the pronoun refers to the meaning of "man" and not to its wording. "Al-zulumat" means disbelief, and "al-nur" means faith.

His saying, Most High, "by His permission": that is, "He enables them to utter the words of faith and to perform its deeds; and He knows their action for that and their commitment to it." This is the definition of permission: knowledge of a thing and enabling of it. Its explanation has already been given in Surah al-Baqarah. "The straight path" is the religion of Allah, His monotheism, and what is built upon it of His law.

Then Allah Most High informed of the disbelief of the Christians who say that Allah is the Messiah. This is one sect of the Christians, and all their sects, despite the difference in their sayings, assign to the Messiah (peace be upon him) a share of divinity. The discussion of the word "al-Masih" has already been given in Surah Al 'Imran.

Then Allah Most High refuted them with His saying to His Prophet: ﴿Say, "Who then could prevent Allah at all"﴾; that is, (p-134) there is no one who can repel the will of Allah Most High concerning the Messiah or concerning anyone else. This is something for which the intellects judge that whoever is subject to the will's full execution is not a god. Then Blessed and Exalted He established His dominion over the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so the Messiah (peace be upon him) becomes the least part of the dominion of Allah Most High. His saying, Most High, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, is an indication of His creating the Messiah in the womb of Mary without a father, rather by origination, like Adam (peace be upon him). The distinction has already been made in Al 'Imran between His saying, Most High, in the story of Zakariyya, ﴿He does what He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40], and in the story of Mary, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾. His saying, Most High, ﴿Allah is over all things competent﴾, is a generality whose meaning is particularization, excluding the Essence, the Attributes, and the impossibilities. And "shay'" (thing) in the language is that which exists.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 18–19:

His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of God and His beloved ones." Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and to Him is the final return."﴾ ﴿O People of the Scripture, indeed Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you after a lapse in the messengers, lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And God is over all things competent.﴾

In the speech there is elision (laff) and brevity (ijaz), leaving the listener to separate it by his own understanding. The apparent wording requires that all the Jews and Christians say of all of them, "We are the children of God and His beloved ones." That is not the case; rather, each sect says specifically, "We are the children of God and His beloved ones." The sonship in their saying is the sonship of tenderness and compassion. They mention that God Most High revealed to the Children of Israel, "My firstborn is among My children," and by this they claimed excellence, and said, "We are the children of God and His beloved ones." Even if what they narrated were sound, its meaning would be firstborn in honour, or in prophethood, or the like. "Ahibba' (beloveds)" is the plural of "habib (beloved)."

This statement from them came when the Prophet (ﷺ) invited them to faith in him and warned them of punishment, and they said, "We do not fear what you say, because we are the children of God and His beloved ones." Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him) mentioned this. They had also said to the Prophet (ﷺ) on several occasions, "We will enter the Fire and remain in it forty days, and then you will succeed us in it." So God refuted their claim, and said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ That is: if your station were above the stations of human beings, He would not have punished you, and you yourselves have acknowledged that He punishes you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This is on the basis that the punishment is the Fire of the Hereafter. The verse may also be understood to mean the punishment God inflicted on them in this world. The Children of Israel, when a man among them committed a sin, would find in the morning written on his door the mention of his sin and the mention of its punishment, and that would be enforced upon him. So this is a punishment in this world for sins, which contradicts that they are sons and beloveds.

Then He left the first speech, turned away from it without invalidating it, and moved on to another matter: establishing that they are human beings like the rest of mankind and creation, the most honoured of whom is the most God-fearing. He guides whom He wills to faith, so He forgives him; and He leads astray whom He wills into disbelief, so He punishes him. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, so by right of dominion He may do what He wills; there is no one to repel His judgment; and to Him is the return of all the world at the Gathering and the Resurrection.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is an address to the Jews and the Christians. The Messenger in His saying "Our Messenger" is Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿after a lapse in the messengers﴾ means: after an interruption in their coming for some period. The fatra (lapse) is a calm after motion in a body, and this term is borrowed for meanings. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "For every deed there is a zeal, and for every zeal there is a lapse." And the poet said:

"Indeed, when I think of you, a lapse overtakes me..."

Its meaning is calm after agitation.

People differed about the length of the lapse that was between ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and Muhammad (ﷺ). Qatada said: five hundred and sixty years. Al-Dahhak said: four hundred and thirty-some years. In the Sahih it is reported that the lapse between them was six hundred years. This verse was revealed because of the saying of the Jews: "God has not sent down anything upon any human after Musa," as Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) said.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"lest you say"﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). The meaning: lest you say, pleading on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿"There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner. But there has come to you..."﴾ and the proof has been established against you. ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾: so He is the Guide, the Misleader, the Bestower of blessings, and the Punisher; there is no lord other than Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 20–22:

His statement, Exalted is He:

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will become losers."﴾ ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. But if they leave it, then we will enter."﴾

The meaning: "Recount to them, O Muhammad, by way of informing them, without their books, so that they may verify your prophethood. Included in this are the favours of God upon them, and their receiving those favours with disbelief, scant obedience and failure to turn back to Him in repentance."

Ibn Muhaysin recited "Ya qawmu" (O people, with a nominative ending) here, and wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. This is also reported from Ibn Kathir. "Ni'mata Allah" (the favour of God) here is an ism al-jins (a generic noun, referring to favours in general). He then enumerated the principal forms of those favours and the prophets who were raised up among them. Their affair is well known, from the time of Israel until the time of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Prophets are a protection (hatah), a means of rescue from the Fire, and a source of honour in this world and the Hereafter. As for His statement, "and made you kings," it may bear several meanings. One is that He reminds them of the kingship of those among the Children of Israel who ruled, because kingship is a form of honour in this world and a protection from its calamities. The other meaning is that He intends: "He rescued you from the Copts (al-qibt) who used to enslave you, so you became free, possessing and not possessed." In this sense they are kings. Al-Suddi and others explained it in this manner. Qatada said: "He only said, 'and made you kings,' because we used to hear that they were the first people whom any of the children of Adam served."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is weak, because the Copts used to enslave the Children of Israel. The apparent situation of the children of Adam is that some of them have subjugated others since they multiplied and spread. The nations differed only regarding the meaning of owning. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and a group of the people of knowledge (p-137) said: whoever has a dwelling, a wife and a servant is a king. It was also said: whoever has a dwelling into which no one may enter without his permission is a king.

As for His statement, Exalted is He, "and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds," Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding it that the address is to the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. This is weak. The majority of the commentators said the address is from Moses, peace be upon him, to his people. Then the commentators differed about what it was that they were given which no one else had received the like of. Mujahid said: the manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud. Others said: the abundance of prophets.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: According to the view that it refers to the abundance of prophets, "the worlds" is general and unrestricted. According to the view that what was given was the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, then "the worlds" is restricted to the time in which they lived, because the community of Muhammad has been given from the signs of Muhammad, peace be upon him, far more than that. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was shaded by a cloud before his mission; stones and animals spoke to him; a tree came to him; the trunk wailed; water gushed from between his fingers; many people were satisfied with a little food through his blessing; the moon was split for him; a staff turned into a sword; and the stone that blocked the trench turned into scattered sand.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This statement from Moses was a preparation (tawti'a) of their souls, so that they would be strengthened and that the command to enter the land of the tyrants would be taken with strength, and the execution of that would be the execution of one whom God has honoured and elevated in rank. "Al-Muqaddasa" means al-mutahhara (the purified). Mujahid said: al-mubaraka (the blessed).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Blessing is a purification from drought, hunger and the like. People differed about identifying it. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is Mount Tur and what surrounds it. Qatada said: it is Syria. Ibn Zayd said: it is Ariha. This was also said by al-Suddi and by Ibn 'Abbas as well. Some people said: it is al-Ghuta, Filastin, and part of al-Urdunn. Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement that it lies between the Euphrates and Arish Misr.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The reports are consistent that Dimashq (Damascus) is the capital of the tyrants.

(p-138) As for His statement, Exalted is He, "which God has prescribed for you," its meaning is: which God has decreed in His decree and His measure, that it is yours; you will inherit it and dwell in it, possessing it. But your trial in entering it lies in the obligation of fighting those who are in it, as a purification and a test. Then Moses, peace be upon him, warned them against turning back on their heels, and that is retreating backwards. It may be that it means turning one's back and returning by the same road from which one came. The "losers" are those whose share has been diminished.

Then He, Exalted and Majestic, mentioned about the Children of Israel that they were obstinate and drew back. They said, "Indeed in it are a people of tyrants." The jabbar is on the pattern fa''al, from al-jabr (compulsion), as if by his strength, his overbearing and his violence, he compels people to his will. A "jabbara" palm tree is a tall one that cannot be reached by hand. The account of the tyrants was that they were a people of power. When Moses sent the twelve nuqaba' (chiefs) to observe the affair and conditions of the tyrants, they saw among them strength and violence, and they imagined that they had no ability to face them. So they came to the Children of Israel, breaking the covenant by informing them of the condition of the tyrants, as we have mentioned in the account of the sending of the chiefs. Of them, only Yushu' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yuqanna kept faith. Then the Children of Israel recoiled and became cowardly, and said: our being slaves to the Copts is easier than fighting these people. Many of them wished to appoint a man over themselves and return with him to the land of Egypt, turning back on their heels. They forgot that when God, Exalted is He, supports the weak, He overcomes the strong. They informed Moses, peace be upon him, that they would never enter the land as long as the tyrants were in it, and they asked him to have God drive out the tyrants by an army from Him, and then the Children of Israel would enter.

Ibn Muhaysin recited "Ya qawmu" (O people, with a nominative ending) here, and wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. This is also reported from Ibn Kathir. "Ni'mata Allah" (the favour of God) here is an ism al-jins (a generic noun, referring to favours in general). He then enumerated the principal forms of those favours and the prophets who were raised up among them. Their affair is well known, from the time of Israel until the time of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Prophets are a protection (hatah), a means of rescue from the Fire, and a source of honour in this world and the Hereafter. As for His statement, "and made you kings," it may bear several meanings. One is that He reminds them of the kingship of those among the Children of Israel who ruled, because kingship is a form of honour in this world and a protection from its calamities. The other meaning is that He intends: "He rescued you from the Copts (al-qibt) who used to enslave you, so you became free, possessing and not possessed." In this sense they are kings. Al-Suddi and others explained it in this manner. Qatada said: "He only said, 'and made you kings,' because we used to hear that they were the first people whom any of the children of Adam served."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is weak, because the Copts used to enslave the Children of Israel. The apparent situation of the children of Adam is that some of them have subjugated others since they multiplied and spread. The nations differed only regarding the meaning of owning. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and a group of the people of knowledge (p-137) said: whoever has a dwelling, a wife and a servant is a king. It was also said: whoever has a dwelling into which no one may enter without his permission is a king.

As for His statement, Exalted is He, "and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds," Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding it that the address is to the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. This is weak. The majority of the commentators said the address is from Moses, peace be upon him, to his people. Then the commentators differed about what it was that they were given which no one else had received the like of. Mujahid said: the manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud. Others said: the abundance of prophets.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: According to the view that it refers to the abundance of prophets, "the worlds" is general and unrestricted. According to the view that what was given was the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, then "the worlds" is restricted to the time in which they lived, because the community of Muhammad has been given from the signs of Muhammad, peace be upon him, far more than that. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was shaded by a cloud before his mission; stones and animals spoke to him; a tree came to him; the trunk wailed; water gushed from between his fingers; many people were satisfied with a little food through his blessing; the moon was split for him; a staff turned into a sword; and the stone that blocked the trench turned into scattered sand.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This statement from Moses was a preparation (tawti'a) of their souls, so that they would be strengthened and that the command to enter the land of the tyrants would be taken with strength, and the execution of that would be the execution of one whom God has honoured and elevated in rank. "Al-Muqaddasa" means al-mutahhara (the purified). Mujahid said: al-mubaraka (the blessed).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Blessing is a purification from drought, hunger and the like. People differed about identifying it. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is Mount Tur and what surrounds it. Qatada said: it is Syria. Ibn Zayd said: it is Ariha. This was also said by al-Suddi and by Ibn 'Abbas as well. Some people said: it is al-Ghuta, Filastin, and part of al-Urdunn. Al-Tabari said: there is no disagreement that it lies between the Euphrates and Arish Misr.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The reports are consistent that Dimashq (Damascus) is the capital of the tyrants.

(p-138) As for His statement, Exalted is He, "which God has prescribed for you," its meaning is: which God has decreed in His decree and His measure, that it is yours; you will inherit it and dwell in it, possessing it. But your trial in entering it lies in the obligation of fighting those who are in it, as a purification and a test. Then Moses, peace be upon him, warned them against turning back on their heels, and that is retreating backwards. It may be that it means turning one's back and returning by the same road from which one came. The "losers" are those whose share has been diminished.

Then He, Exalted and Majestic, mentioned about the Children of Israel that they were obstinate and drew back. They said, "Indeed in it are a people of tyrants." The jabbar is on the pattern fa''al, from al-jabr (compulsion), as if by his strength, his overbearing and his violence, he compels people to his will. A "jabbara" palm tree is a tall one that cannot be reached by hand. The account of the tyrants was that they were a people of power. When Moses sent the twelve nuqaba' (chiefs) to observe the affair and conditions of the tyrants, they saw among them strength and violence, and they imagined that they had no ability to face them. So they came to the Children of Israel, breaking the covenant by informing them of the condition of the tyrants, as we have mentioned in the account of the sending of the chiefs. Of them, only Yushu' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yuqanna kept faith. Then the Children of Israel recoiled and became cowardly, and said: our being slaves to the Copts is easier than fighting these people. Many of them wished to appoint a man over themselves and return with him to the land of Egypt, turning back on their heels. They forgot that when God, Exalted is He, supports the weak, He overcomes the strong. They informed Moses, peace be upon him, that they would never enter the land as long as the tyrants were in it, and they asked him to have God drive out the tyrants by an army from Him, and then the Children of Israel would enter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 23–26 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:
﴿Two men of those who feared (Allah), upon whom Allah had bestowed His favour, said: "Enter upon them through the gate. When you have entered it, you will surely be victorious. And upon Allah put your trust, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother. So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ ﴿He said: "It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people."﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid read "يُخافُونَ" with a *damma* on the *ya'* (yukhafūna, "who are made to fear"). The majority read "يَخافُونَ" with a *fatha* on the *ya'* (yakhāfūna, "who fear"). Most of the exegetes said: the two men were Yusha' ibn Nun, who was the son of Musa's sister, and Kalib ibn Yuqana. It is also said of him "Kilab," and it is said "Kalūth" with a *tha'* (with three dots). It is said of his father's name "Qafiya," and he was the son-in-law of Musa through his sister. Al-Tabari said: the name of his wife was Maryam bint 'Imran.

The meaning of "يَخافُونَ" is: they fear Allah. And Allah bestowed upon them both sound faith, steadfastness of heart, and firmness in the truth. Some people said the meaning is: they fear the enemy, but Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon them both faith and steadfastness despite their fear. The first interpretation is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Two men of those who fear Allah, upon whom He bestowed favour said..."

As for the one who reads with a *damma* on the *ya'*, his reading has three meanings. The first: it is narrated that the two men were among the giants (al-jabbārīn), who believed in Musa and followed him, so they were among the people who were feared; but Allah bestowed upon them the faith in Musa. They said: "We know our people better." The second meaning: they were Yusha' and Kalūth, but they were among those who are venerated, whose words are heeded, and who are held in awe because of their piety and virtue; so they are "feared" in this sense. The third meaning: the verb is from "akhāfa" (to make fear), and the meaning is: among those who are made to fear by the commands, prohibitions, threats and admonitions of Allah. Then this would be praise for them, similar to the praise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]. And His saying, "upon whom Allah had bestowed favour," is a description of the two men.

"Al-bāb" (the gate), according to what the exegetes mentioned, is the gate of the city of the giants. The meaning is: "Strive and struggle until you enter the gate." His saying "you will surely be victorious" is an opinion and a hope on their part, and an inference: that is, by this you will break their resolve, and terror will fall into their hearts, so you will overcome them. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "upon them, woe to you, enter."

Their saying "And upon Allah put your trust, if you are believers" implies that they doubted the faith of the people when they saw them disobeying the Messenger and cowering, despite Allah's promise of victory to them.

Then the Children of Israel persisted in their disobedience. They heard from the ten chieftains (al-nuqabā') who were spies, and who had frightened them about the matter of the giants and described to them the power of the giants and their great stature. So they resolved to oppose the command of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here."﴾ This is a statement that implies disbelief. Some people held that the meaning is: "Go, you, and your Lord will help you," and that the statement is an act of disobedience, not disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Their saying "fa-qātilā" (so fight, both of you) decides in favour of this (latter) interpretation being wrong. Al-Naqqash reported from some exegetes that the intended meaning of "the Lord" here is Harun, because he was older than Musa, and was esteemed among the Children of Israel and beloved for the breadth of his character and the openness of his heart. So it is as if they said: "Go, you and your elder."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a far-fetched interpretation. Harun was only a minister to Musa and a follower of his in the matter of the message. But it is an interpretation that saves the Children of Israel from disbelief.

Al-Tabari reported from Qatada that he said: "It reached us that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to fight the Quraysh in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, he gathered the army and spoke to the people about it. Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad said to him: 'We do not say to you what the Children of Israel said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here.﴾ Rather we say: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are fighting with you both."'" Al-Naqqash reported that the Ansar said this statement to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: All of this is a mistake. Qatada (may Allah have mercy on him) was wrong about the time of the incident, and al-Naqqash was wrong about who made the statement. The conversation took place at the Battle of Badr, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) halted at Dhafiran. He spoke to the people and said: "Advise me, O people." Al-Miqdad said this statement in a long speech; Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned it. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh spoke from among the Ansar with a similar meaning, but al-Miqdad had preceded him in citing the verse as an illustration.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Al-Miqdad's citing of it, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of that, indicates that "the Lord" was intended to refer to Allah, exalted is He. It also gives comfort concerning the faith of the Children of Israel, because al-Miqdad said: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight," and there is no meaning to his statement except that Allah, exalted is He, helps you, and His angels fight with you, and His victory (is with you). So perhaps the Children of Israel meant that: "Go, you, and Allah will drive them out of the city by His victory and power; then we will enter it." But their expression was ugly because it was associated with refusal, while al-Miqdad's expression was beautiful because it was associated with obedience and boldness.

When Musa, peace be upon him, heard their saying and saw their disobedience, he disowned them before Allah, exalted is He, and said, invoking (a curse) against them: ﴿My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother.﴾ He meant Harun. As for his saying "wa-akhī" (and my brother), its i'rab (grammatical case) may be *raf'* (nominative), either as a beginning (the sentence being: "and my brother has no control except over himself"), or as a conjunction with the pronoun in "amliku" (I have control), its implied sense being "I do not have control, I"; and it may be *nasb* (accusative), as a conjunction with "nafsī" (myself). That is because Harun used to obey Musa, so he stated that Musa had control over him. Al-Hasan read: "illā nafsī wa-akhī," with a *fatha* on the *ya'* in both.

His saying "fa-furq baynanā" (so separate us) is a supplication of distress. Al-Suddi said: it was a hasty act that Musa, peace be upon him, committed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: "Decide between us and them with a judgement that separates this dispute and gathers the scattered." So the meaning is: "Judge with a judgement that divides this discord and gathers the dispersed."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: According to this interpretation there is no hastiness in the supplication. Some people said the meaning is: "Separate us and them in the Hereafter, so that the station of the obedient is distinct from the station of the disobedient sinner." The supplication may also mean: "Let us be separated from them," in the sense that he says: "We have lost sight of their faces, and let us be separated from them so that we are not harmed by their wickedness." In this sense, haste does come into the supplication. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read: "fa-afriq" with a *kasra* on the *ra'*.

﴿He said: "It is forbidden to them..."﴾ The meaning is: "Allah said." The subject is omitted in all these verbs for brevity, because the sense of the speech indicates what is intended. Allah, exalted is He, forbade all the Children of Israel to enter that city for forty years, and left them during that period wandering in the land, that is, in the land of that calamity. It is the wilderness of al-Tih, which, as is related, is about eighty miles in length by six farsakhs in breadth, lying between Egypt and Syria. It is narrated that it happened that everyone who had said "we will never enter it" died, and none of that generation entered the city except Yusha' and Kalūth. It is narrated that Harun, peace be upon him, died in the wilderness of al-Tih during this period, and there is no disagreement on this. And it is narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, died there eight years after Harun; and it is said: six and a half months after him. And that Yusha' was made a prophet after the full forty years were completed, and he went out with the Children of Israel and fought the giants and conquered the city; and in that battle the sun stood still for him for an hour until the defeat of the giants was complete. It is also narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, lived until the forty years were completed, went out with the people, and fought the giants, with Yusha' and Kalib at his vanguard; and that he conquered the city and killed 'Uj ibn 'Anaq with his own hand. It is said: Musa's height was ten cubits, and the length of his staff was ten cubits, and he leapt from the ground into the sky ten cubits. Then he caught up with 'Uj's ankle and struck him with his staff on the ankle, and he fell down dead. It is also narrated that 'Uj had uprooted a rock to throw upon the camp of the Children of Israel; so Allah sent a hoopoe with a diamond stone, which it turned around the rock, so that it was split open and entered 'Uj's neck; and Musa struck him and he died. Al-Tabari related that 'Uj's height was eight hundred cubits. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: when he fell, he became a bridge over the Nile for a year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The Nile is not in those regions. All of this is weak, and Allah knows best. Al-Zajjaj related from some people that Musa and Harun were not in the wilderness.

The word governing "forty" (arba'īna) may be "muḥarramatun" (forbidden), that is: "It has been forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land during this period, then it will be opened to them; whoever reaches it reaches it, and whoever dies before it dies." Abu Ishaq rejected that the governing word is "muḥarramatun," but that is an unfair attack on his part. The governing word may also be an implied "yatīhūna" (they will wander), indicated by the later "yatīhūna"; and his saying "fa-innahā muḥarramatun" (for it is forbidden) would be a continuing statement, meaning that they understood from it that those addressed would never enter it, and that they—along with that—would wander in the land for forty years, during which whoever died would die.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The address according to this interpretation is more difficult in its stance, and more pressing in its despair. It is related that whoever had passed twenty years of age did not live to come out of the wilderness, and that those under twenty lived.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is as if the adults did not survive. Al-Zajjaj pointed to this.

Al-tīh (wandering) is walking in the land without a known destination. It is related that the Children of Israel used to travel at night and would walk the whole night in circles and similar aimless wandering, with irregular progress, until in the morning they found themselves all in the place where they had been at the beginning of the night. Mujahid and others said: they would walk during the day at times and during the night at times, so they would be in the evening where they had been in the morning, and in the morning where they had been in the evening; and this was over a distance of six farsakhs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Their wandering may have been caused by the division of their word, the scarcity of unified opinion, and Allah, exalted is He, casting discord among them; and they knew that it had been forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered across that wilderness, and they continued to move from place to place in no order or unity, until this period was completed and Allah permitted their departure. This wandering is possible and conceivable by human custom. The other kind that Mujahid mentioned is a breaking of custom and a wonder of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

During that wandering, the cloud was made to shade them, and they were provided with manna and quails, along with other things narrated about their circumstances; and this has passed in surat al-Baqara.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾ means: do not be sorrowful. It is said: "asiya al-rajulu, ya'sā, asan," when a man grieves. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Standing there, my companions upon their mounts, saying to me: "Do not perish in grief, but bear up."

And from it is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:

I said to them: "Grief begets grief..." ... "Leave me, for all of this is the grave of Malik."

The address in this verse is to Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people, and grieved over them. So Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾.

Some of the exegetes said: the address in these words is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiantly disobedient" are meant his contemporaries. That is, these are the deeds of their forefathers; so do not grieve, on account of their wicked deeds towards you and their rejection of you, for it is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

They said: "We know our people better." Their saying "And upon Allah put your trust, if you are believers" implies that they doubted the faith of the people when they saw them disobeying the Messenger and cowering, despite Allah's promise of victory to them.

Then the Children of Israel persisted in their disobedience. They heard from the ten chieftains (al-nuqabā') who were spies, and who had frightened them about the matter of the giants and described to them the power of the giants and their great stature. So they resolved to oppose the command of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. Qatada (may Allah have mercy on him) was wrong about the time of the incident, and al-Naqqash was wrong about who made the statement. The first interpretation is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Two men of those who fear Allah, upon whom He bestowed favour said..."

As for the one who reads with a *damma* on the *ya'*, his reading has three meanings. The first: it is narrated that the two men were among the giants (al-jabbārīn), who believed in Musa and followed him, so they were among the people who were feared; but Allah bestowed upon them the faith in Musa. They said: "We know our people better." The second meaning: they were Yusha' and Kalūth, but they were among those who are venerated, whose words are heeded, and who are held in awe because of their piety and virtue; so they are "feared" in this sense. The third meaning: the verb is from "akhāfa" (to make fear), and the meaning is: among those who are made to fear by the commands, prohibitions, threats and admonitions of Allah. Then this would be praise for them, similar to the praise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3]. And His saying, "upon whom Allah had bestowed favour," is a description of the two men.

"Al-bāb" (the gate), according to what the exegetes mentioned, is the gate of the city of the giants. The meaning is: "Strive and struggle until you enter the gate." His saying "you will surely be victorious" is an opinion and a hope on their part, and an inference: that is, by this you will break their resolve, and terror will fall into their hearts, so you will overcome them. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "upon them, woe to you, enter."

Their saying "And upon Allah put your trust, if you are believers" implies that they doubted the faith of the people when they saw them disobeying the Messenger and cowering, despite Allah's promise of victory to them.

Then the Children of Israel persisted in their disobedience. They heard from the ten chieftains (al-nuqabā') who were spies, and who had frightened them about the matter of the giants and described to them the power of the giants and their great stature. So they resolved to oppose the command of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "O Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here."﴾ This is a statement that implies disbelief. Some people held that the meaning is: "Go, you, and your Lord will help you," and that the statement is an act of disobedience, not disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Their saying "fa-qātilā" (so fight, both of you) decides in favour of this (latter) interpretation being wrong. Al-Naqqash reported from some exegetes that the intended meaning of "the Lord" here is Harun, because he was older than Musa, and was esteemed among the Children of Israel and beloved for the breadth of his character and the openness of his heart. So it is as if they said: "Go, you and your elder."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a far-fetched interpretation. Harun was only a minister to Musa and a follower of his in the matter of the message. But it is an interpretation that saves the Children of Israel from disbelief.

Al-Tabari reported from Qatada that he said: "It reached us that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to fight the Quraysh in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, he gathered the army and spoke to the people about it. Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad said to him: 'We do not say to you what the Children of Israel said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here.﴾ Rather we say: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are fighting with you both."'" Al-Naqqash reported that the Ansar said this statement to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: All of this is a mistake. Qatada (may Allah have mercy on him) was wrong about the time of the incident, and al-Naqqash was wrong about who made the statement. The conversation took place at the Battle of Badr, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) halted at Dhafiran. He spoke to the people and said: "Advise me, O people." Al-Miqdad said this statement in a long speech; Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned it. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh spoke from among the Ansar with a similar meaning, but al-Miqdad had preceded him in citing the verse as an illustration.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Al-Miqdad's citing of it, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of that, indicates that "the Lord" was intended to refer to Allah, exalted is He. It also gives comfort concerning the faith of the Children of Israel, because al-Miqdad said: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight," and there is no meaning to his statement except that Allah, exalted is He, helps you, and His angels fight with you, and His victory (is with you). So perhaps the Children of Israel meant that: "Go, you, and Allah will drive them out of the city by His victory and power; then we will enter it." But their expression was ugly because it was associated with refusal, while al-Miqdad's expression was beautiful because it was associated with obedience and boldness.

When Musa, peace be upon him, heard their saying and saw their disobedience, he disowned them before Allah, exalted is He, and said, invoking (a curse) against them: ﴿My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother.﴾ He meant Harun. As for his saying "wa-akhī" (and my brother), its i'rab (grammatical case) may be *raf'* (nominative), either as a beginning (the sentence being: "and my brother has no control except over himself"), or as a conjunction with the pronoun in "amliku" (I have control), its implied sense being "I do not have control, I"; and it may be *nasb* (accusative), as a conjunction with "nafsī" (myself). That is because Harun used to obey Musa, so he stated that Musa had control over him. Al-Hasan read: "illā nafsī wa-akhī," with a *fatha* on the *ya'* in both.

His saying "fa-furq baynanā" (so separate us) is a supplication of distress. Al-Suddi said: it was a hasty act that Musa, peace be upon him, committed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: the meaning is: "Decide between us and them with a judgement that separates this dispute and gathers the scattered." So the meaning is: "Judge with a judgement that divides this discord and gathers the dispersed."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: According to this interpretation there is no hastiness in the supplication. Some people said the meaning is: "Separate us and them in the Hereafter, so that the station of the obedient is distinct from the station of the disobedient sinner." The supplication may also mean: "Let us be separated from them," in the sense that he says: "We have lost sight of their faces, and let us be separated from them so that we are not harmed by their wickedness." In this sense, haste does come into the supplication. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read: "fa-afriq" with a *kasra* on the *ra'*.

﴿He said: "It is forbidden to them..."﴾ The meaning is: "Allah said." The subject is omitted in all these verbs for brevity, because the sense of the speech indicates what is intended. Allah, exalted is He, forbade all the Children of Israel to enter that city for forty years, and left them during that period wandering in the land, that is, in the land of that calamity. It is the wilderness of al-Tih, which, as is related, is about eighty miles in length by six farsakhs in breadth, lying between Egypt and Syria. It is narrated that it happened that everyone who had said "we will never enter it" died, and none of that generation entered the city except Yusha' and Kalūth. It is narrated that Harun, peace be upon him, died in the wilderness of al-Tih during this period, and there is no disagreement on this. And it is narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, died there eight years after Harun; and it is said: six and a half months after him. And that Yusha' was made a prophet after the full forty years were completed, and he went out with the Children of Israel and fought the giants and conquered the city; and in that battle the sun stood still for him for an hour until the defeat of the giants was complete. It is also narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, lived until the forty years were completed, went out with the people, and fought the giants, with Yusha' and Kalib at his vanguard; and that he conquered the city and killed 'Uj ibn 'Anaq with his own hand. It is said: Musa's height was ten cubits, and the length of his staff was ten cubits, and he leapt from the ground into the sky ten cubits. Then he caught up with 'Uj's ankle and struck him with his staff on the ankle, and he fell down dead. It is also narrated that 'Uj had uprooted a rock to throw upon the camp of the Children of Israel; so Allah sent a hoopoe with a diamond stone, which it turned around the rock, so that it was split open and entered 'Uj's neck; and Musa struck him and he died. Al-Tabari related that 'Uj's height was eight hundred cubits. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: when he fell, he became a bridge over the Nile for a year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The Nile is not in those regions. All of this is weak, and Allah knows best. Al-Zajjaj related from some people that Musa and Harun were not in the wilderness.

The word governing "forty" (arba'īna) may be "muḥarramatun" (forbidden), that is: "It has been forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land during this period, then it will be opened to them; whoever reaches it reaches it, and whoever dies before it dies." Abu Ishaq rejected that the governing word is "muḥarramatun," but that is an unfair attack on his part. The governing word may also be an implied "yatīhūna" (they will wander), indicated by the later "yatīhūna"; and his saying "fa-innahā muḥarramatun" (for it is forbidden) would be a continuing statement, meaning that they understood from it that those addressed would never enter it, and that they—along with that—would wander in the land for forty years, during which whoever died would die.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The address according to this interpretation is more difficult in its stance, and more pressing in its despair. It is related that whoever had passed twenty years of age did not live to come out of the wilderness, and that those under twenty lived.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is as if the adults did not survive. Al-Zajjaj pointed to this.

Al-tīh (wandering) is walking in the land without a known destination. It is related that the Children of Israel used to travel at night and would walk the whole night in circles and similar aimless wandering, with irregular progress, until in the morning they found themselves all in the place where they had been at the beginning of the night. Mujahid and others said: they would walk during the day at times and during the night at times, so they would be in the evening where they had been in the morning, and in the morning where they had been in the evening; and this was over a distance of six farsakhs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Their wandering may have been caused by the division of their word, the scarcity of unified opinion, and Allah, exalted is He, casting discord among them; and they knew that it had been forbidden to them for forty years, so their dwellings scattered across that wilderness, and they continued to move from place to place in no order or unity, until this period was completed and Allah permitted their departure. This wandering is possible and conceivable by human custom. The other kind that Mujahid mentioned is a breaking of custom and a wonder of the power of Allah, exalted is He.

During that wandering, the cloud was made to shade them, and they were provided with manna and quails, along with other things narrated about their circumstances; and this has passed in surat al-Baqara.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾ means: do not be sorrowful. It is said: "asiya al-rajulu, ya'sā, asan," when a man grieves. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Standing there, my companions upon their mounts, saying to me: "Do not perish in grief, but bear up."

And from it is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayra:

I said to them: "Grief begets grief..." ... "Leave me, for all of this is the grave of Malik."

The address in this verse is to Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Musa regretted his supplication against his people, and grieved over them. So Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾.

Some of the exegetes said: the address in these words is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the defiantly disobedient" are meant his contemporaries. That is, these are the deeds of their forefathers; so do not grieve, on account of their wicked deeds towards you and their rejection of you, for it is a wicked disposition inherited among them.

**The Qur'anic verse (5:27–29):**

﴿Recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah only accepts from the righteous.﴾ ﴿If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I will not stretch out my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya's Commentary

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

"Recite" (*wa-tlu*): its meaning is "recount" and "make them hear it." This is from the knowledge of the earlier scriptures, which Muhammad (ﷺ) had no connection to except through revelation. So it is one of the proofs of his prophethood (ﷺ).

The pronoun in "to them" (*'alayhim*), according to its apparent sense, is intended to refer to the Children of Israel, for two reasons. First, the discourse preceding this was concerning them, and the establishing of proofs against them because of their intention to stretch out their hands against Muhammad (ﷺ). Second, the knowledge of the story of the two sons of Adam is only with them, in the obscure parts of their books, and the proof is established against them in its transmission.

"Naba'" means "news." According to the majority of the exegetes (*mufassirun*), the two sons of Adam were from his own loins, and they are Qabil and Habil. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri said: the two sons of Adam were not from his loins, and offerings (*qaraabin*) existed only among the Children of Israel.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is an error. How could anyone among the Children of Israel be ignorant of the form of burial, so as to be guided by the crow? The correct view is that of the majority. It is narrated that their offering of sacrifices was voluntary worship and devotion. Qabil was a man of crops, so he deliberately chose the worst and lowest of what he had and offered it. Habil was a man of sheep, so he deliberately chose the best of his rams and offered it. At that time, the custom was that the one offering would bring his offering and stand (p-145) and pray and prostrate. If a fire came down and consumed the offering, that was a sign of acceptance; otherwise, its being left was a sign of non-acceptance. When these two offered as I have mentioned, the fire came down, took Habil's ram, lifted it up, and hid it from view, and left Qabil's crops. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that ram continued to graze in Paradise until it was sent down to Ibrahim as a ransom for his son.

The narrators of this account said: Qabil envied Habil and said to him, "Do you walk on the earth while people see you as better than me?" Qabil was the eldest son of Adam. It is also narrated that Adam traveled to Makkah to see the Ka'bah and left Qabil as guardian over his children, so this incident took place during his absence. A group of exegetes, among them Ibn Mas'ud, related that the cause of this offering was that Hawwa' used to give birth to a male and a female in every pregnancy, and a male would marry the female of the other pregnancy, and it was not permitted for him to marry his twin sister. A beautiful sister was born with Qabil, and a less beautiful sister with Habil. When Adam wanted to marry them, Qabil said, "I have more right to my sister." Adam ordered him, but he did not comply, so they agreed to offer sacrifices. It is also narrated that Adam was present at that, and Habil's offering was accepted, and it became necessary for him to take Qabil's sister. At that point, Qabil said to him, "I will surely kill you."

Habil's saying, "Allah only accepts from the righteous," is a statement preceded by an omitted clause, whose implied meaning is: "Why do you kill me when I have committed no crime, and I am not responsible for Allah's acceptance of my offering? Indeed, I fear Him, and you were to me the most beloved of creation. Allah only accepts from the righteous."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The consensus of the people of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) regarding the meaning of these words is that they refer to guarding against shirk. Whoever guards against it while being a monotheist, his deeds in which his intention is sincere are accepted. As for one who guards against shirk and sins, he has the highest degree of acceptance and the decree of mercy. This is known from the report of Allah, the Exalted, not that it is obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted, by reason. 'Adi ibn Thabit and others said: The offering of the righteous of this Ummah is prayer.

People differed about why Habil said, "I will not stretch out my hand against you to kill you." Mujahid said: At that time it was obligatory upon them that no one should draw a sword, and that the one intended to be killed should not defend himself. Abdullah ibn 'Amr and the majority of people said: Habil was stronger than Qabil, but he refrained out of scruple.

(p-146) The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the most apparent view. From here it is strengthened that Qabil was a sinner, not an unbeliever, for if he had been an unbeliever, there would have been no sense in refraining. The point of refraining in this case is that the one who refrains refuses to fight a monotheist, and accepts being wronged in order to be rewarded in the Hereafter. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) did something similar to this.

As for his saying, "Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin," and the rest of the verse: this is not a wanting of love or desire, but a choice between two evils, as the Arabs say: "In evil there is a choice." The meaning is: "If you kill me, and that was decreed, then my choice is to be wronged, and Allah will support me in the Hereafter." "To bear" (*tabu'a*) means "to go forth bearing." His saying, "my sin and your sin," it has been said its meaning is: the sin of killing me and all your other sins that made your offering not accepted. It has also been said that the meaning is: the sin of killing me and your sin in aggression against me, since being aggressive and intending to kill is sinful even if you do not carry out the killing. It has also been said that the meaning is: "the sin of me if I fought you and killed you, and the sin of yourself in fighting me and killing me."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the sin that is implied by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, so what about the one killed?" He said: "He was eager to kill his companion." So it is as if Habil meant: "I am not eager to kill you, so the sin that would fall upon me had I been eager to kill you, I want you to bear it, along with your sin in killing me."

It has also been said that the meaning is: "the sin that is specifically mine concerning what has passed for me," meaning: "it is taken from my evil deeds and cast upon you because of your wronging me, so you bear your sin in killing me." This interpretation is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and some of the good deeds of the wrongdoer will be taken and added to the good deeds of the wronged, until he is compensated. If the wrongdoer has no good deeds, some of the evil deeds of the wronged will be taken and cast upon him."

(p-147) As for His saying, the Exalted, "That is the recompense of the wrongdoers," it is possible that it is the statement of Habil to his brother, and it is possible that it is an informing from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ).
