The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is an error. How could anyone among the Children of Israel be ignorant of the form of burial, so as to be guided by the crow? The correct view is that of the majority. It is narrated that their offering of sacrifices was voluntary worship and devotion. Qabil was a man of crops, so he deliberately chose the worst and lowest of what he had and offered it. Habil was a man of sheep, so he deliberately chose the best of his rams and offered it. At that time, the custom was that the one offering would bring his offering and stand (p-145) and pray and prostrate. If a fire came down and consumed the offering, that was a sign of acceptance; otherwise, its being left was a sign of non-acceptance. When these two offered as I have mentioned, the fire came down, took Habil's ram, lifted it up, and hid it from view, and left Qabil's crops. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that ram continued to graze in Paradise until it was sent down to Ibrahim as a ransom for his son.

The narrators of this account said: Qabil envied Habil and said to him, "Do you walk on the earth while people see you as better than me?" Qabil was the eldest son of Adam. It is also narrated that Adam traveled to Makkah to see the Ka'bah and left Qabil as guardian over his children, so this incident took place during his absence. A group of exegetes, among them Ibn Mas'ud, related that the cause of this offering was that Hawwa' used to give birth to a male and a female in every pregnancy, and a male would marry the female of the other pregnancy, and it was not permitted for him to marry his twin sister. A beautiful sister was born with Qabil, and a less beautiful sister with Habil. When Adam wanted to marry them, Qabil said, "I have more right to my sister." Adam ordered him, but he did not comply, so they agreed to offer sacrifices. It is also narrated that Adam was present at that, and Habil's offering was accepted, and it became necessary for him to take Qabil's sister. At that point, Qabil said to him, "I will surely kill you."

Habil's saying, "Allah only accepts from the righteous," is a statement preceded by an omitted clause, whose implied meaning is: "Why do you kill me when I have committed no crime, and I am not responsible for Allah's acceptance of my offering? Indeed, I fear Him, and you were to me the most beloved of creation. Allah only accepts from the righteous."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The consensus of the people of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) regarding the meaning of these words is that they refer to guarding against shirk. Whoever guards against it while being a monotheist, his deeds in which his intention is sincere are accepted. As for one who guards against shirk and sins, he has the highest degree of acceptance and the decree of mercy. This is known from the report of Allah, the Exalted, not that it is obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted, by reason. 'Adi ibn Thabit and others said: The offering of the righteous of this Ummah is prayer.

People differed about why Habil said, "I will not stretch out my hand against you to kill you." Mujahid said: At that time it was obligatory upon them that no one should draw a sword, and that the one intended to be killed should not defend himself. Abdullah ibn 'Amr and the majority of people said: Habil was stronger than Qabil, but he refrained out of scruple.

(p-146) The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the most apparent view. From here it is strengthened that Qabil was a sinner, not an unbeliever, for if he had been an unbeliever, there would have been no sense in refraining. The point of refraining in this case is that the one who refrains refuses to fight a monotheist, and accepts being wronged in order to be rewarded in the Hereafter. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) did something similar to this.

As for his saying, "Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin," and the rest of the verse: this is not a wanting of love or desire, but a choice between two evils, as the Arabs say: "In evil there is a choice." The meaning is: "If you kill me, and that was decreed, then my choice is to be wronged, and Allah will support me in the Hereafter." "To bear" (*tabu'a*) means "to go forth bearing." His saying, "my sin and your sin," it has been said its meaning is: the sin of killing me and all your other sins that made your offering not accepted. It has also been said that the meaning is: the sin of killing me and your sin in aggression against me, since being aggressive and intending to kill is sinful even if you do not carry out the killing. It has also been said that the meaning is: "the sin of me if I fought you and killed you, and the sin of yourself in fighting me and killing me."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the sin that is implied by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, so what about the one killed?" He said: "He was eager to kill his companion." So it is as if Habil meant: "I am not eager to kill you, so the sin that would fall upon me had I been eager to kill you, I want you to bear it, along with your sin in killing me."

It has also been said that the meaning is: "the sin that is specifically mine concerning what has passed for me," meaning: "it is taken from my evil deeds and cast upon you because of your wronging me, so you bear your sin in killing me." This interpretation is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and some of the good deeds of the wrongdoer will be taken and added to the good deeds of the wronged, until he is compensated. If the wrongdoer has no good deeds, some of the evil deeds of the wronged will be taken and cast upon him."

(p-147) As for His saying, the Exalted, "That is the recompense of the wrongdoers," it is possible that it is the statement of Habil to his brother, and it is possible that it is an informing from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat al-Māʾida, verses 30–31:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him, and he killed him, and became among the losers.﴾ ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth, to show him how to conceal his brother's nakedness. He said, "Woe is me! Am I incapable of being like this crow and concealing my brother's nakedness?" And he became among the regretful.﴾

The reading of the majority (qirāʾa al-jumhūr) is ﴿fa-ṭawwaʿat﴾. The meaning is that killing, in itself, is very difficult for souls. This stubborn, commanding-to-evil soul made him comply, submitting to it, until the owner of this soul actually committed it. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan, al-Jarrāḥ, al-Ḥasan ibn ʿImrān and Abū Wāqid read ﴿fa-ṭāwaʿat﴾. The meaning is as if killing was calling to his self, because of the spite and envy that had afflicted Qābīl. And as if the self refused it and found it hard, and each of the two sides wanted the other to obey it, until the matter escalated, and the self obeyed the killing and committed it.

It is narrated that he sought an opportunity to kill him, until he found him asleep among his sheep, and he smashed his head with a stone. It is also narrated that he did not know how to kill him, so Iblīs came with a bird or another animal and began to smash its head between two stones, so that Qābīl would follow its example, and he did so. It is also narrated that when Qābīl returned to Ādam, he said to him, "Where is Hābīl?" He said, "I do not know. It is as if you had entrusted me with guarding him." Ādam said to him, "Did you do it? By Allah, his blood is calling out to me from the earth. O Allah, curse the earth that drank Hābīl's blood." It is narrated that from that time no earth has drunk blood. Then Ādam (ﷺ) remained for a hundred years without smiling, until an angel came and said to him, "May Allah greet you and make you laugh, O Ādam." Ādam said, "What makes me laugh?" The angel said, "Something that made you laugh." It is narrated that Ādam (ʿalayhi al-salām) then said:

> The lands have changed, and whoever is upon them,
> so the face of the earth is dust-colored and ugly.

> Every thing of taste and color has changed,
> and the beaming face has grown scarce in its brightness.

Thus is the poetry, with the object ﴿bashāshata﴾ in the accusative and the tanwīn dropped.

It is narrated from Mujāhid that he said: one of the killer's legs was bound by its shank to its thigh from that day until the Day of Resurrection, and his face turned toward the sun wherever it turned. Upon him in summer is an enclosure of fire, and upon him in winter is an enclosure of ice.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If this is authentic, then it is part of his loss which is contained in His saying, ﴿and became among the losers﴾. And among his loss is what is narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, that he said: "We find that the son of Ādam who was the killer shares with the people of the Fire a correct division of punishment: upon him is half of their punishment." And among his loss is what is established and authenticated from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Ādam bears a share of its blood-guilt," because he was the first to establish killing.

His saying ﴿fa-aṣbaḥa﴾ ("and he became") is an expression for all of his times; part of the time is used in place of all of it. The morning (al-ṣabāḥ) was singled out for this because it is the beginning of the day, the setting-out toward affairs, and the vehicle of energy. From this is the saying of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ḍabʿ:

> I have become one who no longer carries a weapon...

And from this is the saying of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ: "Then the Banū Asad came to reproach me for Islam," along with other uses of this word by the Arabs, as we have mentioned.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth, to show him how to conceal his brother's nakedness﴾: it is narrated concerning its meaning that Qābīl put his brother in a sack and carried him on his neck for a hundred years. It was said: for one year. It was said: rather, on the second morning after the killing he sought to conceal the matter of his brother, but he did not know what to do with him. So Allah sent a living crow to a dead crow, and it began to scratch in the earth and throw dirt over the dead crow. It is narrated that Allah sent two crows, which fought until one killed the other; then the killer began to scratch and cover the dead one. It is also narrated that Allah sent only one crow, which began to scratch and throw dirt over Hābīl.

The apparent meaning of this verse is that Hābīl was the first dead person among the sons of Ādam; for this reason the custom of burial was unknown. Thus al-Ṭabarī related from Ibn Isḥāq, from some people of knowledge, from what is in the earlier books.

(p. 149) And ﴿yabḥathu﴾ means: it searches the dirt with its beak and stirs it up. From this, the sūra of [Barāʾa] was named "al-Buḥūth," because it searched out (fatashat) the hypocrites. And from this is the saying of the poet:

> If people cover me, I cover myself from them;
> but if they search me out, there are in them searchings (mabāḥith).

And in the saying: "Do not be like the one who searches for the blade (al-bāḥith ʿan al-shafra)."

The pronoun in His saying ﴿sawʾata akhīhi﴾ may refer back to Qābīl, and "the brother" would then be Hābīl. It may also refer back to the searching crow, and "the brother" would then be the dead crow. The first is more well-known in interpretation. The sawʾa is the ʿawra (the private parts). It was singled out for mention, although what is meant is concealing the whole body, out of concern for it and because covering it is more emphatic. It may also be meant that the sawʾa is the state which offends the viewer as a whole. It is attributed to the one who was killed in terms of the calamity that befell him, not as a way of belittling him; rather, the blame falls upon the killer, who is the one who brought about the sawʾa.

The majority read ﴿fa-uwāriya﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and al-Fayyāḍ ibn Ghazwān read ﴿fa-uwārī﴾ with a sukūn on the yāʾ, and this is a dialect form because of the succession of vowels.

When Qābīl saw the crow's action, he became aware of what should be done with his brother, and he saw the deficiency of his own self and the ignorance of humankind in such matters. So he said, ﴿Woe is me! Am I incapable…﴾, to the end of the verse, and he belittled himself, and for this reason he regretted it. The majority read ﴿yā wayletā﴾ ("O woe"), and the original is ﴿yā wayletī﴾, but some Arabs change the yāʾ into an alif and vocalize the yāʾ with a fatḥa for this reason, saying ﴿yā wayletā﴾ and ﴿yā ghulāmā﴾; and some of them stop on the hāʾ of pause, (p. 150) saying ﴿yā wayletāh﴾. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read ﴿yā wayletī﴾.

The vocative of wayla is according to the sense: "Come forth, for this is your time." This is the category of His saying "O regret!" (yā ḥasratan), and of their saying "O wonder!" (yā ʿajaban), and what is similar to it, the calling upon these things which do not understand; these are meanings. The majority read ﴿aʿjaztu﴾ with a fatḥa on the jīm; Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḥasan, al-Fayyāḍ and Ṭalḥa ibn Sulaymān read ﴿aʿajiztu﴾ with a kasra on the jīm, and this is a dialect form.

Then Qābīl concealed his brother, and regretted what he had done of disobedience to Allah in killing him, at a time when regret would not benefit him. The scholars differed concerning Qābīl: was he among the disbelievers or among the sinners? The apparent view is that he was among the sinners. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah has struck for you the example of the two sons of Ādam, so take the better of the two and leave the evil."

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 32:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to mankind entirely. And Our messengers came to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, after that, were transgressors in the land.﴾

The majority of people hold that His saying, ﴿Because of that﴾, is connected to His saying, "We prescribed" (kataba-na), meaning: "because of this incident; and on account of it, We prescribed." Others said: rather, it is connected to His saying, ﴿among the regretful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31], meaning: he regretted because of what had occurred. According to this view, the pause is on "that" (dhalika), and the others hold that the pause is on "among the regretful."

It is said: "ajala al-amr, ajalan wa ajlan" (he brought about the matter, or drew it on), when one commits it or brings it about and drags it along; from this is the verse of Khawwat:

Among a household of a good tent, whose mutual affairs are sound,
They have fought one another over something of the immediate, and I am its delayed consequence.

It is said: "fa'altu dhalika min ajlika" with a fatḥah on the hamzah, and "min ijlika" with a kasrah. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "min ijli dhalika" with the alif joined and a kasrah on the nun before it. This is on the basis that the vowel of the hamzah was transferred onto the nun, as they say: "kam ibiluka?" with a kasrah on the mim and the alif joined, and "min ibrahim" with a kasrah on the nun.

"Kataba-na" means: it was prescribed by Our command in books revealed to them, which contained the obligation of that. God, Exalted, singled out the Children of Israel for mention, although nations before them had also considered killing a soul forbidden among them, for two reasons. The first, as is narrated, is that the Children of Israel were the first nation for whom the threat concerning killing a soul was revealed in a book, and the matter was made more severe for them in accordance with their transgression and their shedding of blood. The second is to make their blameworthiness evident, in that this was prescribed for them while they nonetheless did not refrain or desist; rather they intended to kill the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, unjustly. So they were singled out for mention because of their presence as opponents of what had been prescribed for them.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"without a soul"﴾, means: without a person having killed a soul, thereby deserving to be killed. God, Exalted, has forbidden the soul of a believer except for one of three things: disbelief after belief, or adultery after ihsan (chastity/marriage, a condition for stoning), or the killing of a soul unjustly and transgressively. Here the one who wages war (al-muharib, one who commits armed robbery or brigandage) is included.

Corruption in the land (al-fasad fi al-ardi) comprises adultery, apostasy, and hirabah (armed highway robbery). Al-Hasan read ﴿"or corruption in the land"﴾ with the accusative on "corruption" (fasadan), governed by a verb that is omitted, its estimated form being "or he committed corruption" or "he created corruption." The governing verb was omitted because the sense of the speech indicates it.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿then it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾. The words of the exegetes differed concerning the arrangement of this comparison. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the meaning is: whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever gives him life, by strengthening his arm and supporting him, it is as if he had given life to mankind entirely.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: this is a view that the wording does not support.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the meaning is: whoever kills one soul and violates its sanctity, he is like one who kills mankind entirely; and whoever refrains from killing one soul, preserves its sanctity, and is ashamed to kill it, he is like one who gives life to mankind entirely.

'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas also said: the meaning is: it is as if he had slain mankind entirely in the sight of the one slain; and whoever gives life to it and rescues it from destruction, it is as if he had given life to mankind entirely in the sight of the one rescued.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, and others: the meaning is: whoever kills a soul and thereby destroys his own soul, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely, since he will burn in the Fire because of that; and whoever is spared from killing it, it is as if he were spared from killing mankind entirely.

Mujahid said: whoever kills a believing soul deliberately, God has made his recompense Hell, and He is angry with him, curses him, and has prepared for him a great punishment. He says: even if he had killed all mankind, it would not add anything beyond that; and whoever does not kill anyone, mankind has been given life through him.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the qawad (retaliation) and qisas (legal equal retribution) that he would incur had he killed mankind entirely. He said: "and whoever gives it life" means: whoever pardons the one who is owed death. This was also said by al-Hasan; that is, it is pardoning after the ability to exact it. Mujahid said: "and whoever gives it life" means: he rescues it from burning or drowning.

Some people said: since all believers seek the killer, he is like one who killed mankind entirely.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: this is a view that is self-contradictory, and the comparison does not reach a definite point in any of these views. What I say is: the resemblance between the killer of a soul and the killer of all is not uniform from all aspects; rather the resemblance is established from three aspects. The first is qawad, for it is one. The second is the threat, for God has threatened the killer of a soul with eternal abiding in the Fire, and that is the utmost punishment; if we suppose that he will leave the Fire afterwards because of tawhid (monotheism), then likewise the killer of all, if that were to happen. The third is the violation of sanctity, for one soul and all souls are equal in that; and the violator of one is regarded in the same light as the violator of all. An example of this: two men swore an oath concerning two trees that they would not eat any of their fruit; one of them ate one fruit from his tree, and the other ate all the fruit of his tree; they are equal in having broken the oath.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"and whoever gives it life"﴾ contains a figurative usage (tajawwuz), because it is an expression for leaving alone and rescuing. Otherwise, giving life in its literal sense, which is bringing into existence, belongs only to God, Exalted. This giving of life is like the saying of Nimrod: ﴿"I give life and cause death"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]; he named leaving alone "giving life." The one who gives life to one soul is like the one who gives life to all in preserving sanctity and deserving praise.

Then God, Exalted, informed about the Children of Israel that messengers from God came to them with clear proofs concerning this and concerning other matters. Then many of them, after that, continued in every age to be transgressors, exceeding the limits. In this verse there is an allusion to the deed of the Jews in their intention to kill the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and others, and to the rest of their deeds.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 33–34 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:
﴿The only recompense for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a great punishment.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The meaning of this verse requires that *innama* (the "only" particle, *innama*) be a restrictive particle (*hasr*) of complete restriction. People differed about the occasion of revelation of this verse. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that it was revealed concerning a people from the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant, cut off the road, and spread corruption in the land.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that it was the incident of the Banu Qurayza when they intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Ikrima and al-Hasan said: The verse was revealed concerning the polytheists.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In this there is weakness, because the repentance of a polytheist is accepted even after one has gained power over him. In any case, Anas ibn Malik, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and others said: The verse was revealed concerning a group from 'Ukl and 'Uraina. They came to (p-154) the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam. Then they fell ill, and the climate of Madina did not agree with them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to stay with the milch camels of the charity (*sadaqa*), and said: "Drink from their milk and urine." They went out with them, and when they recovered, they killed the herdsmen and drove off the camels. A messenger (*sarikh*) came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this. He gave an order and it was proclaimed among the people: "O cavalry of Allah, mount!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode after them and they were captured. Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me with a group of Muslims, until when we caught up with them, they had already reached their dwellings, and we brought them to the Prophet (ﷺ). All the narrators said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides, and branded their eyes with hot iron (*samar*) – and it is also narrated: he blinded them (*samal*) – and he left them on the side of the lava field (*harra*), asking for water, but they were not given water. In the hadith of Jarir: They used to say, "Water!" and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would say, "Fire!"

In some narrations from Anas, it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned them with fire after he had killed them. Abu Qilaba said: These people disbelieved, killed, took property, and waged war against Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).

Al-Tabari related from some scholars that this verse abrogated (*naskh*) the Prophet's (ﷺ) action toward the 'Uraniyyin, and confined the matter to these prescribed punishments (*hudud*). Some said: Allah made it a rebuke to His Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the blinding of eyes. It is related from a group of scholars that this verse does not abrogate that act, because that occurred against apostates.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Especially since in some chains it is related that they blinded the eyes of the herdsmen. They said: This verse concerns the believing *muharib* (one who wages war). Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not blind the eyes of the 'Uraniyyin; rather, he intended to do so, and then the verse was revealed forbidding it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a weak opinion, contradicted by the widespread narrations.

(p-155) There is no disagreement among scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to those who wage war from among the people of Islam. They differed about who truly deserves the name of *hiraba* (waging war, brigandage). Malik ibn Anas (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The *muharib* in our view is one who bears arms against people in a city (*misr*) or in the open country (*barriyya*), and overpowers them regarding their persons and property, without any feud, grudge, or enmity. A group of scholars said this too. Abu Hanifa and his companions, and a group of scholars, said: The *muharib* is only one who cuts the road against people outside the cities; as for within a city, there is no (such punishment).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: They mean that the highwayman within a city is liable to the punishment for what he committed, whether killing, theft, usurpation, or the like. *Hiraba* has grades: the least of them is merely terrorizing the road, yet this still entails the status of *hiraba*. Then, beyond that, taking property along with terrorizing; then, beyond that, killing along with terrorizing; then, beyond that, combining all of these. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) and a group of scholars said: Whatever grade the *muharib* falls into, the ruler (*imam*) has the choice regarding him, to punish him with whichever of these penalties he sees fit; and it is considered good (*istihsan*) to take the mildest penalties with the one who did not kill.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Especially if it was a slip, and he was not known for evil conduct. As for one who killed, his killing is unavoidable. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz, Qatada, and others of the scholars said: Rather, for each grade of *hiraba* there is a grade of punishment. Whoever only terrorized the roads, his punishment is banishment; whoever took property without killing, his punishment is the cutting of the hand and foot on opposite sides; whoever killed without taking property, his punishment is execution; and whoever combined all of these is killed and crucified. The proof of this view is that *hiraba* does not take a person outside of faith, and the blood of a believer is forbidden except in one of three cases: apostasy, or adultery after being married (*ihsan*), or murder. So the *muharib* who did not kill has no way to be killed. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan as well, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and others, the same view as Malik's: that the ruler has the choice. The proof for this view is that whatever in the Qur'an is in the form "or... or," it is for choice, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a ransom of fasting (p-156) or charity or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqara: 196]; and like the verse on the expiation of an oath, and the verse on the compensation for hunting.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Al-Tabari preferred the other view. And it is more cautious for the one issuing the legal opinion (*mufti*), and for the blood of the *muharib*. Malik's view is more effective in blocking the means (*sadd al-dhara'i*) and more protective of people and roads, and the one who causes fear is treated as a killer. Along with that, Malik sees the taking of the mildest penalties as a matter of *istihsan*. Al-Tabari related from Anas ibn Malik that he said: «The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about the ruling concerning the *muharib*, and he said: "Whoever terrorizes the road and takes property, cut off his hand for the taking and his foot for the terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever combines all of that, crucify him."»

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What remains is banishment for the one who only terrorizes.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They wage war against Allah﴾ is an intensification; it makes the commission of His prohibitions equivalent to waging war. It was also said: The implied meaning is: they wage war against the servants of Allah, so there is an omitted noun in the phrase.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and strive in the land to spread corruption﴾ is an explanation of *hiraba*; that is: "and they strive by their waging war." It is possible that the meaning is: "and they strive, spreading corruption that is joined to the waging of war." The link to these prescribed penalties is only the waging of war.

The majority of readers read ﴿yuqattalu, aw yusallabu, aw tuqatta'a﴾ with the intensive form (*tashdid*) in these verbs, for emphasis and multiplication. The multiplication here refers only to the number of those upon whom it is inflicted, as in the slaughtering (*tadhbih*) of the Children of Israel, in the reading of the one who doubled the letter in *yudhabbihun*. And al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read *yuqtalu*, *yusbalu*, and *tuqta'a* with the light form (*takhfif*) in all three verbs.

As for the killing of the *muharib*, it is by the sword, a blow to the neck. As for his crucifixion, the majority of scholars hold that he is crucified alive and then killed by being stabbed on the wooden post. This was related from Malik, and it is the most apparent meaning of the verse, and it is the more severe as a deterrent (*nakal*). As for the cutting off, the right hand is cut from the wrist, and the left foot from the joint (p-157).

It was related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to cut off the hand from the fingers, leaving the palm, and the foot from the middle of the foot, leaving the heel.

The scholars differed about banishment (*nafy*). Al-Suddi said: It means that he is pursued forever with horses and on foot until he is caught, and then the prescribed penalty of Allah is applied to him, and he is expelled from the abode of Islam.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that he said: His banishment is that he is pursued. Anas ibn Malik said the same; and this is related from al-Layth and Malik ibn Anas, except that Malik said: no Muslim should be compelled to enter the abode of polytheism. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Banishment is from the abode of Islam to the abode of polytheism. A group of scholars, among them 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, said: Banishment for those who wage war is that they be exiled from one town to another that is far away. Al-Shafi'i said: He banishes him from his place of work. Abu al-Zinad said: In the past, banishment was to Dahlak and Ba'idh, and these are from the farthest parts of Yemen. Abu Hanifa and his companions, and a group, said: Banishment for those who wage war is imprisonment; that is their expulsion from the earth.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The apparent meaning is that "the land" in this verse is the land of the incident. People in ancient times used to avoid the land in which they committed sins. From this is the hadith of the one who turned his chest toward the holy land. It is appropriate for the ruler, if this banished *muharib* is feared and it is thought that he will return to mischief and corruption, to imprison him in the town to which he is exiled. If he is not feared, he is released (*yutraku musarhan*). This is the clear position of Malik's school: that he be exiled and imprisoned wherever he is exiled. And this is the more common case regarding one who is feared. Al-Tabari preferred this view, and it is the sounder one, because his banishment from the land of the incident or from Islam is the explicit text of the verse; and his imprisonment afterward depends on the fear of him. So when he repents and his condition is understood, he is released.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is a disgrace for them﴾ refers to these prescribed penalties which fall upon them. Allah intensified the threat regarding the sin of waging war by informing that for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment, along with the penalty in this world. This is separate from the sins mentioned in the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «"Whoever commits any of those and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him."»

(p-158) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is possible that the disgrace is for the one who is punished, and the punishment of the Hereafter is for the one who is safe in this world. This sin is treated like other sins. And this threat is conditional in its enforcement upon the will of Allah. Nevertheless, fear prevails over them according to the threat and the greatness of the sin. The "disgrace" in this verse means: exposure, humiliation, and abhorrence.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them﴾: Exalted and Majestic is He excepted the one who repents before he is overpowered; and He informed of the removal of the rights of Allah from him by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The people differed about the meaning of the verse. Qatada and al-Zuhri in his book *al-Ashraf* said: That refers to the people of polytheism.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is because they saw the threat as coming after the punishment; and this is weak. The scholars are of the view that the verse concerns believers, and that if the *muharib* repents before he is overpowered, the ruling of *hiraba* has fallen from him, and the ruler has no authority over him except as over other Muslims. If anyone claims him for a killing, the ruler examines the matter and executes retaliation (*qisas*) against him, if the claimant is the rightful heir (*wali*). Likewise, he is pursued for whatever property of others is found with him, and for the value of the property he destroyed. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*), as related by Ibn al-Mundhir. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: He is only required to return the property that is found with him in its own form; as for what he consumed, it is not claimed from him.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on surah 5, verses 33–34 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tabari mentioned this from Malik, through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from him. This is also what is apparent from the action of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding Haritha ibn Badr al-Ghudani, for he had been a highway robber (muharib), and then he repented before he was overpowered. So 'Ali wrote for him a public document (kitab mansur) dropping the claims to property and blood.

Al-Tabari also related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "The repentance of a muharib is not accepted; for if it were accepted, they would become bold, and there would be much corruption. But if he fled to the enemy and then came back repentant, I do not see any punishment upon him."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "I do not know whether he meant apostasy or not." Al-Awza'i said something similar, except that he said: "If he joined the abode of war and apostatized from Islam, or remained upon it, and then came back repentant before he was overpowered, his repentance is accepted."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The correct position in all of this is the view of the jurists which I have just established: that the ruling of hirabah falls away, and he remains like the rest of the Muslims. There is disagreement when the property is less than the amount for which a thief is cut off. Malik said: that is like the large amount. Al-Shafi'i and the Companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: none of the muharibin is cut off except one who took what would make a thief liable to amputation."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them﴾: Exalted and Majestic is He excepted the one who repents before he is overpowered; and He informed of the removal of the rights of Allah from him by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The people differed about the meaning of the verse. Qatada and al-Zuhri in his book *al-Ashraf* said: That refers to the people of polytheism.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is because they saw the threat as coming after the punishment; and this is weak. The scholars are of the view that the verse concerns believers, and that if the *muharib* repents before he is overpowered, the ruling of *hiraba* has fallen from him, and the ruler has no authority over him except as over other Muslims. If anyone claims him for a killing, the ruler examines the matter and executes retaliation (*qisas*) against him, if the claimant is the rightful heir (*wali*). Likewise, he is pursued for whatever property of others is found with him, and for the value of the property he destroyed. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*), as related by Ibn al-Mundhir. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: He is only required to return the property that is found with him in its own form; as for what he consumed, it is not claimed from him.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on surah 5, verses 33–34 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tabari mentioned this from Malik, through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from him. This is also what is apparent from the action of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding Haritha ibn Badr al-Ghudani, for he had been a highway robber (muharib), and then he repented before he was overpowered. So 'Ali wrote for him a public document (kitab mansur) dropping the claims to property and blood.

Al-Tabari also related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "The repentance of a muharib is not accepted; for if it were accepted, they would become bold, and there would be much corruption. But if he fled to the enemy and then came back repentant, I do not see any punishment upon him."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "I do not know whether he meant apostasy or not." Al-Awza'i said something similar, except that he said: "If he joined the abode of war and apostatized from Islam, or remained upon it, and then came back repentant before he was overpowered, his repentance is accepted."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The correct position in all of this is the view of the jurists which I have just established: that the ruling of hirabah falls away, and he remains like the rest of the Muslims. There is disagreement when the property is less than the amount for which a thief is cut off. Malik said: that is like the large amount. Al-Shafi'i and the Companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: none of the muharibin is cut off except one who took what would make a thief liable to amputation."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 35–37:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him, and strive in His cause that you may succeed.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve – if they had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them; and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿They will want to leave the Fire, but they will not emerge therefrom; and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾

This verse is an admonition from Allah, the Exalted, following the mention of the punishments that descend upon those who wage war (muharibun). This is among the most eloquent forms of admonition, because it strikes souls that are fearful and trembling. It is the habit of human beings, when they see or hear of one who is afflicted with dreadful hardships, to be softened and humbled; so the admonition came in this state.

"Wabtaghu" means: seek. "Al-wasilah" means: nearness (al-qurbah), and the cause of success in the desired aim. From this is the saying of 'Antarah to his wife:

Indeed, men have a means (wasilah) to you, / that they may take you; so adorn yourself with kohl and dye.

As for the wasilah sought for Muhammad (ﷺ), it is also of this sense, because the supplication for him for the wasilah and the fadilah is that he be granted both in this world, and be characterized by them, and that the fruit of that in the Hereafter be intercession in the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud). From this word is the saying of the poet:

When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union, / and the purity between us returns, and the means (wasa'il).

Al-Tabari cited it.

As for His saying, ﴿and strive in His cause﴾, jihad was singled out for mention for two reasons: first, its prominence among acts of righteousness, and that it is the pillar of Islam; it is included in meaning in His saying ﴿and seek the means to Him﴾, but it was singled out for honour. The second reason is that it is the worship suited to every one forbidden from warfare, and he is prepared for it by his state, his age, his strength, and the eagerness of his soul; so between him and turning to jihad there is nothing but Allah's granting of success.

The lam in His saying "li-yaftadu" is the lam of purpose (lam kay). The majority of readers read "tuqubbila" with a damma on the ta' and the qaf, in the passive form (ma lam yusamma fa'iluh). Yazid ibn Qutayb read "taqabbala" with a fatha on it, meaning: "what Allah, the Exalted, has accepted."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"yuridun"﴾ is a report that they wish this in their hearts; and in more than one verse it is stated that they utter this desire. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: when the Fire separates them, they draw near its edges; then they desire to come out and hope for it; and this is His saying, ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some people have interpreted this desire to mean "yakadun" (they almost), in accordance with this account related by al-Hasan. This should not be interpreted except where true desire cannot apply, like His saying, ﴿a wall that wants to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf: 77]; but regarding the desire of the children of Adam, no, except by a great figurative extension.

The majority of readers read ﴿"yakhrujuna"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22] with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ra'. Yahya ibn Wathhab and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "yukhrajuna" with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ra'.

Allah, the Exalted, informed concerning these disbelievers that they are not going to emerge from the Fire; rather their punishment therein is lasting and everlasting. Al-Tabari related from Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, the Kharijite, that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "O you blind in sight, blind in heart! You claim that a people will come out of the Fire, while Allah has said, ﴿and they will not be removed from it﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "Woe to you! Read what comes before it; this verse concerns the disbelievers."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 38:**

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they committed, as an exemplary punishment from God. God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The majority of the reciters (qurrā') read ﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ﴾ with *raf'* (nominative case). 'Īsā ibn 'Umar and Ibrāhīm ibn Abī 'Ablah read *"wa-s-sāriqa wa-s-sāriqata"* with *naṣb* (accusative case). Sībawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "The preferred form in Arabic speech is the *naṣb*, as when you say: *Zaydan iḍribhu* (Zayd, strike him). But the common reciters, meaning the majority of the reciters, insisted on the *raf'*." Sībawayh said: "The *raf'* in this case, and in His statement ﴿وَالزَّانِيَةُ وَالزَّانِي﴾ [al-Nur: 2], and in God's statement ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], is according to the meaning: 'concerning what has been prescribed for you'."

The *fa'* (fā', "then") in His statement ﴿فَاقْطَعُوا﴾ turned the independent clause into a dependent one, because His statement "the thief, male and female, [concerning what has been prescribed for you]" is a sentence whose nature and apparent form is independence. But the intended meaning lies only in His statement "cut off." This *fa'* is what connected the second statement to the first, and it made the first one appear dependent here. Abū al-'Abbās al-Mubarrad, and this is the view of a group of the Basrans, said: "I prefer that ﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ﴾ be in the *raf'* as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*), because the intent is not directed at one specific individual. It is not like your saying 'Zayd, so strike him'; rather it is like your saying 'Whoever steals, cut off his hand'." Al-Zajjāj said: "It is the preferred one."

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Sībawayh placed the category of the thief in the position of a specific individual. 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd and Ibrāhīm al-Nakha'ī read: *"wa-s-sāriqūna wa-s-sāriqātu fa-qṭa'ū aymānahum"* (the male thieves and the female thieves, so cut off their right hands). Al-Khaffāf said: It was found in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: *"wa-s-Surraqu wa-s-Surraqatu"*. These two words are vocalized with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (with a shadda) and a *fatḥa* on the *rā'* (with a shadda) in both. Abū 'Amr vocalized them in this way.

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It seems likely that this is a scribal error (*taṣḥīf*) by the vocalizer, because the reading of the majority, when written as *"al-sāriq"* without an *alif*, matches this form in the script.

The taking of another's property (*akhdh mulk al-ghayr*) varies according to its circumstances (*qarā'in*). Among it is usurpation (*ghaṣb*), whose circumstance is that the one from whom the property is seized knows at the time of the seizure, or that someone else present witnesses it. Among it is embezzlement (*khiyāna*), whose circumstance is that the embezzler has gained access to the property through some form of disposal. Among it is theft (*sariqa*), whose circumstances are that property is taken to which the thief had no access, without the knowledge of the owner of the stolen property, and in secrecy from all people as far as the thief can see. This is the act for which the hand alone must be cut off, out of all the kinds of taking of property, because this mode is evil and there is little excuse for it. God, through the tongue of His Prophet, gave people guidance that cutting off [the hand] occurs only with these circumstances: among them is removal from a protected place (*ḥirz*); among them is the amount stolen, on which the scholars differ; and among them is that the thief knows the prohibition of theft, and that the theft is of something whose ownership is not lawful to him. So the word "the thief" in the verse is a general term (*'umūm*) whose meaning is in fact specific (*khuṣūṣ*).

As for the amount stolen, a group said: There is no cutting except for a quarter of a dinar or more. This was the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān, 'Alī, 'Ā'isha, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz, al-Awzā'ī, al-Layth, al-Shāfi'ī, and Abū Thawr, may God be pleased with them all. There is a ḥadīth from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The cutting [of the hand] is for a quarter of a dinar or more." Mālik, may God have mercy on him, said: The hand is cut off for a quarter of a dinar or for three dirhams. If someone steals two dirhams, which is a quarter of a dinar, because of the decline of the exchange rate (*inḥiṭāṭ al-ṣarf*), the hand is not cut off. Likewise, for goods (*'urūḍ*) no cutting is applied unless they reach the value of three dirhams, whether the exchange rate is low or high. Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: If the value of the commodity is a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams, the hand is cut off for either, whether the exchange rate is low or high. There is a fourth opinion regarding the cutting, which is that there is no cutting except for five dirhams or their value. This was reported from 'Umar, and it was the view of Sulaymān ibn Yasār, Ibn Abī Layla, and Ibn Shubrumah. From this is the statement of Anas ibn Mālik: "Abū Bakr cut off [the hand] for a shield whose value was five dirhams."

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: There is no proof in this that five is the prescribed limit (*ḥadd*).

Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, and 'Aṭā', said: There is no cutting for less than ten dirhams. Abū Hurayra and Abū Sa'īd al-Khudrī said: The hand is not cut off for less than four dirhams. 'Uthmān al-Battī said: The hand is cut off for one dirham or more. Al-Ṭabarī reported that 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr cut off [the hand] for one dirham. It is reported from al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan that he said: The hand is cut off for anything that has a value, whether little or much, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. Al-Ṭabarī reported something similar from Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both. This is the view of the people of the apparent meaning (*ahl al-ẓāhir*) and the view of the Khawārij. It is also reported from al-Ḥasan that he said: "We discussed in the time of Ziyād how much the cutting applies to, and our opinion agreed on two dirhams."

Most scholars hold that repentance does not remove the cutting from the thief. It is reported from al-Shāfi'ī that if he repents before he is apprehended, and before the hand of the authorities reaches him, the cutting falls from him, by analogy with the one who wages war (*muḥārib*). The majority of people hold that cutting applies only to one who removed the property from a protected place. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: If he gathers the garments inside the house, he is cut off, even if he does not take them out.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿فَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾ (cut off their hands). He used the plural *aydī* (hands) because each thief has one right hand, which is the one exposed to cutting for theft in the first place. So the thieves have hands, and the female thieves have hands. It is as if He said: "Cut off the right hands of both kinds." The dual in the pronoun refers only to the two kinds. Al-Zajjāj said, on the authority of some grammarians: The dual of a body part of which a person has only one was made plural, like His statement ﴿صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], because most of his organs come in pairs, so what has only one was treated on the pattern of that. Abū Isḥāq said: The reality of this matter is that what exists singly in a thing is not made dual, but is pronounced in the plural form, because the possessive construction (*iḍāfa*) clarifies it. So when you say "I filled their bellies," it is understood that the two have two bellies.

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It seems that they disliked the combination of two duals in one word.

The scholars differed concerning the order of the cutting. The school of Mālik, may God have mercy on him, and the majority of people hold that the right hand of the thief is cut off first; then, if he returns to theft, his left foot is cut off; then, if he returns again, his left hand is cut off; then, if he returns again, his right foot is cut off; and if he steals again after that, he is disciplined (*'uzzira*) and imprisoned. 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, al-Zuhrī, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: His right hand is cut off; then, if he steals again, his left foot is cut off; then, if he steals again, he is disciplined and imprisoned. It is reported from 'Aṭā' ibn Abī Rabāḥ: In theft only the right hand is cut off, and nothing more; then, if he steals again, he is disciplined and imprisoned.

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is an adherence to the apparent meaning of the verse, and the opinion is anomalous (*shādhdh*). According to the apparent meaning of the verse, it would follow that the hand is cut off, then the hand. The position of the majority of jurists is that the cutting of the hand is at the wrist (*rusgh*), and of the foot at the joint (*mafṣil*). It is reported from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, that the cutting of the hand is at the fingers, and of the foot at the middle of the sole.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا﴾ (as a recompense for what they committed). He put it in the accusative (*naṣb*) as an infinitive of the verb (*maṣdar*). Al-Zajjāj said it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*). Likewise ﴿نَكَالًا مِّنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (an exemplary punishment from God). *Al-nakāl* means punishment (*'adhāb*), and *al-nakl* means the shackle (*qayd*). The rest of the meaning of the verse is clear, and in it there is some grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*) by way of description (*ḥikāya*).

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 39–41:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿O Messenger, let not those hasten to disbelief grieve you, of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed; and of those who are Jews, listeners to falsehood, listeners to another people who have not come to you.﴾

The meaning, according to the majority of the scholars, is that whoever repents from theft, regrets what has passed, ceases (the sin) in what is to come, and makes amends by returning the wrongfully taken property if he is able to do so, and if not, by spending it in the way of Allah, and also makes amends in all his other deeds, and rises above (the sin): Allah will turn to him, and He will remove from him the ruling of theft between him and Allah the Exalted. He is hoped for, by the Promise, to be within the Will (of Allah). But repentance does not remove from him the worldly ruling of amputation (qat') if he confesses, or if testimony is given against him. Mujahid said: "Repentance and amends are that the prescribed punishment (hadd) be carried out upon him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a harshness, and Allah has made two doors for the exit from sins: one is the prescribed punishment (hadd), and the other is repentance.
