They sent to the Jews of Medina and to their allies among the hypocrites that they should ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the incident, hoping that he would agree with them on flogging and blackening, so that their affair would be strengthened by that. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about that, he rose with a group of his companions to the house of study (bayt al-midrās), and there he gathered the rabbis and asked them about what is in the Torah. They said: "We do not find stoning in it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed it contains stoning; bring it out and unfold it." It was unfolded, and one of them placed his hand over the verse of stoning. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: "Lift your hand." He lifted his hand, and there was the verse of stoning. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) judged by it with stoning, and enforced it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this hadith there are variations of wording and many narrations. Among them, it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a Jewish man and a Jewish woman who had committed adultery, and they had been flogged and blackened. He said: "Is this your law, O assembly of Jews?" They said: "Yes." He said: "No." Then he went to the house of study, exposed them, and judged in those two cases by stoning, and said: "I will surely be the first to revive the ruling of the Torah when they have caused it to die."

It is also related that the two adulterers were not in Medina, and that the Jews of Fadak were the ones who said to the Jews of Medina: "Ask Muhammad. If he gives you a ruling in accordance with what we follow, of flogging and blackening, then take it. And if he gives you a ruling of stoning, then beware of stoning." This was said by al-Sha'bi and others. Qatada ibn Di'ama and others said: The occasion of the verse: the Jews mentioned that the Banu al-Nadir had raided the Banu Qurayza, so that if a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayza, he was killed in return for him; and if a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayza, he was given the blood-money (diya).

It was also said: the blood-money of a Qurayzi was half the blood-money of a Nadhiri. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, Qurayza requested equality, since they were cousins, going back to one grandfather, and they requested that the case be referred to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then the Nadir said to one another: "If he judges by what we were upon, then take it; otherwise, beware."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All these incidents occurred, and others occurred that resemble them, and it is fitting that the occasion of the verse be the exposure of the Jews in their distortion of words and their attacks upon the religion. The narrations on this are numerous and varied.

In some chains concerning the hadith of Abu Hurayra it occurred that he said, regarding the story of stoning: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose to their house of study, and we rose with him." This implies that the matter was at the end of the Prophet's (ﷺ) period, because Abu Hurayra embraced Islam in the year of Khaybar, at the end of the sixth year after the Hijra. The Nadir had already been expelled, and Qurayza and Quraysh had been killed, and the Jews in Medina were nothing. So how could they have had a house of study at that time? Or if they had a house in a state of humiliation, would the Prophet (ﷺ), with the manifest dominance of his religion, have needed to argue with them in that manner? The apparent sense of the hadith of the house of study is that it was at the beginning of the Hijra. Unless it was that from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the might of his word, he intended to remove their ruling from the hands of their rabbis by the proof against them from their own book; therefore he went to their house of study, while being able to overpower them. But this, in my view, is remote, because at that time they were not causing him grief, nor was there any state of his that required consolation, (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

As for the disagreement of people about who is meant by His saying: ﴿those who hasten to disbelief among those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed﴾, al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar, whom they claimed was Abu Lubaba ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir. Qurayza pointed to him on the day of their siege: "What is the matter, and what judgment will we come down to?" So he gestured to his throat, meaning slaughter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, and Abu Lubaba is among the excellent Companions. Even if he made that gesture, he said: "By Allah, my feet did not move until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger." Then he came to the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ), tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque, and swore that he would not leave it in that state until Allah the Exalted turned to him in forgiveness and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased with him. That gesture of his was only a slip, which was caused by compassion for a people with whom he had an old affection and partnership, may Allah be pleased with him and with all the Companions.

Al-Sha'bi and others said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of Jews who wished to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about a man among them who had killed another. They commissioned a man from among the Muslims to ask, and they said: "If he gives a ruling for blood-money, we will accept his word; and if he gives a ruling for killing, we will not accept it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is similar to what preceded from Qatada concerning the matter of the killing of the Nadir and Qurayza.

'Abdullah ibn Kathir, Mujahid, and others said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿of those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed﴾, is meant to refer to the hypocrites; and His saying after that, ﴿listeners to falsehood, listeners to another people﴾, is meant to refer to the Jews.

As for the arrangement of the meaning of the verse according to these views, it is possible that the meaning is: "O Messenger, let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you, from among the hypocrites and from among the Jews." And His saying "listeners" would be the predicate of an implied subject.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "Let not those who hasten to disbelief among the Jews grieve you." He described them as those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but their hearts have not believed, as a reproach to them, since they had distorted their Torah and altered its rulings. So they say with their mouths, "We believe in the Torah and in Moses," while their hearts have not believed, since they altered it, and denied what is in it of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things that are disbelief on their part. The support for this interpretation is His saying after this: ﴿And those are not believers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 43]. On this interpretation, His saying ﴿and of those who are Jews﴾ comes as if He had said "and of them," but He explicitly mentioned the Jews, since the group of listeners is a different group from the group that alters the Torah with knowledge of it.

Most people read "sammā'ūna" (listeners, nominative). Al-Nahhas read "sammā'īna" (listeners, accusative). In my view its grammatical basis is that it is in the accusative for dispraise, according to the arrangement of one who says: "Let not those among these who hasten grieve you: listeners (sammā'īna)." As for the meaning in His saying ﴿listeners to falsehood﴾, it is possible that it is a description of the hypocrites and of the Children of Israel, because all of them listen to falsehood from one another and accept it; and therefore the expression of their listening came in the form of intensive hyperbole (mubalagha), since the meaning is that they accept and seek more of what they hear. And His saying, Exalted is He, "for falsehood" (lil-kadhib), may mean "listeners to falsehood," and it may mean "listeners to your words from you, in order to be against you, and to transmit your speech, and add to a word many times its falsehood." Al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "lil-kidhb," with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the dhal.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿listeners to another people who have not come to you﴾, may mean: they listen from them. Al-Tabari related from Jabir that the "other people" are the Jews of Fadak. It was also said: the Jews of Khaybar. It was also said: the people of the adulterers. It was also said: the people of the dispute over killing and blood-money. These other people are the ones described as "who have not come to you" (the Prophet (ﷺ)). It is also possible that it means "listeners on behalf of a people," in the sense of spies who eavesdrop on speech in order to convey it to another people; and this is something that the hypocrites and the Jews of Medina may be described by. It was said to Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna: "Is there any mention of the spy (jasus) in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Yes," and recited this verse: ﴿listeners to another people﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verse 42**

[Beginning of the passage]

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿They distort words from their places. They say, "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware." And whomever God intends to test, you cannot avail him anything against God. Those are the ones whose hearts God did not intend to purify. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 41]

﴿Listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain. So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them.﴾

The people in general (al-jumhur) read *al-kalima* (الكَلِمَ) with a fatha on the kaf and a kasra on the lam. Some people read *al-kilmi* (الكِلْمِ) with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the lam, which is a weak dialect form of *kalima* (كَلِمَةٌ, "word").

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They distort the words﴾, describes the Jews regarding what they distorted of the Torah, since that is the gravest matter in which they distorted. It is also possible that it describes them and the hypocrites together, regarding what they distort of statements when lying, because the origins of their lies must be based on things that were said or done. This is the decorated lie that is readily accepted. As for a lie that is not supported by any principle, it has little effect on people's souls.

His saying, ﴿from their places﴾, means: after it had been placed in its proper places and its upright aspects were intended. Regarding this, it was said that it refers to the blackening of the face and flogging for adultery; it was said that it refers to accepting blood money in a matter of killing; and it was said that it refers to the Nadir preserving their honor over the Qurayza. This is according to the earlier disagreement concerning the verse.

Then God, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet, in a manner of cutting off hope regarding them: ﴿And whomever God intends to test, you cannot avail him anything against God﴾. That is: do not follow your own desire regarding their affairs. The *fitna* (test, trial) here means the ordeal of disbelief and punishment in the Hereafter. Then God informed that they are those for whom it was previously decreed in God's knowledge that He would not purify their hearts, and that they would be defiled by disbelief. Then God established for them disgrace in this world. The meaning is humiliation and wretchedness which were imposed upon them throughout the regions of the earth and in every nation. And He established for them punishment in the Hereafter because of their disbelief.

His saying, ﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾: if the first description refers to the Children of Israel, then this is a repetition for emphasis and intensification. If the first description refers to the hypocrites, then this is also a report about the Children of Israel.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿devourers of unlawful gain﴾: *fa"ālūn* (فَعّالُونَ) is an intensive pattern, meaning that their consuming of it is repeated and frequent. *Al-suḥt* (السُحْتُ) is everything whose earnings are not lawful from property. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamza read *al-suḥti* (اَلسُّحْتِ) with a sukun on the ḥa, lightened. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i read *al-suḥutti* (اَلسُّحُّتِ) with a damma on the ḥa, and doubled. It is narrated from Kharija ibn Musʿab, from Nafiʿ, *al-siḥti* (اَلسِّحْتِ) with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the ḥa. The word is derived from their saying *saḥata* and *asḥata*, meaning to uproot and destroy. From the triliteral form is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so He will destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. From the quadriliteral form is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"................. ∗∗∗ except one who is stripped bare or one who is shaved"

*Al-suḥt* and *al-suḥut* (with damma on the sin and lightening or doubling of the ḥa) are two dialect forms for the name of the thing that is destroyed. *Al-saḥt* (with fatha on the sin and sukun on the ḥa) is the verbal noun, and the thing that is destroyed was named by it, just as the hunted game was called *ṣayd* in His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95], and as the pledged thing was called *rahn*. This is common.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Unlawful property was called *suḥt* because it goes away, and misfortunes uproot it, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever acquires property from confusion, God will take it away in ruin." Makki said: unlawful property was called *suḥt* because it goes away from the point where it destroys acts of obedience, that is, it takes them away little by little. Mahdawi said: from the point where it destroys their religions.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is rejected, because evil deeds do not nullify good deeds; except that it may be assumed that it preoccupies one from acts of obedience, so it destroys them by making one not act. But as for an obedience already accomplished, this cannot be said of it. Mahdawi said: the wage of the cupper was called *suḥt* because it destroys the manly honor of the one who takes it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is more fitting.

Tabari said: The origin of *suḥt* is the gnawing of hunger. It is said: "So-and-so has a stomach that is consumed (*masḥūt al-maʿida*)" when he is never found except hungry, his stomach consuming what is in it. So what he takes through bribery is, because of greed, like the hunger of one who is always hungry and never satisfied.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is because bribery destroys (*tansaḥit*). So the meaning is as we have already mentioned. In Tabari's expression there is some confusion, because "one whose stomach is consumed" is derived from uprooting and going away, and the gnawing of hunger is not in fact the origin of *suḥt*. The *suḥt* that the Jews were meant to consume is bribery in judgments, and endowments that are eaten, whose consumption is supported by uttering falsehoods, deceiving the common people, and the like.

Abu Hurayra and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: "The wage of a prostitute is *suḥt*, the stud fee of a stallion is *suḥt*, the earnings of a cupper are *suḥt*, and the price of a dog and of wine is *suḥt*." Ibn Mas'ud said: "*Suḥt* is that someone you have helped in his need or his right gives you a gift and you accept it." It was said to ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "We used to count *suḥt* only as bribery in judgment." He said: "That is disbelief." It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and a great many others that *suḥt* is bribery in judgment. It has also been narrated from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "Every flesh that grew from *suḥt*, the Fire is more deserving of it." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is *suḥt*?" He said: "Bribery in judgment."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Everything mentioned regarding the meaning of *suḥt* is examples, and among the greatest of them is bribery in judgment, and payment for killing a soul. It is a term that covers every unlawful earning.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾, is a choice given to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and to the rulers of his community after him, to judge between them when they agree to refer their cases. ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: this choice is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by His saying: ﴿and that you judge between them by what God has sent down﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 49]. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: two verses were abrogated from [Surat al-Ma'ida]: His saying ﴿and the garlands﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 97], which was abrogated by the verse of the sword; and His saying ﴿or turn away from them﴾, which was abrogated by ﴿and that you judge between them by what God has sent down﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 49].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Many scholars said: it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and the rulers' choice remains. This is the most evident view, God willing.

The jurisprudence of this verse is that the community, as far as it knows, agrees that the ruler of the Muslims judges between the people of the *dhimma* (protected non-Muslims) in cases of wrongdoing, and has authority over them to change it, and removes its form however it occurred, so he changes that. Among wrongdoing is withholding goods that have been sold, usurping property, and other such things. As for cases of judgment in which there is no wrongdoing by one of them against the other, but are rather disputed claims, requests for what is lawful and what is unlawful, and a seeking of a way out from sin in the Hereafter, then the judge is free to choose in these. And if both litigants consent to him, it is still necessary, in addition, to have the consent of the bishops or the rabbis. Ibn al-Qasim said this in *al-ʿUtbiyya*. He said: But if the bishops consent without the two litigants, or the two litigants consent without the bishops, then he is not permitted to judge.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Consider whether, if the bishops consent to the cases because of their difficulty among them, without the two litigants consenting, then they are subject to disagreement. And consider when the two litigants consent, and no objection came from the rabbis, and the judge judged, then the rabbis wished to reject that judgment: are cases equal in this, like stoning two adulterers and a ruling concerning property passing from one of them to the other? And consider when the two litigants consent: is it incumbent upon the judge to inquire what the rabbis have, or is he satisfied that no opposition came from them? Malik, may God have mercy on him, recommends that the ruler of the Muslims turn away from them and leave them to their religion. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others said: God's saying ﴿if they come to you﴾ means the people of the case of the two adulterers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Then the verse, after that, encompasses all the other cases.

[End of passage]

﴿And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42] ﴿How can they make you a judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God? Then after that they turn away. And those are not believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted with of the Book of God and to which they were witnesses. So do not fear people but fear Me, and do not exchange My signs for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾

God, Exalted is He, assured His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, against their harm if he turned away from them, and He belittled their status in this matter. The meaning is: you are victorious and apparently in a dominant position in every circumstance. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He, to the believers: ﴿they will not harm you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111]. Then He said: ﴿and if you judge﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42], meaning: if you choose to judge between them in some incident, ﴿then judge between them with justice﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42], meaning with equity. It is said: aqsata al-rajul (he acted justly), when a man is just and judges with truth, and qasata (he acted unjustly) when he oppresses. From this is His saying: ﴿As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. God's love for the just consists of the blessings of His that appear upon them.

Then God mentioned, after their appointing the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, as judge, that they did so without sincerity. By sound analogy, He clarifies that they only appoint him out of desire for his inclination toward their whims and his leaning toward their appetites. This is because He said: ﴿How can they make you a judge﴾, with a sincere intention, when they have opposed the judgment of the Book in which they believe, and the prophethood of the one who brought it, and have turned away from God's judgment concerning both? You, whom they do not believe in and do not accept, are more deserving that they would oppose your judgment.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿after that﴾, meaning: after the judgment of God in the Torah concerning stoning and what resembles it of the matters in which they opposed the command of God, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and those are not believers﴾, means: in the Torah and in Moses. This is a binding argument against them, because whoever opposes the judgment of the Book of God, his claim to faith in it is unsound.

This verse strengthens that His saying at the beginning of the verse, ﴿among those who say with their mouths "We believe," while their hearts have not believed﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 41], refers to the Jews.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah﴾ and the verse [continues]. Qatada said: It has been related to us that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to say when this verse was revealed: "Today we judge over the Jews and over others among the people of religions." Guidance (al-huda) is direction in belief and in laws. Light (al-nur) is that by which one is illuminated through its commands and prohibitions. The prophets who submitted are those who were sent from the time of Moses son of 'Imran until the period of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. These two are the bounds of this group mentioned in this verse. "Aslamu" (submitted) means: they devoted their faces and their aims to God, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for those who were Jews﴾, is connected to "yahkumu" (judge): meaning, "they judge according to the requirement of the Torah for the children of Israel and against them." His saying, Exalted is He, "al-rabbaniyyun" (the rabbis), is conjoined to "al-nabiyyun" (the prophets), meaning: "and by it the rabbaniyyun judge." They are the scholars. In al-Bukhari it is said: al-rabbani is the one who raises people by teaching them the small matters of knowledge before its great matters. It was also said: al-rabbani is related to "al-Rabb" (the Lord), meaning he has knowledge of Him and of His religion. The letter nun was added to "rabbani" for emphasis, as they say "manzarani" and "makhbarani," and for one of great neck, "raqabani." And al-ahbar (the rabbis) are also the scholars; its singular is "hibr," with a kasra on the ha', and it is also said with a fatha on it, but the use of the fatha became more common in it, to distinguish it from the hibr (ink) with which one writes.

Al-Suddi said: What is meant here by the rabbaniyyin and the ahbar who judge by the Torah are the two sons of Suriya. One of them was a rabbani and the other a hibr. They had given the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, a pledge that he would not ask them about anything from the matter of the Torah except that they would inform him of it. So he asked them about the verse of stoning, and they informed him of it accurately. Then the verse was revealed pointing to the two of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In this there is room for doubt. The sound narration is that the two sons of Suriya and others denied the matter of stoning, and 'Abdullah ibn Salam exposed them in it. The wording is general, referring to every upright rabbi in past times. As for the period of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, had one been found, he would have embraced Islam, and so he would not be called "hibr" or "rabbani."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿by what they were entrusted with﴾, meaning: because of God's, Exalted is He, entrusting them with the matter of the Torah, and His taking from them a covenant to act upon it and to speak by it, and His informing them of what is in it, so that they became witnesses to it. But these people neglected what they were entrusted with, until the Torah was altered. The Qur'an is different from this, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], and praise belongs to God. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear people but fear Me﴾, is a recounting of what was said to the scholars of the children of Israel. His saying: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾, is a prohibition of all corrupt gains through knowledge and of contriving for worldly gain through religion. This very meaning encompasses the scholars of this community and its rulers. It is possible that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear people﴾ up to the end of the verse, is an address to the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The scholars differed regarding the intended meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾

(p-176) One group said: what is meant by "the disbelievers," "the wrongdoers," and "the defiantly disobedient" is the Jews. A hadith has been transmitted on this from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, through al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.

A great group of the people of knowledge said: the verse encompasses everyone who does not judge by what God has revealed, but for the rulers of this community it is disbelief of disobedience, which does not take them out of faith.

It was said to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman: "Was this verse revealed concerning the children of Israel?" He said: "The children of Israel are excellent brothers for you. If you have all the sweetness, they have all the bitterness. You will certainly follow their path the length of a shirak (a sandal thong)."

Al-Sha'bi said: "the disbelievers" was revealed regarding the Muslims, "the wrongdoers" regarding the Jews, and "the defiantly disobedient" regarding the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: I know of no basis for this specification unless a hadith from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is sound concerning it. However, he took into account those mentioned with each report from these three, so that what was said regarding the Muslims applies only insofar as they were addressed by His saying: "So do not fear people." (p-177) Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: these verses were revealed regarding the children of Israel, and then they were approved for this community as well.

﴿And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42] ﴿How can they make you a judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God? Then after that they turn away. And those are not believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars, by what they were entrusted with of the Book of God and to which they were witnesses. So do not fear people but fear Me, and do not exchange My signs for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾

God, Exalted is He, assured His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, against their harm if he turned away from them, and He belittled their status in this matter. The meaning is: you are victorious and apparently in a dominant position in every circumstance. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He, to the believers: ﴿they will not harm you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111]. Then He said: ﴿and if you judge﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42], meaning: if you choose to judge between them in some incident, ﴿then judge between them with justice﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42], meaning with equity. It is said: aqsata al-rajul (he acted justly), when a man is just and judges with truth, and qasata (he acted unjustly) when he oppresses. From this is His saying: ﴿As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. God's love for the just consists of the blessings of His that appear upon them.

Then God mentioned, after their appointing the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, as judge, that they did so without sincerity. By sound analogy, He clarifies that they only appoint him out of desire for his inclination toward their whims and his leaning toward their appetites. This is because He said: ﴿How can they make you a judge﴾, with a sincere intention, when they have opposed the judgment of the Book in which they believe, and the prophethood of the one who brought it, and have turned away from God's judgment concerning both? You, whom they do not believe in and do not accept, are more deserving that they would oppose your judgment.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿after that﴾, meaning: after the judgment of God in the Torah concerning stoning and what resembles it of the matters in which they opposed the command of God, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and those are not believers﴾, means: in the Torah and in Moses. This is a binding argument against them, because whoever opposes the judgment of the Book of God, his claim to faith in it is unsound.

This verse strengthens that His saying at the beginning of the verse, ﴿among those who say with their mouths "We believe," while their hearts have not believed﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 41], refers to the Jews.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah﴾ and the verse [continues]. Qatada said: It has been related to us that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to say when this verse was revealed: "Today we judge over the Jews and over others among the people of religions." Guidance (al-huda) is direction in belief and in laws. Light (al-nur) is that by which one is illuminated through its commands and prohibitions. The prophets who submitted are those who were sent from the time of Moses son of 'Imran until the period of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. These two are the bounds of this group mentioned in this verse. "Aslamu" (submitted) means: they devoted their faces and their aims to God, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for those who were Jews﴾, is connected to "yahkumu" (judge): meaning, "they judge according to the requirement of the Torah for the children of Israel and against them." His saying, Exalted is He, "al-rabbaniyyun" (the rabbis), is conjoined to "al-nabiyyun" (the prophets), meaning: "and by it the rabbaniyyun judge." They are the scholars. In al-Bukhari it is said: al-rabbani is the one who raises people by teaching them the small matters of knowledge before its great matters. It was also said: al-rabbani is related to "al-Rabb" (the Lord), meaning he has knowledge of Him and of His religion. The letter nun was added to "rabbani" for emphasis, as they say "manzarani" and "makhbarani," and for one of great neck, "raqabani." And al-ahbar (the rabbis) are also the scholars; its singular is "hibr," with a kasra on the ha', and it is also said with a fatha on it, but the use of the fatha became more common in it, to distinguish it from the hibr (ink) with which one writes.

Al-Suddi said: What is meant here by the rabbaniyyin and the ahbar who judge by the Torah are the two sons of Suriya. One of them was a rabbani and the other a hibr. They had given the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, a pledge that he would not ask them about anything from the matter of the Torah except that they would inform him of it. So he asked them about the verse of stoning, and they informed him of it accurately. Then the verse was revealed pointing to the two of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In this there is room for doubt. The sound narration is that the two sons of Suriya and others denied the matter of stoning, and 'Abdullah ibn Salam exposed them in it. The wording is general, referring to every upright rabbi in past times. As for the period of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, had one been found, he would have embraced Islam, and so he would not be called "hibr" or "rabbani."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿by what they were entrusted with﴾, meaning: because of God's, Exalted is He, entrusting them with the matter of the Torah, and His taking from them a covenant to act upon it and to speak by it, and His informing them of what is in it, so that they became witnesses to it. But these people neglected what they were entrusted with, until the Torah was altered. The Qur'an is different from this, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], and praise belongs to God. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear people but fear Me﴾, is a recounting of what was said to the scholars of the children of Israel. His saying: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾, is a prohibition of all corrupt gains through knowledge and of contriving for worldly gain through religion. This very meaning encompasses the scholars of this community and its rulers. It is possible that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear people﴾ up to the end of the verse, is an address to the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The scholars differed regarding the intended meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers.﴾

(p-176) One group said: what is meant by "the disbelievers," "the wrongdoers," and "the defiantly disobedient" is the Jews. A hadith has been transmitted on this from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, through al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.

A great group of the people of knowledge said: the verse encompasses everyone who does not judge by what God has revealed, but for the rulers of this community it is disbelief of disobedience, which does not take them out of faith.

It was said to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman: "Was this verse revealed concerning the children of Israel?" He said: "The children of Israel are excellent brothers for you. If you have all the sweetness, they have all the bitterness. You will certainly follow their path the length of a shirak (a sandal thong)."

Al-Sha'bi said: "the disbelievers" was revealed regarding the Muslims, "the wrongdoers" regarding the Jews, and "the defiantly disobedient" regarding the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: I know of no basis for this specification unless a hadith from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is sound concerning it. However, he took into account those mentioned with each report from these three, so that what was said regarding the Muslims applies only insofar as they were addressed by His saying: "So do not fear people." (p-177) Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: these verses were revealed regarding the children of Israel, and then they were approved for this community as well.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verse 45:**

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation. But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers.﴾

The verb *kataba* (prescribed, written) in this verse is used in its literal sense: it was written on the tablets. In meaning, it is the writing of obligation and binding duty. The pronoun in *'alayhim* ("upon them") refers to the Children of Israel, and the pronoun in *fīhā* ("therein") refers to the Torah.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *anna an-nafsa bi-n-nafs* with *an-nafsa* in the accusative, as the noun of *anna* (*ism anna*), and the words that follow are coordinated in the accusative with *an-nafsa*. They read *wal-jurūḥu qiṣāsun* in the nominative, as a separate, independent sentence (*jumla maqṭū'a*). Nafi', Hamza and 'Asim read all of it in the accusative, with *qiṣāsun* as the predicate (*khabar*) of *anna*. Al-Waqidi narrated from Nafi' that he read *wal-jurūḥu* in the nominative. Al-Kisa'i read *anna an-nafsa bi-n-nafs* with the accusative and put the words after it in the nominative.

Whoever reads *wal-'ayna* in the accusative makes the conjunction *wāw* coordinate (*'aṭf tashrīk*) with the governing particle *anna* in its operation, and does not separate the speech from what precedes it. Whoever reads *wal-'aynu* in the nominative, the grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*) of this reading requires that the sentence be separated from what precedes it, and the *wāw* of coordination becomes the coordination of a new sentence, not coordination of sharing in the governing word. It is also possible that the *wāw* is coordinating according to meaning (*'alā al-ma'nā*), because the meaning of His words *"And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life"* is: "We said to them, the life is for the life." A parallel to this is the case of His words, *"They will be served with a cup from a flowing spring"* (al-Saffat 37:45), whose meaning is "they will be given a cup from a flowing spring," so that *"and wide-eyed maidens"* is coordinated with that. It is also possible that His words *"wal-'ayna"* are coordinated with the concealed pronoun (*al-dhikr al-mustatir*) in *al-ṭarq* (the verb of the predicate), even though the coordinated-upon element was not emphasized with a detached pronoun, as it was emphasized in His words, *"Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them"* (al-A'raf 7:27). A similar example without emphasis occurs in His words, *"Neither we nor our fathers would have associated anything"* (al-An'am 6:148).

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, held regarding this verse that the coordination was permissible without emphasis by a detached pronoun, because the speech was lengthened by *wa-lā* in the words *"wa-lā ābā'unā"*, so *wa-lā* served as a substitute for the emphasis, just as the speech is lengthened in the expression "The judge attended today, a woman" (*ḥaḍara al-qāḍī al-yawma imra'a*).

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: This can only be a substitute if it occurs before the coordinating particle, for then it is a substitute for the pronoun that occurs before the coordinating particle. But if it occurs after the coordinating particle, it does not fill the place of the pronoun. Do you not see that if you said, "Attended a woman the judge today," the lengthening of the speech in a place other than where it should occur would not suffice?

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The statement of Sibawayh is sound according to grammatical reasoning, although the lengthening before the coordinating particle is more complete. Nevertheless, after the coordinating particle it is effective, especially in this verse, because *wa-lā* linked the meaning, since a negation preceded it, and it itself also negates regarding the fathers, so the coordination was made firm.

Abu 'Ali said: Whoever reads *wal-jurūḥu qiṣāsun* in the nominative, cutting it off from what precedes it, that reading admits these three possibilities which were admitted by the nominative *wal-'aynu*.

It is also permissible to begin *wal-jurūḥu* as a new sentence, not on the basis that it is among what was prescribed for them in the Torah, but on the basis of the beginning of a new obligation and the initiation of a legal ruling (*ibtidā' sharī'a*). What strengthens that it is among what was prescribed for them is the accusative reading of whoever read it in the accusative.

Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited *"an-nafsu bi-n-nafs"* with *an* lightened and *an-nafsu* in the nominative, and then put the nominative on what follows until the end of the verse. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *an-nafsa* in the accusative and what follows it, and then recited *"wa-an al-jurūḥu qiṣāsun,"* with the addition of the light *an* and *al-jurūḥu* in the nominative.

The meaning of this verse is an account that Allah, Exalted is He, prescribed an obligation upon the Children of Israel: that whoever kills a soul, his own soul must be taken in return for it. Likewise, these mentioned limbs are the same. This ruling then continued among this community according to what is known of the law and rulings of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the consensus (*ijmā'*) of the people has been established upon it.

A group of scholars went to the generalization of His words *"the life for the life,"* so they executed a free man for a slave, and a Muslim for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). The majority hold that it is a general statement (*'umūm*) by which the specific is intended, in the case of two equals. This is the position of Malik, and on it there is the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A Muslim shall not be killed for a disbeliever." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah granted a concession to this community and made it easier for them by means of blood money (*diya*), and He did not make blood money for the Children of Israel in what was revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, and was prescribed for them.

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this verse there is a clarification of the corruption of the Children of Israel's behavior in exercising power (*ta'azzuz*) over one another, and of the fact that the Banu al-Nadir were in a position of double the blood money of the Banu Qurayza, or that one of them could not be retaliated against, but would be content with blood money. So Allah exposed them through this verse and informed that they had opposed their Book. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas: There was fighting between two clans of the Ansar, so there were killings between them, and one of them had superiority over the other. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) came and made the free for the free and the slave for the slave. Al-Thawri said: It has reached me from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Then it abrogated it (*nasakhat-hā*) with His words: *"the life for the life."*

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Likewise His words, Exalted is He, *"and for wounds is retaliation,"* is a general statement by which the specific is intended, concerning wounds of retaliation (*qawad*), which are those from which no fear of death arises. As for wounds from which harm is feared, such as the wound that reaches the brain (*ma'mūma*), the breaking of the thigh, and the like, there is no retaliation for them. *Qiṣāṣ* (retaliation) is derived from *qaṣṣ al-athar* (tracing a trail), which is following it. It is as if the perpetrator's trace is followed, and he is pursued in what he did, so he is killed as he killed.

His words, Exalted is He, *"But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him,"* admit three meanings.

The first: that *man* refers to the one who was wounded, or the guardian (*walī*) of the slain, and the pronoun in *lahu* ("for him") also returns to him. The meaning is: whoever gives away his wound, or the blood of his guardian, and pardons his right in that matter, that pardon is an expiation for him for his sins, and Allah magnifies his reward for that and expiates for him. This interpretation was held by 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Abu al-Darda', who mentioned that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "No Muslim is afflicted in any part of his body and then forgoes it, except that Allah raises him a degree by it and removes a sin from him." Makki mentioned a hadith through the route of al-Sha'bi that he is expiated of his sins to the extent of what he pardoned of the blood money. And Allah knows best. Qatada and al-Hasan also held this view.

The second meaning: that *man* refers to the wounded or the guardian of the slain, and the pronoun in *lahu* returns to the wrongdoer or the killer, when the wounded person gives his wound to the wrongdoer and pardons him. Then that pardon is an expiation for the wrongdoer for that sin, just as retaliation is an expiation, so pardon is likewise an expiation. As for the reward of the one who pardons, it is upon Allah, Exalted is He. The pronoun has returned to one who was not previously mentioned, because the meaning requires it. This interpretation was held by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, Mujahid, Ibrahim, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third meaning: that *man* refers to the wrongdoer or the killer, and the pronoun in *lahu* also returns to him. The meaning: "If a perpetrator commits an act, and it is unknown and his matter is hidden, and then he gives charity by making himself known, and enables the right to take from himself, then that act is an expiation for his sin." Those who held this interpretation argued by the report of Mujahid, who said: If a man strikes another man and the one struck does not know who struck him, and then the striker confesses to him, that is an expiation for the striker. It is also related that 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr struck a man's eye near the Corner (*al-Rukn*) while people were touching it, and the one who was struck did not know who had struck him. 'Urwa said to him: "I struck you, and I am 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr. If there is any harm to your eye, then I am responsible for it."

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Note that *tasaddaqa* in this interpretation may be derived from *ṣadaqa* (charity) or from *ṣidq* (truthfulness).

Makki ibn Abi Talib and others mentioned that some people interpreted the verse to mean: "And for wounds is retaliation. So whoever gives the blood money for the wound, and gives it as charity, that is an expiation for him, if it is accepted from him and received."

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is weak (*qalaq*). The discussion of His words, *"And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed,"* has already preceded. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, the reading is: *"And whoever gives it in charity, then it is an expiation for him."* (p-178) (p-179) (p-180) (p-181)

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 46–48:**

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We sent after them, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah. We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, and confirming what was before it of the Torah, as guidance and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein. Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, confirming what was before it of the Book, and as a guardian over it.﴾

"Wa-qaffaynā" (and We caused to follow): this is a figure of speech. It is as if the coming of Jesus, peace be upon him, was in the wake of the coming and passing of the prophets. The pronoun in "āthārihim" (their footsteps) refers to the prophets mentioned in His statement: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44]. "Muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl). "Al-Tawrāh" (the Torah) is "before" Jesus because it came before him, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is "before" the Hour. The discussion of this meaning has already been presented in more than one place.

"Al-Injīl" (the Gospel) is a non-Arabic name, which has been treated as though it were derived (from Arabic roots) from "najala," meaning to extract and bring forth. People recite it with a kasra on the hamza, except al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan, who recited "al-Anjīl" with a fatḥa on the hamza. The discussion of this has already been presented at the beginning of Surat Āl ʿImrān.

"Al-Hudā" (guidance) is direction and the call to the Oneness of God and the revival of His rulings. "Al-Nūr" (light) is what is in it by which one is illuminated. "Muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is an emphatic circumstantial clause, coordinated with the position of the sentence "fīhi hudan" (in it is guidance), for it is a sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause. Makkī and others said: "Muṣaddiqan" is coordinated with the first.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In this there is a disturbance from the perspective of the coherence of the meanings. People recited "wa-hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan" (and guidance and admonition) in the accusative, which is coordinated with "muṣaddiqan." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "wa-hudan wa-mawʿiẓatun" in the nominative, and that is well-directed. The God-fearing are singled out for mention because they are the intended audience in the knowledge of God, although all are called and admonished; but for other than the God-fearing it is blindness and confusion.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb recited "wa-an liyaḥkuma" with the addition of "an." Ḥamza alone recited "wa-liyaḥkuma" with a kasra on the lām and a fatḥa on the mīm, as the lām of purpose (lām al-kay) with the verb put in the subjunctive after it. The meaning is: "And We gave him the Gospel so that it would contain guidance, light and confirmation, so that its people would judge by what God revealed therein." The rest of the seven readers recited "wa-l-yaḥkum," with the lām, which is the lām of command, pronounced with sukūn, and the verb is in the jussive. The meaning of His command to them to judge is: "Thus it is obligatory upon them." It was appropriate that after this there should follow the warning against those who oppose what God has revealed. Among the readers there are those who recite the lām of command with a kasra and put the verb in the jussive. A parallel to this verse has already been presented. Its statement that these attributes apply to whoever does not judge by what God has revealed is by way of emphasis. The most correct thing said about them is that they encompass every believer and every disbeliever: all of this applies to the disbeliever in its fullest aspects, and to the believer in the sense of the disbelief of disobedience, its wrongdoing, and its defiance.

Then God informed, after this, of the sending down of this Qur'an. His statement "bi-l-ḥaqq" (with the truth) may mean: comprising the realities of matters, as if it came down with them. It may also mean that He sent it down in a way that this was right, not that it was obligatory upon God, but that it was right in itself; and He sent it down, may He be exalted, as a benefit for His servants. His statement "min al-kitāb" (of the Book) means of the revealed books, so it is a noun of genus. The commentators differed in the meaning of "muhaymin" (guardian). Ibn ʿAbbās said: "muhaymin" means a witness. He also said: trusted. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is confirming. al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: trustworthy. al-Zajjāj related: near. The word "al-muhaymin" is more specific than these terms, because the one who is "muhaymin" over a thing is the one charged with its affair, a witness to its realities, the guardian of its essentials, so he does not admit into it what is not from it. God, blessed and exalted, is the "muhaymin" over His creatures and His servants. The guardian of an orphan is "muhaymin" over his ward and his property; the leader is "muhaymin" over his subjects and their conditions. God made the Qur'an "muhaymin" over the books: it bears witness to the realities in them, and to what the distorters attributed to them, so it confirms the realities and nullifies the distortion. This is witness, confirmer, trusted, trustworthy, and guardian.

The form "muhaymin" is the pattern of the active participle. Abū ʿUbayda said: no words in the speech of the Arabs came in this pattern except four: "musayṭir" (dominating), "mubayṭir" (a veterinarian), "muhaymin," and "mujaymir" (a sort of fugitive). Abū al-Qāsim al-Zajjāj, in his commentary on the opening of "Adab al-Kitāb," mentioned also "mubayqir," from "bayqara al-rajul," meaning when a man travelled from the Ḥijāz to al-Shām and from one horizon to another. "Bayqara" also means he played al-bayqarā, a game with which children play. Mujāhid said: the statement of the Exalted, "wa-muhaymanan ʿalayhi" (and a guardian over it), means Muḥammad (ﷺ), that he is trusted over the Qur'an.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: al-Ṭabarī, may God have mercy on him, erred in this word with respect to Mujāhid, for he interpreted its meaning according to the people's reading "wa-muhayminan" with a kasra on the second mīm, so the interpretation became remote. Mujāhid, may God have mercy on him, only recited, he and Ibn Muḥayṣin: "muhaymanan ʿalayhi," with a fatḥa on the second mīm, so it is the pattern of the passive participle, and it is a circumstantial clause from "al-kitāb" coordinated with his statement "muṣaddiqan." On this basis it is apparent that the one entrusted over it is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and "ʿalayhi" is in the position of the nominative, on the assumption that it is a passive object whose agent is not named. This is according to the reading of Mujāhid. Makkī, may God have mercy on him, likewise followed this course and went deeply into al-Ṭabarī's path on this point.

Abū al-ʿAbbās Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad, may God have mercy on him, said: "muhaymin" originally is "mu'aymin," from the family of amīn (trustworthy); its hamza was changed to hā', as they said "arraqtu al-māʾ" (I poured out the water) and "haraqtuhu" (I poured it out). Al-Zajjāj said: this is good according to Arabic grammar, and it agrees with what came in the tafsīr, that the meaning of "muhaymin" is "trusted." Ibn Qutayba related what al-Mubarrad said in some of his books. al-Naqqāsh related that this reached Thaʿlab, and he said: "What Ibn Qutayba said is wretched." He said: "This is false, and the assault upon the Qur'an is severe. He (Mubarrad) did not hear the ḥadīth from a strong (narrator) or a weak one; he only collected books." The words of Thaʿlab end here.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: From "muhaymin" is said: "haymana al-rajul ʿalā al-shayʾ," when he preserved it, guarded it, and became standing over it as a trustworthy one. It is possible that "muṣaddiqan" and "wa-muhayminan" are two circumstantial clauses from the kāf in "ilayka" (to you), and this does not restrict it to the reading of Mujāhid alone, as Makkī claimed.

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿So judge between them by what God has revealed, and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you. For each of you We have appointed a law and a path. Had God willed, He would have made you one community, but He tests you in what He has given you. So race to the good deeds. To God is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of that over which you differed.﴾

Some scholars said: this verse abrogates His statement: ﴿or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42]. This has already been mentioned. (This is the discussion of naskh, abrogation, meaning one ruling superseded by a later one.)

The majority said: it is not an abrogation, and the meaning is: "If you choose to judge, then judge between them by what God has revealed."

Then God, may He be exalted, warned His Prophet against following their desires, that is, their appetites and their wills, which are a passion and a messenger of the self. The self commands evil, so its passion is destructive without doubt. The use of "ʿan" (from) here in His statement ﴿away from the truth that has come to you﴾ is apt, since the speech is in the sense of: "Do not turn away, or do not be diverted by their desires, from what has come to you."

The interpreters differed over the meaning of His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a path﴾. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, Qatāda, and the majority of the theologians said: the meaning is: for each community among you We have appointed a law and a path. That is, the Jews have a law and a path, the Christians likewise, and the Muslims likewise.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is according to them regarding the rulings, but as for belief, the religion is one for all the world: monotheism, faith in the Resurrection, and confirmation of the messengers. God, may He be exalted, has mentioned in His Book a number of prophets whose laws differ. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. This, according to the scholars, applies to beliefs only. As for laws, this verse is the one that decides them: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a path﴾.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The first interpretation is the one most people hold. It is possible that the intended meaning of His statement ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a path﴾ is the nations, as we have stated. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the prophets, especially since their mention and the mention of what was revealed to them has preceded. Those who interpreted hold that "al-shirʿa" (law) and "al-minhāj" (path) in this verse are two words with one meaning. That is because "al-shirʿa" and "al-sharīʿa" mean the path to water and other things that are frequented. Among this is the poet's verse:

"And in the sharāʾiʿ, from Jallān, is a hunter,
ragged of garments, low of voice, cunning."

He meant: in the paths to the water. From this comes "al-shāriʿ" (the street), which are the alleys of cities, and from it the people's saying: "and in it the door is opened." "Al-minhāj" also means the path, and from it is the poet's verse:

"Whoever is in doubt, this is a clear road,
a sweet water and a plain path."

He meant: clear. "Al-minhāj" is an intensive pattern in this sense.

Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: ﴿law and path﴾ means: a way and a custom.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The wording of the verse may allow that by "al-shirʿa" is meant the rulings, and by "al-minhāj" the belief, meaning that it is one for all of you. But this possibility is remote.

The readers recite "shirʿatan" with a kasra on the shīn. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "sharʿatan" with a fatḥa on the shīn.

Then God, may He be exalted, informed that had He willed, He would have made the world one community. But He did not will it, because He wanted to test them and try them in what He had given them of Books and laws. So said Ibn Jurayj and others. So they have no recourse but to strive in carrying out the commands, and this is racing to good deeds. Therefore He commanded them with what is best in outcome for them. Then God, may He be exalted, urged them by admonition and reminder of the return in His statement: ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾. The meaning is: "So hasten, hasten." His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿and He will inform you of that over which you differed﴾ means: "The reward and the punishment will become manifest, and you will be informed of it with the informing of a certainty." Otherwise, God had already announced the truth in this world concerning that over which the nations differed.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This verse is eloquent in its excellence. It gathers many meanings into few words. All of the Book of God, may He be exalted, is like this, except that, because of the shortcomings of our understanding, it becomes clear to some of us in some parts more than in others.

"Wa an uḥkum baynahum bimā anzala Allāh..." (49–50)

Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat al-Māʾidah, verses 49–50:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. But if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiant.﴾ ﴿Is it the judgment of the Time of Ignorance that they seek? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾

"Wa an uḥkum" (And judge): it is coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "al-Kitāb" in His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 48]. Makkī said that it is coordinated with "bil-ḥaqq" in His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book with the truth﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 48]. Both views are good. It is also read with a ḍammah on the nūn of "an-uḥkum" in consideration of the ḍammah on the ʿayn of the imperfect verb. It is read with a kasrah on it according to the usual rule for the meeting of two consonants (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn).

This verse is, according to some scholars, abrogating (nāsikhah) of the choice granted in His saying: ﴿or turn away from them﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 42]. This has already been mentioned. Then the Exalted forbade him from following the desires of the Children of Israel, since they lead astray. Desire (hawā) in most cases is used to refer to what contains no good, though it sometimes occurs qualified by what contains good. Among this is the statement of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb in the story of his opinion and the opinion of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding the captives of Badr: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) inclined to the opinion (fahawā) of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him." Among it also is the saying of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, when he was asked: "What is the most delightful thing to you?" He said: "A truth that agrees with a desire (hawā)." "Al-hawā" is maqṣūr (with a short final vowel), its pattern is faʿal, and its plural is "ahwāʾ." "Al-hawāʾ" is mamdūd (with a long final vowel), and its plural is "ahwiyah."

Then He, Blessed and Exalted, warned against them, lest they tempt him, meaning, lest they divert him by their testing and trying him, away from some of the rulings Allah revealed to him (ﷺ). This is because they wanted to deceive the Prophet (ﷺ). They would repeatedly say to him: "Judge for us in such-and-such a case according to such-and-such, and we will follow you in your religion."

As for His saying, "fa-in tawallaw" (But if they turn away): before it, something is omitted from the speech, which the apparent wording indicates. Its implied meaning is: "Do not follow them, and beware of them. If they nevertheless submit to your judgment and go straight, then that is excellent. But if they turn away, then know..." It is good that this omitted counterpart be supplied after His saying "la-fāsiqūn" (defiant).

As for His saying, "fa-iʿlam" (then know), etc., it is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning them. He fulfilled it through the story of Banū Qaynuqāʿ, the story of Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr, the expulsion of the people of Khaybar by ʿUmar, Fadak, and others. The Exalted restricted their affliction to "some of their sins" and not all of them, because this threat applies only in this world. Their sins in this world are of two kinds: one kind pertains only to them, such as drinking wine, their usury, their bribery, and the like; and another kind extends to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, such as their dealings with the disbelievers and their statements about the religion. It is this second kind that provided them the opening against them, and through it they were destroyed, and through it Allah threatened them in this world. Therefore He restricted it to "some," not "all." They will be punished for all of them in the Hereafter.

As for His saying, ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiant﴾: it is a reference to them, but the expression came in general terms so as to include them and others, that those others who were in defiance, hypocrisy, and turning away from the Prophet (ﷺ) might be alerted, so that they see that they too are under the threat.

The reciters differed regarding His saying: ﴿Is it the judgment of the Time of Ignorance that they seek?﴾. The majority read "ḥukma" with a fatḥah on the mīm, as the verb governed by an implied verb that follows the interrogative alif (alif al-istifhām), which this apparent wording subsequently explains.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-Sulamī, Abū Rajāʾ, and al-Aʿraj read "ḥukmu" with a ḍammah on the mīm. Ibn Mujāhid said: "It is an error." Abū al-Fatḥ said: "It is not so, but it is a valid reading other than that, and stronger than it, and it has occurred in poetry." Abū al-Najm said:

﴿Umm al-Khiyār has come to claim against me ∗∗∗ a sin, all of which I did not commit﴾

with "kullu" in the nominative.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is indeed the transmitted wording, and with it the correct meaning is completed, because he intended to disclaim all of the sin. Had he put "kulla" in the accusative, the apparent meaning of his statement would be that he committed part of it. This is the omission of the pronoun from the predicate (khabar), which is bad. The full form would be: "yabghūnahu" (they seek it) and "lam aṣnaʿhu" (I did not commit it). The pronoun is frequently omitted from the relative clause (ṣila), as in His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ [al-Furqān: 41], and as you say: "I passed by the one whom you honored." It is omitted less often from the qualifier (ṣifah), and its omission from the predicate is bad, as in the verse of Abū al-Najm. His verse can be justified in two ways: first, that there is no interrogative alif in the beginning of his statement that seeks a verb, as there is in His saying "fa-ḥukma" (then the judgment of); second, that in the verse there is a substitute for the omitted hāʾ, namely the letter of extension (ḥarf al-iṭlāq), that is, the yāʾ in "aṣnaʿī." Thus the reading of the one who reads "ḥukmu" with ḍammah is weakened, because the verb after it has no pronoun in it and no substitute for the pronoun. Yet the interrogative alif that seeks a verb, and with which the accusative is preferred even if the pronoun is pronounced, is present. The reading is justified only if the implied meaning is: "Is the judgment of the Time of Ignorance a judgment they seek?" Thus you do not make "yabghūna" the predicate, but rather the qualifier of an omitted predicate and an omitted noun described. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 46], its implied meaning being: "a people who distort." So the noun was omitted and the qualifier put in its place. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

﴿And time is nothing but two turns; from them ∗∗∗ I die, and another I seek life, striving﴾

Sulaymān ibn Mihrān read "afa-ḥakama" with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, the kāf, and the mīm. It is a noun of genus (ism jins), and it is permissible to make a genus noun annexed (muḍāf) in the manner of their saying: "I was denied Iraq, its qafīz and its dirham; and Egypt, its ardabb." It has similar examples.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is as if he said: "Is it the judgment of the soothsayers of the Time of Ignorance that they seek?" This refers to the soothsayers (kuhhān) who used to take gifts (ḥulwān) and judge according to them, and according to desires. Then this reading returns in meaning to the first, because the implied meaning is: "Is the judgment of the judges of the Time of Ignorance?"

Ibn ʿĀmir read "tabghūna" with a tāʾ, addressing them, meaning: "Say to them." The rest of the seven read "yabghūna" with a yāʾ at the beginning. The meaning of "yabghūna" is: they seek and desire.

His saying: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment﴾ is an affirmation: meaning, no one is better than Him in judgment, Blessed and Exalted. The entry of the lām in His saying "li-qawmin" (for a people) is justified semantically as: "This becomes clear and manifest for a people who are certain."
