**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Mā'idah, verses 51–52**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. And whoever among you allies with them is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Him, and they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful.﴾

In this verse Allah, Exalted is He, forbids the believers from taking the Jews and the Christians as allies in support, in close association that leads to intermingling, and in mutual backing. The ruling of this verse is still in effect. Whoever frequently associates with these two groups has his share of the abhorrence contained in His saying, "indeed he is one of them." As for dealing with a Jew or a Christian without close association or intimate contact, this does not fall under the prohibition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dealt with a Jew and pledged his armour to him as collateral.

The exegetes (mufassirūn) differed concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) of this verse. ʿAṭiyyah ibn Saʿd, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Isḥāq and others said: its occasion was that when the battle of Badr was over and the affair of Banū Qaynuqāʿ became acute, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to kill them. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl stood in their defence, for he was their ally. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit also had an alliance with them similar to that of ʿAbd Allāh. When ʿUbādah saw the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) resolve, and what the Jews had pursued of opposition to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I disavow to Allah the alliance and loyalty of the Jews. I take as allies none but Allah and His Messenger." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said: "As for me, I will not disavow the loyalty to the Jews, for I cannot do without them. I am a man who fears misfortunes."

Ibn Isḥāq related in al-Sīrah: "He (ʿAbd Allāh) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), put his hand into the pocket of his coat of mail, and said: 'O Muḥammad, be good to my allies.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Release the coat of mail from your hand.' He said: 'No, by Allah, not until you spare them for me. They are three hundred men wearing armour and four hundred unarmoured. Will you let them be mown down by you in a single morning?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have spared them for you.'" And the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Suddī said: the occasion of this verse was that when the affair of Uḥud befell the Muslims, some people were alarmed, and some of them said to others: "Let us take from the Jews a protective bond (ʿiṣm), so that they may support us if a crushing blow from Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs strikes us." So the verse was revealed concerning that.

ʿIkrimah said: the occasion of the verse was the matter of Abū Lubābah ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir and his gesture toward Qurayẓah, that it was slaughter, when they asked him about his opinion on their surrendering to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: all these sayings are possible, and the times of these incidents differ.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās recited: "Do not take the Jews and the Christians as lords, some of them [as lords] over others."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾ is a separate clause (jumlah maqṭūʿah) from the prohibition. It contains a distinction between them and the believers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them﴾ is a censure of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and of everyone who has this attribute of alliance with them. Whoever allies with them in belief and religion is one of them in unbelief, in deserving retribution, and in eternal abiding in the Fire. Whoever allies with them in deeds, such as lending support and the like, without belief and without impairing his faith, is one of them in the abhorrence and blame that falls upon them and upon him. With this verse, Ibn ʿAbbās and others permitted the slaughtered animals of the Arab Christians. He said: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them is one of them﴾, and he said: "Whoever enters the religion of a people is one of them." Ibn Sīrīn (may Allah have mercy on him) was asked about a man who wished to sell his house to Christians who would make it a church (kanīsah), and he recited this verse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is general. It may be intended in a particular sense (khuṣūṣ), concerning those whom Allah's knowledge has preceded as not believing and not being guided; or it may be intended as restricting the period of wrongdoing and of being engaged in its deed, for guidance is not present in wrongdoing, and the wrongdoer, insofar as he is a wrongdoer, is not guided in his wrongdoing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ and the rest of the verse is addressed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and it points to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and the hypocrites who followed him in his position of protecting Banū Qaynuqāʿ. It also includes those among the believers of the Khazraj who followed him out of ignorance and partisanship. This category has its share of the disease of the heart.

The reading of the majority of people is "fatarā" with the tā' at the beginning. If it is taken as seeing with the eye (ruʾyat ʿayn), then "yusāriʿūna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and this is the intended benefit. If it is taken as seeing with the heart (ruʾyat qalb), then "yusāriʿūna" stands in the place of the second object, and "yaqūlūna" is a circumstantial clause. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "fayarā" with the yāʾ at the beginning. The subject in this reading is omitted, and you may supply "Allah sees" or "the seer sees." "Alladhīna" is the object. It is possible that "alladhīna" is the subject, and the meaning would be "that they hasten," with "an" (that) omitted for brevity.

"Yusāriʿūna fīhim" means: in supporting them, in making them comfortable, and in beautifying their mention.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾ is a wording preserved from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy. There is no doubt that many hypocrites said the same as his statement, and the verse indicates this. "Dāʾirah" means: an event of time and a calamity of the occurrences which compels us to our allies among the Jews. These matters are called "dawāʾir" (revolutions) in ancient usage, since night and day are in rotation, so it is as if the event revolves with their revolution until it falls upon whoever it falls upon. From this is Allah's saying: ﴿The revolution of evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98], and: ﴿waiting for you to be [subjected to] revolutions﴾. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And time, with a person, is turning,"* ∗∗∗ ..............

And the saying of another:

*"............... ∗∗∗ and he knows that calamities revolve"*

And the saying of another:

*"He turns away from you the decree that was decreed, ∗∗∗ and the revolutions of time, that they should turn."*

This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, time has come full circle (istadāra)."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: the act of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy in this incident did not outwardly appear as an open contest against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for had he done so, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have fought him. Rather, he would show the Prophet (ﷺ) that he wished to keep them for supporting Muḥammad (ﷺ), and because that was the sound opinion. His saying, "I am a man who fears the revolutions," means: from the Arabs, and from those who would fight Madinah and its people. In all of this he was concealing caution against the Prophet (ﷺ), the believers, and the weakening of their support. This is what he and those with him who were upon his hypocrisy concealed within themselves, some of them being exposed to others.

His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿"Then perhaps Allah"﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers, and it is a promise to them. "ʿAsā" from Allah, Exalted is He, is binding. The interpreters differed concerning the meaning of "bil-fatḥ" (with a conquest) in this verse. Qatādah said: it means the judgement in these incidents, and "al-Fattāḥ" is the judge. This promise was then fulfilled in what happened to Banū Qaynuqāʿ afterward, and to Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr. al-Suddī said: it means the conquest of Makkah.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: the apparent conquest in this verse is the manifestation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the elevation of his word. That is, the independence from the Jews will become evident, and the hypocrite will see that Allah has not opened a path to what he had been hoping from them, namely support in the affair of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and pushing against the breast of his prophethood. Then he will regret what had occurred in him of opposition to the Sharīʿah, and of the cloak of abhorrence from Allah, from His Messenger (ﷺ), and from the believers being spread over him, as happened and became apparent afterward.

(p-193) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or a decision from Him﴾: al-Suddī said: it means the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax). The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it appears that this division is because the promised conquest is that which is built upon the striving of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and which their diligence and their action cause. So the promise of Allah, Exalted is He, is either a conquest in accordance with those actions, or a decision from Him that destroys the enemies of the Sharīʿah, which is also a conquest in which humans have no causal role.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"then they will become"﴾ means: they will remain in that state throughout their lifetime. The morning is specified for mention because a person in his night is thinking and concealed, so at dawn he is seen in the state that his thought or his illnesses have brought about, and similar things. From this is the saying of the poet: "I have become one who does not carry weapons," and other examples besides this.

What they concealed is what we have mentioned of their familiarity with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Jews' preparation for rebellion against him one day. Ibn al-Zuhrī recited: "fayuṣbiḥa al-fussāq ʿalā mā asarrū fī anfusihim nādimīn" (then the defiant ones will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Mā'idah, verses 51–52**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. And whoever among you allies with them is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us." But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a decision from Him, and they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful.﴾

In this verse Allah, Exalted is He, forbids the believers from taking the Jews and the Christians as allies in support, in close association that leads to intermingling, and in mutual backing. The ruling of this verse is still in effect. Whoever frequently associates with these two groups has his share of the abhorrence contained in His saying, "indeed he is one of them." As for dealing with a Jew or a Christian without close association or intimate contact, this does not fall under the prohibition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dealt with a Jew and pledged his armour to him as collateral.

The exegetes (mufassirūn) differed concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) of this verse. ʿAṭiyyah ibn Saʿd, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Isḥāq and others said: its occasion was that when the battle of Badr was over and the affair of Banū Qaynuqāʿ became acute, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to kill them. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl stood in their defence, for he was their ally. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit also had an alliance with them similar to that of ʿAbd Allāh. When ʿUbādah saw the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) resolve, and what the Jews had pursued of opposition to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I disavow to Allah the alliance and loyalty of the Jews. I take as allies none but Allah and His Messenger." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said: "As for me, I will not disavow the loyalty to the Jews, for I cannot do without them. I am a man who fears misfortunes."

Ibn Isḥāq related in al-Sīrah: "He (ʿAbd Allāh) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), put his hand into the pocket of his coat of mail, and said: 'O Muḥammad, be good to my allies.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Release the coat of mail from your hand.' He said: 'No, by Allah, not until you spare them for me. They are three hundred men wearing armour and four hundred unarmoured. Will you let them be mown down by you in a single morning?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have spared them for you.'" And the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Suddī said: the occasion of this verse was that when the affair of Uḥud befell the Muslims, some people were alarmed, and some of them said to others: "Let us take from the Jews a protective bond (ʿiṣm), so that they may support us if a crushing blow from Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs strikes us." So the verse was revealed concerning that.

ʿIkrimah said: the occasion of the verse was the matter of Abū Lubābah ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir and his gesture toward Qurayẓah, that it was slaughter, when they asked him about his opinion on their surrendering to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: all these sayings are possible, and the times of these incidents differ.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās recited: "Do not take the Jews and the Christians as lords, some of them [as lords] over others."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾ is a separate clause (jumlah maqṭūʿah) from the prohibition. It contains a distinction between them and the believers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them﴾ is a censure of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and of everyone who has this attribute of alliance with them. Whoever allies with them in belief and religion is one of them in unbelief, in deserving retribution, and in eternal abiding in the Fire. Whoever allies with them in deeds, such as lending support and the like, without belief and without impairing his faith, is one of them in the abhorrence and blame that falls upon them and upon him. With this verse, Ibn ʿAbbās and others permitted the slaughtered animals of the Arab Christians. He said: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them is one of them﴾, and he said: "Whoever enters the religion of a people is one of them." Ibn Sīrīn (may Allah have mercy on him) was asked about a man who wished to sell his house to Christians who would make it a church (kanīsah), and he recited this verse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is general. It may be intended in a particular sense (khuṣūṣ), concerning those whom Allah's knowledge has preceded as not believing and not being guided; or it may be intended as restricting the period of wrongdoing and of being engaged in its deed, for guidance is not present in wrongdoing, and the wrongdoer, insofar as he is a wrongdoer, is not guided in his wrongdoing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ and the rest of the verse is addressed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and it points to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and the hypocrites who followed him in his position of protecting Banū Qaynuqāʿ. It also includes those among the believers of the Khazraj who followed him out of ignorance and partisanship. This category has its share of the disease of the heart.

The reading of the majority of people is "fatarā" with the tā' at the beginning. If it is taken as seeing with the eye (ruʾyat ʿayn), then "yusāriʿūna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and this is the intended benefit. If it is taken as seeing with the heart (ruʾyat qalb), then "yusāriʿūna" stands in the place of the second object, and "yaqūlūna" is a circumstantial clause. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "fayarā" with the yāʾ at the beginning. The subject in this reading is omitted, and you may supply "Allah sees" or "the seer sees." "Alladhīna" is the object. It is possible that "alladhīna" is the subject, and the meaning would be "that they hasten," with "an" (that) omitted for brevity.

"Yusāriʿūna fīhim" means: in supporting them, in making them comfortable, and in beautifying their mention.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾ is a wording preserved from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy. There is no doubt that many hypocrites said the same as his statement, and the verse indicates this. "Dāʾirah" means: an event of time and a calamity of the occurrences which compels us to our allies among the Jews. These matters are called "dawāʾir" (revolutions) in ancient usage, since night and day are in rotation, so it is as if the event revolves with their revolution until it falls upon whoever it falls upon. And the saying of another:

This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, time has come full circle (istadāra)."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 53–54**

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

The reciters differed regarding this verse. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Nafi' read "yaqulu" (يَقُولُ) without the conjunctive waw and with the lam in the nominative. This is also how it is written in the codices (mashahif) of Madina and Makka. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read "wa-yaqulu" (وَيَقُولُ) with the waw affirmed, and this is how it is written in the codices of the Kufans. (p-194) al-Tabari said: "It is written this way in our codices, the codices of the people of the East." Abu 'Amr alone read "wa-yaqula" (وَيَقُولَ) with the waw affirmed and the lam in the accusative. Abu 'Ali said: "'Ali ibn Nasr related from Abu 'Amr both the accusative and the nominative for the lam."

As for the reading of Ibn Kathir and Nafi', it is consistent with the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, because the waw here is not a conjunction of a single noun to a single noun, sharing the same governing element. Rather, it conjoins one clause to another clause, linking them together, and the two clauses are connected without a waw, since the second clause contains a reference back to the first. "Those who hasten toward them" and "they say, 'We fear'" and "they will become regretful" are the same people who were described as, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths?" When the two clauses are like this, it is good to join them with the waw and it is also good without the waw, just as the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog," and they will say, "Five, the sixth of them being their dog"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:22). Since each of the two clauses contains a reference to what preceded, the reference was sufficient without the waw. Upon this basis is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ (Surah al-Baqara 2:39). Had the waw entered, saying "wa-hum fiha khalidun," it would have been good.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: However, the eloquence of the speech lies in its conciseness. The entry of the waw being good is shown by the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "Seven, and the eighth of them being their dog"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:22). So the omission of the waw in "Those who believe will say" is like its omission in this verse, and its addition in the phrase "thamimuhum" (the eighth of them).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Many of the exegetes held that this saying of the believers occurs only when the victory (al-fath) comes and the regret of the hypocrites becomes evident, and Allah exposes them. At that time the believers will say: ﴿Are these the ones who swore...﴾ until the end of the verse. The verse may also be a report of what the believers said at the time when those in whose hearts is a disease said: ﴿We fear that a misfortune will befall us﴾ (Surah al-Ma'ida 5:52), and at the time of their actions, what they did in the incident of Banu Qaynuqa'. Their secret became apparent in it, and it was understood from them that their clinging to them (the Jews) was only a lying in wait for Allah and His Messenger. So the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers despised them. The Prophet (ﷺ) left Banu Qaynuqa' for the sake of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, out of desire for welfare and unity, and because 'Abd Allah displayed that this was his own opinion, and that the misfortunes he feared were only what would ruin Madina. The believers knew, and every discerning person understood, that 'Abd Allah was acting contrary to what he displayed. Thus that became an occasion in which it was fitting for the believers to say: ﴿Are these the ones who swore...﴾ until the end of the verse.

As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, "wa-yaqula" with the lam in the accusative, then with it the saying of the believers can only be understood to occur at the time of the victory and the manifestation of the regret of the hypocrites and their exposure. This is because the waw is conjoining a verb to a verb, sharing the same governing element. The conjunction of "wa-yaqula" is consistent in three ways:

The first: on the basis of meaning. His saying: ﴿It may be that Allah will bring a victory﴾ (Surah al-Ma'ida 5:52), its meaning is: "It may be that Allah will bring a victory," with the conjunction of His saying "wa-yaqula" upon "yati" (will bring), relying on the meaning. Otherwise it would not be permissible to say, "It may be that Allah will say: the believers." Likewise is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had You not delayed me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun 63:10). The meaning would not have been: "Delay me to a near term, I will give charity." Rather "wa-akun" (and I would be) was taken as jussive, which the meaning requires in His saying "fa-assaddaqa" (so that I would give charity).

The second way: that His saying "an ya'tiya bil-fath" (that He will bring the victory) is a substitute (badal) for the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as it was substituted for the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:63). Then "wa-yaqula" is conjoined to "an yati" (that he will come), because then it is as if you had said: "It may be that he will come..."

The third way: that His saying "wa-yaqula" is conjoined to "fa-yusbihu" (so they become), since it is a verb in the accusative after the fa' in answer to the optative (tamanni). His saying "it may be that Allah..." is an expression of wishing and hope regarding humans. There is a consideration in this way. Likewise, in my view, there is a consideration in their prohibition of "it may be that Allah will bring the believers to say," because Allah, Exalted is He, makes them say it through His support and the manifestation of His religion. So it should be permissible on the basis of meaning.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ (their most solemn oaths), "jahda" is in the accusative as an emphasizing verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad). The meaning is: (p-196) "Are these the ones who swore with exertion of their oaths, that they were with you? Then there has now become evident from them, through their allegiance to the Jews and their abandonment of the Sharia, what contradicts their belief."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ may be a report from Allah, Exalted is He, or it may be a saying of the believers, by way of reporting what came to be in their belief when they saw the hypocrites in these circumstances. It may also be that His saying "Their deeds have become void" is a supplication, either from Allah, Exalted is He, against them, or from the believers. "Habita al-'amal" (the deed became void) means that it becomes nullified after having been established. It may be said "habita" in regard to the deeds of disbelievers, though it did not come to be, by way of likeness. The majority of people read "habitat" with a kasra on the ba'. Abu Waqid and al-Jarrah read it with a fatha on the ba', and this is a dialect.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion...﴾ until the end of the verse. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak, and Qatada said: the verse was revealed as an address to the believers generally, until the Day of Resurrection. The indication by "a people" whom He will bring refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions, who fought the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda). Ibn Jurayj and others said this.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning of the verse, in my view, is that Allah promised this community: whoever of it turns back, then He will bring people who support the religion and who will suffice in place of the apostates. So Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions were among those about whom the report was fulfilled in that era. Likewise, in my view, is the matter of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) with the Kharijites. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari related that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it and said: "They are the people of this one," meaning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. 'Iyad also said this. Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd said: When this verse was revealed, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Am I and my people them, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No, but they are the people of this one," and he pointed to Abu Musa.

Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b also said that the indication is to the people of Yemen, and Shahr ibn Hawshab said this.

(p-197) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All of this, in my view, is one statement, because the people of Yemen are the people of Abu Musa. The meaning of the verse on this view is an address to all who were present in the era of the Prophet (ﷺ), in the sense of alerting them, rebuking them, and warning them. al-Suddi said: the indication by "a people" is to the Ansar.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is on the basis that His saying, Exalted is He, "O you who believe," is an address to the believers present, which includes their believer and their hypocrite, because the hypocrites used to display belief. The indication by the apostasy is to the hypocrites. The meaning is that whoever is hypocritical and apostatizes, then the committed among the Ansar will protect the Sharia, and Allah will close every breach through them.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read "yartadda" (يَرْتَدَّ) with the dal of the root assimilated into the dal. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yartadid" (يَرْتَدِدْ) without assimilation. This is the dialect of the Hijaz (Makka and its surroundings), and assimilation is the dialect of Tamim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿adhillatin 'ala al-mu'minin﴾ (humble toward the believers). Its meaning: humbling themselves out of their own selves, not arrogant. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (Surah al-Fath 48:29), and like His saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "The believer is gentle and soft." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "adhillatin 'ala al-mu'minin, ghuluzan 'ala al-kafirin" (humble toward the believers, harsh toward the disbelievers).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-la yakhafuna lawmata la'im﴾ (and not fearing the blame of any blamer). This is an indication of a refutation of the hypocrites, in that they used to excuse themselves by the blame of the morals and the knowledge of the disbelievers, and they would observe their affairs.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿dhalika fadlu Allah﴾ (that is the bounty of Allah). The indication by "dhalika" (that) is to the people's being those who love Allah and whom He loves. The discussion of the meaning of Allah's love for the servant has already preceded more than once, and that it is the manifestation of blessings that indicate His good pleasure with him, and His clothing him with them. And "wasi'" (All-Encompassing): its meaning is one who has abundance in what He possesses, gives, and bestows.

"Those who hasten toward them" and "they say, 'We fear'" and "they will become regretful" are the same people who were described as, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths?" Since each of the two clauses contains a reference to what preceded, the reference was sufficient without the waw. Upon this basis is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ (Surah al-Baqara 2:39). Had the waw entered, saying "wa-hum fiha khalidun," it would have been good.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: However, the eloquence of the speech lies in its conciseness. The entry of the waw being good is shown by the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "Seven, and the eighth of them being their dog"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:22). So the omission of the waw in "Those who believe will say" is like its omission in this verse, and its addition in the phrase "thamimuhum" (the eighth of them).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Many of the exegetes held that this saying of the believers occurs only when the victory (al-fath) comes and the regret of the hypocrites becomes evident, and Allah exposes them. At that time the believers will say: ﴿Are these the ones who swore...﴾ until the end of the verse. The verse may also be a report of what the believers said at the time when those in whose hearts is a disease said: ﴿We fear that a misfortune will befall us﴾ (Surah al-Ma'ida 5:52), and at the time of their actions, what they did in the incident of Banu Qaynuqa'. Their secret became apparent in it, and it was understood from them that their clinging to them (the Jews) was only a lying in wait for Allah and His Messenger. So the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers despised them. The Prophet (ﷺ) left Banu Qaynuqa' for the sake of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, out of desire for welfare and unity, and because 'Abd Allah displayed that this was his own opinion, and that the misfortunes he feared were only what would ruin Madina. The believers knew, and every discerning person understood, that 'Abd Allah was acting contrary to what he displayed. Thus that became an occasion in which it was fitting for the believers to say: ﴿Are these the ones who swore...﴾ until the end of the verse.

As for the reading of Abu 'Amr, "wa-yaqula" with the lam in the accusative, then with it the saying of the believers can only be understood to occur at the time of the victory and the manifestation of the regret of the hypocrites and their exposure. This is because the waw is conjoining a verb to a verb, sharing the same governing element. The conjunction of "wa-yaqula" is consistent in three ways:

The first: on the basis of meaning. His saying: ﴿It may be that Allah will bring a victory﴾ (Surah al-Ma'ida 5:52), its meaning is: "It may be that Allah will bring a victory," with the conjunction of His saying "wa-yaqula" upon "yati" (will bring), relying on the meaning. Otherwise it would not be permissible to say, "It may be that Allah will say: the believers." Likewise is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had You not delayed me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun 63:10). The meaning would not have been: "Delay me to a near term, I will give charity." Rather "wa-akun" (and I would be) was taken as jussive, which the meaning requires in His saying "fa-assaddaqa" (so that I would give charity).

The second way: that His saying "an ya'tiya bil-fath" (that He will bring the victory) is a substitute (badal) for the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as it was substituted for the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:63). Then "wa-yaqula" is conjoined to "an yati" (that he will come), because then it is as if you had said: "It may be that he will come..."

The third way: that His saying "wa-yaqula" is conjoined to "fa-yusbihu" (so they become), since it is a verb in the accusative after the fa' in answer to the optative (tamanni). His saying "it may be that Allah..." is an expression of wishing and hope regarding humans. There is a consideration in this way. Likewise, in my view, there is a consideration in their prohibition of "it may be that Allah will bring the believers to say," because Allah, Exalted is He, makes them say it through His support and the manifestation of His religion. So it should be permissible on the basis of meaning.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ (their most solemn oaths), "jahda" is in the accusative as an emphasizing verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad). The meaning is: (p-196) "Are these the ones who swore with exertion of their oaths, that they were with you? Then there has now become evident from them, through their allegiance to the Jews and their abandonment of the Sharia, what contradicts their belief."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ may be a report from Allah, Exalted is He, or it may be a saying of the believers, by way of reporting what came to be in their belief when they saw the hypocrites in these circumstances. It may also be that His saying "Their deeds have become void" is a supplication, either from Allah, Exalted is He, against them, or from the believers. "Habita al-'amal" (the deed became void) means that it becomes nullified after having been established. It may be said "habita" in regard to the deeds of disbelievers, though it did not come to be, by way of likeness. The majority of people read "habitat" with a kasra on the ba'. Abu Waqid and al-Jarrah read it with a fatha on the ba', and this is a dialect.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion...﴾ until the end of the verse. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak, and Qatada said: the verse was revealed as an address to the believers generally, until the Day of Resurrection. The indication by "a people" whom He will bring refers to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions, who fought the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda). Ibn Jurayj and others said this.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning of the verse, in my view, is that Allah promised this community: whoever of it turns back, then He will bring people who support the religion and who will suffice in place of the apostates. So Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions were among those about whom the report was fulfilled in that era. Likewise, in my view, is the matter of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) with the Kharijites. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari related that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it and said: "They are the people of this one," meaning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. 'Iyad also said this. Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd said: When this verse was revealed, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Am I and my people them, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No, but they are the people of this one," and he pointed to Abu Musa.

Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b also said that the indication is to the people of Yemen, and Shahr ibn Hawshab said this.

(p-197) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All of this, in my view, is one statement, because the people of Yemen are the people of Abu Musa. The meaning of the verse on this view is an address to all who were present in the era of the Prophet (ﷺ), in the sense of alerting them, rebuking them, and warning them. al-Suddi said: the indication by "a people" is to the Ansar.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is on the basis that His saying, Exalted is He, "O you who believe," is an address to the believers present, which includes their believer and their hypocrite, because the hypocrites used to display belief. The indication by the apostasy is to the hypocrites. The meaning is that whoever is hypocritical and apostatizes, then the committed among the Ansar will protect the Sharia, and Allah will close every breach through them.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read "yartadda" (يَرْتَدَّ) with the dal of the root assimilated into the dal. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yartadid" (يَرْتَدِدْ) without assimilation. This is the dialect of the Hijaz (Makka and its surroundings), and assimilation is the dialect of Tamim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿adhillatin 'ala al-mu'minin﴾ (humble toward the believers). Its meaning: humbling themselves out of their own selves, not arrogant. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (Surah al-Fath 48:29), and like His saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "The believer is gentle and soft." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "adhillatin 'ala al-mu'minin, ghuluzan 'ala al-kafirin" (humble toward the believers, harsh toward the disbelievers).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-la yakhafuna lawmata la'im﴾ (and not fearing the blame of any blamer). This is an indication of a refutation of the hypocrites, in that they used to excuse themselves by the blame of the morals and the knowledge of the disbelievers, and they would observe their affairs.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿dhalika fadlu Allah﴾ (that is the bounty of Allah). The indication by "dhalika" (that) is to the people's being those who love Allah and whom He loves. The discussion of the meaning of Allah's love for the servant has already preceded more than once, and that it is the manifestation of blessings that indicate His good pleasure with him, and His clothing him with them. And "wasi'" (All-Encompassing): its meaning is one who has abundance in what He possesses, gives, and bestows.

﴿Your only guardian is Allah, and His Messenger, and the believers: those who establish prayer and give zakah while bowing﴾ [5:55]. ﴿Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies, indeed the party of Allah will be the victorious﴾ [5:56]. ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, or the disbelievers. And fear Allah, if you are believers﴾ [5:57].

The address in ﴿Your only guardian is Allah﴾ is to the people to whom it was said: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [5:51]. The word "innama" (only, indeed) in this verse is restrictive (ḥāṣira), and it conveys that meaning. "Walī" (guardian, ally) is a noun of genus (ism jins). Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Innama mawlakum Allah" (your only protector is Allah). As for ﴿and those who have believed﴾, the meaning is: and whoever among the people has believed in truth, not in hypocrisy. They are those who ﴿establish prayer﴾, the obligatory prayer with all its conditions, ﴿and give zakah﴾. Here "zakah" is a general term that includes obligatory zakah, voluntary charity, and all acts of righteousness, since it causes good deeds to grow and purifies a person from the filth of sins. Believers give of that, each according to his capacity. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Āmanū wa-alladhīna yuqīmūna" (with a conjunction "wa" before the second group).

As for His saying, ﴿while bowing﴾, it is a clause conjoined to a preceding clause, and its meaning is to describe them as frequent in prayer. Bowing was singled out for mention because it is among the greatest pillars of prayer, and it is a posture of humility, so it is used to express the whole prayer, as He said: ﴿the bowers and the prostrators﴾ [2:125], which refers to those who pray. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. However, it happened that Ali ibn Abi Talib gave charity while he was bowing. Al-Suddi said: this verse applies to all believers, but Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, was passed by a beggar while he was bowing in the mosque, so he gave him his ring. And it is narrated concerning that: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out from his house after the verse had been revealed to him, and he found a poor man, so he said to him, 'Has anyone given you anything?' He said, 'Yes, that man who is praying gave me a silver ring while he was bowing.' The Prophet (ﷺ) looked, and behold, the man he pointed to was Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Allahu Akbar,' and recited the verse to the people."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Mujahid said that the verse was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave charity while bowing. There is an examination of this view, and the correct position is what we have presented from the interpretation of the majority. It has been said to Abu Ja'far: this verse was revealed concerning Ali. He said: "Ali is among the believers." According to this view, the waw in ﴿and they﴾ is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl).

Some people said: the verse, from its beginning, was revealed because of Ubadah ibn al-Samit, when he disavowed the Banu Qaynuqa'. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it was revealed because of a group of People of the Book who had embraced Islam. They came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, our houses are far away, and we have no place to talk except your mosque, and our people have sworn that they will not associate with us or befriend us." So the verse was revealed to comfort them.

Then Allah, Exalted, informed that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies, will surely overcome everyone who opposes him. The expression came in general terms: ﴿indeed the party of Allah will be the victorious﴾, in brevity, because the one who takes them as allies is from the party of Allah, and the party of Allah is victorious; so this person who has taken Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies is victorious. "Man" (whoever) is intended to denote a genus, not a specific individual. "Ḥizb" (party) means the faction, those who are affiliated with the leader of the party, and those who assist in what concerns the party. From this is the saying of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about Hamnah, who used to fight in the affair of the slander: "So she perished among those who perished."

Then Allah, Exalted, forbade the believers from taking the Jews and the Christians as allies, and He marked them with a mark that moves souls to shun them, namely, their taking the religion of the believers as mockery and play. "Al-huzu" (mockery) means ridicule and contempt. It is read as "huzuwan" (with a ḍamma on the zay and a hamza), "huz'an" (with a sukun on the zay and a hamza), and it is stopped upon as "huzzan" (with a shadda on the open zay), and "huzuwan" (with a ḍamma on the zay and tanwin on the waw), and "huzan" (with an open zay and tanwin). Then Allah, Exalted, specified the kind of those people, that they are from the People of the Book: the Jews and the Christians.

The readers differed on the i'rab (grammatical case inflection) of ﴿and the disbelievers﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Hamzah read "wa-al-kuffāra" (with a fatḥa, accusative). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "wa-al-kuffāri" (with a kasra, genitive). Husayn al-Ju'fi narrated from Abu 'Amr the accusative. Abu 'Ali said: the argument of those who read with the genitive is to link the sentence to the nearer of the two governing elements, and this is the usage of the Revelation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to the genitive reading, the disbelievers are included among those who have taken the religion of the believers as mockery. The mockery of the disbelievers is established in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [15:95]. The mockery of the People of the Book is established in the wording of this verse. The mockery of the hypocrites is established in their saying to their devils: ﴿Indeed, we are with you; we are only mockers﴾ [2:14]. Whoever reads "wa-al-kuffāra" with the accusative takes it as governed by the verb which is "do not take," and the disbelievers are excluded from the wording of this verse, so that it does not include their mockery. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-min al-kuffār" (with the addition of "min"), and this supports the genitive reading. Likewise, in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "min qablikum mina alladhīna ashrakū" (from among those who associated partners with Allah).

The verse distinguished between the disbelievers and those who were given the Scripture, in that the term "disbelievers" generally applies to those who associate partners with Allah in worship, through idol worship, because they are furthest in disbelief. Allah, Exalted, has said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [9:73]. So He distinguished between them for the purpose of clarification, although all of them are disbelievers. This is because the worshippers of idols are disbelievers from every aspect, and these groups join them in the ruling of disbelief but differ from them in degrees. The People of the Book believe in Allah and in some of the prophets, while the hypocrites believe with their tongues.

Then Allah, Exalted, commanded them to fear Him, and He alerted souls with His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: truly believers.

The expression came in general terms: ﴿indeed the party of Allah will be the victorious﴾, in brevity, because the one who takes them as allies is from the party of Allah, and the party of Allah is victorious; so this person who has taken Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies is victorious. "Man" (whoever) is intended to denote a genus, not a specific individual. "Ḥizb" (party) means the faction, those who are affiliated with the leader of the party, and those who assist in what concerns the party. From this is the saying of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about Hamnah, who used to fight in the affair of the slander: "So she perished among those who perished."

Then Allah, Exalted, forbade the believers from taking the Jews and the Christians as allies, and He marked them with a mark that moves souls to shun them, namely, their taking the religion of the believers as mockery and play. "Al-huzu" (mockery) means ridicule and contempt. It is read as "huzuwan" (with a ḍamma on the zay and a hamza), "huz'an" (with a sukun on the zay and a hamza), and it is stopped upon as "huzzan" (with a shadda on the open zay), and "huzuwan" (with a ḍamma on the zay and tanwin on the waw), and "huzan" (with an open zay and tanwin). Then Allah, Exalted, specified the kind of those people, that they are from the People of the Book: the Jews and the Christians.

The readers differed on the i'rab (grammatical case inflection) of ﴿and the disbelievers﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Hamzah read "wa-al-kuffāra" (with a fatḥa, accusative). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "wa-al-kuffāri" (with a kasra, genitive). Husayn al-Ju'fi narrated from Abu 'Amr the accusative. Abu 'Ali said: the argument of those who read with the genitive is to link the sentence to the nearer of the two governing elements, and this is the usage of the Revelation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to the genitive reading, the disbelievers are included among those who have taken the religion of the believers as mockery. The mockery of the disbelievers is established in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [15:95]. The mockery of the People of the Book is established in the wording of this verse. The mockery of the hypocrites is established in their saying to their devils: ﴿Indeed, we are with you; we are only mockers﴾ [2:14]. Whoever reads "wa-al-kuffāra" with the accusative takes it as governed by the verb which is "do not take," and the disbelievers are excluded from the wording of this verse, so that it does not include their mockery. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-min al-kuffār" (with the addition of "min"), and this supports the genitive reading. Likewise, in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "min qablikum mina alladhīna ashrakū" (from among those who associated partners with Allah).

The verse distinguished between the disbelievers and those who were given the Scripture, in that the term "disbelievers" generally applies to those who associate partners with Allah in worship, through idol worship, because they are furthest in disbelief. Allah, Exalted, has said: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [9:73]. So He distinguished between them for the purpose of clarification, although all of them are disbelievers. This is because the worshippers of idols are disbelievers from every aspect, and these groups join them in the ruling of disbelief but differ from them in degrees. The People of the Book believe in Allah and in some of the prophets, while the hypocrites believe with their tongues.

Then Allah, Exalted, commanded them to fear Him, and He alerted souls with His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: truly believers.

[p. 201] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿When you call to the prayer, they take it as mockery and play. That is because they are a people who do not use their reason.﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you blame us for nothing except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that in terms of recompense with Allah? It is those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and among whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way."﴾

[p. 201] His statement: ﴿And when you call [to prayer]﴾, to the end of the verse. This is a rebuke of the Jews and a clarification of the evil of their conduct. When they heard the believers rising for the prayer, some of them would say to others: "They have stood up," or "May they not stand up," and other such words by which they made light of the call to prayer and of other things. Everything that has been mentioned of this is an example. al-Suddi mentioned that there was a Christian man in Medina who, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," would say: "May Allah burn the liar." He continued in this way until a lamp fell in his house one night and burned it, and the Christian was burned, may Allah curse him.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned that this act of theirs was only due to the absence of their reason, and that they were lacking it because it did not function as it should, so it was as if it had not existed.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the People of the Scripture: ﴿Do you blame us?﴾ Its meaning is: "Do you count against us a fault or a defect?" It is said "naqama" (with a fatha on the qaf) "yanqimu" (with a kasra), and this is the dialect upon which the recitation of the majority is based. It is also said "naqima" (with a kasra on the qaf) "yanqamu" (with a fatha), and upon this dialect Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu al-Barahsam and al-Nakha'i recited.

This verse is an eloquent and concise dialogue, and similar to it is the words of Allah: ﴿And they did not blame them except that they believed in Allah﴾ [al-Buruj: 8]. A parallel to this purpose in the use of the exception is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are notched with the blows of the ranks."

The majority recited "unzila" with a damma on the hamza, and likewise in the second instance. Abu Nuhayk recited "anzala" with a fatha on the hamza and the zay in both instances.

As for the words of Allah: ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, according to most of the interpreters it is coordinated with His statement "an [amanna]" [that we believed], so that the fact of their being disobedient would fall within what they blame. This meaning is not sound. It has been reported from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he said regarding this: "Due to their disobedience, they blamed us for believing."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This statement is correct in itself, but it does not suffice for establishing the meaning of the wording. It is only sound if the meaning of the dialogue is: "Do you blame us for nothing except the general state of our being believers and you being disobedient?" Then ﴿and that most of you are disobedient﴾ would be something stated by the one addressing them. This is like when you say to someone you are disputing with: "Do you blame me for nothing except that I am truthful and you are a liar?" He does not admit that he is a liar, nor does he blame that, but the meaning of your words is: "Do you blame anything except the whole of this state?"

Some of the interpreters said: His statement "and that most of you" is coordinated with "wa-ma" [and what], as if He said: "except that we believed in Allah, and in His books, and that most of you [are disobedient]."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a sound meaning, because the belief of the believers that the People of the Scripture who persist in disbelief in Muhammad are transgressors is something they blame. Allah mentioned "most of them" because among them are those who believed and were guided.

As for the words of Allah: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾, the majority recited it with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the ba'. Ibn Waththab and al-Nakha'i recited "unbi'ukum" with a sukun on the nun and a light ba', from "anba'a". The people recited "mathuba" with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the waw. Ibn Buraydah, al-A'raj, Nubayh and Ibn 'Imran recited "mathba" with a sukun on the tha' and a fatha on the waw. Abu al-Fath said: This is among what departed from its original pattern and is anomalous compared with its counterparts. Similar to it is the Arabs' saying: "al-fakiha maqwadatun ila al-adha" (with a sukun on the qaf and a fatha on the waw), whereas the analogical form would be "mathabatun" and "maqadatun." As for "mathubatun" with a damma on the tha', its original form is "mathwubatun," with the pattern "mafulatun" with a damma on the ayn; the vowel of the waw was transferred to the tha', and it was previously "mathwuwbatun," like "maqwulatun." The meaning in both readings is: "a return with Allah," that is, at the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. The Arabs say "tha'a, yathubu" when someone returns, and from this is the words of Allah: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125].

The commentators proceeded with this verse on the basis that those to whom it was commanded to say ﴿"Shall I inform you?"﴾ are the Jews and the disbelievers who take our religion as mockery and play. Al-Tabari said this, and others followed him, though he did not attribute anything in this to an earlier authority.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the believers, meaning: "Say, O Muhammad, to the believers: 'Shall I inform you of something worse than the state of these disobedient ones at the time of return to Allah? They are their predecessors whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry.'" In this case the reference of "that" is to their state of most of them being disobedient.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the present Children of Israel, and the reference of "that" is to the state of those present, namely that most of them are disobedient. Then "worse" (bi-sharr) and "further astray" (wa-adall) are comparative adjectives between two things which share in evil and error.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the present Children of Israel, and the reference of "that" is to the belief of the believers and their whole state. The comparative in "worse" and "further astray" can then be understood as meaning that the sharing in evil and error is in the belief of the Jews, whereas in reality there is no evil or error according to the believers, and they have no share with the Jews and the disbelievers in that. On this interpretation, the words ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ to the end of the verse are intended to include all the Children of Israel, both predecessors and successors, because a later generation is blamed and reproached for the blameworthy deeds of earlier ones when the later generation does not dissociate itself from what its predecessors did and does not condemn it, so it falls under the same ruling.

In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "man ghadiba Allahu 'alayhim wa-ja'alahum qiradatan wa-khanazira" [those on whom Allah became angry and whom He made apes and swine]. The curse (al-la'na) is removal from good.

As for the words of Allah "wa-ja'ala" [and made], it means "sayyara" (turned/made). Abu 'Ali, in his book al-Hujja, said it means "khalaqa" (created).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a Mu'tazili tendency from him, may Allah have mercy on him, because His statement ﴿and who worshipped the Taghut﴾ has as its implied construction "and whoever worshipped the Taghut," and the Mu'tazila do not hold that Allah turns anyone into a worshipper of the Taghut. The story of their transformation into apes has already been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. As for their transformation into swine, it is reported that it was due to a woman among the Children of Israel who was a believer. A king among them disbelieved in a city among their cities, and the people of his kingdom disbelieved with him. The woman called a group of people to support the religion, and they answered her. She went out with them, and they were defeated. Then she did it a second and a third time, and each time her group was defeated. She despaired and spent the night in grief. When morning came, she saw the people of that city running about in its surroundings as swine. She said: "Now I know that Allah has honored His religion and preferred His religion." 'Amr ibn Kathir ibn Aflah, a client of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, said: The transformation of the Children of Israel was only at the hands of that woman.

As for the words of Allah ﴿and who worshipped the Taghut﴾, its implied construction is "and whoever worshipped the Taghut." This is coordinated with His statement ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, or it is an object of "wa-ja'ala" [and made]. On this point Abu 'Ali says that "ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" [created].

The readers differed over this word. Hamza alone recited "wa-'abuda al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." This is because "'abud" is an intensive form like "yaqudh" and "nadus"; it is a singular noun intended to refer to a kind, and it is patterned as an adjective, because "'abud" is originally an adjective, even if it is used as a noun, and this does not remove it from the ruling of an adjective. Therefore it is not impossible to form from it the pattern of adjectives. This reading was also recited by al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Waththab, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"O sons of Lubayna, your mother
is a slave-woman, and your father is an 'abud."

Al-Tabari and others cited it with a damma on the ba'. The rest recited ﴿wa-'abada al-taghut﴾ with a fatha on the ayn and the ba', and with the verb governing "al-taghut" in the accusative, which has already been mentioned. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "'abadu al-taghut" with the past verb attached to a plural pronoun. Ibn Mas'ud, as reported by 'Abd al-Ghaffar from 'Alqama from him, recited "wa-'abuda al-taghutu" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', and a damma on the ta' of "al-taghut," on the basis that "'abuda" became like a character trait and a familiar, known matter, so it has the sense of "faqaha," "sharufa" and "zarufa" (to be learned, noble, and refined). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "wa-'abadu al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn and the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-taghut," on the basis that the intended meaning is "'abadat al-taghut" [worshippers of the Taghut], and the ta' marbuta was dropped for lightness. Similar to it is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"He stood, its governors, and they gave him to drink Sarkhad,"

meaning "wulatuha" [its governors], which was shortened for lightness. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, in the transmission of 'Abbad from him, recited "wa-'abdu al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn, a sukun on the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-taghut," and this is taken as a singular noun of kind intended to mean a plural. It has been reported from al-Hasan, through a route other than 'Abbad, that he recited with a fatha on the ayn and the dal, a sukun on the ba', and a fatha on the ta' of "al-taghut." This may be explained in two ways: one is that he intended "wa-'abdan al-taghut" [and worshipping the Taghut] and dropped the tanwin, as in the verse of the poet: "...and not remembering Allah except a little." The other is that he intended the past verb "'abada" and made the ba' sukun, in the manner in which the middle letter of a verb is made sukun in the verse of the poet: "And not everyone who is cheated, even if he trades poorly..." because the lam of "salafa" is sukun. Similar to this is Abu al-Samal's reading "wa-lu'inu bi-ma qalu" [and they were cursed for what they said]. These are readings in which the ayn is a fatha.

Abu Waqid al-A'rabi recited, in the transmission of al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl from him, "wa-'ubbada al-taghuti" with a damma on the ayn, a shadda on the ba' with a fatha, an alif after it, a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta' of "al-taghut." This is the plural of "'abid" [worshipper]. 'Awn al-'Uqayli, also in the transmission of al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl from him, recited "wa-'abidu al-taghuti" on the pattern "fa'il," with the dal in the nominative. Abu 'Amr said: Its implied construction is "wa-hum 'abidu al-taghut" [and they are worshippers of the Taghut].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is then a noun of kind. Ikrima reported from Ibn 'Abbas "wa-'abidu al-taghuti" with a plural pronoun. Some transmitters said of this last reading that it is a permissible possibility (tajwiz), not a recitation. Ibn Buraydah recited "wa-'abida al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn and the dal, a kasra on the ba' and the ta'. Some Basran readers recited "wa-'ibada al-taghuti" with a kasra on the ayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, an alif between them, and a kasra on the ta'. Abu al-Fath said: It is possible that this is the plural of "'abid," like "qa'im" and "qiyam," "sa'im" and "siyam," and it may also be the plural of "'abd," and "'ibad" rarely occurs attached to other than Allah. Sibawayh cited the verse:

"Do you threaten me with your people, O son of Hajl,
with the arrogant ones who think themselves 'ibad?"

Abu al-Fath said: He means "'ibad Adam" [the servants of Adam], peace be upon him. If he meant "'ibad Allah" [servants of Allah], that would be nothing with which anyone is insulted, since all creation are servants of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This linking of "'ibad" to Adam, peace be upon him, is anomalous and far-fetched, and the objection to it remains. This is not something that one imagines the poet intended; rather he meant "al-'abid" [the slaves], but the rhyme drove him to "al-'ibad," since this is said of one who has acquired some kind of dominion. It has been mentioned that the Arabs of al-Hira in Iraq were only called "al-'Ibad" because they entered the obedience of Kisra, and his kingdom subjugated them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 58–60 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tabari mentioned from Buraydah al-Aslami that he used to recite: "wa-'Abida al-Shaytan" (and who worship the Shaytan), with a fatha on the ʿayn, a fatha on the dal, a kasra on the ba', and an alif before it; and he mentioned "al-Shaytan" in place of "al-Taghut." These are readings that contain an alif.

Ibn ʿAbbas, as narrated from ʿIkrimah, and Mujahid and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "wa-ʿUbuda al-Taghut" (and servants of the Taghut), with a damma on the ʿayn and the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is the plural of "ʿabd," like "rahn" and "ruhun," and "saqf" and "suquf." Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab said: it is the plural of "ʿabid," like "sharif" and "shuruf," and from it is the saying of the singing girl:

Ala ya Hamz lil-shuruf al-niwa'
wa-hunna muʿaqqalat bil-fina'

Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: it is the plural of "ʿabid" (sic: of "ʿabid" in the sense of "ʿabid"), and he recited:

Unsub al-ʿabd ila aba'ihi
aswad al-jildah min qawmin ʿubud

(p-208) And al-Aʿmash and others recited: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a shadda on the fathah-marked ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is according to the plural of "ʿabid," like "darib" and "durrab." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, and al-Aʿmash, in the narration of Harun, recited: "wa-ʿUbida al-Taghutu," with a damma on the ʿayn, a kasra on the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a damma on the ta', as you say: "Duriba Zayd." Al-Tabari weakened this reading, though it is well-founded.

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud that he recited: "wa-ʿUbidat al-Taghut," as you say: "Duribat al-mar'ah."

ʿAlqamah narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud: "wa-ʿUbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This also is a form of intensive (mubalaghah), a singular noun intended here as a plural, patterned like "hutam" and "lubad."

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghuta," on the pattern of "fuʿʿal," with a damma on the fa', a shadda on the fathah-marked ʿayn, a fatha on the lam, and a fatha on the ta' as an accusative. This can be explained as him intending "wa-ʿUbbadan" (with tanwin), then the tanwin was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, as in the saying "wa-la dhakir Allah," whose parallel has already been mentioned.

"Al-Taghut" is everything that is worshipped besides Allah, whether an idol, or a human being who is pleased with that, or a devil. I have fully explained its interpretation in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Makanan" (a place/state) may mean: "in the Hereafter," so that "makan" is in its literal sense, i.e., the place, since their place is Jahannam; or it may mean: "in this world," in which case it is a metaphor for standing and condition.

﴿Sawa' al-sabil﴾ means its middle; from it is the saying of the Arabs: "I stood until the middle of my path ended" (qama hatta inqata'a sawaʾi). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55] (p-209). The line of uprightness in paths is firmly established to the utmost degree only in the middles; therefore sawa' was singled out for mention. And from the word sawa' is derived the term "khatt al-istiwa'" (the line of equilibrium).

That is because they are a people who do not use their reason.﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you blame us for nothing except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that in terms of recompense with Allah? The commentators proceeded with this verse on the basis that those to whom it was commanded to say ﴿"Shall I inform you?"﴾ are the Jews and the disbelievers who take our religion as mockery and play. Al-Tabari said this, and others followed him, though he did not attribute anything in this to an earlier authority.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the believers, meaning: "Say, O Muhammad, to the believers: 'Shall I inform you of something worse than the state of these disobedient ones at the time of return to Allah? They are their predecessors whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry.'" In this case the reference of "that" is to their state of most of them being disobedient.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the present Children of Israel, and the reference of "that" is to the state of those present, namely that most of them are disobedient. Then "worse" (bi-sharr) and "further astray" (wa-adall) are comparative adjectives between two things which share in evil and error.

The verse may also allow that the speech is addressed to the present Children of Israel, and the reference of "that" is to the belief of the believers and their whole state. The comparative in "worse" and "further astray" can then be understood as meaning that the sharing in evil and error is in the belief of the Jews, whereas in reality there is no evil or error according to the believers, and they have no share with the Jews and the disbelievers in that. On this interpretation, the words ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾ to the end of the verse are intended to include all the Children of Israel, both predecessors and successors, because a later generation is blamed and reproached for the blameworthy deeds of earlier ones when the later generation does not dissociate itself from what its predecessors did and does not condemn it, so it falls under the same ruling.

In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "man ghadiba Allahu 'alayhim wa-ja'alahum qiradatan wa-khanazira" [those on whom Allah became angry and whom He made apes and swine]. The curse (al-la'na) is removal from good.

As for the words of Allah "wa-ja'ala" [and made], it means "sayyara" (turned/made). Abu 'Ali, in his book al-Hujja, said it means "khalaqa" (created).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a Mu'tazili tendency from him, may Allah have mercy on him, because His statement ﴿and who worshipped the Taghut﴾ has as its implied construction "and whoever worshipped the Taghut," and the Mu'tazila do not hold that Allah turns anyone into a worshipper of the Taghut. The story of their transformation into apes has already been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. As for their transformation into swine, it is reported that it was due to a woman among the Children of Israel who was a believer. A king among them disbelieved in a city among their cities, and the people of his kingdom disbelieved with him. The woman called a group of people to support the religion, and they answered her. She went out with them, and they were defeated. Then she did it a second and a third time, and each time her group was defeated. She despaired and spent the night in grief. When morning came, she saw the people of that city running about in its surroundings as swine. She said: "Now I know that Allah has honored His religion and preferred His religion." 'Amr ibn Kathir ibn Aflah, a client of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, said: The transformation of the Children of Israel was only at the hands of that woman.

As for the words of Allah ﴿and who worshipped the Taghut﴾, its implied construction is "and whoever worshipped the Taghut." This is coordinated with His statement ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, or it is an object of "wa-ja'ala" [and made]. On this point Abu 'Ali says that "ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" [created].

The readers differed over this word. Hamza alone recited "wa-'abuda al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." This is because "'abud" is an intensive form like "yaqudh" and "nadus"; it is a singular noun intended to refer to a kind, and it is patterned as an adjective, because "'abud" is originally an adjective, even if it is used as a noun, and this does not remove it from the ruling of an adjective. Therefore it is not impossible to form from it the pattern of adjectives. This reading was also recited by al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Waththab, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"O sons of Lubayna, your mother
is a slave-woman, and your father is an 'abud."

Al-Tabari and others cited it with a damma on the ba'. The rest recited ﴿wa-'abada al-taghut﴾ with a fatha on the ayn and the ba', and with the verb governing "al-taghut" in the accusative, which has already been mentioned. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "'abadu al-taghut" with the past verb attached to a plural pronoun. Ibn Mas'ud, as reported by 'Abd al-Ghaffar from 'Alqama from him, recited "wa-'abuda al-taghutu" with a fatha on the ayn, a damma on the ba', and a damma on the ta' of "al-taghut," on the basis that "'abuda" became like a character trait and a familiar, known matter, so it has the sense of "faqaha," "sharufa" and "zarufa" (to be learned, noble, and refined). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "wa-'abadu al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn and the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-taghut," on the basis that the intended meaning is "'abadat al-taghut" [worshippers of the Taghut], and the ta' marbuta was dropped for lightness. Similar to it is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"He stood, its governors, and they gave him to drink Sarkhad,"

meaning "wulatuha" [its governors], which was shortened for lightness. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, in the transmission of 'Abbad from him, recited "wa-'abdu al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn, a sukun on the ba', and a kasra on the ta' of "al-taghut," and this is taken as a singular noun of kind intended to mean a plural. It has been reported from al-Hasan, through a route other than 'Abbad, that he recited with a fatha on the ayn and the dal, a sukun on the ba', and a fatha on the ta' of "al-taghut." This may be explained in two ways: one is that he intended "wa-'abdan al-taghut" [and worshipping the Taghut] and dropped the tanwin, as in the verse of the poet: "...and not remembering Allah except a little." The other is that he intended the past verb "'abada" and made the ba' sukun, in the manner in which the middle letter of a verb is made sukun in the verse of the poet: "And not everyone who is cheated, even if he trades poorly..." because the lam of "salafa" is sukun. Similar to this is Abu al-Samal's reading "wa-lu'inu bi-ma qalu" [and they were cursed for what they said]. These are readings in which the ayn is a fatha.

This is the plural of "'abid" [worshipper]. 'Awn al-'Uqayli, also in the transmission of al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl from him, recited "wa-'abidu al-taghuti" on the pattern "fa'il," with the dal in the nominative. Abu 'Amr said: Its implied construction is "wa-hum 'abidu al-taghut" [and they are worshippers of the Taghut].

Some transmitters said of this last reading that it is a permissible possibility (tajwiz), not a recitation. Ibn Buraydah recited "wa-'abida al-taghuti" with a fatha on the ayn and the dal, a kasra on the ba' and the ta'. Some Basran readers recited "wa-'ibada al-taghuti" with a kasra on the ayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, an alif between them, and a kasra on the ta'. Abu al-Fath said: It is possible that this is the plural of "'abid," like "qa'im" and "qiyam," "sa'im" and "siyam," and it may also be the plural of "'abd," and "'ibad" rarely occurs attached to other than Allah. "Do you threaten me with your people, O son of Hajl,
with the arrogant ones who think themselves 'ibad?"
