It has been mentioned that the Arabs of al-Hira in Iraq were only called "al-'Ibad" because they entered the obedience of Kisra, and his kingdom subjugated them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 58–60 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tabari mentioned from Buraydah al-Aslami that he used to recite: "wa-'Abida al-Shaytan" (and who worship the Shaytan), with a fatha on the ʿayn, a fatha on the dal, a kasra on the ba', and an alif before it; and he mentioned "al-Shaytan" in place of "al-Taghut." These are readings that contain an alif.

Ibn ʿAbbas, as narrated from ʿIkrimah, and Mujahid and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "wa-ʿUbuda al-Taghut" (and servants of the Taghut), with a damma on the ʿayn and the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is the plural of "ʿabd," like "rahn" and "ruhun," and "saqf" and "suquf." Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab said: it is the plural of "ʿabid," like "sharif" and "shuruf," and from it is the saying of the singing girl:

Ala ya Hamz lil-shuruf al-niwa'
wa-hunna muʿaqqalat bil-fina'

Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: it is the plural of "ʿabid" (sic: of "ʿabid" in the sense of "ʿabid"), and he recited:

Unsub al-ʿabd ila aba'ihi
aswad al-jildah min qawmin ʿubud

(p-208) And al-Aʿmash and others recited: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a shadda on the fathah-marked ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is according to the plural of "ʿabid," like "darib" and "durrab." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, and al-Aʿmash, in the narration of Harun, recited: "wa-ʿUbida al-Taghutu," with a damma on the ʿayn, a kasra on the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a damma on the ta', as you say: "Duriba Zayd." Al-Tabari weakened this reading, though it is well-founded.

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud that he recited: "wa-ʿUbidat al-Taghut," as you say: "Duribat al-mar'ah."

ʿAlqamah narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud: "wa-ʿUbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This also is a form of intensive (mubalaghah), a singular noun intended here as a plural, patterned like "hutam" and "lubad."

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghuta," on the pattern of "fuʿʿal," with a damma on the fa', a shadda on the fathah-marked ʿayn, a fatha on the lam, and a fatha on the ta' as an accusative. This can be explained as him intending "wa-ʿUbbadan" (with tanwin), then the tanwin was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, as in the saying "wa-la dhakir Allah," whose parallel has already been mentioned.

"Al-Taghut" is everything that is worshipped besides Allah, whether an idol, or a human being who is pleased with that, or a devil. I have fully explained its interpretation in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Makanan" (a place/state) may mean: "in the Hereafter," so that "makan" is in its literal sense, i.e., the place, since their place is Jahannam; or it may mean: "in this world," in which case it is a metaphor for standing and condition.

﴿Sawa' al-sabil﴾ means its middle; from it is the saying of the Arabs: "I stood until the middle of my path ended" (qama hatta inqata'a sawaʾi). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55] (p-209). The line of uprightness in paths is firmly established to the utmost degree only in the middles; therefore sawa' was singled out for mention. And from the word sawa' is derived the term "khatt al-istiwa'" (the line of equilibrium).

[p. 201] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿When you call to the prayer, they take it as mockery and play. That is because they are a people who do not use their reason.﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you blame us for nothing except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that in terms of recompense with Allah? It is those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and among whom He made apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut. Those are worse in position and further astray from the right way."﴾

[p. 201] His statement: ﴿And when you call [to prayer]﴾, to the end of the verse. This is a rebuke of the Jews and a clarification of the evil of their conduct. When they heard the believers rising for the prayer, some of them would say to others: "They have stood up," or "May they not stand up," and other such words by which they made light of the call to prayer and of other things. Everything that has been mentioned of this is an example. al-Suddi mentioned that there was a Christian man in Medina who, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," would say: "May Allah burn the liar." He continued in this way until a lamp fell in his house one night and burned it, and the Christian was burned, may Allah curse him.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned that this act of theirs was only due to the absence of their reason, and that they were lacking it because it did not function as it should, so it was as if it had not existed.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the People of the Scripture: ﴿Do you blame us?﴾ Its meaning is: "Do you count against us a fault or a defect?" It is said "naqama" (with a fatha on the qaf) "yanqimu" (with a kasra), and this is the dialect upon which the recitation of the majority is based. It is also said "naqima" (with a kasra on the qaf) "yanqamu" (with a fatha), and upon this dialect Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu al-Barahsam and al-Nakha'i recited.

This verse is an eloquent and concise dialogue, and similar to it is the words of Allah: ﴿And they did not blame them except that they believed in Allah﴾ [al-Buruj: 8]. A parallel to this purpose in the use of the exception is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are notched with the blows of the ranks."

The majority recited "unzila" with a damma on the hamza, and likewise in the second instance. Abu Nuhayk recited "anzala" with a fatha on the hamza and the zay in both instances.

As for the words of Allah: ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, according to most of the interpreters it is coordinated with His statement "an [amanna]" [that we believed], so that the fact of their being disobedient would fall within what they blame. This meaning is not sound. It has been reported from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he said regarding this: "Due to their disobedience, they blamed us for believing."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This statement is correct in itself, but it does not suffice for establishing the meaning of the wording. It is only sound if the meaning of the dialogue is: "Do you blame us for nothing except the general state of our being believers and you being disobedient?" Then ﴿and that most of you are disobedient﴾ would be something stated by the one addressing them. This is like when you say to someone you are disputing with: "Do you blame me for nothing except that I am truthful and you are a liar?" He does not admit that he is a liar, nor does he blame that, but the meaning of your words is: "Do you blame anything except the whole of this state?"

Some of the interpreters said: His statement "and that most of you" is coordinated with "wa-ma" [and what], as if He said: "except that we believed in Allah, and in His books, and that most of you [are disobedient]."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a sound meaning, because the belief of the believers that the People of the Scripture who persist in disbelief in Muhammad are transgressors is something they blame. Allah mentioned "most of them" because among them are those who believed and were guided.

It has been mentioned that the Arabs of al-Hira in Iraq were only called "al-'Ibad" because they entered the obedience of Kisra, and his kingdom subjugated them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 58–60 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tabari mentioned from Buraydah al-Aslami that he used to recite: "wa-'Abida al-Shaytan" (and who worship the Shaytan), with a fatha on the ʿayn, a fatha on the dal, a kasra on the ba', and an alif before it; and he mentioned "al-Shaytan" in place of "al-Taghut." These are readings that contain an alif.

Ibn ʿAbbas, as narrated from ʿIkrimah, and Mujahid and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "wa-ʿUbuda al-Taghut" (and servants of the Taghut), with a damma on the ʿayn and the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is the plural of "ʿabd," like "rahn" and "ruhun," and "saqf" and "suquf." Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab said: it is the plural of "ʿabid," like "sharif" and "shuruf," and from it is the saying of the singing girl:

Ala ya Hamz lil-shuruf al-niwa'
wa-hunna muʿaqqalat bil-fina'

Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: it is the plural of "ʿabid" (sic: of "ʿabid" in the sense of "ʿabid"), and he recited:

Unsub al-ʿabd ila aba'ihi
aswad al-jildah min qawmin ʿubud

(p-208) And al-Aʿmash and others recited: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a shadda on the fathah-marked ba', a fatha on the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This is according to the plural of "ʿabid," like "darib" and "durrab." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, and al-Aʿmash, in the narration of Harun, recited: "wa-ʿUbida al-Taghutu," with a damma on the ʿayn, a kasra on the ba', a fatha on the dal, and a damma on the ta', as you say: "Duriba Zayd." Al-Tabari weakened this reading, though it is well-founded.

It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud that he recited: "wa-ʿUbidat al-Taghut," as you say: "Duribat al-mar'ah."

ʿAlqamah narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud: "wa-ʿUbada al-Taghut," with a damma on the ʿayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, and a kasra on the ta'. This also is a form of intensive (mubalaghah), a singular noun intended here as a plural, patterned like "hutam" and "lubad."

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "wa-ʿUbbada al-Taghuta," on the pattern of "fuʿʿal," with a damma on the fa', a shadda on the fathah-marked ʿayn, a fatha on the lam, and a fatha on the ta' as an accusative. This can be explained as him intending "wa-ʿUbbadan" (with tanwin), then the tanwin was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, as in the saying "wa-la dhakir Allah," whose parallel has already been mentioned.

"Al-Taghut" is everything that is worshipped besides Allah, whether an idol, or a human being who is pleased with that, or a devil. I have fully explained its interpretation in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Makanan" (a place/state) may mean: "in the Hereafter," so that "makan" is in its literal sense, i.e., the place, since their place is Jahannam; or it may mean: "in this world," in which case it is a metaphor for standing and condition.

﴿Sawa' al-sabil﴾ means its middle; from it is the saying of the Arabs: "I stood until the middle of my path ended" (qama hatta inqata'a sawaʾi). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55] (p-209). The line of uprightness in paths is firmly established to the utmost degree only in the middles; therefore sawa' was singled out for mention. And from the word sawa' is derived the term "khatt al-istiwa'" (the line of equilibrium).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 61–64:**

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they entered with disbelief and they left with it. And Allah knows best what they were concealing.﴾ ﴿You see many of them hastening toward sin and transgression and consuming what is unlawful. How evil is what they have been doing!﴾ ﴿Why do the rabbanis (divine scholars) and the rabbis not forbid them from their sinful speech and their consumption of what is unlawful? How evil is what they have been producing!﴾ ﴿The Jews say, "Allah's hand is chained." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they have said. Rather, His hands are both outstretched; He spends as He wills. What has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it, and they strive upon the earth in corruption. And Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾

The pronoun in "jā'ūkum" (they came to you) refers to the Jews contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ), and especially to the hypocrites. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and al-Suddi stated this explicitly.

Then Allah informed about them that they entered while they were disbelievers, and they left in the same state. Admonition did not benefit them, and reminder had no effect on them. His statement "wa-hum" (while they) is a clarification that removes the possibility that the sentence might mean that some people enter in disbelief and then believe, and others leave while they are disbelievers. Thus, the phrase "they have entered with disbelief and they have left with it" would apply to all of them. The statement of Allah, "wa-hum qad kharajū bihi" (and they have indeed left with it), removed this possibility; meaning, they themselves, in their very persons. Then He exposed them with His statement, "Allah knows best what they were concealing," meaning, of disbelief.

His statement to His Prophet, "wa-tarā" (and you see), may be from sight by the eye, or from sight by the heart. In that case, "yusāri'ūna" (they hasten) is the second object. According to the first possibility, "yusāri'ūna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

"Fī al-ithm" (in sin) means in the things that necessitate sin, since sin is essentially the judgment attached to the person who commits disobedience, and the status he comes to bear when the wrongdoing occurs. Among them is their disbelief. "Wal-'udwān" (and transgression) is a verbal noun from "'adā al-rajul," meaning he wronged and exceeded the limit. "Al-suḥt" (what is unlawful) is bribery and all of their evil earnings. The lām in "labi'sa" (how evil) is the lām of oath. Abu Haywa recited "wal-'idwān" with a kasra on the 'ayn.

His statement, "Why do the rabbanis and the rabbis not forbid them…", is a specification which, within it, contains a rebuke to them, since they abandoned what was obligatory. Al-Ṭabarī said: "All the scholars say there is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke of the scholars than this verse, nor more frightening for them." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an that I fear more than this one: that we do not forbid." Ibn 'Abbas said something similar. Al-Jarrāḥ and Abu Wāqid recited "al-rabbāniyyūn" with a kasra on the rā'. Its singular is "rabbī," either attributed to the knowledge of the Lord (rabb), or from the nurturing of people with the basics of knowledge before its advanced parts. The nūn was added to the nisba for emphasis, as in "sha'rānī," "manẓarānī," and "makhbarānī." Al-Ḥasan said: "al-rabbānī" is a scholar of the Gospel, and "al-ḥabr" is a scholar of the Torah.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His statement regarding "al-rabbānī" is anomalous and far-fetched.

"Al-aḥbār" (the rabbis): its singular is "ḥabr," with a kasra or fatḥa on the ḥā'. They are the scholars who do not exert themselves to reform people, nor are they burdened with that. The rabbānī is the scholar who manages and reforms. His statement, "'an qawlihimu al-ithm" (from their sinful speech), clearly means that sin here refers to disbelief. It may also refer to the rest of their abhorrent statements about the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. Ibn 'Abbas recited "bi'sa mā kānū yaṣna'ūn" without the lām of oath.

His statement, "And the Jews said…" up to "…does not love the corrupters": this verse enumerates a major part of their statements and disbelief. That is, "whoever says this monstrous thing should not be surprised if he is hypocritical toward you, O Muhammad, and strives to reject the command of Allah which was revealed to you." Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the interpreters said: the meaning of their statement is stinginess (tabkhīl). They were afflicted by a drought and hardship, so they uttered this phrase, meaning that Allah was stingy toward them with provision and abundance. This meaning resembles His statement, "And do not make your hand chained to your neck" (al-Isrā' 29). The intent there is "do not be stingy." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The example of the miser and the one who gives charity…" (the hadith). Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naqqāsh mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Finḥāṣ the Jew, and that he said it. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: their statement, "Allah's hand is chained," means only "from His punishment," so it is, according to this, in the sense of their statement, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved" (al-Mā'ida 18). Al-Suddī said: they meant by it that His hand is chained until He returns our kingdom to us.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It seems they meant that His strength had diminished, until they were overcome in their kingdom. The apparent doctrine of the Jews, may Allah curse them, in this statement is anthropomorphism (tajsīm). Likewise, many of their statements imply this.

His statement, "ghullat aydīhim" (their hands are chained), is an invocation against them, and it may also be a report. Both possibilities are valid, and it may refer to this world or to the Hereafter. If it is a report about this world, the meaning is: "their hands were chained from goodness, from spending in the way of Allah, and the like." If it is a report about the Hereafter, the meaning is: "they are chained in the fire of Jahannam," that is: "this has been decreed upon them, and the decree has been carried out, just as the curse has been decreed upon them because of this statement of theirs and what is similar to it." Abu al-Sammāl recited "wa-lu'inū" with a sukūn on the 'ayn, and that is intended for lightness, especially here for the descent from a ḍamma to a kasra.

His statement, "bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān" (rather, His hands are both outstretched): the creed regarding this meaning is the negation of likeness to Allah, that He is not a body, nor has He a limb, nor is He likened, nor is He given a modality, nor is He confined to a direction like the substances, nor do events inhere in Him, exalted is He above what the falsifiers say.

Then the scholars differed about what should be believed regarding His statement "bal yadāhu," and His statement "bi-yadayya" (Ṣād 75), "'amilat aydīnā" (Yā-Sīn 71), "yadu Allāhi fawqa aydīhim" (al-Fatḥ 10), "wa-li-tuṣna'a 'alā 'aynī" (Ṭā-Hā 39), "tajrī bi-a'yuninā" (al-Qamar 14), "wāṣbir li-ḥukmi rabbika fa-innaka bi-a'yuninā" (al-Ṭūr 48), and "kullu shay'in hālikun illā wajhahu" (al-Qaṣaṣ 88), and what is similar to these. A group of scholars, among them al-Sha'bī, Ibn al-Musayyib, and Sufyān, said: "These things are believed in and recited as Allah stated them, one does not strain to interpret them, nor does one probe deeply into them."

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a position that is unstable, because those who hold it agree that these expressions are not to be taken literally in the language of the Arabs. When they do this, they have already reflected, and silence about the matter after this becomes something that misleads the common people and bewilders the ignorant.

The majority of the Ummah said: "Rather, these matters are interpreted according to the rules of language, the figurative usage of metaphor, and other of the varieties of Arabic speech." They said regarding "al-'ayn" and "al-a'yun" that it is an expression for knowledge and perception, as one says, "So-and-so is under the watch of so-and-so," when he is cared for in his affairs even though he is absent from him. They said regarding "al-wajh" that it is an expression for the essence and its attributes. They said regarding "al-yad," "al-yamīn," and "al-aydī" that they sometimes come with the meaning of "power," as the Arabs say, "I have no hand (yad) in such-and-such." Sometimes they come with the meaning of "favour," as it is said, "So-and-so has a hand (yad) with so-and-so." They may mean "dominion," as you say, "So-and-so's hand is over his land." When these meanings come from Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, they are expressed by "yad," or "aydī," or "yadayn," in use according to the eloquence of the Arabs and because of the brevity it contains. This is the position of Abu al-Ma'ālī and the skilled scholars.

A group of scholars, among them al-Qāḍī Ibn al-Ṭayyib, said: all of these are attributes additional to the essence, affirmed for Allah without any likeness or limitation. Al-Ṭabarī and others mentioned this.

Ibn 'Abbas said regarding this verse: "yadāhu" means "His two favours." Then the people's expressions differed in specifying the two favours. It was said: the favour of this world and the favour of the Hereafter. It was said: the outward favour and the inward favour. It was said: the favour of rain and the favour of plants.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What appears is that His statement, "bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān," is an expression for His bounty in general, and it was expressed with two hands in accordance with the manner of the Arabs in their saying, "So-and-so spends with both his hands." From this is the statement of the poet, al-A'shā:

*Your two hands are hands of glory: one palm is beneficial,*
*and a palm which, when wealth is withheld, spends.*

What supports that the two hands here mean bounty is the context of spending. Abu 'Amr al-Dānī said: Abu 'Abd Allāh recited "bal yadāhu basṭatān" (with the feminine dual of basṭa), as one says "yadun basṭah," meaning unrestricted. It is narrated from him as "bas̱ṭān."

His statement, "wa-la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa-kufran" (what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief): this is an announcement to Muhammad (ﷺ). These Jews were so obstinate and far from the truth that when they hear these secrets which are theirs, and the statements that no one other than them knows, descending upon you, they transgress and disbelieve. Their proper response would have been to believe, since they know that you could not know them except from Allah. But they are so obstinate that this increases them in transgression. Allah specified "kathīran" (many), since among them are those who believed in Allah, and those who do not transgress entirely.

His statement, "wa-alqaynā baynahumu al-'adāwata wal-baghḍā'" (We have cast among them enmity and hatred): it is coordinated with His statement, "And the Jews said," so these are narratives, some of which are conjoined to others. Enmity (al-'adāwa) is more specific than hatred (al-baghḍā'), because every enemy hates, but one may hate someone who is not an enemy. It seems enmity is a well-known thing from which action and war arise, whereas hatred may not go beyond the souls. Allah has cast both matters upon the Children of Israel.

His statement, "kullamā awqadū nāran lil-ḥarbi aṭfa'ahā Allāh" (every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it): this is an eloquent metaphor which indicates the breaking up of their gatherings, the scattering of their opinions, and the dispersal of their word. The verse may be an informing about the condition of their ancestors, that is, since they disobeyed and transgressed, and Allah destroyed their kingdom, He struck them with these matters, so no banner of theirs rises until the Day of Resurrection, and they do not fight together except in fortified villages. This is the statement of al-Rabī' and al-Suddī and others. Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: every time they kindle a fire for war against Muhammad, Allah extinguishes it. According to this, the verse is good tidings for Muhammad (ﷺ) and the believers, and an allusion to the Jews present in his time.

His statement, "wa-yas'awna fil-arḍi" (and they strive upon the earth): the meaning of "sa'y" (striving) in this verse is action and deed. Striving may also come in the sense of moving on foot, as in His statement, "fa-isʿaw ilā dhikri Allāh" (so hasten to the remembrance of Allah) (al-Jumu'a 9). Although Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Muwaṭṭa' that the striving in "fa-isʿaw ilā dhikri Allāh" is action and deed, other people of knowledge understood it as on foot, and this is the apparent meaning given the context of the narrowness of time and the transitivity with "ilā" (to). The recitation of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb supports it: "fa-amḍū ilā dhikri Allāh" (so proceed to the remembrance of Allah).

His statement, "wallāhu lā yuḥibbu al-mufsidīn" (and Allah does not love the corrupters): that is, there does not appear from their actions, in this world and the Hereafter, anything that would necessitate love.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What appears is that His statement, "bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān," is an expression for His bounty in general, and it was expressed with two hands in accordance with the manner of the Arabs in their saying, "So-and-so spends with both his hands." From this is the statement of the poet, al-A'shā:

*Your two hands are hands of glory: one palm is beneficial,*
*and a palm which, when wealth is withheld, spends.*

What supports that the two hands here mean bounty is the context of spending. Abu 'Amr al-Dānī said: Abu 'Abd Allāh recited "bal yadāhu basṭatān" (with the feminine dual of basṭa), as one says "yadun basṭah," meaning unrestricted. It is narrated from him as "bas̱ṭān."

His statement, "wa-la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa-kufran" (what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief): this is an announcement to Muhammad (ﷺ). These Jews were so obstinate and far from the truth that when they hear these secrets which are theirs, and the statements that no one other than them knows, descending upon you, they transgress and disbelieve. Their proper response would have been to believe, since they know that you could not know them except from Allah. But they are so obstinate that this increases them in transgression. Allah specified "kathīran" (many), since among them are those who believed in Allah, and those who do not transgress entirely.

His statement, "wa-alqaynā baynahumu al-'adāwata wal-baghḍā'" (We have cast among them enmity and hatred): it is coordinated with His statement, "And the Jews said," so these are narratives, some of which are conjoined to others. Enmity (al-'adāwa) is more specific than hatred (al-baghḍā'), because every enemy hates, but one may hate someone who is not an enemy. It seems enmity is a well-known thing from which action and war arise, whereas hatred may not go beyond the souls. Allah has cast both matters upon the Children of Israel.

His statement, "kullamā awqadū nāran lil-ḥarbi aṭfa'ahā Allāh" (every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it): this is an eloquent metaphor which indicates the breaking up of their gatherings, the scattering of their opinions, and the dispersal of their word. The verse may be an informing about the condition of their ancestors, that is, since they disobeyed and transgressed, and Allah destroyed their kingdom, He struck them with these matters, so no banner of theirs rises until the Day of Resurrection, and they do not fight together except in fortified villages. This is the statement of al-Rabī' and al-Suddī and others. Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: every time they kindle a fire for war against Muhammad, Allah extinguishes it. According to this, the verse is good tidings for Muhammad (ﷺ) and the believers, and an allusion to the Jews present in his time.

His statement, "wa-yas'awna fil-arḍi" (and they strive upon the earth): the meaning of "sa'y" (striving) in this verse is action and deed. Striving may also come in the sense of moving on foot, as in His statement, "fa-isʿaw ilā dhikri Allāh" (so hasten to the remembrance of Allah) (al-Jumu'a 9). Although Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Muwaṭṭa' that the striving in "fa-isʿaw ilā dhikri Allāh" is action and deed, other people of knowledge understood it as on foot, and this is the apparent meaning given the context of the narrowness of time and the transitivity with "ilā" (to). The recitation of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb supports it: "fa-amḍū ilā dhikri Allāh" (so proceed to the remembrance of Allah).

His statement, "wallāhu lā yuḥibbu al-mufsidīn" (and Allah does not love the corrupters): that is, there does not appear from their actions, in this world and the Hereafter, anything that would necessitate love.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 65–68:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic:

﴿If the People of the Book had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do.﴾ ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you are not upon anything until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord. What has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.﴾

This verse may refer to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), but the more apparent meaning is that it refers to their predecessors. Those contemporaries are included in these circumstances in meaning. The purpose is to inform about those whose fires Allah extinguished and whom He humiliated because of their disobedience. If they had believed in Allah and His Book, and been mindful in carrying out His commands and prohibitions, their misdeeds would have been covered over, meaning concealed and removed, and they would have been admitted into Paradise.

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah﴾, that is, they had manifested its rulings. Its upholding is like the establishing of a market and the establishing of prayer. All of this is a metaphor drawn from the standing of a person, since standing is the most manifest posture of a human being.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"and the Gospel"﴾ implies that the Christians are included in the expression "People of the Book" in this verse. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what was revealed to them from their Lord﴾ means: "from revelation and sunnahs (ways) conveyed through the tongues of the prophets."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of ﴿from above them and from beneath their feet﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said the meaning is: "The sky would have given them its rain and its blessing, and the earth its plants, by the grace of Allah, exalted is He." Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and others reported that the expression is a metaphor and an exaggeration in abundance, as one says: "So-and-so has been overwhelmed by good from his head to his foot." Al-Naqqash mentioned that the meaning is: "They would have eaten from above them," that is, from the provision of Paradise, "and from beneath their feet," that is, from the provision of this world, since it comes from the plants of the earth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾. Its meaning: upright, balanced. Qasd (moderation) and iqtisad (moderation) mean balance, gentleness, and the good middle course in words and deeds.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is that among the Children of Israel there are those who are moderate regarding 'Isa (peace be upon him). They say, "He is the servant of Allah, a messenger, and a spirit from Him." Most of them went to extremes concerning him. Some of them said, "He is a god." On this path went the Romans, and whoever entered the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) at a later time. Others among them, who are the majority of the Children of Israel, said, "He is a human being born out of wedlock." Thus both extremes disbelieved. Mujahid said: "The moderate community" refers to the Muslims among the People of the Book, past and present.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: On this interpretation, al-Tabari's statement is derived. No one says of 'Isa, "He is a servant and a messenger," except a Muslim. Ibn Zayd said: they are the people of obedience to Allah among the People of the Book. This is the preferred view. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that by "the moderate community" he means the groups that did not oppose the prophets with the opposition of the unrestrained, open rebels.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is only appropriate to describe them as moderate in comparison with the rebellious, as one says of Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham: "He is moderate," in comparison with Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him.

Then He, exalted is He, described most of them with evil deeds in general. Al-Tabari held that this refers to their denial of the prophets, and the disbelief of the Jews in 'Isa, and the disbelief of all of the People of the Two Books in Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Sa'a﴾ in this verse is the conjugable (muta-sarrifah) form, as when you say, "the matter was bad (sa'a al-amr); it is bad (yasu'u)." Sa'a may also be used in the manner of ni'ma (excellent) and bi'sa (wretched), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the example﴾ [al-A'raf: 177]. That usage is different from this one. The usage in His saying ﴿Evil is the example﴾ [al-A'raf: 177] requires supposition and an implied element to be determined, in the way that ni'ma and bi'sa require it. But there is room to examine this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, to His saying: ﴿over the disbelieving people﴾.

This verse is a command from Allah to His Messenger to convey in full and completeness, because he had already conveyed. What is commanded in this verse is that he should not hold back from anything out of fear of anyone. That is because his message (ﷺ) included criticism of various kinds of disbelievers and an exposure of the corruption of their condition. He would encounter hardship from them, and at times he feared them before the revelation of this verse. So Allah said to him: ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, meaning completely and fully. Then He threatened him, exalted is He, with His saying: ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾, meaning: "If you leave out one thing, it is as if you have left out everything, and what you conveyed will not be counted as conveyed." So His saying ﴿and if you do not﴾ means "and if you do not complete it." A similar statement is the poet's verse:

You were asked and you neither withheld nor gave a gift,
So it is equal; there is no blame upon you, nor praise.

That is, you did not give what would be counted as a gift; otherwise the verse would be false.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالَتَهُ﴾ (fa-ma ballaghta risalatahu) in the singular. They recited in "al-An'am" ﴿حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسالاتِهِ﴾ (wherever He places His messages) in the plural, and likewise in "al-A'raf" ﴿بِرِسالاتِي﴾ (with My messages). Ibn Kathir recited the word risalah in the singular in all three places. Nafi' recited ﴿رِسالاتِهِ﴾ in the plural, and likewise in "al-An'am," but used the singular in "al-A'raf." Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited risalah in the plural in all three places. Hafs, transmitting from 'Asim, recited the singular in "al-'Uqud" and "al-An'am," and the plural in "al-A'raf." Whoever recites the singular, risalah, does so because the whole Sharia is one thing, a single whole, some of which derives from the rest. Whoever recites the plural does so because the Sharia contains many meanings, which came in pieces at different times.

'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her), said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad concealed any part of the revelation has indeed committed a great slander, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿O Messenger﴾," and the rest of the verse.

'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was being followed by his companions, who were guarding him. When this was revealed: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾, he went out and said: 'O people, go back to your places, for Allah has protected me.'"

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: This verse ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ was revealed because of the Bedouin who drew the sword of the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to kill him with it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: He was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, and the incident occurred during the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'.

Ibn Jurayj said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) feared the Quraysh. When this verse was revealed, up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾, he lay down on his back and said: 'Whoever wishes, let him abandon me'," twice or three times.

Ya'simuka (He will protect you) means: He will guard you and place a shield around you. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43]. From this is also the poet's verse:

I said, "Upon you is Malik, for Malik
...will protect you, if there is any protector among the people."

The protection (ismah) mentioned in the verse is from the fears that could cause a person to hold back from some part of the conveying, such as killing, capture, and bodily harm, and the like. As for the words of the disbelievers and the like, they are not included in the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. It is either specific to those whom Allah's knowledge has already determined will not believe, or it is general, on the basis that there is no guidance in disbelief, and Allah does not guide the disbeliever along the paths of his disbelief.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet Muhammad (upon him be blessings and peace) to say to the People of the Book present with him: ﴿You are not upon anything﴾, meaning: "upon anything upright, until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel." In upholding these two is faith in Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ refers to the Qur'an, as said by Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and others. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed His Prophet that many of them would rebel, because of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that the revelation of the Qur'an and the Sharia would increase them in disbelief and envy. Then He consoled him about them and belittled them with His saying: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, meaning: do not be sorrowful that they did not believe, and do not be concerned about them. Al-asa means grief. It is said, "The man grieved (asiya), yasa, asan," when he became sorrowful. From this is the verse of the rajaz poet:

And his eyes overflowed from the excess of grief.

Al-Tabari transmitted, through a chain going back to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: "Rafi' ibn Jariyah, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf, and Rafi' ibn Huraymilah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, that you believe in the Torah and in the prophethood of Musa, and that all of that is true?' He said: 'Yes, but you have introduced innovations, changed, and concealed.' They said: 'We hold to what is in our hands, for it is the truth, and we do not believe you or follow you.' So this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Say: O People of the Book﴾," up to the end of the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said the meaning is: "The sky would have given them its rain and its blessing, and the earth its plants, by the grace of Allah, exalted is He." Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and others reported that the expression is a metaphor and an exaggeration in abundance, as one says: "So-and-so has been overwhelmed by good from his head to his foot." Al-Naqqash mentioned that the meaning is: "They would have eaten from above them," that is, from the provision of Paradise, "and from beneath their feet," that is, from the provision of this world, since it comes from the plants of the earth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾. Its meaning: upright, balanced. Qasd (moderation) and iqtisad (moderation) mean balance, gentleness, and the good middle course in words and deeds.

Al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is that among the Children of Israel there are those who are moderate regarding 'Isa (peace be upon him). They say, "He is the servant of Allah, a messenger, and a spirit from Him." Most of them went to extremes concerning him. Some of them said, "He is a god." On this path went the Romans, and whoever entered the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) at a later time. Others among them, who are the majority of the Children of Israel, said, "He is a human being born out of wedlock." Thus both extremes disbelieved. Mujahid said: "The moderate community" refers to the Muslims among the People of the Book, past and present.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: On this interpretation, al-Tabari's statement is derived. No one says of 'Isa, "He is a servant and a messenger," except a Muslim. Ibn Zayd said: they are the people of obedience to Allah among the People of the Book. This is the preferred view. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that by "the moderate community" he means the groups that did not oppose the prophets with the opposition of the unrestrained, open rebels.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is only appropriate to describe them as moderate in comparison with the rebellious, as one says of Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham: "He is moderate," in comparison with Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him.

Then He, exalted is He, described most of them with evil deeds in general. Al-Tabari held that this refers to their denial of the prophets, and the disbelief of the Jews in 'Isa, and the disbelief of all of the People of the Two Books in Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Sa'a﴾ in this verse is the conjugable (muta-sarrifah) form, as when you say, "the matter was bad (sa'a al-amr); it is bad (yasu'u)." Sa'a may also be used in the manner of ni'ma (excellent) and bi'sa (wretched), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the example﴾ [al-A'raf: 177]. That usage is different from this one. The usage in His saying ﴿Evil is the example﴾ [al-A'raf: 177] requires supposition and an implied element to be determined, in the way that ni'ma and bi'sa require it. But there is room to examine this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, to His saying: ﴿over the disbelieving people﴾.

This verse is a command from Allah to His Messenger to convey in full and completeness, because he had already conveyed. What is commanded in this verse is that he should not hold back from anything out of fear of anyone. That is because his message (ﷺ) included criticism of various kinds of disbelievers and an exposure of the corruption of their condition. He would encounter hardship from them, and at times he feared them before the revelation of this verse. So Allah said to him: ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, meaning completely and fully. Then He threatened him, exalted is He, with His saying: ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾, meaning: "If you leave out one thing, it is as if you have left out everything, and what you conveyed will not be counted as conveyed." So His saying ﴿and if you do not﴾ means "and if you do not complete it." A similar statement is the poet's verse:

You were asked and you neither withheld nor gave a gift,
So it is equal; there is no blame upon you, nor praise.

That is, you did not give what would be counted as a gift; otherwise the verse would be false.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالَتَهُ﴾ (fa-ma ballaghta risalatahu) in the singular. They recited in "al-An'am" ﴿حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسالاتِهِ﴾ (wherever He places His messages) in the plural, and likewise in "al-A'raf" ﴿بِرِسالاتِي﴾ (with My messages). Ibn Kathir recited the word risalah in the singular in all three places. Nafi' recited ﴿رِسالاتِهِ﴾ in the plural, and likewise in "al-An'am," but used the singular in "al-A'raf." Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited risalah in the plural in all three places. Hafs, transmitting from 'Asim, recited the singular in "al-'Uqud" and "al-An'am," and the plural in "al-A'raf." Whoever recites the singular, risalah, does so because the whole Sharia is one thing, a single whole, some of which derives from the rest. Whoever recites the plural does so because the Sharia contains many meanings, which came in pieces at different times.

'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her), said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad concealed any part of the revelation has indeed committed a great slander, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿O Messenger﴾," and the rest of the verse.

'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was being followed by his companions, who were guarding him. When this was revealed: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾, he went out and said: 'O people, go back to your places, for Allah has protected me.'"

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: This verse ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ was revealed because of the Bedouin who drew the sword of the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to kill him with it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: He was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, and the incident occurred during the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'.

Ibn Jurayj said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) feared the Quraysh. When this verse was revealed, up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾, he lay down on his back and said: 'Whoever wishes, let him abandon me'," twice or three times.

I said, "Upon you is Malik, for Malik
...will protect you, if there is any protector among the people."

The protection (ismah) mentioned in the verse is from the fears that could cause a person to hold back from some part of the conveying, such as killing, capture, and bodily harm, and the like. As for the words of the disbelievers and the like, they are not included in the verse.

It is either specific to those whom Allah's knowledge has already determined will not believe, or it is general, on the basis that there is no guidance in disbelief, and Allah does not guide the disbeliever along the paths of his disbelief.

Al-Tabari transmitted, through a chain going back to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: "Rafi' ibn Jariyah, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf, and Rafi' ibn Huraymilah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, that you believe in the Torah and in the prophethood of Musa, and that all of that is true?' He said: 'Yes, but you have introduced innovations, changed, and concealed.' They said: 'We hold to what is in our hands, for it is the truth, and we do not believe you or follow you.' So this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿Say: O People of the Book﴾," up to the end of the verse.

(p-219)His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿We had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a party [of them] they denied, and a party they killed.﴾

"Those who" is a term general to every believer of the community of Muhammad and of other religious communities. It is as though the words of the verse encompass all people and clarify the sects in their diversity. This is the interpretation of the majority of the exegetes. Al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, is the hypocrites, so the meaning is: "Indeed, those who believed with their mouths, while their hearts did not believe."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is as though the words of the verse enumerated the sects that could transfer to faith, then negated fear and grief from them on condition of their transferring to belief in Allah and the Last Day. According to the first interpretation, His saying "whoever believed" is within the scope of the believers, meaning: "persisted and continued." The explanation of "Jews" (hadu), of "Sabeans" (al-sabi'in), and of "Christians" (al-nasara) has already been given in Surat al-Baqara.

The reciters differed regarding the grammatical case (i'rab) of "al-Sabi'un" in this verse. The majority read "wa-al-Sabi'una" with a nominative (raf') ending, and this is the reading in the codices of the major cities and the Seven Reciters. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Jahdari read "wa-al-Sabi'in" with a genitive (jarr) ending, and this is a reading whose grammatical case is clear. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "wa-al-Sabiyyun" with a kasra on the ba' and a damma on the ya', without hamza, and this was mentioned in Surat al-Baqara.

As for the majority's reading "wa-al-Sabi'un," the view of Sibawayh, al-Khalil, and the grammarians of Basra is that it belongs to what is "preposed" in meaning but "postponed" in intention (al-muqaddam alladhi ma'nahu al-ta'khir), and this is what is meant. It is as though he said: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve; and the Sabeans and the Christians likewise." Al-Zajjaj cited a parallel for this:

"Otherwise know that we and you
are rebels, as long as we remain in dissension."

Then his saying "and you" (wa-antum) is preposed in wording but postponed in meaning, i.e., "and you likewise."

Al-Zajjaj related from al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' that they said: "wa-al-Sabi'un" is conjoined to "alladhina" (those who), since the original status of "alladhina" is the nominative, and the accusative after "inna" is weak. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: "inna" is the strongest of the accusative-governing particles. It is also related from al-Kisa'i that he said: "wa-al-Sabi'un" is conjoined to the pronoun in "hadu," and the sense is: "they were Jews, they and the Sabeans." This view is refuted by the meaning, because it implies that the Sabeans were Jews. It has also been said that "inna" here means "ni'ma" (how excellent), and what follows it is nominative as a subject of a nominal sentence. It is related from some of them that he read: ["wa-al-Sabun," without hamza].

The connection of this verse with the one before it is that they were told: the truth in itself is not as you claim, that you are the sons of Allah and His beloved; rather you are not upon anything upright until you believe and establish the revealed Books. Then he resumed the report about the truth in itself: that whoever believes, in all the world, is the one who attains success, for whom there is no fear.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, etc., is a resumed report about the deeds of their forefathers, the covenants they broke, and the crimes they committed. That is: "Indeed the staff is from the stock," and these, O Muhammad, are of those; so the ugliness of their deed is no novelty.

"Kullama" is an adverb of time, and its governing element is "kadhdhabu" and "yaqtulun." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with what their souls did not desire﴾ (p-221) implies that their desire was other than the truth, and this is the apparent meaning of "hawa al-nafs" (desire of the soul) whenever it is used without qualification; but when it is qualified by good, that is permissible. From this is the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the story of the captives of Badr: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, inclined to what Abu Bakr said, and did not incline to what I said."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a party they denied﴾ means: they only denied them, meaning a party of the messengers, and they did not kill them; and a party of the messengers they denied and killed. He mentioned only the killing, since it encompasses the denial.

are rebels, as long as we remain in dissension."

Then his saying "and you" (wa-antum) is preposed in wording but postponed in meaning, i.e., "and you likewise."

Al-Zajjaj related from al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' that they said: "wa-al-Sabi'un" is conjoined to "alladhina" (those who), since the original status of "alladhina" is the nominative, and the accusative after "inna" is weak. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: "inna" is the strongest of the accusative-governing particles. It is also related from al-Kisa'i that he said: "wa-al-Sabi'un" is conjoined to the pronoun in "hadu," and the sense is: "they were Jews, they and the Sabeans." This view is refuted by the meaning, because it implies that the Sabeans were Jews. It has also been said that "inna" here means "ni'ma" (how excellent), and what follows it is nominative as a subject of a nominal sentence. It is related from some of them that he read: ["wa-al-Sabun," without hamza].

The connection of this verse with the one before it is that they were told: the truth in itself is not as you claim, that you are the sons of Allah and His beloved; rather you are not upon anything upright until you believe and establish the revealed Books. Then he resumed the report about the truth in itself: that whoever believes, in all the world, is the one who attains success, for whom there is no fear.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, etc., is a resumed report about the deeds of their forefathers, the covenants they broke, and the crimes they committed. That is: "Indeed the staff is from the stock," and these, O Muhammad, are of those; so the ugliness of their deed is no novelty.

"Kullama" is an adverb of time, and its governing element is "kadhdhabu" and "yaqtulun." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with what their souls did not desire﴾ (p-221) implies that their desire was other than the truth, and this is the apparent meaning of "hawa al-nafs" (desire of the soul) whenever it is used without qualification; but when it is qualified by good, that is permissible. From this is the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the story of the captives of Badr: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, inclined to what Abu Bakr said, and did not incline to what I said."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a party they denied﴾ means: they only denied them, meaning a party of the messengers, and they did not kill them; and a party of the messengers they denied and killed. He mentioned only the killing, since it encompasses the denial.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 71–72**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf; then God turned to them in forgiveness; then many of them became blind and deaf again. And God is Seeing of what they do.﴾ ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who said, "Indeed, God is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord. Indeed, whoever associates others with God, God has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾

The meaning of this verse: these disbelievers and sinners among the Children of Israel thought that God would not test them, nor seize them in this world, nor purify them. So they persisted in their desires and became blind to them, since they did not perceive the truth. They were likened to the blind. They became deaf, since they did not hear it, and they were likened to the deaf. A similar saying is the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement: "Your love for a thing makes you blind and deaf."

As for His saying, ﴿Then God turned to them in forgiveness﴾: a group of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir) said: this repentance was their return to Jerusalem after the first expulsion, and the restoration of their kingdom and their condition. Then they became blind and deaf again after that, until they were expelled a second time, and they were never restored again. Another group said: "Then God turned to them in forgiveness" refers to the sending of Jesus (peace be upon him) to them. Another group said: God's turning to them in forgiveness is the sending of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him). He restricted this meaning to many of them, because a few of them believed. Then He warned them with His saying: ﴿And God is Seeing of what they do.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿أَلَّا تَكُونَ﴾ (*alla takuna*) with a fatha on the nun. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿أَنْ لَا تَكُونُ﴾ (*an la takuna*) with a damma on the nun. They all agreed on the nominative of ﴿فِتْنَةٌ﴾ (*fitnah*, trial), because *kana* here is the complete verb (*kana al-tammah*, meaning "to occur" or "to exist"). The reading with the fatha is explained by taking *an* to be the light particle that governs the subjunctive. The reading with the damma is explained by taking it to be the lightened form of the heavy *inna* (*al-mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*). Its use is good because *la* (not) has prepared the way for a verb to follow it, and it stands in place of the omitted pronoun as a substitute for it. In such a case there must be a substitute, as in your saying, "I knew that Zayd will surely stand," and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He knew that there would be among you sick people﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and your saying, "I knew that Zayd will surely stand," and "an la takuna fitnah."

As for His saying, ﴿And that man has nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], the omission of a substitute is good there, because *laysa* (is not) is not a true verb. Verbs are of three kinds. One kind is treated like *tayaqqantu* (I became certain), such as *'alimtu* (I knew) and *daraytu* (I knew). This kind is followed by the heavy *anna*, which suits it in affirmation and the occurrence of the event. A second kind is the opposite of this, such as *tamia'tu* (I hoped greedily), *raja'tu* (I hoped), and *khiftu* (I feared). It is clearly stated that the event has not occurred. This kind is followed by *an*, the light form, because it suits it. An example is His saying: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82], and "you fear that the people will snatch you away," ﴿If you fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], ﴿So we feared that it would overwhelm them with transgression and disbelief﴾ [al-Kahf: 80], ﴿Are you apprehensive that you will offer charity before...?﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 13], and similar examples. A third kind sometimes inclines toward the first and sometimes toward the second, such as *zanantu* (I thought), *hasibtu* (I reckoned), and *za'amtu* (I supposed). It is treated like *arju* (I hope) and *atma'u* (I hope greedily) in respect of supposition, claim and reckoning, since these are matters that are neither fixed nor settled. They may be placed in the position of knowledge, in that they are used as knowledge is used, as in His saying: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20].

The majority of people read ﴿عَمُوا وَصَمُّوا﴾ (*'amu wa-sammu*) with a fatha on the 'ayn and the sad. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read ﴿عُمُوا وَصُمُّوا﴾ (*'umu wa-sumu*) with a damma on the 'ayn and the mim, with the mim lightened, and with a damma on the sad. This is according to treating it like *zukima al-rajul* (the man had a cold in the head) and *azkamahu Allah* (God gave him a cold in the head), and *humma al-rajul* (the man had a fever) and *ahammahu Allah* (God gave him a fever). One does not say *zakamahu Allah* or *hamahu Allah*. Likewise this form comes as *'Umiya al-rajul* (the man became blind) and *a'maahu ghayruhu* (another made him blind), and *Summa* (he became deaf) and *asammahu ghayruhu* (another made him deaf). One does not say *'amaytuhu* or *sammamtuhu*.

His saying, ﴿Then God turned to them in forgiveness﴾, means: He brought them back to obedience and to the truth. Part of the eloquence of the expression is the attribution of this noble act to God, Exalted is He, and the attribution of blindness and deafness, which are metaphors for misguidance, to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿كَثِيرٌ﴾ (*kathir*, many) is in the nominative for one of three reasons. It may be a substitute (*badal*) for the *waw* in ﴿عَمُوا وَصَمُّوا﴾. Or it may be according to the plurality of the verb, even though the verb comes first, following the dialect of one who says *akalunī al-barāghīthu* (the fleas ate me). Or it may be that *kathir* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

Then God, Exalted is He, informed, with the emphasis of the oath particle, of the disbelief of those who said: ﴿Indeed, God is the Messiah, the son of Mary.﴾ This is the saying of the Ya'qubiyyah (a Christian sect). Then God, Exalted is He, informed of the Messiah's saying to them and his communication of it, and how it was. He said: ﴿And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel..."﴾ These meanings are the Messiah's words in the terms of his language, and they are the very same found in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and in other verses. Jesus (peace be upon him) informed them that God, Exalted is He, is his Lord and their Lord. They deviated, and they disbelieved because of the signs they saw at his hands.

Al-ma'wa (refuge) is the place where a person dwells and to which he returns. His saying, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, may be from the saying of Jesus (peace be upon him) to the Children of Israel. It may also be a new report addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). The discussion of the term *al-Masih* (the Messiah) has already been given in the commentary on Surah Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 73–75:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Certainly, they have disbelieved who said, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three," and there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿So will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; those before him [too] were messengers. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are turned away.﴾

This verse is an emphatic report, like the one before it, about this sect that speaks of the Trinity. They are, it is said, "the Melkites" (al-Malikiyya), and they comprise several sects, among them "the Nestorians" (al-Nusturiyya) and others. There is no point in mentioning their opinions in a book of tafsir. The truth is that they, despite the variety of their conditions, are disbelievers, in that they assigned a number to divinity, and in that they attributed a divine status to 'Isa (peace be upon him).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Third of three"﴾ permits only the idafa (construct) and the genitive case of "thalatha" (three), because the meaning is: one of three. If you say, "Zayd is the third of two," or "the fourth of three," it is permissible for you to use the idafa, as has preceded, and it is also permissible not to use the idafa and to put "thalathatan" (three) in the accusative, in the sense of "Zayd makes the three a fourth."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾ is a declaration that cuts through with the truth; He is the Creator, the Originator, characterized by the most exalted attributes, exalted above what the falsifiers say.

Then He, blessed and exalted, threatened these sayers of this monstrous statement with the touch of punishment; that is a threat of punishment in this world, by killing and captivity, and of punishment in the Hereafter after that, from which none of them will escape.

Then He, exalted be He, was gentle with them by urging them to repentance and to seeking forgiveness; then He described Himself with forgiveness and mercy, to attract the repentant and to comfort them, so that they might be confident of benefiting from their repentance.

Then Allah, exalted be He, informed of the reality of the matter of the Messiah, that he was a messenger, a human being, like the messengers who came before him.

"Khalat" means: passed away, and it has preceded in the sense of emptiness from the earth. Hittan ibn 'Abd Allah al-Raqashi recited: "qad khalat min qablihi rusulun" (with "rusul" indefinite), and likewise he recited: ﴿"Muhammad is not but a messenger; the messengers have passed away before him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144]. The discussion of the mode of this reading has already passed there.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his mother was a supporter of truth﴾ is an attribute in the intensive pattern (sighat mubalagha) from "al-sidq" (truthfulness); it may also be from "al-tasdiq" (affirmation), and by this Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was named, for his affirmation. This description of Maryam refutes the saying of one who said: "She was a prophetess." It is found in the authentic hadith that angels spoke to people without prophethood, such as the story of the three: the leper, the bald man, and the blind man, and others; there was no prophethood there. Likewise is the matter of Maryam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ is an indication of the deficiency of humanity and of a state of need for nourishment, with which divinity is negated. Makki, al-Mahdawi, and others mentioned that it is an expression for the need to defecate; this is a vile opinion, and there is no necessity that compels us to intend this meaning by the mention; rather it is an expression for the need for nourishment, and there is no doubt that whoever reflects with his mind on the concomitants of nourishment will find that, and other things.

Then Allah, exalted be He, commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), and implicitly his community, to consider the misguidance of these people and their distance from the paths of truth, and that the signs are made clear to them and displayed in the utmost clarity; then after that they are turned away, that is, their own motives turn them away, and their laziness removes them from the truth.

"Kayfa" in this verse is not a question about a state; rather it is an expression for a state about which one would ask with "kayf" (how). This is like your saying: "Be however you wish; you are a friend."

"Anna" means: from what direction; Sibawayh said: its meaning is "how" and "from where."

"Yu'fakun" means: they are turned away; from it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿From it is turned away whoever is turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 9]. And "al-ard al-ma'fukah" is the land that has been turned away from receiving rain; in reality the rain is what is turned away, but it is said "a ma'fuka land" because it is [turned away] from it.

And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿So will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; those before him [too] were messengers. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are turned away.﴾

This verse is an emphatic report, like the one before it, about this sect that speaks of the Trinity. They are, it is said, "the Melkites" (al-Malikiyya), and they comprise several sects, among them "the Nestorians" (al-Nusturiyya) and others. There is no point in mentioning their opinions in a book of tafsir. The truth is that they, despite the variety of their conditions, are disbelievers, in that they assigned a number to divinity, and in that they attributed a divine status to 'Isa (peace be upon him).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Third of three"﴾ permits only the idafa (construct) and the genitive case of "thalatha" (three), because the meaning is: one of three. If you say, "Zayd is the third of two," or "the fourth of three," it is permissible for you to use the idafa, as has preceded, and it is also permissible not to use the idafa and to put "thalathatan" (three) in the accusative, in the sense of "Zayd makes the three a fourth."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾ is a declaration that cuts through with the truth; He is the Creator, the Originator, characterized by the most exalted attributes, exalted above what the falsifiers say.

Then He, blessed and exalted, threatened these sayers of this monstrous statement with the touch of punishment; that is a threat of punishment in this world, by killing and captivity, and of punishment in the Hereafter after that, from which none of them will escape.

Then He, exalted be He, was gentle with them by urging them to repentance and to seeking forgiveness; then He described Himself with forgiveness and mercy, to attract the repentant and to comfort them, so that they might be confident of benefiting from their repentance.

Then Allah, exalted be He, informed of the reality of the matter of the Messiah, that he was a messenger, a human being, like the messengers who came before him.

"Khalat" means: passed away, and it has preceded in the sense of emptiness from the earth. Hittan ibn 'Abd Allah al-Raqashi recited: "qad khalat min qablihi rusulun" (with "rusul" indefinite), and likewise he recited: ﴿"Muhammad is not but a messenger; the messengers have passed away before him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144]. The discussion of the mode of this reading has already passed there.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his mother was a supporter of truth﴾ is an attribute in the intensive pattern (sighat mubalagha) from "al-sidq" (truthfulness); it may also be from "al-tasdiq" (affirmation), and by this Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was named, for his affirmation. This description of Maryam refutes the saying of one who said: "She was a prophetess." It is found in the authentic hadith that angels spoke to people without prophethood, such as the story of the three: the leper, the bald man, and the blind man, and others; there was no prophethood there. Likewise is the matter of Maryam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ is an indication of the deficiency of humanity and of a state of need for nourishment, with which divinity is negated. Makki, al-Mahdawi, and others mentioned that it is an expression for the need to defecate; this is a vile opinion, and there is no necessity that compels us to intend this meaning by the mention; rather it is an expression for the need for nourishment, and there is no doubt that whoever reflects with his mind on the concomitants of nourishment will find that, and other things.

Then Allah, exalted be He, commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), and implicitly his community, to consider the misguidance of these people and their distance from the paths of truth, and that the signs are made clear to them and displayed in the utmost clarity; then after that they are turned away, that is, their own motives turn them away, and their laziness removes them from the truth.

"Kayfa" in this verse is not a question about a state; rather it is an expression for a state about which one would ask with "kayf" (how). This is like your saying: "Be however you wish; you are a friend."

"Anna" means: from what direction; Sibawayh said: its meaning is "how" and "from where."

"Yu'fakun" means: they are turned away; from it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿From it is turned away whoever is turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 9]. And "al-ard al-ma'fukah" is the land that has been turned away from receiving rain; in reality the rain is what is turned away, but it is said "a ma'fuka land" because it is [turned away] from it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 76–78:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Say: "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you? And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the sound way."﴾ ﴿Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel by the tongue of David and Jesus, the son of Mary. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to confront them about their worship of a human being who has no power to harm them nor to benefit them.

As for "min dūn" (besides), and "dūn fulān" (beside so-and-so), and whatever comes of this word, it is only attached to someone who is not in the situation in which the statement is made; and explaining it as "ghayr" (other than) is not a consistently applicable meaning.

"Ḍarr" (harm), with a fatḥah on the ḍād, is the verbal noun (maṣdar), while "ḍurr", with a ḍammah, is the noun (ism); and it is the absence of good.

"Al-Samī'" (the All-Hearing) points to His comprehending their words; and "al-ʿAlīm" (the All-Knowing) to their intentions. Some of the exegetes said: these two attributes serve as a reminder of the deficiency of human beings; that is, "Allah the Exalted is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing absolutely, not Jesus nor anyone else"; and they acknowledge that Jesus was, for a period, one who did not hear and did not know. Makkī said something similar.

(p-227) Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet Muḥammad to forbid them from exaggeration (ghuluww) in their religion. Ghuluww is going beyond the limit. "Ghalā al-sahm" (the arrow flew beyond): when it exceeds the intended target and reaches its full extent of range; that distance is its ghalwah. Just as his saying "lā taghlū" (do not exceed) means "do not say and do not adhere to", the word "ghayr" is put in the accusative; and the meaning of this verse is not: "Avoid from your religion, which you are upon, the exaggeration"; rather its meaning is: "in your religion which ought to be your religion", because every person is required to follow the true religion, and it is fitting that he follow it and adhere to it. This address is to the Christians who exaggerated regarding Jesus, peace be upon him; and the people whose desires the Christians were forbidden to follow are the Children of Israel. The meaning of the verse is: "Do not you follow your desires as those people followed their desires", so the meaning is: "do not follow their ways". What prompted this interpretation is that the Christians in their exaggeration were not upon the desires of the Children of Israel; they were in opposition to them in statements; rather they came together in following a type of desire. So the verse is like your saying to one whom you blame for crookedness: "This is the way of so-and-so", representing him with another who has become crooked in a different kind of crookedness, even though their circumstances differ.

Allah the Exalted described the Jews as having strayed long ago and as having led many of their followers astray; then He emphasized the matter by repeating His saying, Exalted is He: "and strayed from the sound way". Some of those who interpreted it held that the meaning is: "O People of the Scripture from among the Christians, do not follow the desires of these Jews who strayed before — that is, their forefathers strayed, and they were before the coming of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him — and led many of the hypocrites astray; and they strayed from the sound way now after the truth has become clear."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel" — the verse etc. — it has been established in more than one place in the Qur'an what occurred during the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, of some of them disbelieving and being insolent; and likewise their conduct with Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was witnessed at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an. So this verse specified Dāwūd and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both, to inform that they were cursed in the four books, and that they were cursed by the tongue of others than Mūsā, peace be upon him, and Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: They were cursed in every tongue: they were cursed at the time of Mūsā, peace be upon him, in the Torah; at the time of Dāwūd, peace be upon him, in the Zabūr; at the time of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, in the Injīl; and at the time of Muḥammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Qur'an.

Ibn Jurayj narrated that connected to their curse by the tongue of Dāwūd, peace be upon him, was that they were transformed into swine; this is because Dāwūd, peace be upon him, passed by a group of them who were in a house, and he said: "Who is in the house?" They said: "Swine" — in the sense of being veiled. He said: "O Allah, make them swine," and they became swine. Then ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, invoked against those who slandered him that they become apes, and they became apes.

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: Rather, they were transformed into apes in the time of Dāwūd, peace be upon him, and into swine in the time of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. Al-Zajjāj related something similar.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The mention of transformation is not something the wording of the verse conveys; rather the wording of the verse conveys that Allah the Exalted cursed them and removed them far from His mercy, and informed the believing servants of that by the tongue of the Prophet Dāwūd in his time, and by the tongue of ʿĪsā in his time. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: Those of the Sabbath were cursed by the tongue of Dāwūd, and those who disbelieved concerning the Table were cursed by the tongue of ʿĪsā.

His saying, Exalted is He: "That" is a reference to their curse; and the rest of the verse is clear.
