**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 79–81:**

Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿They did not forbid one another from the wrongdoing they committed. How evil was what they were doing.﴾ ﴿You see many of them allying themselves with those who disbelieve. How evil is what their souls have sent ahead for them, that Allah became angry with them, and in the punishment they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿If they had believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies. But many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

Allah censures this accursed group because ﴿they did not forbid one another from the wrongdoing they committed﴾. That is, they openly committed sins. If one of them did forbid it, he did so without earnestness. Rather, the one who abstained did not refrain from keeping company with, eating with, or mingling with the sinner. Ibn Mas'ud reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from the Children of Israel would see his brother committing a sin and would forbid him from it, as a reprimand. Then on the next day, what he had seen did not prevent him from being his companion and table-mate. When Allah saw this from them, He set the hearts of some of them against others, and He cursed them through the tongue of their Prophet Dawud and 'Isa, peace be upon them both." Ibn Mas'ud said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been reclining, then he sat up and said: "No, by Allah, you must indeed seize the wrongdoer by the hands and force him toward the truth, forcing him firmly."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is consensus (ijma') that forbidding wrongdoing is obligatory upon whoever is able to do it, who forbids with kindness, and who is safe from harm to himself and to the Muslims. If someone is unable to forbid it for any of these reasons, then it is obligatory upon him to reject it in his heart and not to mix with the one committing the wrong.

The skilled scholars said: It is not a condition for the one who forbids that he be free of sin. Rather, sinners forbid one another. Some of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) said: It is obligatory upon those who engage in drinking vessels (i.e., wine) that they forbid one another. The proponent of this view derived it from this verse, because His saying "they did not forbid one another" and "they committed it" implies that they shared in the act, and He censured them for abandoning mutual forbidding.

As for His saying, ﴿How evil was what they were doing﴾: the lam is the lam of an oath. Al-Zajjaj took "ma" to be a verbal noun (masdariyya), and said the sense is: "How evil was their doing a thing."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This requires examination. Others said: "ma" is an indefinite descriptive noun, and the sense is: "How evil is the thing that they were doing, an act."

As for His saying to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿You see many﴾: it may be a seeing of the heart. In that case, it may mean: from the predecessors mentioned, that is, "you see now, when We inform you." It may also mean: from the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), because he used to see that among their affairs and the indications of their conditions. It may also be a seeing of the eye, in which case it means only the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for His saying, ﴿How evil is what their souls have sent ahead for them﴾: that is, their souls sent it ahead for the Hereafter and committed it. Then His saying, ﴿that Allah became angry with them﴾ explains that. "That Allah became angry" is in the position of an apposition (badal) for "what." It may also be that the sense is: "it is that Allah became angry with them." Al-Zajjaj said: "that" is in a position of accusative, in the sense of "because Allah became angry with them."

As for His saying, "and the Prophet": if the intended ones are the predecessors, then the Prophet is Dawud and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. If the intended ones are the contemporaries of Muhammad, then the Prophet is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ are the worshippers of idols. The majority among them were singled out for defiant disobedience, since among them there were a few who had believed.

Some exegetes held that His saying, ﴿You see many of them﴾, is a statement detached from the mention of the Children of Israel, and that it refers to the hypocrites. Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, said: ﴿If they had believed﴾ and the verse that follows refers to the hypocrites.

The skilled scholars said: It is not a condition for the one who forbids that he be free of sin. Rather, sinners forbid one another. Some of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence) said: It is obligatory upon those who engage in drinking vessels (i.e., wine) that they forbid one another. The proponent of this view derived it from this verse, because His saying "they did not forbid one another" and "they committed it" implies that they shared in the act, and He censured them for abandoning mutual forbidding.

As for His saying, ﴿How evil was what they were doing﴾: the lam is the lam of an oath. Al-Zajjaj took "ma" to be a verbal noun (masdariyya), and said the sense is: "How evil was their doing a thing."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This requires examination. Others said: "ma" is an indefinite descriptive noun, and the sense is: "How evil is the thing that they were doing, an act."

As for His saying to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿You see many﴾: it may be a seeing of the heart. In that case, it may mean: from the predecessors mentioned, that is, "you see now, when We inform you." If the intended ones are the contemporaries of Muhammad, then the Prophet is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ are the worshippers of idols. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 82–83:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers to be those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses."﴾

The lam in His saying "la-tajidanna" (surely you will find) is the lam of inception (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam). Al-Zajjaj said it is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). The heavy nun (nun al-thaqila) was added in order to separate the present from the future.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an unrestricted statement that applies to all time, and the situation remains so until now. The reason is that the Jews became accustomed to denying the prophets and killing them, practiced rebellion and sin, and persisted in incurring the curse and in being struck with humiliation and wretchedness. Their enmity has therefore grown harsh and their envy has increased, so they are the most intense of the people in enmity toward the believers. Likewise are the polytheists, the idol-worshippers among the Arabs and the fire-worshippers among the Magians, because faith has obliterated them, has demolished their structures, and has made clear that they had no basis from the beginning. Nothing remained for them, so their enmity is severe.

As for the Christians, the People of the Book, our Law judges that their original state was sound, except that they went astray. They believe they have not gone astray, and that this verse did not abrogate their law. They honor those among the people of Islam in whom they sense the soundness of a religion, and they belittle those in whom they perceive wickedness. When they fight, their fighting is out of pride and for gain, not because their law commands them to do so. When they make peace, their peace is pure. What supports this is that they are a people of noble character, possessing fidelity and the four qualities that 'Amr ibn al-'As mentioned in Sahih Muslim. Consider also that the Prophet (ﷺ) was pleased when the Romans defeated the Persians, because the Romans were People of the Book; and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not intend that Roman dominance should continue. He was pleased only by the victory of the People of the Book over the people who worship fire. In addition to this, the lesser enemy was defeated and the thorn of the greater enemy, who was feared for Islam, was broken.

As for the Jews, may Allah curse them, they have none of this character. Rather, their nature is corruption and twisting with their tongues. In the midst of your kindness to a Jew, he seeks to bring you ruin, except for the rare exception among them, one who might be specially disciplined with good manners and matters other than what was taught at first.

Allah, exalted is He, did not describe the Christians as people of affection. He only described them as nearer than the Jews and the polytheists, so it is a nearness of affection in comparison with those who are far off.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those who say, "We are Christians"﴾, there is an indication that the Christians who were contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) were not in the true reality of Christianity. Rather, their being Christians was merely a statement from them and a claim.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks﴾, its meaning is: that is because among them are people of fear of Allah, of devotion to Allah, and of worship, even if they were not upon guidance. They incline toward the people of worship and fear of Allah. Among the Jews there are not, and never were, people of monasteries, cloisters, or withdrawal from the world. Rather, they glorify the world, competing in building and worldly affairs, to the point that it is as if they do not believe in the Hereafter. Therefore no ascetic is seen among them.

It is said "qass" with a fatha on the qaf and also with a kasra, and "qissis." It is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized. The word "al-qass" in Arabic speech means slander, but it has nothing to do with this.

As for "ruhban," it is the plural of "rahib," and this is an Arabic designation. "Al-rahab" means fear. Among the evidences that ruhban is a plural is the saying of the poet:

Monks of Madyan, had they seen you, would have descended,
and the wild goats, from the passion of the captivated minds, the fleeing ones.

It has also been said that "al-ruhban" is a singular noun, and the evidence for it is the saying of the poet:

Had she seen the monk of a monastery at the summit (of a hill), the monk would have come down walking and descended.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is also narrated as "wa-yazil" with a ya', from "al-zalal" (slipping). This narration is more eloquent in expressing the overwhelming effect of this woman on the mind of this monk.

Allah, exalted is He, described the Christians as not being arrogant, and this is clearly present among them until now. The Jew, whenever he finds an opportunity for pride, transgresses and becomes arrogant. Allah humiliated them, the fever has laid them low, and the weight of the Law has trampled them. The religion of Islam, Allah has raised high.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a delegation that the Negus sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that they might see him and learn his condition. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, and they wept, believed, and returned to the Negus, and he believed too, and he remained a believer until he died. The Prophet (ﷺ) then prayed over him.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is also narrated that the bier of the Negus was uncovered for the Prophet (ﷺ), so he could see it from his place in Medina. News came after a period of time that the Negus had been buried on the day the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed over him. Al-Suddi mentioned that they were twelve: seven priests and five monks. Abu Salih said they were sixty-seven men. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said they were seventy, wearing woolen garments, and each of them was a possessor of a cloister, chosen by the Negus, the best of them and then the best of them. Al-Suddi also mentioned that the Negus went out as a migrant and died on the way.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, and none of the scholars of the biography (sira) mentioned it.

Qatada said: These verses were revealed concerning a people who were believers, and then they believed in Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Al-Tabari distinguished between these two statements, though they are one and the same.

Salman al-Farisi narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "That is because among them are truthful ones (siddiqin) and monks."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes...﴾ and the rest of the verse: The pronoun in "sami'u" (they heard), its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to those among these arrivals from the land of Abyssinia who believed, since they recognized the truth and said, "We have believed." Not all the Christians do this. The beginning of the verse, concerning nearness in affection, is general regarding them. It is not appropriate to hold that the beginning of the verse is specific to those who believed, because whoever believed is among those who believed, and it is not said of him, "They said, 'We are Christians,'" nor is it said of believers, ﴿That is because among them are priests﴾, nor is it said, "They are nearer in affection." Rather, whoever believed is a person of pure affection. The specification came only from His saying, ﴿And when they heard﴾, while the pronoun came in general form, since a group may be praised for the action of one of them. In this there is an invitation to the Christians and a gentleness from Allah toward them. Indeed, the overflowing of tears is often found among them, even if they do not believe.

It is narrated that a delegation from Najran came to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq concerning some of their affairs. He ordered someone who recites the Qur'an to recite in their presence, and they wept intensely. Abu Bakr said: "This is how we used to be, but the hearts have hardened."

It is also narrated that a monk from the monasteries of Syria looked at the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), saw their worship and their earnestness in fighting their enemy, so he marveled at their condition and wept, and said: "Those who were sawn with saws upon the religion of Jesus were not more patient than these, nor more diligent in their religion."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The people who were described as having recognized the truth are those whom the Negus sent to see the Prophet (ﷺ) and hear what he had. When they saw him, he recited the Qur'an to them, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾. Their eyes overflowed with tears out of the fear of hearts.

"Al-ru'ya" is sight of the eye. "Tafid" (overflowing) is a circumstantial clause (hal) for "al-a'yun" (the eyes). "Yaqulun" (they say) is also a circumstantial clause. The meaning of "amanna" is: "We affirm that this is Your Messenger, and what was heard is Your Book." "Al-shahidun" (the witnesses) are Muhammad and his community, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, and others.

Al-Tabari said: If someone said that the meaning of that is: "with the witnesses to Your Oneness from all the world, those who came before and those who came after," that would be correct.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the meaning of al-Tabari's statement, and it is a sound statement. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, specified the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the basis of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], and the rest of the verse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 84–87:**

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And why should we not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth, and hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?﴾ ﴿So Allah rewarded them, for what they said, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.﴾

His saying, "Wa ma lana" (And why should we not): it is a rebuke directed at themselves, or an argument against those among the disbelievers who opposed them, as if he said to them: "You have believed and hastened to it." They replied: "What is it that would prevent us from believing, when the right course has become clear and the manifest truth has come?"

"Wa ma lana" is an inchoative sentence (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). "La nu'minu" (we do not believe) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). However, it is a circumstantial clause that is itself the purpose, and the benefit lies in it, just as you say: "Zayd came riding," when you have been asked: "Did he come on foot or riding?"

In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "Wa ma lana la nu'minu billahi wa ma anzala ilayna rabbuna" (And why should we not believe in Allah and in what our Lord has sent down to us).

"Wa natma'u" (and we hope): its implied form is "wa nahnu natma'u" (and we, we hope). The waw is therefore conjunctive of a nominal sentence upon a nominal sentence, not conjunctive of a verb upon a verb. The "righteous people" (al-qawm al-salihun) are Muhammad and his companions, as stated by Ibn Zayd and other exegetes.

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned what He rewarded them with of bliss, for their faith and their good-doing. Then He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers who denied, and that they are companions of the Blazing Fire. The meaning, known from more than one verse of the Book of Allah, is that this is a necessary, constant, everlasting association.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intentionally bound by oaths. Its expiation is feeding ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾

"Eat" (kulū) in this verse is an expression meaning: "enjoy eating, drinking, clothing, riding, and the like." Eating is singled out because it is the greatest of the intended benefits and the most particular of the uses a person derives [from provision].

According to the People of the Sunna, provision (rizq) is whatever benefit can be validly derived from. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: provision is whatever can validly be owned, and what is unlawful is not provision, since it cannot validly be owned. This is refuted by saying that it follows for them that one who eats what is unlawful is not provided for by Allah, Exalted is He. Some noble scholars have drawn from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him: a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba: 15], that what is unlawful is provision. He said: He mentioned forgiveness, indicating that provision may contain what is unlawful. Abu al-Ma'ali, in al-Irshad, refuted the Mu'tazila by saying: if they say "provision is what is owned," it follows that whatever is owned is provision, and Allah's ownership of things cannot validly be described as His provision.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This objection that was imposed is not binding, so consider it carefully." The remainder of the verse is clear.

The discussion of His saying, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths﴾, has already been presented in Surat al-Baqara, in a parallel to this. As for His saying, ﴿for what you have intentionally bound by oaths﴾, its meaning is: "you have strengthened (them)."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ʿaqqadtum (with the qaf doubled). ʿĀsim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ʿaqadtum (with the qaf light). Ibn 'Amir read ʿāqadtum (with an alif), on the pattern of fā'altum. Abu 'Ali said: whoever doubles the qaf admits two possibilities: one is that it is for intensifying the action, since it addresses a group; the other is that ʿaqqada is like ḍaʿʿafa, not intended to indicate intensification, just as ḍāʿafa is not intended to indicate an action between two parties. Whoever reads ʿaqadtum, lightening the qaf, may intend by it either the frequent or the occasional performance of the action. The binding of an oath is like the tying of a rope and of a covenant. Al-Hutay'a said:

"A people who, when they bind a pledge to their neighbor,
they tighten the rope and tighten the pact above it."

Whoever reads ʿāqadtum admits two patterns: one is like ṭāraqtu al-naʿl ("I made the sandal repaired") and ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ ("I punished the thief"); the other is that it is intended as fā'altu, which requires two agents, as though the meaning were: "He will hold you accountable for what you have made a pact upon with oaths." ʿĀqada is construed with ʿalā because it has the sense of ʿāhada ("to covenant"). Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And who fulfills what he covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. This is like how nādaytum ilā al-ṣalāt ("you called to prayer") [al-Ma'ida: 58] is construed with ilā, though its usual form is nādaytu Zayd-an ("I called Zayd"). And ﴿We called him from the right side of the mountain﴾ [Maryam: 52]. But since it has the sense of "I invited to such-and-such," as in His saying, ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 33], nādā is construed with ilā. Then the construction is extended in His saying ʿāqadtum ʿalayhi al-aymān ("you have made pacts upon them with oaths"): the preposition is dropped, and the verb reaches its object directly. Then the pronoun that refers back to the relative is dropped from the clause, and the intended meaning is: "He will hold you accountable for what you have bound as oaths," just as it is dropped in His saying, ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 94].

Al-aymān is the plural of yamīn, which is an oath (al-ālīyya). It was called yamīn ("right hand") because it was their custom to clasp each other's right hands when swearing.

His saying, ﴿fa-kaffāratuhu﴾, means: "so the thing that covers the sin of breaking the oath is feeding..." According to the grammatical convention, the pronoun refers to mā ("what"). In this position, mā may be relative (meaning "that which") or it may be verbal-masdarial. The pronoun, given the meaning we have mentioned, refers to the sin of breaking the oath, though no valid mention of it has preceded; but the meaning requires it.

Feeding ten needy people (iṭ'ām ʿashara masākīn) means satisfying them with food once. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if one gathers them together, he feeds them a single full meal; and if he gives them [food] individually, he gives each one a mikūk (a unit of measure). The ruling for these is that none of them should be repeated in a single expiation of an oath, whether they are fed individually or as a group at one time. In none of this is a dhimmi (non-Muslim under Muslim protection) valid. And if a child is fed, [he receives a large share]. It is not permissible to feed a slave, nor a relative whose maintenance is obligatory on him. If [the recipient] is one whose maintenance is not obligatory upon the one making expiation, Malik said: "I do not like that he feed him; but if he does, and the recipient is poor, it suffices him." It is not permissible to feed a wealthy person from it; and if one feeds a wealthy person unknowingly about his wealth, then in al-Mudawwana and other books it is stated that it does not suffice; and in al-Asadiyya it is stated that it suffices.

People differed on the meaning of His saying, ﴿from the average (min awsat)﴾. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group with him, took it to mean moderation in quantity. A group took it to mean moderation in kind. The correct view is that the word "average" encompasses both quantity and kind. Malik held that the needy person in Medina should be fed one mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is a ritl and a third of flour; this was due to the hardship of living in Medina. He held that elsewhere one should be more generous; for this reason he approved of lunch and dinner. Ibn Wahb issued a legal opinion in Egypt for a mudd and a half, and Ashhab for a mudd and a third. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: a mudd and a third is the average of the living standard of the inhabitants of the cities for lunch and dinner. Ibn Habib said: bread alone does not suffice; rather it must be with olive oil, milk, meat, or the like. In the commentary of Ibn Muzayn it is stated that bread alone suffices. Those who said that the average refers to kind held that the one making expiation should avoid the lowest food that people eat in the town, and step down from the highest, and make expiation with the middle of that. The school of al-Mudawwana holds that the one making expiation should take into account the living standard of the town; but in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz it is stated that the standard to be considered is his own household's living standard, specific to him.

It seems that the verse, on the first interpretation, means: "from the average of what you, O people, feed your families in general, from a city or a region." On the second interpretation, it means: "from the average of what a person feeds his household."

The majority read ʾahlīkum (the plural of ahl, in the sound masculine plural form). Ja'far ibn Muhammad read min awsat mā tuṭʿimūna ahālīyakum, which is a broken plural. Abu al-Fath said: ahālī is like layālin ("nights"); as though its singular were ahlāt and laylāt. The Arabs say ahl and ahla; and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a people of friendship whose affection I have renounced..."

It is also said laylah and laylāh; and Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"Every day and every night of his
until whoever sees him says, when he sees him:
Oh woe to him, what a wretched camel!"

The majority read ﴿aw kiswatuhum﴾ with a kasra on the kaf, meaning the clothing of garments. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read aw kusūtuhum with a damma on the kaf. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read aw ka-isāratihim, from al-iswa (example/pattern). Abu al-Fath said: it is as though he said, "or with what suffices people like them." So it is by omission of the annexed noun, with the sense "or like the sufficiency of their pattern." He said: if you wish, you can make al-iswa itself mean sufficiency, and then you need not posit an omitted annexed noun.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is room for scrutiny here, and the reading contradicts the script of the Mushaf. Its meaning is also contrary to what the scholars have interpreted: that one who breaks an oath sworn by Allah, Exalted is He, has a choice between feeding, clothing, or freeing [a slave]. The scholars agree that freeing a slave is the most excellent of these, then clothing, then feeding; Allah, Exalted, began with His servants by the easiest, then the easier. It may be that in a time of hardship and famine, feeding is more excellent than freeing; but that is rare and not customary, and the ruling follows the more common case.

The scholars differed about the limit of clothing (kiswa). Some considered the wording itself: if the one making expiation is clothed and the needy person is clothed, the requirement is met. This status is attained with a single garment, whatever garment it is, since people agree that a cap alone does not suffice for expiation of an oath. Mujahid said: one garment, or more, suffices for expiation of an oath. Al-Hasan said: kiswa is one garment for each needy person; and Tawus said the same. Mansur said: kiswa is a garment, a shirt, a cloak, or a loincloth; so said Abu Ja'far, 'Ata', and Ibn 'Abbas; and he said: a mantle may suffice in expiation, and likewise a shamla (wrap). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: a turban suffices for expiation of an oath. Mujahid said: anything suffices except the tubban (short underwear). It is reported from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The tubban is a fine garment," which al-Tabari transmitted with a chain. al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba said: a turban with which one wraps his head suffices.

Others considered the customary dress and the commonly known clothing. Some of them said: a single garment does not suffice unless it is comprehensive, of the sort with which one dresses, such as a cloak or a wrapper. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: a comprehensive garment suffices; a shirt, a coat, or a headscarf is not a comprehensive garment.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A complete shirt may be comprehensive and a customary dress. Some said: clothing in expiation is a waist-wrap, a shirt, and a cloak; so said Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that clothing in expiation is two garments for each needy person. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, tied the ruling to what suffices in prayer; and this is the best consideration. He said: for a man, one garment suffices. Ibn Habib said: he is clothed with a shirt or a wrap that is long enough to wrap around himself in the manner of ishtimāl (wrapping oneself). Ibn Habib's statement is an explanation. Malik said: a woman is clothed with a long shirt and a veil. Ibn al-Qasim said in al-'Utbiyya: if he clothes a young girl, then [it is] a long shirt and a veil, like the adult; and the expiation is one, and nothing is reduced for a child. Ibn al-Mawwaz said of this: I do not approve of clothing nursing infants at all; but as for one who is commanded to pray, he clothes him with a shirt, and it suffices. Ibn al-Mawwaz said from his own opinion: rather, it must be the clothing of an adult man; otherwise it does not suffice. Ashhab said: a female who has not reached the age of prayer is given a man's garment, and it suffices; and Ibn al-Majishun said the same.

His saying, ﴿or freeing a slave (taḥrīr raqaba)﴾: taḥrīr means removing from bondage. It is also used of captivity, hardships, the toil of the world, and the like. From it is His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the mother of Mary: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one devoted (muḥarraran)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]; that is, free from the toil of the world. And from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"O Banu Ghudana, indeed I freed you,
then I gave you to 'Atiyya ibn Ji'al."

That is: I freed you from satire. The neck (raqaba) is specified from the human body because it is the member in which the shackle is placed, and binding is typically done on animals; so it is the locus of ownership, and therefore taḥrīr is attributed to it.

The people differed over the description of the freed slave in expiation: how should he be? A group of scholars said: this is an unrestricted "neck" (raqabah) that is not qualified by oaths; so it is permissible in the expiation for oaths to free a disbeliever. This is the view of al-Tabari and a group of scholars. Another group said: every unrestricted (mutlaq) term in the Qur'an of this kind is referred back to the restricted (muqayyad) one concerning freeing a neck in the case of accidental killing (al-qatl al-khata'); so no disbeliever suffices for any of the expiations. This is the opinion of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group along with him. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: a blind person, a leper, or an insane person does not suffice. Ibn Shihab and a group said likewise. Regarding the one-eyed (a'war) there are two opinions within the school (madhhab); and likewise regarding the deaf and the eunuch (khasi). Among the scholars there are those who held that all of these suffice. Al-Nakha'i made a distinction: he permitted freeing one who performs his tasks and service, and forbade freeing one who does not work, such as the blind, the paralysed (mu'aqad), and one whose two hands are useless (ashall al-yadayn). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: in my view a non-Arabic speaker (a'jami) suffices when the expense is reduced, but others are more beloved to me. Sahnun said: he means after he has accepted Islam; but if the a'jami has not accepted it, yet is among those who are compelled to accept Islam, such as an adult Magian and a young non-Arab of the People of the Book from the warring nations, then Ibn al-Qasim said: his freeing suffices even if he has not become Muslim. Ashhab said: it does not suffice until he becomes Muslim. According to Malik, whoever has a share of freedom (shu'bat hurriyyah), such as the mudabbar, the umm walad, and the like, does not suffice.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Whoever does not find"﴾; its meaning: he does not find in his possession any one of these three things: feeding, clothing, or freeing a neck. The scholars differed over the limit of this one who lacks the means, such that fasting is valid for him. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group of scholars said: if the one making expiation owns only his sustenance and the sustenance of his dependants for his day and night, then he may fast; but if he has, beyond that, what would feed ten needy persons, feeding is obligatory upon him. This is also the view of Malik and his companions. Malik said in al-Mudawwanah: fasting does not suffice for him while he is able to do one of the three things. It is reported from Ibn al-Qasim that whoever has a surplus of one day's sustenance does not fast. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: the one who has broken his oath does not fast until he finds nothing but his sustenance, or he is in a land where no one would show him kindness. Ibn al-Qasim said in the Kitab Ibn Muzayn: if the one who has broken his oath has a surplus over the sustenance of his day, he should feed (others), unless he fears hunger, or he is in a land where no one would show him kindness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: if he has only three dirhams, he should feed. Qatadah said: if he has only the amount with which he makes expiation, he should fast. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if he has two dirhams, he should feed. Al-Tabari said: others said: it is permissible for one who does not have two hundred dirhams to fast, and he is one who does not find. Others said: it is permissible for one who has no surplus over the capital with which he conducts his livelihood to fast.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "then a fast of three days, consecutive (muttabi'at)"; and likewise 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. A group of scholars held this view, including Mujahid and others. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: if one makes them consecutive, that is good; and if one separates them, it suffices.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"That is the expiation of your oaths"﴾; it refers to the three things mentioned.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"when you swear"﴾; its meaning: "then you intend to break it, or you have fallen into it." The remainder of the verse is an exhortation and a reminder of the blessing and of faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have intentionally bound by oaths. Its expiation is feeding ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾

"Eat" (kulū) in this verse is an expression meaning: "enjoy eating, drinking, clothing, riding, and the like." Eating is singled out because it is the greatest of the intended benefits and the most particular of the uses a person derives [from provision].

According to the People of the Sunna, provision (rizq) is whatever benefit can be validly derived from. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: provision is whatever can validly be owned, and what is unlawful is not provision, since it cannot validly be owned. This is refuted by saying that it follows for them that one who eats what is unlawful is not provided for by Allah, Exalted is He. Some noble scholars have drawn from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him: a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ [Saba: 15], that what is unlawful is provision. He said: He mentioned forgiveness, indicating that provision may contain what is unlawful. Abu al-Ma'ali, in al-Irshad, refuted the Mu'tazila by saying: if they say "provision is what is owned," it follows that whatever is owned is provision, and Allah's ownership of things cannot validly be described as His provision.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "This objection that was imposed is not binding, so consider it carefully." The remainder of the verse is clear.

The discussion of His saying, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths﴾, has already been presented in Surat al-Baqara, in a parallel to this. As for His saying, ﴿for what you have intentionally bound by oaths﴾, its meaning is: "you have strengthened (them)."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ʿaqqadtum (with the qaf doubled). ʿĀsim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ʿaqadtum (with the qaf light). Ibn 'Amir read ʿāqadtum (with an alif), on the pattern of fā'altum. Abu 'Ali said: whoever doubles the qaf admits two possibilities: one is that it is for intensifying the action, since it addresses a group; the other is that ʿaqqada is like ḍaʿʿafa, not intended to indicate intensification, just as ḍāʿafa is not intended to indicate an action between two parties. Whoever reads ʿaqadtum, lightening the qaf, may intend by it either the frequent or the occasional performance of the action. The binding of an oath is like the tying of a rope and of a covenant. Al-Hutay'a said:

"A people who, when they bind a pledge to their neighbor,
they tighten the rope and tighten the pact above it."

Whoever reads ʿāqadtum admits two patterns: one is like ṭāraqtu al-naʿl ("I made the sandal repaired") and ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ ("I punished the thief"); the other is that it is intended as fā'altu, which requires two agents, as though the meaning were: "He will hold you accountable for what you have made a pact upon with oaths." ʿĀqada is construed with ʿalā because it has the sense of ʿāhada ("to covenant"). Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And who fulfills what he covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. This is like how nādaytum ilā al-ṣalāt ("you called to prayer") [al-Ma'ida: 58] is construed with ilā, though its usual form is nādaytu Zayd-an ("I called Zayd"). And ﴿We called him from the right side of the mountain﴾ [Maryam: 52]. But since it has the sense of "I invited to such-and-such," as in His saying, ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 33], nādā is construed with ilā. Then the construction is extended in His saying ʿāqadtum ʿalayhi al-aymān ("you have made pacts upon them with oaths"): the preposition is dropped, and the verb reaches its object directly. Then the pronoun that refers back to the relative is dropped from the clause, and the intended meaning is: "He will hold you accountable for what you have bound as oaths," just as it is dropped in His saying, ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 94].

Al-aymān is the plural of yamīn, which is an oath (al-ālīyya). It was called yamīn ("right hand") because it was their custom to clasp each other's right hands when swearing.

His saying, ﴿fa-kaffāratuhu﴾, means: "so the thing that covers the sin of breaking the oath is feeding..." According to the grammatical convention, the pronoun refers to mā ("what"). In this position, mā may be relative (meaning "that which") or it may be verbal-masdarial. The pronoun, given the meaning we have mentioned, refers to the sin of breaking the oath, though no valid mention of it has preceded; but the meaning requires it.

Feeding ten needy people (iṭ'ām ʿashara masākīn) means satisfying them with food once. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if one gathers them together, he feeds them a single full meal; and if he gives them [food] individually, he gives each one a mikūk (a unit of measure). The ruling for these is that none of them should be repeated in a single expiation of an oath, whether they are fed individually or as a group at one time. In none of this is a dhimmi (non-Muslim under Muslim protection) valid. And if a child is fed, [he receives a large share]. It is not permissible to feed a slave, nor a relative whose maintenance is obligatory on him. If [the recipient] is one whose maintenance is not obligatory upon the one making expiation, Malik said: "I do not like that he feed him; but if he does, and the recipient is poor, it suffices him." It is not permissible to feed a wealthy person from it; and if one feeds a wealthy person unknowingly about his wealth, then in al-Mudawwana and other books it is stated that it does not suffice; and in al-Asadiyya it is stated that it suffices.

People differed on the meaning of His saying, ﴿from the average (min awsat)﴾. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group with him, took it to mean moderation in quantity. A group took it to mean moderation in kind. The correct view is that the word "average" encompasses both quantity and kind. Malik held that the needy person in Medina should be fed one mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is a ritl and a third of flour; this was due to the hardship of living in Medina. He held that elsewhere one should be more generous; for this reason he approved of lunch and dinner. Ibn Wahb issued a legal opinion in Egypt for a mudd and a half, and Ashhab for a mudd and a third. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: a mudd and a third is the average of the living standard of the inhabitants of the cities for lunch and dinner. Ibn Habib said: bread alone does not suffice; rather it must be with olive oil, milk, meat, or the like. In the commentary of Ibn Muzayn it is stated that bread alone suffices. Those who said that the average refers to kind held that the one making expiation should avoid the lowest food that people eat in the town, and step down from the highest, and make expiation with the middle of that. The school of al-Mudawwana holds that the one making expiation should take into account the living standard of the town; but in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz it is stated that the standard to be considered is his own household's living standard, specific to him.

It seems that the verse, on the first interpretation, means: "from the average of what you, O people, feed your families in general, from a city or a region." On the second interpretation, it means: "from the average of what a person feeds his household."

The majority read ʾahlīkum (the plural of ahl, in the sound masculine plural form). Ja'far ibn Muhammad read min awsat mā tuṭʿimūna ahālīyakum, which is a broken plural. Abu al-Fath said: ahālī is like layālin ("nights"); as though its singular were ahlāt and laylāt. The Arabs say ahl and ahla; and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a people of friendship whose affection I have renounced..."

It is also said laylah and laylāh; and Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"Every day and every night of his
until whoever sees him says, when he sees him:
Oh woe to him, what a wretched camel!"

The majority read ﴿aw kiswatuhum﴾ with a kasra on the kaf, meaning the clothing of garments. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read aw kusūtuhum with a damma on the kaf. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read aw ka-isāratihim, from al-iswa (example/pattern). Abu al-Fath said: it is as though he said, "or with what suffices people like them." So it is by omission of the annexed noun, with the sense "or like the sufficiency of their pattern." He said: if you wish, you can make al-iswa itself mean sufficiency, and then you need not posit an omitted annexed noun.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is room for scrutiny here, and the reading contradicts the script of the Mushaf. Its meaning is also contrary to what the scholars have interpreted: that one who breaks an oath sworn by Allah, Exalted is He, has a choice between feeding, clothing, or freeing [a slave]. The scholars agree that freeing a slave is the most excellent of these, then clothing, then feeding; Allah, Exalted, began with His servants by the easiest, then the easier. It may be that in a time of hardship and famine, feeding is more excellent than freeing; but that is rare and not customary, and the ruling follows the more common case.

The scholars differed about the limit of clothing (kiswa). Some considered the wording itself: if the one making expiation is clothed and the needy person is clothed, the requirement is met. This status is attained with a single garment, whatever garment it is, since people agree that a cap alone does not suffice for expiation of an oath. Mujahid said: one garment, or more, suffices for expiation of an oath. Al-Hasan said: kiswa is one garment for each needy person; and Tawus said the same. Mansur said: kiswa is a garment, a shirt, a cloak, or a loincloth; so said Abu Ja'far, 'Ata', and Ibn 'Abbas; and he said: a mantle may suffice in expiation, and likewise a shamla (wrap). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: a turban suffices for expiation of an oath. Mujahid said: anything suffices except the tubban (short underwear). It is reported from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The tubban is a fine garment," which al-Tabari transmitted with a chain. al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba said: a turban with which one wraps his head suffices.

Others considered the customary dress and the commonly known clothing. Some of them said: a single garment does not suffice unless it is comprehensive, of the sort with which one dresses, such as a cloak or a wrapper. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: a comprehensive garment suffices; a shirt, a coat, or a headscarf is not a comprehensive garment.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A complete shirt may be comprehensive and a customary dress. Some said: clothing in expiation is a waist-wrap, a shirt, and a cloak; so said Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that clothing in expiation is two garments for each needy person. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, tied the ruling to what suffices in prayer; and this is the best consideration. He said: for a man, one garment suffices. Ibn Habib said: he is clothed with a shirt or a wrap that is long enough to wrap around himself in the manner of ishtimāl (wrapping oneself). Ibn Habib's statement is an explanation. Malik said: a woman is clothed with a long shirt and a veil. Ibn al-Qasim said in al-'Utbiyya: if he clothes a young girl, then [it is] a long shirt and a veil, like the adult; and the expiation is one, and nothing is reduced for a child. Ibn al-Mawwaz said of this: I do not approve of clothing nursing infants at all; but as for one who is commanded to pray, he clothes him with a shirt, and it suffices. Ibn al-Mawwaz said from his own opinion: rather, it must be the clothing of an adult man; otherwise it does not suffice. Ashhab said: a female who has not reached the age of prayer is given a man's garment, and it suffices; and Ibn al-Majishun said the same.

His saying, ﴿or freeing a slave (taḥrīr raqaba)﴾: taḥrīr means removing from bondage. It is also used of captivity, hardships, the toil of the world, and the like. From it is His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the mother of Mary: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one devoted (muḥarraran)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]; that is, free from the toil of the world. And from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"O Banu Ghudana, indeed I freed you,
then I gave you to 'Atiyya ibn Ji'al."

That is: I freed you from satire. The neck (raqaba) is specified from the human body because it is the member in which the shackle is placed, and binding is typically done on animals; so it is the locus of ownership, and therefore taḥrīr is attributed to it.

A group of scholars said: this is an unrestricted "neck" (raqabah) that is not qualified by oaths; so it is permissible in the expiation for oaths to free a disbeliever. This is the view of al-Tabari and a group of scholars. Another group said: every unrestricted (mutlaq) term in the Qur'an of this kind is referred back to the restricted (muqayyad) one concerning freeing a neck in the case of accidental killing (al-qatl al-khata'); so no disbeliever suffices for any of the expiations. Ibn Shihab and a group said likewise. Regarding the one-eyed (a'war) there are two opinions within the school (madhhab); and likewise regarding the deaf and the eunuch (khasi). Among the scholars there are those who held that all of these suffice. Al-Nakha'i made a distinction: he permitted freeing one who performs his tasks and service, and forbade freeing one who does not work, such as the blind, the paralysed (mu'aqad), and one whose two hands are useless (ashall al-yadayn). Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: in my view a non-Arabic speaker (a'jami) suffices when the expense is reduced, but others are more beloved to me. Sahnun said: he means after he has accepted Islam; but if the a'jami has not accepted it, yet is among those who are compelled to accept Islam, such as an adult Magian and a young non-Arab of the People of the Book from the warring nations, then Ibn al-Qasim said: his freeing suffices even if he has not become Muslim. Ashhab said: it does not suffice until he becomes Muslim. According to Malik, whoever has a share of freedom (shu'bat hurriyyah), such as the mudabbar, the umm walad, and the like, does not suffice.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Whoever does not find"﴾; its meaning: he does not find in his possession any one of these three things: feeding, clothing, or freeing a neck. The scholars differed over the limit of this one who lacks the means, such that fasting is valid for him. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group of scholars said: if the one making expiation owns only his sustenance and the sustenance of his dependants for his day and night, then he may fast; but if he has, beyond that, what would feed ten needy persons, feeding is obligatory upon him. This is also the view of Malik and his companions. Malik said in al-Mudawwanah: fasting does not suffice for him while he is able to do one of the three things. It is reported from Ibn al-Qasim that whoever has a surplus of one day's sustenance does not fast. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: the one who has broken his oath does not fast until he finds nothing but his sustenance, or he is in a land where no one would show him kindness. Ibn al-Qasim said in the Kitab Ibn Muzayn: if the one who has broken his oath has a surplus over the sustenance of his day, he should feed (others), unless he fears hunger, or he is in a land where no one would show him kindness. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: if he has only three dirhams, he should feed. Qatadah said: if he has only the amount with which he makes expiation, he should fast. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if he has two dirhams, he should feed. Al-Tabari said: others said: it is permissible for one who does not have two hundred dirhams to fast, and he is one who does not find. Others said: it is permissible for one who has no surplus over the capital with which he conducts his livelihood to fast.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "then a fast of three days, consecutive (muttabi'at)"; and likewise 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. A group of scholars held this view, including Mujahid and others. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: if one makes them consecutive, that is good; and if one separates them, it suffices.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"That is the expiation of your oaths"﴾; it refers to the three things mentioned.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"when you swear"﴾; its meaning: "then you intend to break it, or you have fallen into it." The remainder of the verse is an exhortation and a reminder of the blessing and of faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 90–92:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear notification.﴾

The address is to the believers as a whole, because these things are appetites and habits with which they were afflicted in the Jahiliyyah, and they had overpowered the souls; so some of them remained in many believers' souls. As for intoxicants, they had not yet been prohibited. As for gambling (maysir), it contains gambling (qimar), pleasure for the idle soul, and benefit as well in some respect. As for idolatrous altars (ansab), they are stones upon which they would slaughter for a virtue they believed in them; and it has been said: they are the worshipped idols, to which they would slaughter and at which they would do so in the Jahiliyyah. If the intended meaning in this verse is only the stones upon which slaughter is performed, then that is because there remained in the souls of the weaker believers something of the glorification of those stones, and this is like the saying of the wife of Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi to her husband: "Do you fear for the children anything from Dhu al-Shara?" And "Dhu al-Shara" was an idol of the Daws. And if the intended meaning in this verse is the idols, then they were joined with these matters so that the deficiency in these might become evident when they are joined with the idols; and it is not to be understood that there remained in the soul of a believer anything of the glorification of idols and of being involved with them, such that it would be said to him: avoid it.

As for divining arrows (azlam), they are the three that most people would use: on one of them was written "no," on another "yes," and the third was blank. These are the ones that Suraqah ibn Ju'shum withheld when he pursued the Prophet (ﷺ) at the time of the Hijrah; and they would venerate them, and something of them remained in some souls. Of this kind is the desire for augury by birds, and seeking omens from them in books, and the like of what people do today. It is also said of the arrows of gambling that they are "azlam," and the zalm is the arrow. Among the azlam were also those kept with the soothsayers, and among them were arrows at the idols; and these are the ones by which lots were cast over 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, father of the Prophet (ﷺ); and among the Quraysh in the Ka'bah there were azlam bearing rulings, which Ibn Ishaq and others mentioned. So Allah the Exalted informed that these things are rijs (defilement). Ibn Zayd said: ar-rijs is evil.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Everything disliked is blameworthy, and it may be said of punishment too. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said regarding this verse: rijs is wrath. It may also be said of what is foul-smelling, of filth, and of excrement: "rijs." The rijz is punishment only; the riks is excrement only; and rijs is said of both matters. Allah the Exalted commanded avoidance of these things, and the command form in His saying "fa-ijtanibuhu" was joined by the texts of the hadiths and the consensus of the Ummah; so avoidance attained the rank of prohibition. By this, intoxicants were prohibited by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, the explicit text of the hadith, and the consensus of the Ummah. The explanation and meaning of the word khamr, and the explanation of maysir, have already passed in Surat al-Baqarah; and the explanation of the idolatrous altars and of seeking decisions by the arrows has passed at the beginning of this surah.

People differed concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses. Abu Maysarah said: they were revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), for he mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ) the faults of intoxicants and what befalls people because of them, and he called upon Allah regarding its prohibition, and said: "O Allah, make clear to us a healing explanation concerning it." Then these verses were revealed, and 'Umar said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Mus'ab ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas narrated from his father Sa'd, who said: A man from the Ansar prepared food and invited us, and we drank intoxicants until we became intoxicated; then the Ansar and the Quraysh boasted, and each group said: "We are better than you." Then a man from the Ansar took a jawbone of a camel and struck Sa'd's nose with it, and it split it, so Sa'd had a split nose. Sa'd said: "Concerning me the verse was revealed, to its end."

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: The prohibition of intoxicants was revealed concerning two tribes of the Ansar who drank until, when they became drunk, they became violent; then when they became sober, each one of them saw the trace on his face, his beard, and his body, and would say: "This is the doing of so-and-so to me." So enmities arose between them over this, and these verses were revealed concerning that.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The matter of intoxicants came about gradually, through many incidents, among them the story of Hamzah when he slit open the humps, and he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Are you anything but slaves of my father?" And among them was the recitation of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Maghrib prayer: "Say: O disbelievers, I worship what you worship," so there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [an-Nisa': 43], to the end of the verse. Then incidents continued to afflict people because of it, until this verse was revealed, and it was prohibited in Madinah; and grape wine was scarce there. Their intoxicants were made from five things: from honey, from dates, from raisins, from wheat, and from barley. The Ummah is unanimous on the prohibition of the little and the much of grape wine that has not been touched by fire and not mixed with anything. Most of the Ummah hold that whatever intoxicates in large quantity is also prohibited in small quantity. Abu Hanifah and some jurists of Kufa held the permissibility of what does not intoxicate from among what intoxicates in large quantity, other than grape wine; and this is a rejected position. Some have deduced the prohibition of intoxicants from describing them as "rijs." Allah, blessed and exalted, described in another verse carrion, flowing blood, and the flesh of swine as rijs; so it follows that every rijs is prohibited. The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In this there is room for scrutiny. And ijtinab (avoidance) is making a thing a side or a direction.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, informed His servants that Satan only wants enmity to occur among the believers because of intoxicants and what incites to them, and because of gambling, since they would gamble over wealth and family, until the loser might remain grieved and poor, so grudges and enmity arise from that; and if the matter does not reach the degree of enmity, it becomes hatred. The end of a people who hate one another is not good. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not hate one another, do not envy one another, do not turn your backs on one another, and be servants of Allah, brothers." And by the unity of souls and of the word, religion is protected and the enemy is fought; whereas hatred undoes the bonds of religion and demolishes the pillar of protection. Likewise, Satan also wants to turn the believers away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, and to preoccupy them from it with appetites; so intoxicants, gambling, and betting are all among his greatest instruments in that.

And in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ there is a threat within the form of a question, beyond the meaning of "desist." Since there was in the speech the meaning of "desist," it was good that "and obey" be conjoined to it; and "and obey" was repeated in mention of the Messenger for emphasis. Then Allah, Exalted, warned against opposing the command and threatened the one who turns away with the punishment of the Hereafter; that is: upon the Messenger is only to convey, and upon the One who sent him is to punish or to reward, according to what is disobeyed or obeyed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 93–94:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good; and Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

The occasion of this verse, as related by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Anas ibn Malik, is that: "When the prohibition of wine was revealed, some of the Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about those among us who died while drinking it (p-250) and consuming gambling?' and similar speech. So this verse was revealed."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is similar to their question about those who died while facing the first qibla, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Since the matter of the qibla was grave and one of the landmarks of the religion, some people imagined a deficiency in those who had missed it. Likewise, when wine and gambling came under this great degree of blame, some people became apprehensive and imagined a deficiency in those who had died while engaged in these reprehensible things. So the Blessed and Exalted One informed His servants that blame and blame-worthiness (junah) only attach through acts of disobedience, and those who died before the prohibition had not disobeyed by committing a forbidden act yet; rather these things were disliked, and were not explicitly prohibited, and it was the Law that made them ugly and made avoiding them good. The junah (blame): it is sin and culpability, and it is all of the ruling that characterizes the doer of disobedience and the attribution that follows the disobedient person.

And "ta'imu" (طَعِمُوا): its meaning is "they tasted," and by extension (فَصاعِدًا) it applies to the degrees of eating and drinking; it may be used metaphorically for sleep and other things, but its literal sense is the sense of taste.

The repetition in His saying "ittaqu" (اتَّقُوا) requires that each instance carry an increase over the one before it, and in this there is emphasis in these attributes for them. Some exegetes went on to specify the intended meaning of this repetition: a group said: the first degree is guarding against shirk and the major sins, with faith in its completeness and doing righteous deeds; the second degree is steadfastness and persistence in the aforementioned state; and the third degree is reaching the end of piety in carrying out what is not obligatory of the voluntary acts in prayer, charity and other things, and this is ihsan (excellence).

Another group said: the first degree refers to the past time, the second to the present, and the third to the future.

Another group said: the first guarding (ittiqa') is regarding shirk and adherence to the Law, the second regarding major sins, and the third regarding minor sins.

(p-251) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This verse is not restricted to those who have done all righteous deeds and attained complete piety; rather it applies to every believer, even if he sometimes disobeys, provided he has practised from these praiseworthy qualities what entitles him to be described as a believer who does righteous deeds, mindful of Allah in most of his affairs, and a doer of good. There is no blame on this category for what they have eaten of what was not forbidden to them.

Qudama ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi, one of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with him), interpreted this verse. He was among those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia with his two brothers, 'Uthman and 'Abd Allah; then he emigrated to Madina, witnessed Badr, lived a long life, and was the son-in-law of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, the maternal uncle of 'Abd Allah and Hafsa. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) appointed him over Bahrain, then dismissed him because al-Jarud, the chief of 'Abd al-Qays, came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and testified against him for drinking wine. 'Umar said to him: "Who testifies with you?" He said: "Abu Hurayra." Abu Hurayra came, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "What do you testify to?" He said: "I did not see him drinking, but I saw him drunk, vomiting." 'Umar said to him: "You have gone too far in testimony." Then 'Umar wrote to Qudama asking him to come to him; he came, and al-Jarud said to 'Umar: "Establish the Book of Allah upon this man." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Are you an adversary or a witness?" He said: "Rather, a witness." He said: "You have rendered your testimony," so al-Jarud fell silent. Then he went to 'Umar the next day and said: "Establish the Book of Allah upon Qudama." 'Umar said to him: "I see you as nothing but an adversary, and only one man testified with you." Al-Jarud said: "I adjure you by Allah." 'Umar said: "Either you hold your tongue, or I will harm you." Al-Jarud said: "By Allah, O 'Umar, this is not the truth: that your cousin should drink wine and it should upset me." Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "If you doubt our testimony, send to the daughter of al-Walid and ask her, for she is Qudama's wife." 'Umar sent to Hind bint al-Walid, adjuring her by Allah, and she gave testimony against her husband. 'Umar said to Qudama: "I will apply the prescribed punishment (hadd) to you." He said: "If I had drunk as they say, it would not be permitted for you to flog me." 'Umar said: "Why?" He said: "Because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾; the verse." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "You have erred in the interpretation; if you were mindful of Allah, you would avoid what He has forbidden you." Then 'Umar applied the punishment to him, and he was ill; some of the Companions said to him: "We do not think you should flog him while he is sick." One day 'Umar woke up having resolved to flog him, and said (p-252) to his companions: "What do you think about flogging Qudama?" They said: "We do not think so while he is in pain." 'Umar said: "That I should meet Allah while he is under the whips is dearer to me than that I should meet Him while he is upon my neck." He commanded that Qudama be flogged. Qudama became angry with 'Umar and shunned him until 'Umar performed the Hajj; Qudama also performed the Hajj with him, still angry with him. When 'Umar was at al-Suqya, he slept, then awoke and said: "Hasten Qudama to me, for a comer came to me in a dream and said: 'Reconcile with Qudama, for he is your brother.'" He sent for Qudama, but he refused to come; 'Umar said: "Drag him if he refuses." When he came, 'Umar spoke with him, asked forgiveness for him, and they were reconciled. Ayyub ibn Abi Tamima said: "No one among the people of Badr was punished for wine apart from him."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game﴾: that is, He will certainly try you, to see your obedience from your disobedience, and your patience from your inability regarding the game. Hunting was one of the livelihoods of the Arabs of the desert, widespread among all of them and very commonly practised; so Allah tested them with it, along with the state of ihram or the Sacred Precinct, just as He tested the Children of Israel in not transgressing on the Sabbath.

The "min" (مِن) may be partitive (lit-tab'id), meaning: of the game of the land, not of the sea; this was the view of al-Tabari and others. It may also be that the partitive applies to the state of sanctity (ihram), since ihram may end and one may leave the Sacred Precinct, so the game in some of these circumstances is part of the game in general. It is also permissible that it is explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins). Al-Zajjaj said: this is like your saying: "I will test you with something of provision," and like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30].

His saying "bi-shay'" (بِشَيْءٍ) requires some partitive sense; and many jurists have said that the ba' (بِ) in His saying: ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] conveyed a certain partitive sense.

Ibn Wththab and al-Nakha'i read "yanaluhu" (يَنالُهُ) with a yaa' dotted from below. Mujahid said: the hands reach the chicks, the eggs, and whatever cannot flee; and the spears reach the large game.

(p-253) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The apparent reason that Allah the Exalted specifically mentioned the hands is that they are the greatest instrument of action in hunting, the tool of tools; and into them enter hunting dogs, snares, and whatever is made by hand of traps and nets. The spears are specifically mentioned because they are the greatest means by which game is wounded, and into them enters the arrow and the like. Some people argued from this verse that the game belongs to the one who catches it, not to the one who startles it, because the one who startled it has not yet had his hand or spear reach anything.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"li-ya'lama"⁠﴾ means: so that His knowledge may continue upon it, while it already exists, since Allah the Exalted knew that from eternity.

Al-Zuhri read "li-yu'lima Allah" (لِيُعْلِمَ اللهُ) with a dammah on the yaa' and a kasrah on the lam; that is, so that He may make His servants know.

As for ﴿"bil-ghayb"⁠﴾: al-Tabari said its meaning is: in this world, where the servant does not see his Lord, so He is absent from him. The apparent meaning is: "in the unseen" from people, that is, in privacy; so whoever fears Allah refrains from the game of his own accord, even though it would have been hidden from him had he hunted. Then the Exalted threatened whoever transgresses after this prohibition that is to come, and this is what He intended by His saying: ﴿"la-yabluwannakum"⁠﴾; and His saying "dhalika" pointed to it. The painful punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 93–94:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good; and Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

The occasion of this verse, as related by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Anas ibn Malik, is that: "When the prohibition of wine was revealed, some of the Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about those among us who died while drinking it (p-250) and consuming gambling?' and similar speech. So this verse was revealed."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is similar to their question about those who died while facing the first qibla, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Since the matter of the qibla was grave and one of the landmarks of the religion, some people imagined a deficiency in those who had missed it. Likewise, when wine and gambling came under this great degree of blame, some people became apprehensive and imagined a deficiency in those who had died while engaged in these reprehensible things. So the Blessed and Exalted One informed His servants that blame and blame-worthiness (junah) only attach through acts of disobedience, and those who died before the prohibition had not disobeyed by committing a forbidden act yet; rather these things were disliked, and were not explicitly prohibited, and it was the Law that made them ugly and made avoiding them good. The junah (blame): it is sin and culpability, and it is all of the ruling that characterizes the doer of disobedience and the attribution that follows the disobedient person.

And "ta'imu" (طَعِمُوا): its meaning is "they tasted," and by extension (فَصاعِدًا) it applies to the degrees of eating and drinking; it may be used metaphorically for sleep and other things, but its literal sense is the sense of taste.

The repetition in His saying "ittaqu" (اتَّقُوا) requires that each instance carry an increase over the one before it, and in this there is emphasis in these attributes for them. Some exegetes went on to specify the intended meaning of this repetition: a group said: the first degree is guarding against shirk and the major sins, with faith in its completeness and doing righteous deeds; the second degree is steadfastness and persistence in the aforementioned state; and the third degree is reaching the end of piety in carrying out what is not obligatory of the voluntary acts in prayer, charity and other things, and this is ihsan (excellence).

Another group said: the first degree refers to the past time, the second to the present, and the third to the future.

Another group said: the first guarding (ittiqa') is regarding shirk and adherence to the Law, the second regarding major sins, and the third regarding minor sins.

(p-251) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This verse is not restricted to those who have done all righteous deeds and attained complete piety; rather it applies to every believer, even if he sometimes disobeys, provided he has practised from these praiseworthy qualities what entitles him to be described as a believer who does righteous deeds, mindful of Allah in most of his affairs, and a doer of good. There is no blame on this category for what they have eaten of what was not forbidden to them.

Qudama ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi, one of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with him), interpreted this verse. He was among those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia with his two brothers, 'Uthman and 'Abd Allah; then he emigrated to Madina, witnessed Badr, lived a long life, and was the son-in-law of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, the maternal uncle of 'Abd Allah and Hafsa. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) appointed him over Bahrain, then dismissed him because al-Jarud, the chief of 'Abd al-Qays, came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and testified against him for drinking wine. 'Umar said to him: "Who testifies with you?" He said: "Abu Hurayra." Abu Hurayra came, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "What do you testify to?" He said: "I did not see him drinking, but I saw him drunk, vomiting." 'Umar said to him: "You have gone too far in testimony." Then 'Umar wrote to Qudama asking him to come to him; he came, and al-Jarud said to 'Umar: "Establish the Book of Allah upon this man." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Are you an adversary or a witness?" He said: "Rather, a witness." He said: "You have rendered your testimony," so al-Jarud fell silent. Then he went to 'Umar the next day and said: "Establish the Book of Allah upon Qudama." 'Umar said to him: "I see you as nothing but an adversary, and only one man testified with you." Al-Jarud said: "I adjure you by Allah." 'Umar said: "Either you hold your tongue, or I will harm you." Al-Jarud said: "By Allah, O 'Umar, this is not the truth: that your cousin should drink wine and it should upset me."
