The painful punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter.

(p-254) The address is to all the believers. This prohibition is the trial of which the earlier words "He will surely test you" gave notice. The word *al-sayd* (game, the hunted animal) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) treated as a noun, so it refers to the animal that is hunted. The word *al-sayd* here is general in form, but its meaning is restricted, to exclude the animal which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted to be killed within the sacred precinct (*haram*). It is established from him ﷺ that he said: "Five harmful creatures may be killed in the sacred precinct: the crow, the kite, the mouse, the scorpion, and the rabid dog." Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh adhered to the apparent meaning of this hadith, and so they did not permit the one in the state of ihram (*muhrim*) to kill anything other than what was mentioned. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, extended by analogy from the rabid dog to every creature that rages against people and attacks them, and he regarded it as included in the wording. He said: the one in ihram may kill the lion, the leopard, the panther, the wolf, and every aggressive predator, initiating the killing. As for the cat, the fox and the hyena, the one in ihram may not kill them, and if he kills them he must pay a ransom (*fidya*). The companions of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*, the Hanafis) said: if the predator attacks the one in ihram, he may kill it; but if the one in ihram initiates the attack, he must pay its value. Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: the one in ihram may not kill any predator except one that attacks him. Ibn 'Umar said: whatever predator attacks you, you may attack it. As for the young of a predator before they hunt, Malik said in *al-Mudawwana* (the codified compilation of his doctrine): it is not proper for the one in ihram to kill them. Ashhab said in the book of "Muhammad": if he does so, he must pay the compensation (*jaza'*). Ashhab also said, and Ibn al-Qasim said: there is no compensation for him. It is established from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he commanded those in ihram to kill snakes, and the scholars agreed on the permissibility of killing them. It is also established from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that killing the wasp is permitted, because it is in the ruling of the scorpion. Malik said: the killer must feed something (to the poor). Malik likewise said regarding one who kills the flea, the fly, the ant and the like. The companions of opinion said: there is nothing upon the killer of all of these. As for birds of prey, Malik said: the one in ihram may not kill them, and if he does, he must pay a ransom. Ibn al-Qasim said in the book of "Muhammad": "I prefer that he not kill the crow and the kite until they harm him; but if he does so, there is nothing upon him."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All venomous creatures are in the ruling of the snake, such as the viper and the tarantula. Whatever is other than what we have mentioned is of that which Allah forbade killing in the sanctity of the land or of the state of ihram, and He prescribed compensation for the one who kills it.

"Hurum" (those in the state of sanctity) is the plural of "haram", which means one who has entered the sacred precinct or the state of ihram. "Haram" is used for the masculine, the feminine, the dual and the plural.

The scholars differed regarding the meaning of His words "intentionally" (*muta'ammidan*). Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is one who intentionally kills it while forgetting his ihram. This is the one who must expiate; and likewise, the pure error (*khata' mahd*) requires expiation. But if he kills it intentionally, remembering his ihram, this is too grave and too great to be expiated. Mujahid said: he has become free of ihram, and there is no concession for him. Ibn Jurayj said the same, and al-Mahdawi and others narrated that his pilgrimage is void. Ibn Zayd said: this is left to the vengeance of Allah. A group of the people of knowledge, among them Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, Tawus and others, said: the one who acts intentionally is the one who intends to kill while remembering his ihram; and he must expiate. Likewise the forgetful one and the one who kills by mistake must expiate. Al-Zuhri said: the Qur'an was revealed concerning the intentional killing, and the Sunnah established in the case of killing by mistake that both must expiate. Some people said: the one who kills by mistake is not obliged to expiate.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited *fa-jaza'u mithli ma* (with *jaza'* in the nominative and *mithl* in the genitive), with the *jaza'* annexed to *mithl*. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim recited *fa-jaza'un* (with *jaza'* in the nominative) and *mithlu* (also in the nominative). As for the first recitation, its meaning is: "upon him is compensation of the like of what he killed, that is, its payment and its fine." The word *mithl* here is used as in your saying, "I honour the like of you," while you intend by your saying, "I honour you." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]; the implied meaning is "like one who is in darkness."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His words "*fa-jaza'un mithlu*" may also mean: "upon him is that he must pay the like of what," and then the annexation to *mithl*, which is the thing by which the compensation is paid, occurred by way of extension (*ittisa'an*). As for the second recitation, its meaning is: "so the obligation upon him, or the thing required of him, is a compensation of the like of what," and *mithl*, in this recitation, is an adjective of *jaza'*, that is: "so a similar compensation."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿*min al-na'am*﴾ ("of the cattle") are an adjective of *jaza'* in both recitations.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud recited *fa-jaza'uhu mithlu ma* with the pronoun *hu* made explicit; it may refer to the game (*al-sayd*) or to the hunter who killed it. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman (al-A'raj) recited *fa-jaza'un* with nunation (tanwin) and *mithla ma* in the accusative; Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: *mithla* is in the accusative governed by the verbal noun *jaza'* itself, that is: "upon him is that he must pay the like of what he killed."

The scholars differed regarding how this likeness is to be determined. The majority held that the two arbiters look at the animal killed in its creation and its size of appearance, and so they make from the cattle the compensation for it. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, al-Suddi and a group of jurists said: for the ostrich, the wild ass and the like, a camel (*badana*); for the wild goat (*wa'l*), the camel and the like, a cow; for the gazelle and the like, a ram; for the hare and the like, a sheep in its second year (*thaniyya*); for the jerboa, a young lamb; and for a locust or the like, a handful of food; for birds, their value is estimated in food, and then he may give it in charity, or if he wishes he may fast, one day for each *sa'* (measure). If he finds the eggs of an ostrich, the male is brought to a number of the young she-camels that he has found, and whatever is produced from them he gives as a gift to the House; and whatever spoils from them, there is nothing upon him concerning it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled upon Qabisa ibn Jabir in the case of a gazelle with a sheep. 'Umar and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf also ruled. Qabisa said: "I said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful, its matter is lighter than that you should summon one who will judge with you.'" He said: "So he struck me with the whip (*dirra*) until I outran him in a run. Then he said: 'Did you kill the game while you were in ihram, and then you make light of the legal ruling?'" This story is in the *Muwatta'* with different wording; and it is likewise narrated that the case happened to a companion of Qabisa, and Qabisa is the one who narrated it in both accounts. Allah knows best. As for the hare, the jerboa and the like, the ruling according to Malik is that it is valued in food; and if he wishes he may give it in charity, or if he wishes he may fast in place of each *mudd* (measure) a day. Likewise, according to him, the fasting in the expiation of compensation is entirely a day in place of each *mudd*; according to some, in place of a *sa'*; and according to some, in place of two *mudds*. As for the pigeons of the sacred precinct, according to Malik, there is a sheep for the pigeon; and for other pigeons, a ruling of arbiters (*hukuma*), since they are not like the pigeons of the sacred precinct. As for the eggs of the ostrich and of the rest of birds, according to Malik, for the egg there is a tenth of the price of its mother. Ibn al-Qasim said: whether or not there is a chick in it, provided that the chick does not cry out after it is broken; but if it cries out, then there is the full compensation, like the compensation for the adult of that bird. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: by the ruling of two just arbiters. Ibn Wahb said: if in the egg of the ostrich or what is less than it there is a chick, then a tenth of the price of its mother; and if there is not, then a day's fast, or a *mudd* for each poor person.

A group of the people of knowledge, among them al-Nakha'i and others, held that the likeness is only in value: the killed game is valued, and then with its value a similar animal from the cattle is bought, and then it is offered as a gift. Al-Tabari and others rejected this opinion.

*Al-na'am* (cattle) is a term that applies to camels, cows and sheep when these kinds are together; when each kind is alone, it is not called *na'am* except the camel alone. Al-Hasan recited *min al-nu'm* with the vowelless 'ayn; and this is a dialect form. The compensation is obligatory only by killing the game, not merely by seizing it, according to the ruling of the wording of the verse. This is evident in *al-Mudawwana* from the case of the one who hunted a bird, plucked its feathers, then confined it until its feathers grew back, and it flew away: he said, there is no compensation upon him. The Qur'an restricted this case to two just arbiters who are learned in the ruling of the case and in its estimation. 'Umar and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with them both, ruled; and he ordered Abu Jarir al-Bajali to go to two men of the just, so that they might judge against him concerning a female gazelle (*anz*) of the gazelles which he had hunted. He said: "So I came to 'Abd al-Rahman and Sa'd, and they ruled against me a bearded male goat (*tays a'far*)." Ibn 'Umar summoned Ibn Safwan to judge together with him in a compensation. This is the view of the majority of people and of the jurists of the cities.

Ibn Wahb, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *al-'Utbiyya*: "It is from the Sunnah that the two arbiters give the one who hunted the game a choice, just as Allah gave him the choice: to bring a sacrificial animal (*hady*) reaching the Ka'ba, or an expiation, the food of the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting. If he chooses the sacrificial animal, the two arbiters judge against him with what they consider a counterpart to what he hunted, whether between them and the equivalent of that, a sheep, since it is the lowest of the sacrificial animals; and what does not reach a sheep, they judge concerning it by food; then he is given the choice to feed it, or to fast a day in place of each *mudd*." Likewise Malik said in *al-Mudawwana*: "When the one who hit the game wants to feed, or to fast, even if for what he hit there is a counterpart from the cattle, its game is valued in food, not in dirhams." He said: "If they value it in dirhams, and with the dirhams food is bought, I would hope that it would be ample; but the first is more correct. If he wishes he feeds, otherwise he fasts in its place a day for each *mudd*, even if that exceeds two months or three."

Yahya ibn 'Umar, one of our companions, said: "It is only said: how many people will be satisfied by this game? So the number is known; then it is said: how much food will satisfy this number? If he wishes, he gives out that food; and if he wishes, he fasts the number of its *amdad* (measures)."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a good opinion, in which he exercised caution, because the value of the game in food may be small; so by this consideration the food increases. Some people of knowledge hold that the fasting for the compensation should not exceed two months, saying: because it is the highest of the expiations by fasting.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿*hadyan bala'a al-Ka'ba*﴾ ("a sacrificial animal reaching the Ka'ba"): this wording requires that this sacrificial animal be sent off until it reaches (the Ka'ba). The Ka'ba is mentioned because it is the mother of the sanctuary and the head of its sanctity; and the entire sanctuary is a place of sacrifice for this sacrificial animal. So what is presented at 'Arafa from this compensation is slaughtered at Mina; and what is not presented there is slaughtered at Makka and in the rest of the areas of the sanctuary, on condition that it enters from outside the sacred area (*hill*). It is necessary that there be combined in it both the outside and the sacred area, until it reaches the Ka'ba.

'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj recited *hadiyyan bala'a al-Ka'ba*, with a kasra on the *dal* and a shadda on the *ya'*. *Hadyan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) from the pronoun in *bihi*; and it was said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*). *Bala'a* is in fact indefinite (*nakira*); the annexation did not remove from it the generality (*shiyu'*), so its underlying form is *bala'an al-Ka'ba*, with its tanwin dropped for lightness.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *aw kaffara tun* (with the *kaffara* nunated), *ta'amu masakin* (with *ta'am* in the nominative and annexed to the plural *masakin*). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited *kaffaratu* (with the *kaffara* in the nominative, without nunation), and *ta'ami* in the genitive, annexed, and *masakin* in the plural. Abu 'Ali said: the grammatical status of *ta'am* in the reading of the one who put it in the nominative is that it is a *'atf bayan* (an appositive explanatory apposition), because the food is the expiation; and he did not annex the *kaffara* to the food, because it is not for the food; rather, it is for killing the game.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 95 (part 2 of 2):

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: All of this discussion is based on the premise that the expiation (kaffara) is the food. But this is open to question, because the expiation is the covering of the sin by giving food. The expiation is other than the food, but it is accomplished through it. So with the nominative "ṭaʿām" (food), the most apt reading is that it is in apposition (al-badal al-maḥḍ, pure substitution). The reading of the one who puts the expiation in the genitive construction with the food is also acceptable, understood as an idafa of specification (idafat takhṣīṣ), since the expiation for this killing may be an expiation of a sacrificial animal (hady), or an expiation of food, or an expiation of fasting.

Al-A'raj and Isa ibn Umar read: "aw kaffāratun" with the nominative and tanwin, "ṭaʿāmu" with the nominative without tanwin, and "miskīnin" in the singular, which is a noun of genus (ism jins).

Malik (may God have mercy on him) and a group of scholars said: the one who killed the game has a choice among the three grades, even if he is wealthy, and this is what the particle "aw" (or) implies according to them. Ibn 'Abbas and a group said: the one making expiation does not move from the sacrificial animal to food unless he cannot find an animal; and likewise he does not fast unless he cannot find anything with which to feed. This was also said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. They said: the meaning is "or the expiation of food, if he does not find the hady."

Malik (may God have mercy on him) and a group with him hold that what is valued is the killed game itself, which is valued in food, as has already been stated. The Iraqi scholars said: the recompense is only valued as food. So whoever kills a gazelle, the gazelle is valued according to Malik, and its equivalent is valued in rams or something else according to Abu Hanifa and others. Al-Tabari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) that he said: when the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) hits game, its recompense is adjudged against him from the livestock (al-naʿam). If he finds its recompense, he slaughters it and gives it in charity; if he does not find it, the recompense is valued in dirhams; then the dirhams are valued in wheat; then he fasts one day for every half ṣāʿ. He said: the mention of food is intended only to clarify the matter of fasting, and whoever does not find food, then he is seeking recompense. He also attributed this to al-Suddi.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: this view is objected to by the outward wording of the verse, for it conflicts with it, and the hady can only be in the Haram, as we mentioned earlier.

People differed concerning the food. A group of scholars said: feeding and fasting may be done wherever the one making expiation wishes in the lands. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and others said: the hady and the feeding are in Makkah, and the fasting is wherever you wish.

(p-260) As for His saying, ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾: the majority read "ʿadl" with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, and its meaning is the counterpart of a thing by balance and by equivalence in value (al-miqdār al-maʿnawī). Ibn 'Abbas, Talha ibn Musarrif, and al-Jahdari read "ʿidl" with a kasra on the ʿayn. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) transmitted it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Some people said: "al-ʿadl" with the fatḥa means the measure of a thing of a different kind, and "ʿidluhu" with the kasra means its measure of the same kind. Makki attributed this to al-Kisa'i, and it is a mistake. The correct position from al-Kisa'i is that both are dialect forms for "equivalent." This attributed statement is an objectionable expression, and the intent of its speaker is that "al-ʿidl" with the kasra is the measure of a thing by actual balance, like the two loads of a camel (ʿidlayi al-baʿīr); and "ʿadluhu" is its measure from another thing by a balance in value, as one says of the price of a horse: "this is its equivalent in gold." Kasra on the ʿayn does not seem correct here, as far as I have memorized.

The reference by "dhālika" (that) in His saying "or its equivalent" may refer to the food, and on this basis is built the view of those jurists who said: the days of fasting are according to the number of mudd measures, or ṣāʿ measures, or half of them, depending on the disagreement I have mentioned about that. It is also possible, and indeed necessary, that the reference by "dhālika" is to the killed game. On this basis is built the view of those scholars who said: fasting for killing game is only according to the amount of the one killed.

Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: if the muhrim kills a gazelle, then upon him is a sheep to be slaughtered in Makkah. If he does not find it, then feeding six poor people. If he does not find that, then fasting three days. If he kills an ayyal (a male deer), then upon him is a cow. If he does not find it, then feeding twenty poor people. If he does not find it, he fasts twenty days. If he kills an ostrich or a wild ass, then upon him is a camel. If he does not find it, he feeds thirty poor people. If he does not find it, he fasts thirty days.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) previously stated a view other than this just now, which al-Tabari transmitted from him with two chains. It is not denied that he may have two opinions regarding the form of the expiation.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, in explaining His saying ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾, said: he fasts three days, up to ten.

As for His saying ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his deed﴾: "dhawq" (tasting) here is used metaphorically, as He said: ﴿Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]; and as He said: ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]; and as Abu (p-261) Sufyan said: "Taste, ʿUqaq." The literal meaning of tasting is in the sense of the tongue, and in all of this it is metaphorical for what is experienced by the self. "Al-wabāl" is the evil consequence, and "al-marʿā al-wabīl" is the pasture that one is harmed by after eating it. He expressed by "amrihi" (his affair) his whole condition: from killing, expiation, the judgment against him, the loss of his property, or his hardship through fasting.

The interpreters differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿Allah has pardoned what has passed﴾. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and a group with him said: its meaning is: "Allah has pardoned what passed in your jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period), from your killing of game while in the sacred state. And whoever returns now in Islam: if he is one who considers it lawful, then Allah will take vengeance on him in the Hereafter, and he is expiated in the outward judgment; and if he is one who disobeys, then the retribution is only in imposing the expiation alone." They said: whenever the muhrim returns, he makes expiation.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: the scrupulous fear that the retribution remains along with the expiation. This is the view of the jurists: Malik and his counterparts and companions (may God have mercy on them). Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: the muhrim who kills repeatedly while forgetting his state of ihram, then he makes expiation each time. As for the one who kills intentionally and knowingly of his ihram, he makes expiation the first time, and God pardons his sin along with the expiation. If he returns a second time, then no judgment is passed against him, and it is said to him: "Allah will take vengeance on you," as Allah said. Shurayh the qadi, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and Mujahid held this view. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: killing game was permitted once; whoever returns, Allah does not leave him alone until He takes vengeance on him.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: this statement from him (may God be pleased with him) is an admonition through the verse; and he, despite that, holds that judgment should be passed against him for returning, and that he should make expiation; but he feared, despite that, the persistence of retribution.

(p-262) Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse ﴿Allah has pardoned what has passed﴾ is: for you, O believers, regarding killing game before this prohibition and this forbiddance. He said: as for whoever returns and kills game while knowing its sanctity and intentionally killing, this one is not judged, and he is left to the retribution of Allah. The meaning of His saying ﴿"intentionally"﴾ at the beginning of the verse is: intentionally killing, while forgetting the sanctity.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: this section has already been mentioned.

Al-Tabari said: some people said: this verse is specific to a particular individual. It is attributed to Zayd ibn al-Mu'alla that a man hit game while in ihram, and he was excused for it; then he returned, so Allah sent a fire upon him that burned him. This is His saying ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take vengeance on him﴾.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ is an alert to two attributes, which requires the fear of one who has insight; and whoever fears is restrained. From this meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever fears sets out at night; and whoever sets out at night reaches the destination."

(p-263) The Almighty's statement:

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travellers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage). And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿Allah made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a means of support for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the hady (sacrificial animals brought to Makka) and the qala'id (garlanded animals), that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and that Allah is Knower of all things.﴾ ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is a ruling permitting the game of the sea, which is every creature caught from its fish. This permission applies both to the one in ihram and to the one not in ihram. Here too "game" (ṣayd) refers to the thing caught, and it is attributed to the sea because it comes from it by way of a means. "Sea" (baḥr) means a large body of water, whether salty or fresh, and every large river is a sea.

(p-263) People differed concerning the meaning of His words "and its food". Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with them both), and a large group of the Companions, the Successors, and those after them, said: it is what the sea casts up and what floats on its surface, because that is food, not game. A man asked Ibn 'Umar about fish that the sea had thrown up, and he forbade them. Then he read the Mushaf and said to Nafi': "Go to him and order him to eat them, for they are the food of the sea." This interpretation looks to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Its water is pure, and its dead animal is lawful."

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and a group said: "its food" is whatever is salted from it and preserved, since those are processed things that enter into food and make it food; game is only the fresh catch. Others said: "its food" is its salt, which forms from its water, and whatever plants and the like are in it.

A group disliked the water pig, while Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "You call it a pig," but his school holds that it is permitted.

The view of Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) is the most preponderant of the opinions, and it is the school of Malik.

Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith read: "wa-ṭu'muhu" (with a damma on the ṭa' and a sukun on the 'ayn, without an alif).

"Provision" (matā'an) is in the accusative as a verbal noun. The meaning is: "He has given it to you as a provision by which you benefit and use as relish." "For you" refers to those present at the sea and its cities. "For the travellers" means the wayfarers. Mujahid said the addressees are the people of the villages, and the travellers are the people of the cities.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems he means the people of the sea's villages, and that the travellers are from the cities other than those villages, who bring it to the cities.

Scholars differed about the implication of His words: ﴿but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram﴾. Some understood it in its general sense, in all its aspects. They said: the one in ihram may not hunt, nor order hunting, nor eat game hunted on his behalf or not on his behalf. The meat of game in any form is forbidden to the one in ihram.

(p-264) It is narrated that 'Uthman performed Hajj, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib performed it with him. 'Uthman was brought meat of game that a non-pilgrim had hunted, and he ate some of it, but 'Ali did not eat. 'Uthman said: "By Allah, we did not hunt it, nor order it, nor point to it." 'Ali said: ﴿and the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram﴾.

It is also narrated that 'Uthman appointed Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith over al-'Urud, and he hunted some wild ewes (ya'aqib), placed them in an enclosure, and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by him, so he cooked them and served them to him. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib came and forbade them to eat, and mentioned something similar to what has been mentioned before. The narrator said: Then when they were in Makka, 'Uthman was told: "Would you like to see 'Ali? Someone has given him a donkey's haunch, and he is eating from it." 'Uthman sent for him and asked him about eating the haunch, and said to him: "As for you, you eat, but as for us, you forbid us." 'Ali said to him: "It was hunted in the first year, and I was not in ihram, so there is no harm for me in eating it. And that (meaning the ewes) was hunted while I was in ihram, and they were slaughtered while I was in ihram." A view like 'Ali's is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Tawus, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) did not see any harm for the one in ihram to eat the meat of game that a non-pilgrim hunted for a non-pilgrim like himself, or for himself. Abu Hurayra was asked about this case, and he gave a ruling permitting it. Then he informed 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said to him: "If you had given any other ruling, I would have struck your head with this whip." Abu al-Sha'tha' asked Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) about this issue, and he said to him: "'Umar used to eat it." He said: "I said: and you?" He said: "'Umar was better than me." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "Whatever is hunted or slaughtered while you are not in ihram is lawful for you; and whatever is hunted or slaughtered while you are in ihram is forbidden for you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is like the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him).

'Ata' narrated from Ka'b, who said: I came with some people in ihram, and we found the meat of a wild donkey (p-265) and they asked me about eating it, and I gave them a ruling permitting it. Then we came to 'Umar and informed him of that. He said: "I have appointed him over you until you return." 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam (may Allah be pleased with them both) said the same as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. This is the sound view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) ate from the donkey that Abu Qatada hunted while he was not in ihram, and the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was in ihram.

Al-Tabari said: Others said: what is forbidden to the one in ihram is only hunting. As for buying game from its owner and slaughtering and eating it, that is not forbidden. He then mentioned that Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman bought a cat while he was at al-'Araj, and ate it, and people criticized him for that.

Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) permits the one in ihram to eat what a non-pilgrim hunted and slaughtered, provided it was not hunted on account of the one in ihram. If it was hunted on his account, he must not eat it. Al-Shafi'i said the same. Then they differed if he ate it: Malik said: he must pay the compensation (jaza'); al-Shafi'i said: there is no compensation for him.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read: "wa-ḥarrama" (with a fatha on the ḥa' and the ra' doubled), "ṣayda" (with a fatha on the dal), "mā dumtum ḥarāman" (with a fatha on the ḥa'). The meaning is: "And Allah has forbidden to you," and "ḥaraman" applies to both the plural and the singular, like "riḍan" and similar words. The meaning is "as long as you are in ihram," so it is, in meaning, like the reading of the majority with a damma on the ḥa' and the ra'.

(p-266) There is no disagreement that what never leaves the water is game of the sea, and what never leaves the land is game of the land. Scholars differed about what lives in one and may also live in the other. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him), Abu Mijlaz, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others said: whatever lives on land and has life there is game of the land. If the one in ihram kills it, he must pay its ransom (fidya). Abu Mijlaz mentioned frogs, tortoises, and crabs in this regard.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Among these are types that never leave the water, so they are without doubt game of the sea. On this basis, Malik's answer about frogs in al-Mudawwana came out: he said, "Frogs are game of the sea." It is narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah a view contrary to what we have mentioned, namely that he considered where the animal spends most of its life. He was asked about the water-son (ibn al-ma'), whether it is game of the land or game of the sea? He said: "Wherever it is found most, it belongs to that; and wherever it breeds, it belongs to that."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The correct view regarding ibn al-ma' is that it is game of the land, a bird that grazes and eats grain.

His Exalted statement: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is an emphasis and a reminder following this permission and prohibition. Then He mentioned the matter of the gathering and the Resurrection, as an intensification of the warning.

Since the sanctity of the Sacred Precinct (haram) and the inviolability conferred by ihram were shown in these verses, for the sake of the Ka'ba, and because it is the House of Allah and the source of these virtues, He mentioned in His statement, Glorified is He: ﴿Allah made﴾ and so on, what He established among the people and guided them to, and what He imposed upon the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyya), from their commitment that the Ka'ba is a qiwam, the hady is a qiwam, and the qala'id are a qiwam. That is, a matter that sustains the people through security and the lawfulness of fighting, just as kings, who are the pillars of the world, do. Since that nation had no king, Allah made these things like a king for them. He informed that the people's adherence to this is among what He legislated and was pleased with. What shows the weight of these matters in their souls is that when Quraysh sent al-Hulays to him at the time of al-Hudaybiya, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, when he saw him: "This is a man who honors the sanctity; so let the sacrificial camels (budn) with marked humps be shown to him." When al-Hulays saw them, it weighed heavily on him, and he said: "These should not be barred," and he returned from his mission.

(p-267) In this verse, "made" (ja'ala) means "rendered." "The Ka'ba" is the House in Makka, and it was called "Ka'ba" because of its squareness. The lexicographers said: every square house is "mukaʿʿab" and "Ka'ba." From this is the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"The people of Khawarnaq, al-Sadir, and Bariq,
and the House with its cubes in Sindad."

They said: there were square houses in it. In the book of the biographies of Ibn Ishaq, it is mentioned that in Khath'am there was a house they called "the Ka'ba of the Yemenis." Others said it was called "Ka'ba" because of its protrusion and its rising above the earth. From this is "ka'aba thady al-jariya" (the girl's breast protruded), from this "ka'b al-qadam" (the ankle), and from this "ku'ub al-qanat" (the joints of the spear).

"Qiyaman" means: a matter that sustains the people with security and benefits, just as the king is the support of the subjects. Their qiyam is said with a ya' (qiyam), like "al-siyam" and similar words, because of the lightness of the ya'. Thus some words originally with a waw are used with a ya'. The original form "qiwam" is also used, as the rajaz poet said:

"The support of this world and the support of religion."

Some interpreters went to the view that the meaning of His statement ﴿qiyaman lil-nas﴾ is: the place where standing (qiyam) in the rites and acts of worship is obligatory, and the restraint of souls in the Sacred Month, and with the hady and the qala'id.

Ibn 'Amir alone read "qiyaman" without an alif as "qiyaman" (qiyam), and this is either as a verbal noun, like "al-shiba'" and similar words, and it was made defective (u'illa) so it was not treated like "iwad" and "ḥiwal," since its verb is defective. Plurals are also made defective because their singulars are defective, so verbal nouns are more fitting to be made defective because their verbs are. "Qiyaman" may also mean that the alif is omitted while it is intended, and the rule for this is that it occurs in poetry and not in ordinary speech.

Al-Jahdari read "qayyiman," with a fatha on the qaf and a doubled, kasra-ed ya'.

"Al-Shahr" here is a generic noun, and the intended meaning is the three months, by consensus of the Arabs. The Sacred Month of Mudar is Rajab, called "al-Asamm," named so because no sound of iron was heard in it, and they called it "Muncil al-Asinna" (the one that removes spearheads), because they used to remove the spearheads of their lances in it. It was the month of Quraysh, and 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas said about it:

"And the month of the Banu Umayya, and the offerings,
when they are driven with their blood flowing."

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) named it "the Month of Allah," that is, "the Month of the Family of Allah," since the people of the Sacred Precinct were called "the Family of Allah." It may also be called "the Month of Allah" because Allah established it and made it firm, since many Arabs did not regard it.

As for the hady, it was a safety for the one who drove it, because he knew he was in worship and had not come for war. As for the qala'id, it was likewise. A man, when he set out wishing to perform Hajj, would hang on himself something from the bark of the acacia or other trees, and that was a safety for him. The matter was great in their souls, which Allah had established, so that one who was not in ihram could not hang anything on himself, out of fear of Allah. Likewise, when they returned, they would hang on themselves something from the trees of the Sacred Precinct.

His Exalted statement: "lil-nas" (for the people) is a general term, and some exegetes said it means the Arabs. The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: There is no basis for this restriction. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Allah made these matters for the people, though they did not hope for Paradise nor fear the Fire. Then Islam reinforced that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 96–98 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted, "That" (dhalika) is a reference to His having made these matters a means of establishment (qiyaman). The meaning is: "He did that so that you may know that Allah, exalted is He, knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your welfare, O people, both before and after; so consider His gentleness toward the servants despite their state of disbelief."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, is general in complete generality, encompassing particulars and the subtleties of existing things, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. Holding otherwise is deviation (ilhad) in the religion and disbelief.

Then Allah, exalted is He, warned His servants and gave them hope by His saying: ﴿Know that Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. Indeed, this is the matter in itself: it is fitting that the servant be fearful, acting in accordance with fear, mindful of God (muttaqi), and at ease in accordance with hope.

(p-263) The Almighty's statement:

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travellers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage). And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿Allah made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a means of support for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the hady (sacrificial animals brought to Makka) and the qala'id (garlanded animals), that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and that Allah is Knower of all things.﴾ ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The meaning is: "He did that so that you may know that Allah, exalted is He, knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your welfare, O people, both before and after; so consider His gentleness toward the servants despite their state of disbelief."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, is general in complete generality, encompassing particulars and the subtleties of existing things, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. Holding otherwise is deviation (ilhad) in the religion and disbelief.

Then Allah, exalted is He, warned His servants and gave them hope by His saying: ﴿Know that Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. Indeed, this is the matter in itself: it is fitting that the servant be fearful, acting in accordance with fear, mindful of God (muttaqi), and at ease in accordance with hope.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 99–102:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey, and Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal.﴾ ﴿Say: "Not equal are the evil and the good, even though the abundance of the evil may impress you. So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you may succeed."﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned them, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿A people before you asked about such things, and then became disbelievers because of them.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾. This is an informing of the believers. It cannot be conceived that it is a verse of truce (mu'ada'ah) abrogated (mansukhah) by the verses of fighting. Rather, this is the condition of one who has believed and testified to the truth of the testimony. Since he has secured from the Messenger his property and his blood, the Messenger has no obligation toward him beyond conveying the message. Allah, after that, knows what his breast conceals, and He is the One who recompenses him, according to that, with reward or punishment.

Al-balagh (conveying) is a verbal noun from "ballagha, yuballighu." The meaning of the verse is a warning to the believers if they deviate and do not comply with what was conveyed to them.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: "Not equal are...﴾, the verse is a general expression covering all matters. It applies to earnings, to numbers of people, and to knowledge and the like. Thus the evil in all of these does not prosper, nor is it noble, nor is its outcome good. The good, even if it is little, is beneficial and has a pleasant outcome.

This verse is compared with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad comes forth only sparsely﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. Al-khubth (evil) is the hidden corruption in things, such that one might think they are sound, whereas the good is the opposite of that. Likewise is evil in a person. The word "khabith" (evil) may also be used of a person to mean the corruption of his lineage. A word of this kind, in this intention, obliges the one who says it to the prescribed punishment (hadd).

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding﴾, it is an alert to the necessity of the good in belief and in action. He specified "people of understanding" for mention because they are the foremost in discerning these matters, and it is not fitting for them to neglect them while they possess their intellects and perception. It seems that the reference of "these intellects" is to the core of experience (lubb al-tajribah), which exceeds the core of legal responsibility (lubb al-taklif), through sagacity, insight drawn out by reasoning, and far-reaching reflection.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ [and the rest of the verse]: the narrators differed about its cause. A group, among them Anas ibn Malik and others, said: it was revealed on account of the question of 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi. That is because "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended the pulpit in anger and said: 'Do not ask me today about anything except that I will inform you of it.' A man stood and said: 'Where am I?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'In the Fire.' 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi stood up, and he was being slandered regarding his lineage, and said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafah.'"

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The hadith contains, which al-Tabari did not mention: "Another stood and said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Salim, mawla of Abu Shaybah.' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, then knelt on his knees and said: 'We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Prophet. We seek refuge in Allah from the trials.' The people wept because of the anger of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed on account of these questions."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Messenger of Allah's ﷺ ascending the pulpit in anger was only because of the questions of the Bedouins, the ignorant, and the hypocrites. Among them was one who would say: "Where is my camel?" and another who would say: "What is it that has befallen me on this journey?" and the like, from what is ignorance, or mockery, or trouble-making.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all, (their wording differs, but the meaning is one) said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed the people and said: 'O people, the Hajj has been prescribed upon you.' He recited to them: ﴿And for Allah is a duty upon the people to make pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?' He remained silent, and they repeated. He said: 'No. And if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory.'" Abu Hurayrah said: 'Ukashah ibn Mihsan said; Murrah said: Mihsan al-Asadi said; another said: a man of the Banu Asad stood up; and some of them said: "A Bedouin stood and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained silent, then said: 'Who is the questioner?' It was said: 'So-and-so.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory; and had it become obligatory, you would not have been able to bear it; and if you had left it, you would have perished.' Then this verse was revealed" on account of that.

This is strengthened by the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, the greatest of the Muslims in crime against the Muslims is one who asks about a thing that was not forbidden, and it is then forbidden because of his question."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The verse was revealed on account of a people who asked about the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah, and the like of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is reported that when Allah, may He be exalted, explained in these verses the matter of the Ka'bah, the sacrificial animals, and the garlands, and informed that their sanctity is what He established, since they are beneficial matters, ancient, from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, some Arabs went to ask about the rest of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah, to see whether they would be joined to those or not. For they had believed all of them to be sunnah, not distinguishing between what is from Allah and what is from the devil's inspiration, and between the changers of the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and others. Concerning 'Amr ibn Luhayy the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire, and he was the first to set loose the sawa'ib (free-roaming camels)."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent meaning of the reports is that the Bedouins and the ignorant pressed upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with various kinds of questions, as we have mentioned, so Allah, may He be exalted, rebuked them against that with this verse.

"Ashya'" (things) is a collective noun (ism jam') for "shay'" (thing). Its original form, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is "shay'a'" on the pattern of "fa'la'," then it was changed to "la fa'a'" because of the heaviness of the juxtaposition of two hamzahs. Abu Hatim said: "ashya'," its measure is "af'al," and it is the plural of "shay'," and the omission of its diptote-ness (tark al-sarf) in it is by transmission (sama'). Al-Kisa'i said: "ashya'" is not declined, due to its resemblance at the end to "hamra'" (the feminine ending with alif of the extended form), and due to its frequent use. The Arabs say "ashya'at," as they say "hamra'at." It would follow from this that "asma'" should not be declined, since they say "asma'at." Al-Akhfash said: "ashya'," its origin is "ashyi'a'," on the measure of "af'ila'," the juxtaposition of the two hamzahs was felt to be heavy, so the first was changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, then the ya' was dropped for lightness. It would follow from this that the singular of "ashya'" is "shayyi'," like "hayyin," and "ahwina'."

Most people read: ﴿in tubda﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the dal, with the verb in the passive. Mujahid read: "in tabdu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the dal, the verb in the active. Al-Sha'bi read: "in yabdu lakum" with a ya' at the beginning, fathah, and the dal with a damma, "yasu'kum," with a ya' at the beginning, meaning: "Allah will disclose it to you."

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: its meaning: "Do not ask about things in which the disclosure of them would cause you distress, either by a legal obligation that would fall upon you, or by a news that would grieve you, as was said to the one who said: 'Where am I?' But when the Qur'an is revealed concerning a matter, and your Lord begins to address you with a command, then at that time, if you ask about its detail and explanation, it will be explained to you and made manifest."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The pronoun in His saying "'anha" (about them) refers to their type, not to the first things about which He forbade asking.

Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Indeed Allah has imposed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has pardoned things without forgetfulness, so do not search into them.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr used to say: "Indeed Allah made lawful and made unlawful. So what He made lawful, make lawful; and what He made unlawful, avoid. And between these He left things which He neither made lawful nor made unlawful; that is a pardon from Allah, He has pardoned it." Then he recited this verse.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾ may carry the meaning of a warning, as if He said: "Do not ask; and if you ask, you will meet the burden of that and its difficulty, because you will be imposing on yourselves and hastening to know what will distress you, like the one who was told: 'Indeed he is in the Fire.'"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾: He left them and did not define them. This word "'afa" (pardoned) supports that the things which are in the legal obligations are viewed in this way. The saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, supports this: "Indeed Allah has pardoned you regarding the charity of horses."

﴿"And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing"﴾: two attributes that suit pardon, leaving aside excessive inquiry, and generosity in matters.

Most people read: "qad sa'alaha" with a fatha on the sin. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read: "qad si'alaha" with a kasrah on the sin. The intended meaning of this reading is imalah (inclination of the vowel), according to the dialect of the one who says "silta, tasal" (from the root sa'ala/sala). It is related from the Arabs: "huma yatasawalan." This indicates that this dialect is from the waw, not from the hamzah. So the imalah is only intended, and this is permitted because of the kasrah before the lam in "silta," just as imalah came in "khaafa," due to the coming of a kasrah on the kha' of "khiftu."

The meaning of the verse is that these questions, which are tangled and seek excess, and are proposals and disputes, were asked before you by the nations, then they disbelieved because of them. Al-Tabari said: like the people of Salih in their asking for the she-camel, and the Children of Israel in their asking for the table spread. Al-Suddi said: like the asking of Quraysh that Allah make al-Safa into gold for them.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is only fitting regarding Quraysh as an example that they asked for a sign, and when He split the moon for them, they disbelieved. This meaning is said only of one who asked the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Where is my camel?" and as the Bedouin said to him: "What is in the belly of this my she-camel?" As for one who asked him about the Hajj: "Is it every year?", the saying of His, may He be exalted, ﴿A people asked about such things﴾ [and the rest of the verse] is not explained by this, nor by its like. Rather, it is explained by the fact that nations in earlier times sought to go to extremes in religion from their prophets, and then did not fulfill what they were obligated to do.

Thus the evil in all of these does not prosper, nor is it noble, nor is its outcome good. The good, even if it is little, is beneficial and has a pleasant outcome.

This verse is compared with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad comes forth only sparsely﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. Al-khubth (evil) is the hidden corruption in things, such that one might think they are sound, whereas the good is the opposite of that. Likewise is evil in a person. The word "khabith" (evil) may also be used of a person to mean the corruption of his lineage. A word of this kind, in this intention, obliges the one who says it to the prescribed punishment (hadd).

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding﴾, it is an alert to the necessity of the good in belief and in action. He specified "people of understanding" for mention because they are the foremost in discerning these matters, and it is not fitting for them to neglect them while they possess their intellects and perception. It seems that the reference of "these intellects" is to the core of experience (lubb al-tajribah), which exceeds the core of legal responsibility (lubb al-taklif), through sagacity, insight drawn out by reasoning, and far-reaching reflection.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ [and the rest of the verse]: the narrators differed about its cause. A group, among them Anas ibn Malik and others, said: it was revealed on account of the question of 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi. That is because "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended the pulpit in anger and said: 'Do not ask me today about anything except that I will inform you of it.' A man stood and said: 'Where am I?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'In the Fire.' 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi stood up, and he was being slandered regarding his lineage, and said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafah.'"

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The hadith contains, which al-Tabari did not mention: "Another stood and said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Salim, mawla of Abu Shaybah.' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, then knelt on his knees and said: 'We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Prophet. We seek refuge in Allah from the trials.' The people wept because of the anger of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed on account of these questions."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Messenger of Allah's ﷺ ascending the pulpit in anger was only because of the questions of the Bedouins, the ignorant, and the hypocrites. Among them was one who would say: "Where is my camel?" and another who would say: "What is it that has befallen me on this journey?" and the like, from what is ignorance, or mockery, or trouble-making.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all, (their wording differs, but the meaning is one) said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed the people and said: 'O people, the Hajj has been prescribed upon you.' He recited to them: ﴿And for Allah is a duty upon the people to make pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?' He remained silent, and they repeated. He said: 'No. And if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory.'" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained silent, then said: 'Who is the questioner?' It was said: 'So-and-so.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory; and had it become obligatory, you would not have been able to bear it; and if you had left it, you would have perished.' Then this verse was revealed" on account of that.

This is strengthened by the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, the greatest of the Muslims in crime against the Muslims is one who asks about a thing that was not forbidden, and it is then forbidden because of his question."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The verse was revealed on account of a people who asked about the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah, and the like of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is reported that when Allah, may He be exalted, explained in these verses the matter of the Ka'bah, the sacrificial animals, and the garlands, and informed that their sanctity is what He established, since they are beneficial matters, ancient, from the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, some Arabs went to ask about the rest of the rulings of the Jahiliyyah, to see whether they would be joined to those or not. For they had believed all of them to be sunnah, not distinguishing between what is from Allah and what is from the devil's inspiration, and between the changers of the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and others. Concerning 'Amr ibn Luhayy the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire, and he was the first to set loose the sawa'ib (free-roaming camels)."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The apparent meaning of the reports is that the Bedouins and the ignorant pressed upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with various kinds of questions, as we have mentioned, so Allah, may He be exalted, rebuked them against that with this verse.

Its original form, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is "shay'a'" on the pattern of "fa'la'," then it was changed to "la fa'a'" because of the heaviness of the juxtaposition of two hamzahs. Abu Hatim said: "ashya'," its measure is "af'al," and it is the plural of "shay'," and the omission of its diptote-ness (tark al-sarf) in it is by transmission (sama'). Al-Kisa'i said: "ashya'" is not declined, due to its resemblance at the end to "hamra'" (the feminine ending with alif of the extended form), and due to its frequent use. The Arabs say "ashya'at," as they say "hamra'at." It would follow from this that "asma'" should not be declined, since they say "asma'at." It would follow from this that the singular of "ashya'" is "shayyi'," like "hayyin," and "ahwina'."

Mujahid read: "in tabdu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the dal, the verb in the active. Al-Sha'bi read: "in yabdu lakum" with a ya' at the beginning, fathah, and the dal with a damma, "yasu'kum," with a ya' at the beginning, meaning: "Allah will disclose it to you."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: its meaning: "Do not ask about things in which the disclosure of them would cause you distress, either by a legal obligation that would fall upon you, or by a news that would grieve you, as was said to the one who said: 'Where am I?' But when the Qur'an is revealed concerning a matter, and your Lord begins to address you with a command, then at that time, if you ask about its detail and explanation, it will be explained to you and made manifest."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The pronoun in His saying "'anha" (about them) refers to their type, not to the first things about which He forbade asking.

Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Indeed Allah has imposed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has pardoned things without forgetfulness, so do not search into them.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr used to say: "Indeed Allah made lawful and made unlawful. So what He made lawful, make lawful; and what He made unlawful, avoid. And between these He left things which He neither made lawful nor made unlawful; that is a pardon from Allah, He has pardoned it." Then he recited this verse.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾ may carry the meaning of a warning, as if He said: "Do not ask; and if you ask, you will meet the burden of that and its difficulty, because you will be imposing on yourselves and hastening to know what will distress you, like the one who was told: 'Indeed he is in the Fire.'"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾: He left them and did not define them. This word "'afa" (pardoned) supports that the things which are in the legal obligations are viewed in this way. The saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, supports this: "Indeed Allah has pardoned you regarding the charity of horses."

﴿"And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing"﴾: two attributes that suit pardon, leaving aside excessive inquiry, and generosity in matters.

Most people read: "qad sa'alaha" with a fatha on the sin. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read: "qad si'alaha" with a kasrah on the sin. The intended meaning of this reading is imalah (inclination of the vowel), according to the dialect of the one who says "silta, tasal" (from the root sa'ala/sala). It is related from the Arabs: "huma yatasawalan." This indicates that this dialect is from the waw, not from the hamzah. So the imalah is only intended, and this is permitted because of the kasrah before the lam in "silta," just as imalah came in "khaafa," due to the coming of a kasrah on the kha' of "khiftu."

The meaning of the verse is that these questions, which are tangled and seek excess, and are proposals and disputes, were asked before you by the nations, then they disbelieved because of them. Al-Tabari said: like the people of Salih in their asking for the she-camel, and the Children of Israel in their asking for the table spread. Al-Suddi said: like the asking of Quraysh that Allah make al-Safa into gold for them.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is only fitting regarding Quraysh as an example that they asked for a sign, and when He split the moon for them, they disbelieved. This meaning is said only of one who asked the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Where is my camel?" and as the Bedouin said to him: "What is in the belly of this my she-camel?" As for one who asked him about the Hajj: "Is it every year?", the saying of His, may He be exalted, ﴿A people asked about such things﴾ [and the rest of the verse] is not explained by this, nor by its like. Rather, it is explained by the fact that nations in earlier times sought to go to extremes in religion from their prophets, and then did not fulfill what they were obligated to do.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 103–105:

(p-275) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahira, sa'iba, wasila, or ha'm. But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, what is upon you is yourselves. Those who are astray cannot harm you once you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about what you used to do.﴾

When a people asked about these rulings that existed in the pre-Islamic period, whether they should be attached to the ruling of Allah concerning the veneration of the Ka'ba and the Sacred Precinct (haram), Allah, exalted is He, informed in this verse that He had not made any of them, nor had He prescribed them for His servants. The meaning is: "But the disbelievers did this, for their elders and leaders, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and others, invent lies against Allah, saying: 'This is an act of devotion to Allah and a matter that pleases Him.' And most of them—meaning the followers—do not reason; rather they follow these matters by blind imitation and misguidance without any proof."

As for "ja'ala" (made, instituted) in this verse, it cannot be taken to mean "khalaqa Allah" (Allah created), because Allah, exalted is He, created all these things; nor does it mean "sayyara" (rendered, turned into), due to the absence of a second object. Rather, it means "sanna" (ordained) or "shara'a" (legislated), and so it takes one object, just as the verb that has this meaning does.

Al-bahira is on the pattern of fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula, from "bahara," meaning he split. When a she-camel gave birth to ten young, they would split her ear lengthwise into two halves; she was then called mabhura. She was left to graze and to come to water, and no benefit was taken from her. Her meat, if she died, was forbidden to women but permitted to men. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They did this to her when she gave birth to five young." Masruq said: "When she bore five or seven, they split her ear."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What appears from what is related on this matter is that the Arabs differed on the number at which the ears of she-camels were split; each had its own practice, and all of it is misguidance. Ibn Sida said: It is said that the bahira is the one left unherded, and a copious she-camel is also called bahira.

(p-276) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I see that the bahira is one that is well-fed and grows fat, and whose milk is abundant, so the abundant ones are likened to the sea (bahr). On this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"In it, from the thin-eared, startled (she-camel), is a rumbling, the roar of the rumbling of the large camels amid the herd of the sea-like."

He means the large camels, even if their ears were not split.

Al-Sha'bi related, from Abu al-Ahwas, from his father, who said: "I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and he said to me: 'Have you seen your camels? Do you not bring them forth with unsplit ears, then you take the knife and cut their ears and say: "These are bahr," and you cut their skins and say: "These are sirum," and you forbid them to yourself and your family?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Indeed what Allah has given you is lawful for you, and the help of Allah is stronger, and the knife of Allah is sharper.'"

As for the sa'iba: it is the she-camel that is let loose for the idols. A she-camel was also let loose when she gave birth to twelve females in succession with no male among them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Aktham ibn al-Jawn al-Khuza'i: "O Aktham, I have seen 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'a ibn Khandaq dragging his intestines in the Fire, and I have not seen anyone more like him than you."
