They regarded this as akin to the freeing of a human being. This was mentioned by al-Suddi and others. The Arabs believed that whoever encountered these she-camels and took them, or benefited from them in any way, would be subject to punishment from the Fire.

(p-277) As for the wasila: most people said that the wasila concerns sheep. They said: when a ewe gave birth to three or five litters, if the last of them was a male kid, they slaughtered it for the house of the idols; if it was a female, they spared her; and if it was a male and a female together, they spared both. They said: "This female has joined (wasalat) her brother, so she has prevented him from being slaughtered."

Although the reports from most people concern the wasila among sheep, it is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that the wasila among camels was: when a she-camel first bore a female, then bore another female after it, they said: "She has joined two females," and they would slit their noses for their idols or slaughter them; al-Tabari was uncertain about one of the two words.

As for the ha'm: it is the stallion camel which has covered (she-camels) for ten years; it is also said: when ten of his offspring have been born from his loins; and it is also said: when he has been born from the offspring of his offspring. They said: "His back has been protected," so they let him go free; he was not ridden nor put to any work. 'Alqama said to one who asked him about these things: "What do you want with something that was from the practice of the people of ignorance and has passed away?" Ibn Zayd said something similar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sum of what appears from these matters is that Allah, exalted is He, made these livestock a kindness for His servants, a blessing He enumerated for them, and a far-reaching benefit. The people of ignorance cut off the path of benefit, (p-278) and they destroyed the blessing of Allah in them, and they removed the welfare intended for the servants in those camels. For this reason these matters differ from endowments (ahbas) and waqfs, for the owner who has the right to give and to give in charity has the right to direct the benefit toward any path of righteousness, and the path to it was not blocked entirely, as was done with the bahira and the sa'iba.

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: endowments (ahbas) and waqfs are not permissible, and they analogized them to the bahira and the sa'iba. The difference is clear. If a man deliberately took an estate of his and said: "This shall be a habs, its fruit not to be gathered, its land not to be cultivated, and no benefit taken from it whatsoever," then it would be permissible to liken this to the bahira and the sa'iba. But a clearly defined habs, whose path is known and whose benefit continues, is not of this kind. Sufficient for you is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning a property of his: "Make it a habs, its principal not to be sold." And the Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, made endowments.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But those who disbelieve﴾ and the rest of the verse: it has already been mentioned that the inventors of lies are the innovators, and that those who do not reason are the followers. Al-Sha'bi and others stated this explicitly, and it is what the verse indicates. Muhammad ibn Abi Musa said: "Those who disbelieved and invented lies are the People of the Book, and those who do not reason are the idol-worshippers."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the interpretation of one who detaches the words at the end of the verse from what precedes it, and from the meaning connected with it, and from what follows it, namely His saying: ﴿"And when it is said to them"﴾. The first of the two interpretations is more probable.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿"it is said to them"﴾ refers to the disbelievers who follow these practices. ﴿"Come"﴾ is a clear call; this is its basic meaning, and then it is used both where righteousness is intended and where its opposite is intended. ﴿"To what Allah has revealed"﴾ means the Qur'an, in which is the sound prohibition. ﴿"Sufficient for us"﴾ means: enough for us. His saying ﴿"Even though their fathers"﴾: the interrogative alif entered upon the conjunctive waw, as though they joined this clause to the first (p-279) and committed themselves to a shocking statement. The interrogation is in fact a rebuke to them, as though they were saying after it: "Yes, even if they were like that."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, what is upon you is yourselves. Those who are astray cannot harm you once you are guided﴾. People differed in the interpretation of this verse. Abu Umayya al-Sha'bani said: "I asked Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani about this verse, and he said: 'You have asked about it one who is well-informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "Enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil; but when you see worldly gain given precedence, stingy greed obeyed, and every person pleased with his own opinion, then keep to yourself and leave the common people, for behind you are days in which the reward of the one who acts therein is like the reward of fifty of you."'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the interpretation in the presence of which no one has any need to deliberate, because it comprehends the good, and it issues from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

It appears from the words of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that it reached him that some people had interpreted the verse as meaning that no enjoining of good or forbidding of evil is required along with it. So he ascended the pulpit and said: "O people, do not be deceived by the saying of Allah: ﴿'upon you is yourselves'﴾, so that one of you says: 'Upon me is myself.' By Allah, you must enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, or else the worst among you will be placed over you, and they will inflict upon you the evil torment."

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "This is not the time of this verse. Speak the truth as long as it is accepted from you; but when it is rejected from you, then upon you is yourselves."

(p-280) "It was said to Ibn 'Umar, at some time of trials: 'If only you would leave speaking in these days, so that you neither enjoin nor forbid.' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: "Let the one who is present convey to the one who is absent," and we were present, so it is incumbent upon us to convey to you. And there will come a time when, if the truth is spoken, it will not be accepted.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sum of what the scholars hold on this matter is that enjoining what is good is obligatory whenever acceptance is hoped for, or the redress of wrongs is hoped for, even by force, provided one does not fear harm that would reach him personally, or a strife that he would bring upon the Muslims, whether by splitting the community or by harm reaching a group of people. When this is feared, then "upon you is yourselves" is a binding ruling at which one must stop.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The meaning of this verse, ﴿"O you who have believed, upon you is yourselves"﴾, is: hold fast to your law with what it contains of struggle, enjoining what is good, and other things; and the misguidance of the People of the Book cannot harm you once you are guided.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of the verse is: "O you who have believed, from among the sons of those who split the bahira and let loose the sawa'ib: upon you is yourselves in steadfastness upon the religion; and the misguidance of your forefathers cannot harm you once you are guided." He said: When a man became Muslim, the disbelievers said to him: "You have foolished your fathers, and misguided them, and you did such and such," and the verse was revealed on account of that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: To my knowledge, no one has said that it is a verse of truce with the disbelievers; and likewise nothing that Allah has commanded in other verses, such as upholding justice and enjoining what is good, should be opposed by it. Al-Mahdawi said: It has been said that it is abrogated by the command to enjoin good and forbid evil.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, and its proponent is not known.

Some people said: it was revealed on account of the apostasy of some believers and their being tempted, such as Ibn Abi Sarh and others; so it was said to the believers: their misguidance cannot harm you.

(p-281) The majority of readers recited ﴿lā yaḍurrukum﴾ with a damma on the dad and a shadda on the mushaddad ra; al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited ﴿lā yaḍrukum﴾ with a damma on the dad and sukun on the ra; and Ibrahim recited ﴿lā yaḍirrukum﴾ with a kasra on the dad. All of these are dialects, with the meaning of "ḍarra, yaḍurru" and "ḍārra, yaḍūru, yaḍīru."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾ and the rest of the verse: it is a reminder of the gathering (hashr) and what follows it, and this is a consolation concerning the matters of this world, its disliked and its beloved. It is related from one of the righteous that he said: "There is no day but that Satan comes and says: 'What will you eat? What will you wear? Where will you live?' So I say to him: 'I eat death, I wear the shroud, and I dwell in the grave.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever reflects upon his return to Allah, this is his state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 106–107 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be [the] testimony between you: two just men from among you, or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land and the affliction of death befalls you. You shall detain them both after the prayer, and they will swear by Allah, "We will not sell [this] for any price, even if he were a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed we would then be among the sinful."﴾ ﴿But if it becomes known that the two had committed a sin, then two others shall take their place from among those against whom the [claim] was made, the two nearest [of kin], and they will swear by Allah, "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾

Makki ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "These verses are, according to the people of ma'ani (the scholars of the meanings of the Qur'an), among the most difficult passages of the Qur'an, in i'rab (grammatical analysis), in meaning, and in ruling."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is the statement of one whom the snow (i.e., confusion) did not reach in its tafsir (exegesis); and that is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him. And in Him we seek help."

We know of no disagreement that the occasion of revelation of this verse was: "Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Badda were Christians. They travelled to Madina wanting to go to Syria for their trade. Al-Waqidi said: they were two brothers. Ibn Abi Maria, the client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, also came to Madina wanting to go to Syria as a merchant. So they set out together as a caravan. Ibn Abi Maria fell ill on the journey." Al-Waqidi said: "He wrote a will with his own hand, placed it in his baggage, and entrusted to Tamim and 'Adi that they should deliver his baggage. After some time they came to Madina with his baggage and handed it over. His heirs from the Banu Sahm found his will written down, and they found missing some items that he had listed. They asked the two about them, and they said: 'We do not know; this is what we received for him.' So they brought the two to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the first verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the two swear after the 'Asr prayer. The matter remained for a period. Then at Makka, among his belongings, a large silver vessel decorated with gold was found. It was said to those in whose possession it was found: 'From where did this vessel come to you?' They said: 'We bought it from Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Badda.' So the matter was raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the other verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered two men from the heir(s) of the deceased to swear." Al-Waqidi said: "So 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a swore, and they were entitled [to the property]."

Ibn 'Abbas narrated, "from Tamim al-Dari, that he said: 'The people were cleared of these verses, except me and 'Adi ibn Badda,'" and he mentioned the account, except that he said: "With him was a silver cup, which he intended for the king. Then 'Adi and I took it, and we sold it for a thousand, and we divided its price. When I embraced Islam after the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Madina, I felt guilty about that; so I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred. Then they pounced upon 'Adi, and they brought him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man with him swore, and five hundred was taken away from 'Adi."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The wording of this account differs in the books of record, and what I have mentioned is its main thread. It is not established, to my knowledge, that 'Adi had companionship (suhba) with the Prophet (ﷺ), nor is his Islam established. Some later scholars have listed him among the Companions, but they weakened his status, and in my view there is no basis for mentioning him among the Companions."

As for the meaning of the verse from beginning to end, it is that Allah, may He be exalted, informed the believers that His ruling regarding testimony upon the testator, when death approaches him, is that it should be the testimony of two just men. If he is on a journey, which is the "striking in the land," and no believer is with him, then he should call as witnesses two [men] from among those present of the people of disbelief. When they return and deliver the testimony concerning his will, they both swear after the prayer that they did not lie, nor did they alter [anything], and that what they testified to is true, and that they did not conceal the testimony of Allah; and their testimony is judged by. If, after that, it becomes known that they lied, or betrayed, or [committed] something similar that is a sin, then two men from among the heirs of the testator swear during the journey, and the two witnesses are made to pay what was found against them. This is the meaning of the verse according to the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim [al-Nakha'i], Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, and others. They say: the meaning of His saying "from among you" is from among the believers, and the meaning of "from other than you" is from among the disbelievers. Some of them said: "This is because the verse was revealed when there were no believers except in Madina, and they used to travel for trade in the company of People of the Book, worshippers of idols, and various kinds of disbelievers."

This group differed. The view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Shurayh, and others is that the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). Al-Tabari transmitted through al-Sha'bi that a man whose death approached at Daquqa, and who did not find any believer to call as a witness to his will, called two men from among the People of the Book as witnesses. They came to Kufa and went to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and informed him, and they brought his estate. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not occur in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Then he made them swear after the 'Asr prayer, and he enforced their testimony.

Al-Tabari also transmitted from Shurayh that he did not allow the testimony of a Christian or a Jew against a Muslim, except in the case of a will; and even in a will it was not permitted except when they were on a journey.

The view of a group of those mentioned is that it is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], and by what the consensus (ijma') of the majority of people rests upon, that the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible.

A group of scholars interpreted the verse otherwise than all of this. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "His saying, may He be exalted, 'from among you' means from among your clan and kin; and His saying, '[or] two others from other than you,' means from other than kin and clan." This was also said by 'Ikrima, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Shihab. They said: "Allah commanded calling two just men from among the kin, since they are the most knowledgeable about the circumstances of the will and the most aware of the form of justice in it. If the matter occurs on a journey and no kin are present, then two outsiders are called. When they testify, if no doubt arises, the testimony stands. If doubt arises that they have diverted the will to someone, or added or subtracted [anything], then they swear after the 'Asr prayer, and their testimony stands. If after that it becomes known that they altered it and incurred sin, then two of the kin swear, and the testimony of the first two is invalidated."

Some people said: "The verse is abrogated, and a witness does not swear." This is reported from Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, and the majority of jurists (kafat al-fuqaha').

Al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned that this oath in the verse is only according to the circumstances of the claim (al-tada'i). That is, the first two witnesses swear only if doubt arises; and when doubt arises, a claim is thereby directed against them, so the oath becomes binding upon them. But this doubt arises only from betrayal on their part. If after that it becomes known that they incurred sin, it is considered: if the matter is clear, they are made to pay without the oath of the two heirs; but if it is by a single witness, or by indications that necessitate their betrayal, or something similar, which is like a witness, then it is attributed to the wrongdoer, and the two claimants swear together with whatever witness or proof has been established for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is the disagreement regarding the meaning of the verse and the form of its ruling. Now let us return to the i'rab and speak word by word of the verse, aiming for the statement that is beneficial, because people have mixed greatly in the tafsir of this verse; mentioning that and refuting it would be lengthy, and in clarifying the truth that minds accept with acceptance there is sufficiency. And Allah is the One sought for help."

His saying: ﴿"Testimony between you"﴾. Some people said: the word shahada (testimony) here means "presence" (hudur). Al-Tabari said: shahada means "oath" (yamin), and it is not the testimony that is delivered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "All of this is weak. The correct view is that it is the testimony that is preserved in order to be delivered. Its subject is in the nominative (raf') by way of inception (ibtida'), and the predicate is in His saying 'two' (ithnan). Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] said: the estimate is: 'The testimony between you in your wills is the testimony of two,' so the modified word was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. Another estimated it differently at first, as if he said: 'The one establishing the testimony between you is two.'"

The word testimony (shahada) was attributed to "between" (bayn) as an extension in the adverbial usage, so that it is treated like nouns, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly your bond has been severed [between you]﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

Al-A'raj, al-Sha'bi, and al-Hasan read "shahadatun" with tanwin, and "baynakum" in the accusative. The i'rab of this reading is like the i'rab of the reading of the Seven. It is narrated from al-A'raj and Abu Haywa: "shahadatan" in the accusative with tanwin, and "baynakum" in the accusative. Abu al-Fath [Ibn Jinni] said: the estimate is: "Let two [men] establish a testimony between you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"When death approaches one of you"﴾: its meaning is "when the approach [of death] draws near," since if death has actually arrived, a dead person does not testify. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and like His saying: ﴿When you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. This is common. The governing element of "when" (idha) is the verbal noun which is "testimony." This is on the basis that you make "idha" equivalent to "hina" (when), which does not need an answer (jawab). You may also make "idha" in this verse the one that needs an answer, but the answer has been dispensed with because of what precedes it, in His saying: ﴿"testimony between you"﴾, since the meaning is: "When death approaches one of you, it is appropriate that he should call a witness."

His saying: ﴿"at the time of the will"﴾ is an adverb of time, and the governing element is "approached" (hadara). If you wish, you may make it a substitute (badal) for "idha." Abu 'Ali said: "You may also link it to 'death' (al-mawt); it is not permissible for 'testimony' to govern it, because when it governs one adverb of time, it does not govern another adverb of it."

His saying: ﴿"two just men"﴾ is a qualifier (sifa) for "two"; and "from among you" is also a qualifier, after a qualifier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"from other than you"﴾ is a qualifier for "two others"; and ﴿"you strike in the land"﴾ means "you travel for trade." You say: "ḍarabtu fi al-ard" meaning "I travelled for trade"; and "ḍarabtu al-ard" means "I went in it for the fulfilment of a human need." This travel is the kind in which a believer might lack two believers, so it was singled out for mention, because travel for jihad hardly ever lacks two believers.

Abu 'Ali said: His saying ﴿"you shall detain them both"﴾ is a qualifier for "two others." It is interposed between the qualified and the qualifier by His saying "if you are" up to "death," and this interposition conveys that the turning to "two others from other than [your] religion, or kin" — according to the disagreement of scholars on that — happens only with the necessity of travel and the arrival of death during it. The answer to "if" (in) is dispensed with because of what preceded in His saying: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾.

The majority of scholars said: "The prayer here is the 'Asr prayer, because it is the time when people gather. The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned it regarding one who swears concerning his merchandise, and he ordered li'an (mutual oath) in it." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "It is only after the prayer of the dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects); as for the 'Asr, it has no sanctity for them."

The fa' in His saying: ﴿"then they swear"﴾ is a conjunction of one clause upon another, because the meaning is complete at His saying: ﴿after the prayer﴾. Abu 'Ali said: "If you wish, you need not estimate the fa' as conjoining one clause to another, but make it a conditional response (jaza'), as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And the pupil of my eye: water sometimes dries it up, so it appears; and at other times it overflows and drowns."

Its estimate according to them is: 'When it dries up, it appears; so likewise, when you detain them both, they will swear.'"

(p-287) His saying, "if you doubt" (in Arabic: إنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ), is a condition, and the oath of the two witnesses is not directed except by it. Whenever no doubt or dispute arises, there is no oath. Yet it appears from the ruling of Abu Musa that the oath of the dhimmis (non-Muslim protected people) is required, that by the oath their testimony is completed and the bequest is carried out for its beneficiaries, even if no doubt arose. This doubt, according to the one who does not regard the verse as abrogated (mansukh), arises from suspicion of betrayal, and from an accusation of favouring some of the legatees over others. In his view the oath is still required in these cases. As for the one who regards the verse as abrogated, no oath is imposed except when the doubt concerns betrayal or some form of transgression; the oath is then, in his view, in the manner of an oath upon a denial in a claim, not as a completion of the testimony.

The pronoun in the words of the two swearers, "we will not sell it for any price" (in Arabic: ﴿لا نَشْتَرِي بِهِ ثَمَنًا﴾), refers to the oath. It may also refer to the name of God, may He be blessed and exalted. Abu 'Ali said: it refers to the distortion of the testimony. His saying, "we will not sell" (in Arabic: "لا نَشْتَرِي"), is the answer to what is implied by His saying, "they both swear by God" (in Arabic: "فَيُقْسِمانِ بِاللهِ"), because an oath and the like are introduced by what oaths are introduced by. The construction "for it a price" (in Arabic: "بِهِ ثَمَنًا") is to be read as "possessing a price" (in Arabic: "أيْ: ذا ثَمَنٍ"), because a price is not itself bought. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have sold the signs of God for a small price﴾ [al-Tawba: 9]; its meaning is "possessing a price". It is not permissible that "we will buy" (in Arabic: "نَشْتَرِي") in this verse means "we will sell" (in Arabic: "نَبِيعُ"), because the meaning nullifies it, although that usage exists in the language in other places.

He singled out the near kin for mention because it is the custom of people to incline towards their relatives, and to make light of what they would not make light of when it concerns their own benefit.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾; he attributed "testimony" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةَ") to Him, exalted is He, insofar as He is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment.

Al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi read "wa-la naktumu" (in Arabic: "وَلا نَكْتُمْ") with the mim vowelled with a jazm. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Na'im ibn Maysara, and al-Sha'bi (in a variant from him) read "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً") with tanwin, and "Allah" (in Arabic: "اَللَّهَ") in the accusative governed by "naktumu" (in Arabic: "نَكْتُمُ"), as though the sentence were "and we will not conceal God a testimony". Al-Zahrawi said: it is possible that the meaning is "and we will not conceal a testimony and by God", then the waw was dropped and the verb put in the accusative for brevity. Yahya ibn Adam related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash: "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً"), "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "أللَّهِ"), with the alif cut off without elongation, and the ha' in the genitive. It is also related from al-Sha'bi and others that he would pause on the ha' of "shahada" with sukun, then cut off the written alif without elongation, as has been mentioned. It is also related from him that he read "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "آللَّهِ") with elongation of the interrogative alif in both cases, namely with the ha' of "shahada" quiescent, and with it vowelled as tanwin in the accusative. These readings, namely the tanwin of "shahada" and the elongation of the interrogative alif after it, are related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. Abu al-Fath said: as for the quiescence of the ha' of "shahadah" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةْ") and pausing on it, with the oath beginning anew, this is a good reading, because beginning the oath at the start of the speech is more fitting for it and more awe-inspiring than that it be folded into the general course of speech. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, 'Abd Allah ibn Habib, and al-Hasan al-Basri, as mentioned by Abu 'Amr al-Dani, read "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً") with accusative and tanwin, and "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "آللَّهِ") with elongation of the hamza of interrogation, which is a substitute for the particle of oath "a-nna" (in Arabic: "آنّا") with elongation of the interrogative alif also; it entered to make the swearers stop and reflect, or to establish the truth in their souls, or for those they address. Ibn Muhaysin read "lamina-l-athimin" (in Arabic: "لَمِلّاثِمِينَ") with idgham (assimilation).

His saying, exalted is He: "then if it is discovered" (in Arabic: "فَإنْ عُثِرَ"), is a metaphor for what befalls their knowledge after it had been hidden, by agreement, and after it was not expected and not intended. This is as one says, "you have fallen upon the one who knows" (in Arabic: "عَلى الخَبِيرِ سَقَطْتَ"), and "you came upon such-and-such" (in Arabic: "وَقَعْتَ عَلى كَذا"). Abu 'Ali said: "the sin" (in Arabic: "الإثْمُ") here is the name of the thing taken, because its taker is sinful by taking it, so it is called a sin, just as what is taken without right is called an injustice (in Arabic: "مَظْلَمَةً"). Sibawayh said: "al-maẓlama" is the name of what is taken from you; likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: what appears here is that "the sin" (al-ithm) is in its proper sense, namely the ruling that attaches to the two of them, and the state they incur after their engagement in distorting the testimony, or in taking what is not theirs, or the like.

"Istahaqqa" (in Arabic: "اِسْتَحَقّا") means that they deserved it from God and were fit for it; so this is "istihqaq" in its proper sense, the deserving of a real thing. Had "the sin" meant the thing taken, it would not have been said of it "istahaqqa", because they had done wrong and betrayed in it; rather, they deserved the station of evil and the ruling of disobedience, and that is the sin.

His saying, exalted is He: "then two others" (in Arabic: "فَآخَرانِ"), means: when their corruption is discovered, then two others from the people who are the heirs of the deceased take the oath and establish the case in place of the first two; and their share, or their claim, or their property, or whichever of these estimations you choose, is deserved against them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read "istuhigga" (in Arabic: "اِسْتُحِقَّ") with the ta' vowelled with damma, and "al-awlayani" (in Arabic: "اَلْأولَيانِ") in the dual of "awla". Qurra related from Ibn Kathir: "istahaqqa" (in Arabic: "اِسْتَحَقَّ") with fatha on the ta', and "al-awlayani" in the dual. Hafs also related the same from 'Asim. Hamza and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "istuhigga" with damma on the ta', and "al-awwalina" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلِينَ") as the plural of "awwal". Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "istahaqqa" with fatha on the ta', and "al-awwalani" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلانِ") as the dual of "awwal". Ibn Sirin read "al-awwalayni" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلَيْنِ") as the dual of "awwal", with it in the accusative, on the supposition: "al-awwalayni fa-l-awwalayni", in rank and nearness of kinship.

Abu 'Ali, regarding the reading of Ibn Kathir and those with him, said: the nominative of "al-awlayani" is either as a beginning (mubtada') that has been delayed, so the sense is as though it were "and the two nearest by the command of the dead are two others who stand", so the speech comes as in their saying "I am a Tamimi"; or it is the predicate of an elided beginning, as though it were "then two others stand in their place, they are the nearest"; or it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani"; or it is attributed to "istuhigga". Abu al-Hasan permitted another possibility: that "al-awlayani" be an adjective of "fa-akharani", because when it was described it became specified, and so it was described on account of the particularity that it acquired.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: then Abu 'Ali said, after this speech: as for what "istuhigga" is attributed to, it must be either the shares, or the bequest, or the sin, and the taken thing was called "sin" as one says of what is taken from the wronged: "maẓlama". For this reason it was permissible for "istuhigga" to be attributed to it. Then he said, after a further discussion: if you ask, is it permissible to attribute "istuhigga" to "al-awlayani"? The answer: that is not permissible, because what is deserved is only the bequest or a part of it, and as for the nearest kin of the dead, they cannot themselves be deserved, so "istuhigga" cannot be attributed to them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: there is scrutiny in this speech, and in my view it is permissible to attribute "istuhigga" to "al-awlayani". That is because Abu 'Ali took the word "istihqaq" as literal, so he did not permit it except where true deserving applies to the case; and what is truly deserved is the share and the like. The word "istihqaq" in the verse is only a metaphor, and does not mean "they deserved a sin". For true deserving is here literal, while in "istuhigga" it is figurative, because there is no sense to this deserving except domination over the situation, by virtue of this deceased being alone and having no kin or co-religionists to support him. So "istuhigga" here is like what you say of an oppressor who wrongs you: "this has been deserved against me, my wealth or my house, by his injustice", so you liken it to what is truly deserved, since he has scaled the wall as the owner would scale it and taken possession as the owner would possess. Likewise one says: "so-and-so's time has deserved from him the occupation of such-and-such", when that matter has overcome his hours. In this way "istuhigga" in the verse is in every case, even if it is attributed to the shares and the like, because his saying "istuhigga" is a relative clause (silah) of "alladhina", and "alladhina" refers to the category opposed to the two unjust witnesses. The two witnesses did not in this case deserve anything in the true sense of deserving; they only scaled the wall as one who deserves would do. So we may take "al-awlayani" as a beginning, delayed, and then "istuhigga" is attributed, on this reading, to the wealth or the share and the like, by way of metaphor. The same holds if "al-awlayani" is the predicate of a beginning, and likewise as a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani", and as an adjective on the opinion of Abu al-Hasan. We may also take the sense to be: from the group that was absent, whose right it was and whose desired course was that their guardian attend; so when they were absent and this testator stood alone, this condition deserved, and these two witnesses, being outside the religion, deserved authority and the command over these two nearest kin over this group. Then the verb was put in the passive with this meaning, for brevity. What strengthens this aim is that the verb took "ʿalā" when it indicated power and the taking over of the situation by force. One does not say "istuhigga minhu" or "istuhigga fihi" except in true deserving in its proper form; but "istuhigga ʿalayhi" is said of seizure, domination, and figurative deserving. The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers, in every case in this reading, to the group opposed to the two sinful false witnesses. It is also possible that it refers to the category of which the false witness is one, as we shall show now, God willing, in a reading other than this one.

As for Qurra's transmission from Ibn Kathir, "istahaqqa" with fatha on the ta', it is possible that "al-awlayani" is a beginning, or the predicate of a beginning, and the sense is: "in the group or the tribe that deserved the case against this category of false witnesses". The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the category of the two false witnesses.

(p-291) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: in this interpretation there is a transposition, a restructuring, and a manipulation in "alladhina"; and on it Abu 'Ali's discussion in the book "al-Hujja" is built. It is also possible that the meaning is: "from among those upon whom standing has been deserved". The correct of the two interpretations is that the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to "alladhina", and "al-awlayani" is raised by "istahaqqa". This is explained on three meanings:

The first is that what is intended by "those upon whom it has been deserved" is that their property and their estate were deserved by the two false witnesses; so he called the two false witnesses "awlayayn" (the two nearest), because the first state made them so; that is, the lack of people made them the nearest to this deceased and his estate, so they acted within it.

The second meaning is that what is intended by the group is: those upon whom it was right that the two nearest should be of them; so "istahaqqa" has the sense of "haqqa" and "wajaba", as you say: "this building has deserved" in the sense of "it is right", like "ʿajiba" and "istaʿjaba" and the like.

The third meaning is that "istahaqqa" be taken in the sense of "saʿā" and "istawjaba", so the sense is: "then two others from the people among whom two nearest from them were present, so they strove against them for their right"; that is, they deserved it for them, strove in it, and claimed it with their oaths and their kinship. A similar meaning to that which the transitive use with "ʿalā" gives is the verse of the poet:

I strive against the living of the Banu Malik,
each man is a striver in his own affair.

Likewise in the hadith, in some routes of the hadith of the three men, one of whom mentioned his dutifulness to his parents, when the rock came down upon them: "I used to tend the flock over them" (in Arabic: "كُنْتُ أرْعى عَلَيْهِمُ الغَنَمَ").

As for Hamza's reading, its meaning is: "from the people upon whom their affair has been deserved", that is, they were overcome by it; then he described them as "first", that is, in mention in this verse, and that is in His saying: ﴿two men of justice from among you﴾; then after that He said: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 5, verses 106–107 (part 3 of 3):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they both swear by Allah﴾; meaning the other two who stand in the place of the two witnesses of distortion. And their saying: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾; that is: "What we have reported, and what we have mentioned of the text of the matter, is more worthy than what the first two mentioned, and distorted in it." ﴿"And we have not transgressed"﴾; we, in this our statement, nor have we exceeded the limit." And their saying: ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾; a disavowal in the form of declaring great and abhorrent the act of wrongdoing (ẓulm). And ẓulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verses 106–107 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who have believed, when death approaches one of you, let there be [the] testimony between you: two just men from among you, or two others from other than you, if you are travelling in the land and the affliction of death befalls you. You shall detain them both after the prayer, and they will swear by Allah, "We will not sell [this] for any price, even if he were a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed we would then be among the sinful."﴾ ﴿But if it becomes known that the two had committed a sin, then two others shall take their place from among those against whom the [claim] was made, the two nearest [of kin], and they will swear by Allah, "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers."﴾

Makki ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "These verses are, according to the people of ma'ani (the scholars of the meanings of the Qur'an), among the most difficult passages of the Qur'an, in i'rab (grammatical analysis), in meaning, and in ruling."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is the statement of one whom the snow (i.e., confusion) did not reach in its tafsir (exegesis); and that is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him. And in Him we seek help."

We know of no disagreement that the occasion of revelation of this verse was: "Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Badda were Christians. They travelled to Madina wanting to go to Syria for their trade. Al-Waqidi said: they were two brothers. Ibn Abi Maria, the client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, also came to Madina wanting to go to Syria as a merchant. So they set out together as a caravan. Ibn Abi Maria fell ill on the journey." Al-Waqidi said: "He wrote a will with his own hand, placed it in his baggage, and entrusted to Tamim and 'Adi that they should deliver his baggage. After some time they came to Madina with his baggage and handed it over. His heirs from the Banu Sahm found his will written down, and they found missing some items that he had listed. They asked the two about them, and they said: 'We do not know; this is what we received for him.' So they brought the two to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the first verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the two swear after the 'Asr prayer. The matter remained for a period. Then at Makka, among his belongings, a large silver vessel decorated with gold was found. It was said to those in whose possession it was found: 'From where did this vessel come to you?' They said: 'We bought it from Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Badda.' So the matter was raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the other verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered two men from the heir(s) of the deceased to swear." Al-Waqidi said: "So 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a swore, and they were entitled [to the property]."

Ibn 'Abbas narrated, "from Tamim al-Dari, that he said: 'The people were cleared of these verses, except me and 'Adi ibn Badda,'" and he mentioned the account, except that he said: "With him was a silver cup, which he intended for the king. Then 'Adi and I took it, and we sold it for a thousand, and we divided its price. When I embraced Islam after the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Madina, I felt guilty about that; so I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred. Then they pounced upon 'Adi, and they brought him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man with him swore, and five hundred was taken away from 'Adi."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The wording of this account differs in the books of record, and what I have mentioned is its main thread. It is not established, to my knowledge, that 'Adi had companionship (suhba) with the Prophet (ﷺ), nor is his Islam established. Some later scholars have listed him among the Companions, but they weakened his status, and in my view there is no basis for mentioning him among the Companions."

As for the meaning of the verse from beginning to end, it is that Allah, may He be exalted, informed the believers that His ruling regarding testimony upon the testator, when death approaches him, is that it should be the testimony of two just men. If he is on a journey, which is the "striking in the land," and no believer is with him, then he should call as witnesses two [men] from among those present of the people of disbelief. When they return and deliver the testimony concerning his will, they both swear after the prayer that they did not lie, nor did they alter [anything], and that what they testified to is true, and that they did not conceal the testimony of Allah; and their testimony is judged by. If, after that, it becomes known that they lied, or betrayed, or [committed] something similar that is a sin, then two men from among the heirs of the testator swear during the journey, and the two witnesses are made to pay what was found against them. This is the meaning of the verse according to the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim [al-Nakha'i], Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, and others. They say: the meaning of His saying "from among you" is from among the believers, and the meaning of "from other than you" is from among the disbelievers. Some of them said: "This is because the verse was revealed when there were no believers except in Madina, and they used to travel for trade in the company of People of the Book, worshippers of idols, and various kinds of disbelievers."

This group differed. The view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Shurayh, and others is that the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). Al-Tabari transmitted through al-Sha'bi that a man whose death approached at Daquqa, and who did not find any believer to call as a witness to his will, called two men from among the People of the Book as witnesses. They came to Kufa and went to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and informed him, and they brought his estate. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not occur in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Then he made them swear after the 'Asr prayer, and he enforced their testimony.

Al-Tabari also transmitted from Shurayh that he did not allow the testimony of a Christian or a Jew against a Muslim, except in the case of a will; and even in a will it was not permitted except when they were on a journey.

The view of a group of those mentioned is that it is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], and by what the consensus (ijma') of the majority of people rests upon, that the testimony of a disbeliever is not permissible.

A group of scholars interpreted the verse otherwise than all of this. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "His saying, may He be exalted, 'from among you' means from among your clan and kin; and His saying, '[or] two others from other than you,' means from other than kin and clan." This was also said by 'Ikrima, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Shihab. They said: "Allah commanded calling two just men from among the kin, since they are the most knowledgeable about the circumstances of the will and the most aware of the form of justice in it. If the matter occurs on a journey and no kin are present, then two outsiders are called. When they testify, if no doubt arises, the testimony stands. If doubt arises that they have diverted the will to someone, or added or subtracted [anything], then they swear after the 'Asr prayer, and their testimony stands. If after that it becomes known that they altered it and incurred sin, then two of the kin swear, and the testimony of the first two is invalidated."

Some people said: "The verse is abrogated, and a witness does not swear." This is reported from Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, and the majority of jurists (kafat al-fuqaha').

Al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned that this oath in the verse is only according to the circumstances of the claim (al-tada'i). That is, the first two witnesses swear only if doubt arises; and when doubt arises, a claim is thereby directed against them, so the oath becomes binding upon them. But this doubt arises only from betrayal on their part. If after that it becomes known that they incurred sin, it is considered: if the matter is clear, they are made to pay without the oath of the two heirs; but if it is by a single witness, or by indications that necessitate their betrayal, or something similar, which is like a witness, then it is attributed to the wrongdoer, and the two claimants swear together with whatever witness or proof has been established for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is the disagreement regarding the meaning of the verse and the form of its ruling. Now let us return to the i'rab and speak word by word of the verse, aiming for the statement that is beneficial, because people have mixed greatly in the tafsir of this verse; mentioning that and refuting it would be lengthy, and in clarifying the truth that minds accept with acceptance there is sufficiency. And Allah is the One sought for help."

His saying: ﴿"Testimony between you"﴾. Some people said: the word shahada (testimony) here means "presence" (hudur). Al-Tabari said: shahada means "oath" (yamin), and it is not the testimony that is delivered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "All of this is weak. The correct view is that it is the testimony that is preserved in order to be delivered. Its subject is in the nominative (raf') by way of inception (ibtida'), and the predicate is in His saying 'two' (ithnan). Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] said: the estimate is: 'The testimony between you in your wills is the testimony of two,' so the modified word was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. Another estimated it differently at first, as if he said: 'The one establishing the testimony between you is two.'"

The word testimony (shahada) was attributed to "between" (bayn) as an extension in the adverbial usage, so that it is treated like nouns, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly your bond has been severed [between you]﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

Al-A'raj, al-Sha'bi, and al-Hasan read "shahadatun" with tanwin, and "baynakum" in the accusative. The i'rab of this reading is like the i'rab of the reading of the Seven. It is narrated from al-A'raj and Abu Haywa: "shahadatan" in the accusative with tanwin, and "baynakum" in the accusative. Abu al-Fath [Ibn Jinni] said: the estimate is: "Let two [men] establish a testimony between you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"When death approaches one of you"﴾: its meaning is "when the approach [of death] draws near," since if death has actually arrived, a dead person does not testify. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and like His saying: ﴿When you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. This is common. The governing element of "when" (idha) is the verbal noun which is "testimony." This is on the basis that you make "idha" equivalent to "hina" (when), which does not need an answer (jawab). You may also make "idha" in this verse the one that needs an answer, but the answer has been dispensed with because of what precedes it, in His saying: ﴿"testimony between you"﴾, since the meaning is: "When death approaches one of you, it is appropriate that he should call a witness."

His saying: ﴿"at the time of the will"﴾ is an adverb of time, and the governing element is "approached" (hadara). If you wish, you may make it a substitute (badal) for "idha." Abu 'Ali said: "You may also link it to 'death' (al-mawt); it is not permissible for 'testimony' to govern it, because when it governs one adverb of time, it does not govern another adverb of it."

His saying: ﴿"two just men"﴾ is a qualifier (sifa) for "two"; and "from among you" is also a qualifier, after a qualifier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"from other than you"﴾ is a qualifier for "two others"; and ﴿"you strike in the land"﴾ means "you travel for trade." You say: "ḍarabtu fi al-ard" meaning "I travelled for trade"; and "ḍarabtu al-ard" means "I went in it for the fulfilment of a human need." This travel is the kind in which a believer might lack two believers, so it was singled out for mention, because travel for jihad hardly ever lacks two believers.

Abu 'Ali said: His saying ﴿"you shall detain them both"﴾ is a qualifier for "two others." It is interposed between the qualified and the qualifier by His saying "if you are" up to "death," and this interposition conveys that the turning to "two others from other than [your] religion, or kin" — according to the disagreement of scholars on that — happens only with the necessity of travel and the arrival of death during it. The answer to "if" (in) is dispensed with because of what preceded in His saying: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾.

The majority of scholars said: "The prayer here is the 'Asr prayer, because it is the time when people gather. The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned it regarding one who swears concerning his merchandise, and he ordered li'an (mutual oath) in it." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "It is only after the prayer of the dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects); as for the 'Asr, it has no sanctity for them."

The fa' in His saying: ﴿"then they swear"﴾ is a conjunction of one clause upon another, because the meaning is complete at His saying: ﴿after the prayer﴾. Abu 'Ali said: "If you wish, you need not estimate the fa' as conjoining one clause to another, but make it a conditional response (jaza'), as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And the pupil of my eye: water sometimes dries it up, so it appears; and at other times it overflows and drowns."

Its estimate according to them is: 'When it dries up, it appears; so likewise, when you detain them both, they will swear.'"

(p-287) His saying, "if you doubt" (in Arabic: إنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ), is a condition, and the oath of the two witnesses is not directed except by it. Whenever no doubt or dispute arises, there is no oath. Yet it appears from the ruling of Abu Musa that the oath of the dhimmis (non-Muslim protected people) is required, that by the oath their testimony is completed and the bequest is carried out for its beneficiaries, even if no doubt arose. This doubt, according to the one who does not regard the verse as abrogated (mansukh), arises from suspicion of betrayal, and from an accusation of favouring some of the legatees over others. In his view the oath is still required in these cases. As for the one who regards the verse as abrogated, no oath is imposed except when the doubt concerns betrayal or some form of transgression; the oath is then, in his view, in the manner of an oath upon a denial in a claim, not as a completion of the testimony.

The pronoun in the words of the two swearers, "we will not sell it for any price" (in Arabic: ﴿لا نَشْتَرِي بِهِ ثَمَنًا﴾), refers to the oath. It may also refer to the name of God, may He be blessed and exalted. Abu 'Ali said: it refers to the distortion of the testimony. His saying, "we will not sell" (in Arabic: "لا نَشْتَرِي"), is the answer to what is implied by His saying, "they both swear by God" (in Arabic: "فَيُقْسِمانِ بِاللهِ"), because an oath and the like are introduced by what oaths are introduced by. The construction "for it a price" (in Arabic: "بِهِ ثَمَنًا") is to be read as "possessing a price" (in Arabic: "أيْ: ذا ثَمَنٍ"), because a price is not itself bought. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have sold the signs of God for a small price﴾ [al-Tawba: 9]; its meaning is "possessing a price". It is not permissible that "we will buy" (in Arabic: "نَشْتَرِي") in this verse means "we will sell" (in Arabic: "نَبِيعُ"), because the meaning nullifies it, although that usage exists in the language in other places.

He singled out the near kin for mention because it is the custom of people to incline towards their relatives, and to make light of what they would not make light of when it concerns their own benefit.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾; he attributed "testimony" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةَ") to Him, exalted is He, insofar as He is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment.

Al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi read "wa-la naktumu" (in Arabic: "وَلا نَكْتُمْ") with the mim vowelled with a jazm. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Na'im ibn Maysara, and al-Sha'bi (in a variant from him) read "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً") with tanwin, and "Allah" (in Arabic: "اَللَّهَ") in the accusative governed by "naktumu" (in Arabic: "نَكْتُمُ"), as though the sentence were "and we will not conceal God a testimony". Al-Zahrawi said: it is possible that the meaning is "and we will not conceal a testimony and by God", then the waw was dropped and the verb put in the accusative for brevity. Yahya ibn Adam related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash: "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً"), "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "أللَّهِ"), with the alif cut off without elongation, and the ha' in the genitive. It is also related from al-Sha'bi and others that he would pause on the ha' of "shahada" with sukun, then cut off the written alif without elongation, as has been mentioned. It is also related from him that he read "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "آللَّهِ") with elongation of the interrogative alif in both cases, namely with the ha' of "shahada" quiescent, and with it vowelled as tanwin in the accusative. These readings, namely the tanwin of "shahada" and the elongation of the interrogative alif after it, are related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. Abu al-Fath said: as for the quiescence of the ha' of "shahadah" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةْ") and pausing on it, with the oath beginning anew, this is a good reading, because beginning the oath at the start of the speech is more fitting for it and more awe-inspiring than that it be folded into the general course of speech. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, 'Abd Allah ibn Habib, and al-Hasan al-Basri, as mentioned by Abu 'Amr al-Dani, read "shahadatan" (in Arabic: "شَهادَةً") with accusative and tanwin, and "a-llahi" (in Arabic: "آللَّهِ") with elongation of the hamza of interrogation, which is a substitute for the particle of oath "a-nna" (in Arabic: "آنّا") with elongation of the interrogative alif also; it entered to make the swearers stop and reflect, or to establish the truth in their souls, or for those they address. Ibn Muhaysin read "lamina-l-athimin" (in Arabic: "لَمِلّاثِمِينَ") with idgham (assimilation).

His saying, exalted is He: "then if it is discovered" (in Arabic: "فَإنْ عُثِرَ"), is a metaphor for what befalls their knowledge after it had been hidden, by agreement, and after it was not expected and not intended. This is as one says, "you have fallen upon the one who knows" (in Arabic: "عَلى الخَبِيرِ سَقَطْتَ"), and "you came upon such-and-such" (in Arabic: "وَقَعْتَ عَلى كَذا"). Abu 'Ali said: "the sin" (in Arabic: "الإثْمُ") here is the name of the thing taken, because its taker is sinful by taking it, so it is called a sin, just as what is taken without right is called an injustice (in Arabic: "مَظْلَمَةً"). Sibawayh said: "al-maẓlama" is the name of what is taken from you; likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: what appears here is that "the sin" (al-ithm) is in its proper sense, namely the ruling that attaches to the two of them, and the state they incur after their engagement in distorting the testimony, or in taking what is not theirs, or the like.

"Istahaqqa" (in Arabic: "اِسْتَحَقّا") means that they deserved it from God and were fit for it; so this is "istihqaq" in its proper sense, the deserving of a real thing. Had "the sin" meant the thing taken, it would not have been said of it "istahaqqa", because they had done wrong and betrayed in it; rather, they deserved the station of evil and the ruling of disobedience, and that is the sin.

His saying, exalted is He: "then two others" (in Arabic: "فَآخَرانِ"), means: when their corruption is discovered, then two others from the people who are the heirs of the deceased take the oath and establish the case in place of the first two; and their share, or their claim, or their property, or whichever of these estimations you choose, is deserved against them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read "istuhigga" (in Arabic: "اِسْتُحِقَّ") with the ta' vowelled with damma, and "al-awlayani" (in Arabic: "اَلْأولَيانِ") in the dual of "awla". Qurra related from Ibn Kathir: "istahaqqa" (in Arabic: "اِسْتَحَقَّ") with fatha on the ta', and "al-awlayani" in the dual. Hafs also related the same from 'Asim. Hamza and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "istuhigga" with damma on the ta', and "al-awwalina" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلِينَ") as the plural of "awwal". Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "istahaqqa" with fatha on the ta', and "al-awwalani" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلانِ") as the dual of "awwal". Ibn Sirin read "al-awwalayni" (in Arabic: "اَلْأوَّلَيْنِ") as the dual of "awwal", with it in the accusative, on the supposition: "al-awwalayni fa-l-awwalayni", in rank and nearness of kinship.

Abu 'Ali, regarding the reading of Ibn Kathir and those with him, said: the nominative of "al-awlayani" is either as a beginning (mubtada') that has been delayed, so the sense is as though it were "and the two nearest by the command of the dead are two others who stand", so the speech comes as in their saying "I am a Tamimi"; or it is the predicate of an elided beginning, as though it were "then two others stand in their place, they are the nearest"; or it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yaqumani"; or it is attributed to "istuhigga". Abu al-Hasan permitted another possibility: that "al-awlayani" be an adjective of "fa-akharani", because when it was described it became specified, and so it was described on account of the particularity that it acquired.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: then Abu 'Ali said, after this speech: as for what "istuhigga" is attributed to, it must be either the shares, or the bequest, or the sin, and the taken thing was called "sin" as one says of what is taken from the wronged: "maẓlama". For this reason it was permissible for "istuhigga" to be attributed to it. Then he said, after a further discussion: if you ask, is it permissible to attribute "istuhigga" to "al-awlayani"? The answer: that is not permissible, because what is deserved is only the bequest or a part of it, and as for the nearest kin of the dead, they cannot themselves be deserved, so "istuhigga" cannot be attributed to them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: there is scrutiny in this speech, and in my view it is permissible to attribute "istuhigga" to "al-awlayani". That is because Abu 'Ali took the word "istihqaq" as literal, so he did not permit it except where true deserving applies to the case; and what is truly deserved is the share and the like. The word "istihqaq" in the verse is only a metaphor, and does not mean "they deserved a sin". For true deserving is here literal, while in "istuhigga" it is figurative, because there is no sense to this deserving except domination over the situation, by virtue of this deceased being alone and having no kin or co-religionists to support him. So "istuhigga" here is like what you say of an oppressor who wrongs you: "this has been deserved against me, my wealth or my house, by his injustice", so you liken it to what is truly deserved, since he has scaled the wall as the owner would scale it and taken possession as the owner would possess. Likewise one says: "so-and-so's time has deserved from him the occupation of such-and-such", when that matter has overcome his hours. In this way "istuhigga" in the verse is in every case, even if it is attributed to the shares and the like, because his saying "istuhigga" is a relative clause (silah) of "alladhina", and "alladhina" refers to the category opposed to the two unjust witnesses. The two witnesses did not in this case deserve anything in the true sense of deserving; they only scaled the wall as one who deserves would do. So we may take "al-awlayani" as a beginning, delayed, and then "istuhigga" is attributed, on this reading, to the wealth or the share and the like, by way of metaphor. The same holds if "al-awlayani" is the predicate of a beginning, and likewise as a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani", and as an adjective on the opinion of Abu al-Hasan. We may also take the sense to be: from the group that was absent, whose right it was and whose desired course was that their guardian attend; so when they were absent and this testator stood alone, this condition deserved, and these two witnesses, being outside the religion, deserved authority and the command over these two nearest kin over this group. Then the verb was put in the passive with this meaning, for brevity. What strengthens this aim is that the verb took "ʿalā" when it indicated power and the taking over of the situation by force. One does not say "istuhigga minhu" or "istuhigga fihi" except in true deserving in its proper form; but "istuhigga ʿalayhi" is said of seizure, domination, and figurative deserving. The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers, in every case in this reading, to the group opposed to the two sinful false witnesses. It is also possible that it refers to the category of which the false witness is one, as we shall show now, God willing, in a reading other than this one.

As for Qurra's transmission from Ibn Kathir, "istahaqqa" with fatha on the ta', it is possible that "al-awlayani" is a beginning, or the predicate of a beginning, and the sense is: "in the group or the tribe that deserved the case against this category of false witnesses". The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the category of the two false witnesses.

(p-291) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: in this interpretation there is a transposition, a restructuring, and a manipulation in "alladhina"; and on it Abu 'Ali's discussion in the book "al-Hujja" is built. It is also possible that the meaning is: "from among those upon whom standing has been deserved". The correct of the two interpretations is that the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to "alladhina", and "al-awlayani" is raised by "istahaqqa". This is explained on three meanings:

The first is that what is intended by "those upon whom it has been deserved" is that their property and their estate were deserved by the two false witnesses; so he called the two false witnesses "awlayayn" (the two nearest), because the first state made them so; that is, the lack of people made them the nearest to this deceased and his estate, so they acted within it.

The second meaning is that what is intended by the group is: those upon whom it was right that the two nearest should be of them; so "istahaqqa" has the sense of "haqqa" and "wajaba", as you say: "this building has deserved" in the sense of "it is right", like "ʿajiba" and "istaʿjaba" and the like.

The third meaning is that "istahaqqa" be taken in the sense of "saʿā" and "istawjaba", so the sense is: "then two others from the people among whom two nearest from them were present, so they strove against them for their right"; that is, they deserved it for them, strove in it, and claimed it with their oaths and their kinship. A similar meaning to that which the transitive use with "ʿalā" gives is the verse of the poet:

I strive against the living of the Banu Malik,
each man is a striver in his own affair.

Likewise in the hadith, in some routes of the hadith of the three men, one of whom mentioned his dutifulness to his parents, when the rock came down upon them: "I used to tend the flock over them" (in Arabic: "كُنْتُ أرْعى عَلَيْهِمُ الغَنَمَ").

As for Hamza's reading, its meaning is: "from the people upon whom their affair has been deserved", that is, they were overcome by it; then he described them as "first", that is, in mention in this verse, and that is in His saying: ﴿two men of justice from among you﴾; then after that He said: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 5, verses 106–107 (part 3 of 3):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they both swear by Allah﴾; meaning the other two who stand in the place of the two witnesses of distortion. And their saying: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾; that is: "What we have reported, and what we have mentioned of the text of the matter, is more worthy than what the first two mentioned, and distorted in it." ﴿"And we have not transgressed"﴾; we, in this our statement, nor have we exceeded the limit." And their saying: ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾; a disavowal in the form of declaring great and abhorrent the act of wrongdoing (ẓulm). And ẓulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 5, verses 108–109:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿That is more likely to make them bring the testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths. And fear God and listen. God does not guide the defiant people.﴾ ﴿On the Day when God gathers the Messengers and says, "What response did you receive?" they will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾

The reference of "ذَلِكَ" (that) is to everything God has previously prescribed: the detaining of the two witnesses after the prayer for the oath, then, if their dishonesty is discovered, the oath being returned and the two being made to pay a penalty. All of this brings closer the uprightness of this category of people in whatever incidents may occur, because they fear the severe oath sworn right after the prayer, then they fear disgrace and the return of the oath. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both).

It appears from the words of al-Suddi that the reference of "ذَلِكَ" is only to the detention after the prayer (p-293). Then comes His saying, ﴿or fear that oaths will be returned﴾, corresponding to ﴿if it becomes known﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 107], and so on.

The pronoun in "يَأْتُوا" (they bring) and "يَخافُوا" (they fear) is plural because the intended meaning is a category and type of people. The "أو" (or) in this verse, according to al-Suddi's interpretation, is like your saying, "Zayd, you come to me or you anger me," as if you meant, "Otherwise you anger me." Likewise the meaning of the verse is: "That is more likely to make them bring the testimony in its proper form; otherwise they fear the return of oaths." As for the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), the meaning is: "That whole ruling is closer to their bringing [the testimony], and closer to their fearing [consequences]."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿in its proper form﴾ means: "in its upright manner, which has not been altered or distorted."

Then God commanded taqwa (God-consciousness, which is holding fast to God), and listening to these saving matters. He informed that He does not guide the defiant people insofar as they are defiant; otherwise He guides them when they repent. It is possible that the word "الفاسِقِينَ" (the defiant) is general, and the intended meaning is specific to those who do not repent.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Day when God gathers the Messengers﴾. Some exegetes held that the governing element (al-'amil) of "يَوْمَ" (the Day) is what precedes it, namely His saying "does not guide." This is weak. The arrangement and eloquence of the verse indicate that this statement is a new beginning, and the governing element is implied: either "remember" (اذْكُرُوا), or "be mindful" (تَذَكَّرُوا), or "beware" (اِحْذَرُوا), or something similar, whose omission is good because the listener knows it.

The reference of "هَذا اليَوْمِ" (this Day) is to the Day of Resurrection. The Messengers are singled out for mention because they are the leaders of creation, and within their gathering is the gathering of all creatures. They are the first to be addressed.

The meaning of ﴿"What response did you receive?"﴾ is: "What did the nations respond with, of belief or disbelief, obedience or disobedience?" This question to the prophets, the Messengers, is only so that the proof may be established against the nations, and their reckoning begins with what is clear and evident to everyone of natural disposition.

People differed about the meaning of their saying, peace be upon them, ﴿"We have no knowledge."﴾ Al-Tabari said: they were bewildered from the answer because of the terror of the moment. It is reported from al-Hasan that he said: "We have no knowledge of the terror of that Day." And from al-Suddi: "They stood in a station where minds were bewildered, so they said, 'We have no knowledge.' Then they stood in another station where they bore witness against their peoples." And from Mujahid that he said: "They are struck with fear, so they say, 'We have no knowledge.'"

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: (p-294) Some people weakened this approach by the words of God, ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103]. The prophets are in the most severe terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and at the time of crossing the Sirat, they say, "Safety! Safety!" and their condition is greater [than ordinary people's]. God's favor upon them is too great for their minds to be bewildered so that they say what is not true in itself.

Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: the meaning of the verse is: "We have no knowledge except a knowledge which You know better than we do."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This is good; it seems the meaning is: "We have no knowledge that is sufficient and reaches its ultimate end."

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of ﴿"What response did you receive?"﴾ is: "What did they do after you, and what innovations did they introduce?" Therefore they said, "We have no knowledge."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: This is a good meaning in itself, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen,﴾ supports it. But the wording "أُجِبْتُمْ" (you were answered/you received a response) does not support Ibn Jurayj's view except with reluctance. The view of Ibn 'Abbas is the most correct of these approaches, because it is consistent with submission to God, and referring the matter to Him. For His saying, "What response did you receive?", they have no knowledge of its answer except what was conveyed to them during their lifetimes, and what is lacking is what was in the hearts of those they addressed, of hypocrisy and the like. Likewise, what came after them from their community is lacking, while God knows all of that in detail and completeness. So they saw the submission to Him and the humility before His all-encompassing knowledge as proper. Abu Haywa recited "ماذا أجَبْتُمْ" (with a fatḥa on the hamza), reading the verb in the first person, "What did I answer?" (with the consonant pattern of the active first person, ʾajabtum).
