Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 110:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿When Allah said: "O Jesus son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit, so that you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book and wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel; and when you shaped from clay the likeness of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission, and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission; and when you brought forth the dead by My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those of them who disbelieved said, 'This is nothing but evident magic.'"﴾

It is possible that the operative element in "idh" (when) is an implied verb, its estimate being: "Remember, O Muhammad, when you came to them with clear proofs." And "qala" (said) here means "yaqulu" (says), because the apparent meaning of this speech is that it takes place on the Day of Resurrection, as a preface to His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. All of that constitutes rulings for rebuking those who, in their claim of Jesus' divinity, become disbelievers in Allah.

It is also possible that "idh" is a substitute for His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah gathers...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109].

The favour of Allah upon Jesus is prophethood and all that was mentioned, and what is known of it, which cannot be counted. The favour upon his mother was also enumerated to him, since it is a favour that reverts to him and exists because of him.

The majority of readers recite ﴿"ayyadtuka"﴾ with a doubled yā'. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recite "a'yadtuka" on the pattern of "fa'altuka". It appears that the original form in both readings is "ayyadtuka" on the pattern of "af'altuka", then the rules of weak-letter alteration differed. The meaning in both is "I strengthened you," from "al-ayd" (strength). 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

Praise be to Allah, the Mighty, the Most Noble, who strengthened us on the day of the armies of al-Ashram.

The Holy Spirit is Jibril, peace be upon him. His saying "in the cradle" is a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "as a small child." "And in maturity" is also a circumstantial clause, coordinated with the first, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿He calls upon Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Yunus: 12]. Maturity is from forty to fifty; it was also said that it is from thirty-three.

"Al-kitab" in this verse is a verbal noun of "kataba, yaktubu," meaning "I taught you writing." It is possible that it intends a generic noun, including the scrolls of Ibrahim and other things. Then, after that, the Torah and the Gospel were singled out for mention, as an honour.

"Wisdom" is understanding and perception in matters of the Sharia. Allah has granted the prophets from it what they are distinguished by: they are protected and do not speak out of whim.

His saying, "And when" in this verse, wherever it is repeated, is a conjunction to the first one, in which "favour" operated.

"Takhluqu" means: you determine, and prepare with an even, perfected determination. From it is the poet's saying:

And indeed you smooth what you have created, while some people create but do not smooth.

That is: he prepares and determines in order to act and complete, but then does not act. From it is another's saying:

Whoever creates what he is going to do, my resource in it is little.

Jesus, peace be upon him, used to fashion from clay the likenesses of bats, then breathe into them in front of the people, and they would come to life and fly by the permission of Allah. This story has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran."

The majority of readers recite "kahay'ati" with a hamza; it is a verbal noun from their saying "haa'a al-shay'u, yahaa'u," when a thing becomes firm and settles upon a good matter. Al-Lihyani said: it is also said "yahi'u." Al-Zuhri recited "kahayyati" with a doubled yā' and without hamza. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "kahay'ati al-ta'ir."

"Idhn" (permission) in this verse, however it is repeated, means enablement together with knowledge of what is being done and what is intended by calling people to faith.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"fa-tanfukhu fiha"﴾ is the ordinary breathing known from humans. Allah made the matter thus only so that Jesus' being clothed with the miracle and its issuing from him would be manifest. This is like Musa, peace be upon him, throwing down his staff, and like Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, bringing the Qur'an. This is one of the conditions of miracles. And His saying "fiha," with a feminine pronoun, along with the coming of that in "Al 'Imran" as ﴿fa-anfukhu fihi﴾ [Al 'Imran: 49] with a masculine pronoun, is a point over which the commentators have differed. Makki said: in "Al 'Imran" it refers to the bird, and in "al-Ma'idah" it refers to the form; he said the reverse is also valid. Others said the masculine pronoun refers to the clay.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is not valid for this pronoun to refer to the bird, nor to the clay, nor to the form, because the clay, and the bird into which the clay is shaped in its form, has no breath at all; likewise there is no breath into its form specific to its body, which is the one mentioned in the verse; and likewise the clay mentioned in the verse is only general clay, and there is no breathing into that; rather, breathing is into the specific shapes from it, which were arranged by the hand of Jesus, peace be upon him. So the correct view regarding the return of the feminine pronoun is that it refers to what the verse necessarily requires: His saying, ﴿And when you shape from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ requires forms, or bodies, or shapes. Similarly, the masculine pronoun refers to the created thing that "takhluqu" requires. You may also make it refer to what the kaf indicates in the sense of "like," because the meaning is: "and when you shape from clay a likeness like its form." You may also make the pronoun refer to the kaf itself, according to those who allow it to be a noun outside poetry, with the kaf in the accusative position as an adjective of the intended verbal noun; its estimate: "and when you create a creation from clay like the form of a bird."

Abdullah ibn 'Abbas recited: "kahay'ati al-tayri fatanfukhuha fayakunu"; the majority recited "fatakunu" with the ta' from above; 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "fiha fayakunu" with the ya' from below; Nafi' alone recited "fatakuna ta'iran"; and the rest recited "tayran" without an alif. Both readings are widely transmitted among people. "Al-tayr" is the plural of "ta'ir," like "tajir" and "tajr," "sahib" and "sahb," "rakib" and "rakb." "Al-ta'ir" is a singular noun. The meaning on Nafi's reading is: "so every piece of those created things becomes a bird."

Abu 'Ali said: if someone said that "al-ta'ir" may be a plural, like "al-hamil" and "al-baqir," then the meaning of both readings would be one, and that would be sound analogy. This is strengthened by what Abu al-Hasan related of their saying "ta'irah," which would then be of the category of "sha'irah" and "sha'ir," and "tamrah" and "tamr."

The discussion of the blind and the leper has already been mentioned, and the stories of his raising the dead in "Al 'Imran." "Bringing forth the dead" means: from their graves. "The restraining of the Children of Israel from him, peace be upon him," means his being lifted up, when they surrounded him in the house with the disciples. From the first thing Allah protected him from them was the restraint, up to that final incident; there the greatness of the restraint became manifest. "The clear proofs" are his miracles, his Gospel, and all that he brought.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim here, and in Hud and al-Saff, recited ﴿"inna hadha illa sihrun"﴾ without an alif; Hamzah and al-Kisa'i in the four places recited "sahirun" with an alif. Whoever recited "sihrun" made the reference to the clear proofs, the speech, and what he brought; whoever recited "sahirun" made the reference to the person, since he is one possessing magic in their view. This is consistent throughout the Qur'an wherever this difference occurs.

(p-298)

**His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:**

﴿And when I inspired the disciples, "Believe in Me and in My Messenger." They said, "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, is your Lord able to send down to us a table (ma'idah) from heaven?" He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be at rest, and that we may know that you have spoken truly to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"And when I inspired"﴾ is part of the enumeration of the blessings bestowed upon Jesus. "Inspired" (awhaytu) in this place may mean either inspiration of inner suggestion (wahy al-ilham) or inspiration of command (wahy al-amr), as the poet said:

"....................  He inspired her to settle, so she settled."

In general, it is the casting of a meaning into the soul in a hidden manner, which He, Exalted is He, conveys to their souls however He wills.

The Messenger in this verse is Jesus, peace be upon him. The disciples' words, ﴿"and bear witness"﴾, may be an address from them to God, Exalted is He, or it may be addressed to Jesus, peace be upon him. The explanation of the term "al-Hawariyyun" (the disciples, lit. the white-garbed helpers) has already been given in the commentary on Al 'Imran.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the disciples said﴾, to the end of the verse, is an interjection (i'tiradh) inserted in the midst of describing the situation of God's speech to Jesus on the Day of Resurrection. This interjection includes information for Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and his community, about the event of the disciples concerning the table, since it is a beneficial example for every community with its prophet, from whose virtues one may take example and from whose errors (such as asking for signs and the like) one should be restrained.

The majority of people recited: ﴿"is your Lord able"﴾ with a ya' (yastati'u) and with the ra' of "Rabbuka" in the nominative. This is the reading of the Seven, except al-Kisa'i. This does not mean that they doubted God's power over this matter; rather it means: "Will God, Exalted is He, do this? Will He grant a response to it?" This is like what was said to 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd: "Are you able to show me how the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, performed ablution?" The meaning is: "Is it easy for you? Will you do it?" However, there is an indecency (bashaa'ah) in the wording, because of which Jesus said: ﴿"Fear God, if you are believers"﴾; and because of it a group of the Companions and others turned to a different reading. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God be pleased with them all, read: "Is your Lord able" with a ta' (tastati'u) and with the ba' of "Rabbaka" in the accusative. The meaning is: "Are you able to ask your Lord?" 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "The disciples were too well-acquainted with God to say: 'Is your Lord able?'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, exonerated them from the indecency of the wording; otherwise, no ignorance of God, Exalted is He, necessarily follows from it, as has been made clear just now.

With this same reading, al-Kisa'i recited, and he added that he assimilated the lam into the ta' (idgham). Abu 'Ali said: "That is good." The ﴿"that"﴾ (an) in His saying ﴿"that He send down"﴾, according to this reading, is connected to the omitted verbal noun, which is "su'al" (asking), and "an" is the object, since it is in the status of what is explicitly mentioned, even if it is omitted from the wording, because the meaning is not complete without it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is possible to dispense with estimating "su'al" (asking), by taking the meaning to be: "Is your Lord able to send down [a table] by your supplication, or by your standing with Him, and the like?" The meaning then returns you, necessarily, to an implied element indicated by what has been mentioned in the wording.

And "al-ma'idah" (the table) is of the pattern "fa'ilah" from "mada," when it moves (madu), according to the statement of al-Zajjaj; or from "mada" when it gives food and provisions (mara wa atama), as Ru'bah said:

"Heads of the affluent, the equals, are brought as gifts
to the Commander of the Faithful, the one from whom provision is sought."

That is: the table is that from which food is sought and provisions are obtained.

His saying, peace be upon him: ﴿"Fear God, if you are believers"﴾ is a confirmation addressed to them, as you say: "Do such and such, if you are a man." I do not know of any disagreement that the disciples were believers, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse.

Some said: The disciples uttered this statement at the outset, before they knew that he would heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead. The phrase ﴿"Fear God"﴾, from his words, peace be upon him, appears as a rejection of their saying that. This, according to the reading of the one who read "yastati'u" with a ya' from below, is directed at two matters: one of them is the indecency of the wording, and the other is the rejection of seeking signs and exposing oneself to God's wrath by them, and prophethoods are not founded upon being tested. As for the other reading, he rejected from them only the demand (iqtira'), and their lack of tranquility in what had already appeared of His signs. So when he, peace be upon him, addressed them with this statement, they openly declared the motives which led them to seek the table, saying: ﴿"We wish to eat from it"﴾, so that we may be honored in the world.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Because the purpose of this eating is not the filling of the belly.

﴿"and that our hearts may be at rest"﴾: its meaning is that our thought about your matter may be calmed by direct observation, by a matter descending from heaven before our eyes; ﴿"and that we may know"﴾ with the knowledge of necessity and of witnessing, ﴿"that you have spoken truly to us"﴾, so that doubts which arise in the knowledge gained by reasoning (ilm al-istidlal) do not beset us.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: By this the view of the one who said that this was before they knew His signs is strengthened. It also indicates this, that God's inspiration to them, ﴿"that believe"﴾, was only at the outset of the matter, and at that time they uttered this statement; then they believed, saw the signs, persisted, and turned away; and whoever disbelieved perished.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: "wa yu'lama" with a ya' and a damma, in the passive voice (ma lam yusamma fa'iluh).

His saying: ﴿"and that we may be among its witnesses"﴾: its meaning is "among those who bear witness to this sign, conveying it to others, calling to this law because of it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is narrated that what led them to this course of demand was that Jesus, peace be upon him, once said to them: "Would you like to fast thirty days for God, and then, if you ask Him for a need, He will fulfill it?" When they had fasted them, they said: "O teacher of goodness, the right of one who performs a deed is that he be fed; so is your Lord able [to send us a table]?" They wished that the table would come at the conclusion of that fast.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-Ma'idah (5), verses 114–115:**

His statement, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven, which will be for us a festival ('īd) for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."﴾ ﴿Allah said: "Indeed, I will send it down to you. But whoever disbelieves after that among you, I will surely punish him with a punishment by which I will not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that Jesus answered their request and called upon Allah concerning the matter of the table. It is narrated that he wore a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, stood to pray, wept, and supplicated.

As for "Allāhumma" (O Allah), according to Sibawayh (the grammarian), its origin is "Yā Allāh," and the two letters *mīm* were substituted for "yā." "Rabbanā" (our Lord) is a second vocative, and it cannot be an adjective, because "Allāhumma" is treated as a sound (an interjection-like word) on account of the alteration it underwent.

The majority of readers recited "takūnu lanā" (it will be for us), as a description of the table. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited "takun lanā" (let it be for us), as a response to the imperative "anzil" (send down).

"Al-ʿīd" (the festival, ʿīd) means the gathering and the day of witness. Its customary usage is for that which recurs annually, monthly, weekly, or the like. It derives from "ʿāda, yaʿūdu" (to return), so its original root is with *wāw*, but the *yāʾ* became obligatory because of the kasra on the ʿayn.

The majority of reciters read "li-awwalinā wa-ākhirinā" (for the first of us and the last of us). Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Muhayṣin, and al-Jahdari read "li-ūlānā wa-ukhrānā."

The commentators differed about the meaning of this. Al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Juraij, and Sufyan said: "li-awwalinā" means for the first of the community, then for those after them, down to its last. They would take that day as a festival. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning is: "It will be a gathering for all of us, first and last." He said: "The first of the people ate from the table when it was set down, just as the last of them ate."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to this view, "ʿīd" is not intended to mean that which recurs.

His statement: ﴿and a sign from You﴾ means: a sign and proof of my truthfulness and of my honor. So Allah answered Jesus' supplication and said: ﴿Indeed, I will send it down to you﴾. Then He stipulated for them the condition customary among nations: that whoever disbelieves after a sign has been requested will be punished with the most severe punishment.

Nafi', Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀsim read "innī munazziluhā" with a fatha on the *nūn* and a shaddah on the *zāy*. The rest read "munziluhā" with a sukun on the *nūn*. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Mujahid said: When they heard the condition concerning the punishment of whoever disbelieves, they asked to be excused from it, so it did not descend. Mujahid said: This is like the example Allah, exalted is He, set for people so that they would not ask for these signs.

The majority of the exegetes said: The table did descend. Then the narrations differed concerning how it happened. Al-Sha'bi related from Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: The table descended with bread and fish. ʿAtiyya said: The table was a fish in which was the flavor of every food. Ibn ʿAbbas said: A tray descended upon which were bread and fish; they would eat from it wherever they alighted, whenever they wished. Wahb ibn Munabbih also said this. Ishaq ibn ʿAbd Allah said: Seven loaves and seven fish descended upon the table. He said: No day passed until they hoarded and betrayed, so they were transformed into apes and swine. But whoever disbelieves after that among you, I will surely punish him with a punishment by which I will not punish anyone among the worlds."﴾

"Rabbanā" (our Lord) is a second vocative, and it cannot be an adjective, because "Allāhumma" is treated as a sound (an interjection-like word) on account of the alteration it underwent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 116–117:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'" He will say, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ ﴿"I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are, over all things, Witness."﴾

The exegetes differed concerning the time at which this statement occurs. Al-Suddi and others said: When Allah raised Jesus, peace be upon him, to Himself, the Christians said what they said, and claimed that Jesus, peace be upon him, had commanded them to do so. Then the Exalted asked him about their saying, and he said: ﴿"Glory be to You"﴾, to the end of the verse.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to this view, "qala" (he said) comes in the past tense in its proper sense. The Exalted's saying later, ﴿And if You forgive them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 118], that is, by their repentance from disbelief, comes because this is what Jesus, peace be upon him, said while they were still alive in the world.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and the majority of people said: This statement from Allah is in fact on the Day of Resurrection. (p-304) Allah says it to him before the heads of all creatures, so the disbelievers see his disavowal of them, and they know that what they were upon was false.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: According to this interpretation, "qala" carries the meaning of "yaqulu" (he says), and the past tense is used in place of the future to indicate that the matter is certain and established. His saying later, ﴿And if You forgive them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 118], means: If You punish the whole world, it is by Your right; and if You forgive, that too was foreknown in Your knowledge. It is because You are worthy of that; none can repel Your judgment, and none can contend with You. The meaning is not that You must do one of these two things; rather, he said this statement while knowing that Allah does not forgive that He be associated with. The benefit of this questioning, according to the view of those who say it is on the Day of Resurrection, is the manifestation of the sin of the disbelievers in worshipping Jesus, peace be upon him; and it is a questioning of him through which the clarification of the misguidance of the misguided becomes evident.

"Subhanaka" means: an declaration of Your transcendence above that this should be said or uttered.

His saying: ﴿It is not for me to say﴾, to the end of the verse, is a negation supported by the evidence of reason: it is rationally impossible for a created human being to claim divinity. This formula may be used for what is not fitting and is not becoming, even though it is possible; and from it is the saying of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It was not for the son of Abu Quhafa to lead the prayer in front of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace."

Then he said: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾; so Allah granted Jesus, peace be upon him, this conclusive argument. His saying: ﴿You know what is within myself﴾ refers to Allah's encompassing knowledge of him; and he singled out the self for mention because it is the place of concealment and of keeping knowledge hidden. The meaning is that Allah knows what is in the self of Jesus and knows all his affairs, including whatever might not be in his self. His saying: ﴿and I do not know what is within Yourself﴾ means: I do not know what You have of knowledge and what You encompass. The mention of "self" here is a verbal antithesis in the Arabic language, which brevity requires; and this alludes obliquely to His saying: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]; ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15]. Naming the punishment by the name of the sin was prompted only by the pursuit of verbal correspondence, since it is among the eloquent speech and the skilful expression.

Then Jesus, peace be upon him, acknowledged to Allah the Exalted that He is the Knower of the unseen. The meaning is: "I have no knowledge of the unseen, so how could divinity belong to me?" Then he reported what he did in the world and what he said in his conveyance, namely that he did not transgress the command of Allah, in that He commanded them to worship Him, and he acknowledged His lordship. The "an" in His saying: ﴿an u'budu Allah﴾ is explanatory (mufassira) and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). It may be a substitute (badal) for "ma"; it may be in the genitive position, on the estimate of "bi-an u'budu Allah"; and it may be a substitute for the pronoun in "bihi".

Then he, peace be upon him, reported that he was a witness over them as long as he remained among them in the world; so "ma" here is temporal (zarfiyya).

His saying: ﴿When You took me up﴾ means: You took me to Yourself by raising me and placing me in the heavens. And "al-raqib" means: the guardian, the one who observes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 118–120:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah said, "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great attainment."﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾

This verse, according to the view of those who say that the questioning of 'Isa (peace be upon him) took place right after his raising (to heaven), has a sound meaning, because he said this statement about them while they were still alive in the world, and he does not know what they will end up with.

And it, according to the view of those who say that the questioning will take place on the Day of Resurrection, means: "If a word of punishment has preceded for them, as it has preceded, then they are Your servants; You do with them, by right of ownership, whatever You wish, with no objection to You; and if You forgive them, by repentance, as You forgave others, then indeed You are the Exalted in Might in Your power, the Wise in (p-306) Your actions, not opposed in any state." It is as if he said: "If there are among the people those who will be punished, then they are Your servants; and if there are those who will be forgiven, then Your might and Your wisdom require all of this."

And this, in my view, is the more preponderant opinion, and it is strengthened by what follows it. That is because when 'Isa (peace be upon him) affirmed that Allah, Exalted is He, has the right to do with His servants whatever He wills, of punishment and forgiveness, Allah made manifest to His servants what the prophets used to inform them of, as if he were saying: "This is a matter that has been completed; whoever has been destined for mercy has been singled out for it, and whoever has been destined for punishment has been singled out for it." So He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾. Thus every believer in Allah, Exalted is He, enters under this expression, and whoever was most pious is more inclusive within the expression. Then this expression came pointing to 'Isa in his state at that time and his truthfulness in what he said, so he obtained thereby a great honor on that standing, even though the wording includes him and others. And He, Exalted, mentioned what He has prepared for them by His mercy and His bounty, up to His saying: ﴿That is the great attainment.﴾

Nafi' alone recited: "Hadha yawma" with the accusative on "yawma"; the rest recited "yawmu" with the nominative, as the predicate of the subject which is "hadha"; and "yawmu" is in construct with "yanfa'u". The subject and predicate are in a position of accusative as the object of the saying, since "qala" governs whole sentences. As for Nafi''s recitation, it admits two possibilities. One is that "yawma" is an adverbial complement of the saying, as if the estimate were: "Allah said, this narrative, or this report, [occurs] on the day when...".

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This meaning, in my view, removes the arrangement of the verse and its splendor of expression.

The second meaning is that what follows "qala" is a relation of what preceded it of His saying to 'Isa, pointing to him; and the predicate of "hadha" is omitted for brevity, as if the estimate were: "Allah said: this one who is recounted occurs or takes place on the day when the truthful benefit..."

(p-307) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The address, according to this, is to Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) and his community, and this is more fitting than the previous one; and the eloquent and well-directed reading is the recitation of the majority.

Abu 'Ali said: It is not permissible that "yawma" be in a position of nominative according to Nafi''s recitation, because this verb to which it is added is inflected; and the indeclinability is only acquired by the noun in construct from the noun it is added to when the latter is indeclinable, such as: ﴿from the punishment of that day﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11]. It does not resemble the saying of the poet:

"At the time I reproached the white hair for youth, and said: Will I ever awaken while gray hair is restraining?"

Because the past verb in the verse is indeclinable, while the present verb in the verse is inflected.

Al-Hasan ibn al-'Abbas al-Shami recited: "Hadha yawmun", with nominative and tanwin.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾, to the end of the verse: it may be that it is among what will be said on the Day of Resurrection, and it may be that it is separated from that, addressed to Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) and his community. On both views, there is in it a support for what 'Isa said: "If You punish the people, they are Your servants," according to the interpretation of the majority that preceded.

The commentary on Surah "al-Ma'idah" is complete; and Allah is the One sought for help, and He is sufficient for me and the best Disposer of affairs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 5, verse 118–120:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah said, "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great attainment."﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾

This verse, according to the view of those who say that the questioning of 'Isa (peace be upon him) took place right after his raising (to heaven), has a sound meaning, because he said this statement about them while they were still alive in the world, and he does not know what they will end up with.

And it, according to the view of those who say that the questioning will take place on the Day of Resurrection, means: "If a word of punishment has preceded for them, as it has preceded, then they are Your servants; You do with them, by right of ownership, whatever You wish, with no objection to You; and if You forgive them, by repentance, as You forgave others, then indeed You are the Exalted in Might in Your power, the Wise in (p-306) Your actions, not opposed in any state." It is as if he said: "If there are among the people those who will be punished, then they are Your servants; and if there are those who will be forgiven, then Your might and Your wisdom require all of this."

And this, in my view, is the more preponderant opinion, and it is strengthened by what follows it. That is because when 'Isa (peace be upon him) affirmed that Allah, Exalted is He, has the right to do with His servants whatever He wills, of punishment and forgiveness, Allah made manifest to His servants what the prophets used to inform them of, as if he were saying: "This is a matter that has been completed; whoever has been destined for mercy has been singled out for it, and whoever has been destined for punishment has been singled out for it." So He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾. Thus every believer in Allah, Exalted is He, enters under this expression, and whoever was most pious is more inclusive within the expression. Then this expression came pointing to 'Isa in his state at that time and his truthfulness in what he said, so he obtained thereby a great honor on that standing, even though the wording includes him and others. And He, Exalted, mentioned what He has prepared for them by His mercy and His bounty, up to His saying: ﴿That is the great attainment.﴾
